A different se: a specific person (reflexive) or se replacing le before lo/la.
Before writing the verb, look at what goes with it: one or several things without “a” → agreement; people with “a”, an infinitive or nothing → singular; a verb that already has se → use uno.
“We buy second-hand cars.”
“At this company, customers are treated very kindly.”
“In hospitals, talking on your mobile is forbidden in some areas.”
“In the mountains you get up very early.”
“Last year two new parks were opened in my city.”
Guadalajara, Mexico. Paola Ríos runs a language school and is writing the rules for new students. Her colleague Hugo gives her his notes, but they are written with “we” and “you”.

Official notices and news use three more resources: se ruega a + people + que + subjunctive, se les recuerda (with les for the people being reminded), and the ser + participle passive, which you only need to recognise for now.
Notice: “Residents are asked not to use the lift during the works.”
Notice: “Please remember that the water will be cut off on Tuesday.”
News: “The market was built in 1931.” Which sentence means the same in a more spoken register?
Museum sign, more polite than “Don’t touch the works”.

You can now talk about what is done without saying who does it. The natural next step: talking about the result of those actions, the state things are left in: “The door is closed”, “The pavements are repaired”.

Irene Castillo is leaving the flat she has rented for two years. Today, Saturday, at ten, Mauricio Vega from the letting agency checks it with her before she hands back the keys. Mauricio reads his list: “Have the walls been painted? Have the windows been closed?” Irene answers with the result: “Yes, the walls are painted and the windows are closed.” Today you learn to describe the state an action leaves behind with estar + past participle.
Irene and her brother have painted the walls. (what they did)
Pablo is painting the hall. (still in progress)
The walls are painted. (the state now)
“Las ventanas están cerradas” is about…
They closed the balcony door. Now the balcony door is closed.
Which sentence says the action has not finished yet?
What state is something (or someone) in after an action?
The oven is unplugged and the fridge is switched off.
The living-room furniture is sold.
Irene is tired, but happy.
The kitchen boxes are already open.
Careful: the bathroom mirror is broken.
When Irene moved in two years ago, the kitchen was already painted.
Irene has closed the windows. (the action; the participle never changes)
The windows are closed. (the state; the participle agrees)

With some verbs, the state is normally expressed with an adjective: limpiar → la cocina está limpia (the kitchen is clean); llenar → lleno (full); vaciar → vacío (empty); secar → seco (dry); despertar → despierto (awake). With haber you use the regular participle: he limpiado, he vaciado, se ha despertado. “La cocina está limpiada” sounds very odd.
I’ve already emptied the wardrobes: there’s nothing left inside.
Mauricio opens the wardrobes: they’re empty.
—And the oven? —I cleaned it this morning.
What state did something end up in after an event or a process?
After the knock, the wardrobe door ended up crooked.
In the rush, the garage light was left on.
We sign the handover report and the flat is officially handed back.
What have you got done already? How much have you done so far?
Pablo already has the bed taken apart.
Irene has written twelve labels so far; she has eight to go.
Nobody switched the heating off: it stayed on all weekend.
I’ve already got the kitchen boxes closed.
Of the thirty books, Pablo has packed fifteen so far.

You will also hear sentences like “El edificio fue construido en 1980” (The building was built in 1980). That is ser + participle, the passive: it is about the action (and sometimes who did it), not the state. Today you only recognise it; in class 121 you compare it with estar + participle.
The plants on the balcony are dead: nobody watered them in August.
Pablo has taken down the bedroom curtains.
Good morning, Ms Castillo. I have the inventory here. Shall we start with the kitchen?
Of course. As you can see, the kitchen is clean and the oven is unplugged.
Very good. According to the list, the fridge has to be left empty with the door open.
I emptied it this morning. Look, the door is open so it doesn’t smell.
Perfect. Let’s go to the living room. The walls are painted, aren’t they? It smells of paint.
Yes, my brother and I painted them this week. By Thursday we had everything painted except the hall.
Let’s go to the bathroom… There’s a tile here that is broken.
It was already broken when I moved in two years ago. It’s written in the inventory: look at page three.
You’re right, it says so here. And the bedroom blind? It won’t come down.
Yesterday it got stuck halfway. I’m sorry, I don’t know what happened.
Don’t worry, I’ll make a note of it. And how’s the move going?
Fine: I’ve got the suitcases packed and I’ve closed twenty boxes so far. I only have the books left.
Why is the fridge door open?
What does Irene say about the broken tile?
What does Irene still have left to do for the move?
It’s cold in here: the balcony door is open.
Pablo, have you put the beds together yet?
Bad luck: two plates are broken.
In the rush, the bedroom window stayed open all night.
By eight, Irene already had all the books in place.
The living-room windows are open.
I’ve already got the suitcases packed.
The blind got stuck again.
Why is Mauricio calling?
What state are the wardrobes in?
What does Mauricio say about the broken tile?
What is wrong with the bedroom blind?
What is Mauricio going to send this afternoon?

Mauricio talks about the “depósito” (deposit): that is the common word in much of Latin America. In Spain people mostly say “fianza”. And what in many countries is an “apartamento” (flat) is usually a “piso” in Spain. Today’s grammar is the same everywhere: el depósito está devuelto, la fianza está devuelta.
the state an action leaves; it agrees (abierto, roto, hecho, escrito, puesto…)
the action and who does it; it never agrees
the final state; with “se”, often unintended
what you already have ready; what is done so far; it agrees with the object

Ask yourself: am I talking about the action or the state? For the action, haber + participle in -o: “He cerrado las ventanas.” For the state, estar + participle, which agrees: “Las ventanas están cerradas.” With quedar you say how something ended up, and with tener what you already have ready: “Tengo hechas las maletas.” And for limpiar, llenar or vaciar, use the adjective: está limpio, lleno, vacío.
Sorry, the pharmacy is already closed.
The technician has fixed the washing machine: it works now.
—And the report? —It’s written: I’ll send it to you now.
Nobody turned off the tap and the bath stayed full all morning.
Of the forty exams, I’ve marked thirty so far; I have ten left.
Lorena is closing a small company’s office before the August holidays. Transform her sentences to describe how everything is left.

Other verbs also present a result with a participle that agrees. Dejar + participle: how you leave something when you go (“I left the boxes ready”). Dar por + participle: to declare something finished or accepted (“We consider the inspection finished”). Tener dicho (colloquial) shows repetition: “Te tengo dicho que cierres con llave” = I’ve told you many times to lock the door. Recién + participle = very recently: “Careful: wet paint.” And in informal speech, “Estoy muerto / muerta” means I’m exhausted.
Before leaving, Irene left all the windows closed.
“Well, everyone, I declare the meeting closed.”
“I’ve told you again and again to lock the door!” means…
“Careful: wet paint.”
“I’m not going out tonight: I’m exhausted.”

You can now describe the state an action leaves with estar + participle and tell it apart from the action with haber. In class 121 you compare estar + participle with ser + participle, the passive: “The painting was painted in 1950; now it is finished.” It is the natural next step: from the state of something to how and by whom it was done.

In Valdemora, the old railway station opens this week as the City Museum. At the entrance there is a plaque: “This station was built in 1890. It was restored between 2024 and 2026.” And today, when you go in, you see the result: the station is restored and the rooms are open. Today you learn to separate what happened from how something is.
The station was restored between 2024 and 2026. (an action: someone restored it)
Today the station is restored. (the result we can see now)
“La estación fue construida en 1890” is about…
“Las salas están abiertas” is about…
What happened? When? Who did it?
The station was built in 1890 by the engineer Ramón Gil.
The last trains were withdrawn in 1985.
The mural in the hall was painted by Elena Ruiz, a local painter.
How is it now? How was it?
Now the station is restored and the rooms are open.
In 2023 the building was abandoned.
The station square is closed for works.
The mural was painted in 1950.
The rooms are open now.
The museum was opened yesterday. (the opening ceremony)
The museum is already open. (you can visit it now)
The building was closed for forty years.

With a date you are talking about the action: “El museo fue inaugurado en 1995”. “Está inaugurado” is possible but rare: to say it is already working, the natural choice is “el museo ya está abierto”.
The exhibition was opened yesterday by the mayor.
When we arrived at ten, the ticket office was already open.
The station was closed for almost forty years, from 1985 to 2025.
The station was built in 1890 by Ramón Gil. (written, formal)
It was built in 1890. / Ramón Gil built it. (more usual in speech)
Now it is restored and it is beautiful. (any register)

In conversation, “se construyó” does not normally take an agent: we do not say “se construyó por Ramón Gil”. If you want to name the person, use the active sentence: “La construyó Ramón Gil”. The passive with ser + por sounds written: it is correct, but in a chat with friends it is less common.
A friend asks you about the station. Which answer sounds most natural in conversation?
Where would you expect to read “El puente fue inaugurado en 1912”?
The benches on the platform were repaired by a local carpenter.
You can’t go into room 3: it’s closed.
Nuria, to start, a bit of history. When was the station built?
In 1890. It was built by a local engineer, Ramón Gil. The plaque at the entrance says so.
And then the bad years came…
Yes. The last trains were withdrawn in 1985, and the building was closed for almost forty years.
I remember going in to play as a kid. The windows were broken and everything was covered in dust.
Well, now it is completely restored. Look at the mural: it was painted in 1950 and it was cleaned inch by inch.
It’s beautiful. And the rooms? Are they finished yet?
Almost. The first three are set up; in the fourth we still need the lights.
And who is opening the door on Saturday?
The mayor, at six. On Sunday the news will say: “The door was opened by the mayor.” But I prefer another sentence: “At one minute past six, the door was already open to everyone.”
What was the station like when Raúl was a child?
What is still missing in the fourth room?
Why does Nuria prefer “la puerta ya estaba abierta para todos”?
These benches were made in 1910 for the waiting room.
The lift is out of order. Please use the stairs.
This clock was made in Switzerland in 1889 and arrived in Valdemora in 1891.
The invitations are already printed: they’re in the blue box.
On 3 May 1936 the station was damaged by a fire.
The rooms are open until eight.
In 2023 the windows were broken.
The fourth room is already finished.
What is the main idea?
Who opened the main door?
What is going on with the station clock?
What is still closed?
How does he recommend getting to the museum?
what happened; typical of news, plaques and history books
how something is or was: the result
same participle, different meaning
in speech, more common than ser + participle

Ask yourself: am I telling what happened, or describing how something is? An action, with a date or “por” + agent: ser (“fue construida en 1890”). The result, now or at a past moment: estar (“está restaurada”, “estaba abierta”). In both cases the participle agrees. And in speech, for the action, prefer “se construyó” or the active.
This castle was built in the 12th century.
We can’t get through here: the street is closed for works.
When the police arrived, the window was already broken.
The new libraries were opened yesterday by the minister.
The theatre was closed for two years for refurbishment and now it is open again.
In the next village, the old library also has a plaque. Your friend does not understand the “bookish” sentences. Explain each one in conversational words or with the state it is in now.

In the news, ser + participle does not only appear in the indefinido. You will read “ha sido restaurado” (present perfect: a recent action), “será inaugurada” (future: an action that will happen) and “es visitado” (present: something habitual). You only need to understand them. One more note: some adjectives change meaning with ser and estar (ser listo = clever / estar listo = ready; also malo, rico, aburrido): you will see them in class 237.
“La nueva sala será inaugurada el próximo lunes.” What does it mean?
“El museo es visitado por miles de turistas cada verano.” What does it mean?
For a message to your brother, which version is more natural?

Today you saw that, in speech, the active usually sounds more natural than the passive: “La construyó Ramón Gil”, “Lo pintó Elena Ruiz”. Pronouns do a lot of work in those sentences. In class 122 you combine them and put them in the right place: “Te lo explico”, “Ya se lo he dicho”, “Quiero enseñárselo”. It is the natural next step to tell what happened with smooth, conversational sentences.

Clara Ibarra and Daniel Soto are getting married on Saturday at a country house. Noelia, Clara’s sister, is organizing everything, and Bruno Vega, Daniel’s best friend, is helping her. Bruno wants to know which song the couple will dance to, but it is a secret. Noelia smiles and says: “I’d tell you, but it’s a secret.” Today you combine two pronouns with any verb form: the conditional, the present perfect, commands, the infinitive and the gerund.
I’d tell you the name of the song, but it’s a secret.
I’d tell you, but it’s a secret.
In “Te lo diría”, what is “lo”?
Why do the pronouns come before “diría”?
“Can you tell me the time of the ceremony?” “Sure, I’ll tell you right now.”
Are there two pronouns together? The order never changes: “se” first, then the person, then the thing.
Clara sent us the invitations in June.
The speech is for Clara, but I haven’t shown it to her yet.
The photo list? Óscar gave it to me yesterday.

“Se lo di” can mean to him, to her, to you (usted), or to them. If it is not clear, add the person at the end: “Se lo di a ella”. With two pronouns, “se” stays even when you name the person: “Se lo di a Clara”.
Daniel needs the rings. Bruno is giving them to him tomorrow.
The bouquet is for Clara. Noelia takes it to her room.
“Who sent you the flowers?” “Grandma sent them to us.”
I have already given the rings to Daniel.
Which sentence is NOT correct?
It’s a negative command: don’t show it to Clara.

Attach both pronouns and find the stressed syllable of the verb: it does not move. Because you add two syllables after it, the word takes a written accent: dárselo, decírmelo, tráemela. Compare “Dime” and “Dímelo”.
Which one is spelled correctly?
Which word does NOT need an accent?
Is there a “se” and another person pronoun? “Se” always goes first: se me olvidó, never “me se”.
Oh, I left the keys in the car (I forgot them).
Daniel dropped a ring, but he found it right away.
She loves the dress: she tried it on three times.
Oh no! I forgot the present at home.
It’s cold, Bruno. Your jacket: put it on.
Clara took her shoes off at midnight because her feet hurt.
I have already sent the photos to my grandparents.
The surprise: please don’t tell Daniel about it.
Bruno is explaining the dinner plan to the waiters now.
Bruno, have you got the rings? Daniel told me he gave them to you yesterday.
Yes, here they are. Tomorrow I’ll give them to him just before the ceremony.
No, better give them to me: you’ll be really nervous tomorrow.
OK, here you go. Hey, what about your speech for Clara? Have you shown it to her yet?
No way! I’m not going to show it to her: it’s a surprise. And don’t you tell her, OK?
Don’t worry. By the way, which song are they going to dance to?
I’d tell you, but I promised Clara I wouldn’t tell anyone.
Fine, fine. And the keys to the house? The owner wants us to give them back to him on Sunday.
Oh, the keys… I left them in the car!
Stay here, I’ll go. Look, there’s Daniel’s grandmother with his grandfather’s watch. She’s giving it to him now!
How lovely! He’s going to wear it tomorrow. Hey, and the musicians? Did you tell them the time?
Yes, I told them this morning, and tonight I’m going to send it to them in writing.
Why does Noelia want the rings?
What does Clara know about the speech?
Where are the keys to the house?
Clara needs the dress. Noelia is taking it to her room now.
“Bruno, can I borrow your sunglasses?” “Sure, here you are.”
“When are you giving them the list?” “I’m going to give it to them at twelve.”
“Relax, I’ll give them to you in a moment.”
“The watch is for Daniel. Give it to him before the ceremony, please.”
I’d tell her, but I don’t want to worry her.
Don’t give them to him yet.
I’m going to explain it to her this afternoon.
What is the main idea?
What does Noelia have to do with the keys?
Why does their mother want the dress?
What happens to the presents?
What can Noelia tell Bruno now?

Clara says “se lo quiere llevar”: with querer + infinitive, the pronouns go before the first verb. Just as correct: “quiere llevárselo”. Here “se” is reflexive (llevarse: to take something away with you) and “lo” is the dress.
le / les become se; before haber; between “no” and the verb
always with a written accent
before the first verb or at the end; never in the middle or twice
never “me se”; the meaning comes in class 150

Two questions. Which order? Se first, then the person, then the thing (le / les become se). Which place? Look at the verb: conjugated or with “no” → before; affirmative command, infinitive or gerund → attached, with an accent; periphrasis → either position. The two pronouns always stay together, and appear only once.
“Have you thanked your boss?” “Yes, I already have.”
Your friend tells everyone: “Don’t tell Lucía, OK?” (ustedes)
Which sentence is correct?
Oops! I spilled coffee on my shirt.
Rocío is leaving her job at a library and handing her tasks over to her colleague Hugo. Transform her sentences with two pronouns.

Four cases to go further. 1. In everyday speech in many Latin American countries, when the receiver is plural and the thing singular, the plural moves onto the thing: “se los dije” (= I told it to them). It is very common in conversation; formal writing prefers “se lo dije (a ellos)”. 2. With “hay que”, pronouns can only be attached: “hay que decírselo”. 3. Nosotros commands drop the final -s of “demos” before “se”: démoselo, digámoselo. 4. Attribute “lo” also goes before or attached in a periphrasis: “no lo va a ser” = “no va a serlo”.

If you hear “Ya se los expliqué” about one thing and several people, understand “I already explained it to you all / to them”. It is a regional variety. You can always use “se lo”, which is correct everywhere.
“Guys, I already told you the answer yesterday.” In the general norm it would be…
The present is for Ana. Let’s give it to her tonight, OK?
The exam looks easy, but it isn’t going to be.

You can now combine two pronouns in the right order and place with any verb form. Pronouns agree with what they replace; in class 123 you work on another tricky agreement: the verb with collective nouns and quantities (“La gente está contenta”, “La mitad de los invitados…”). It is the natural next step: from pronoun agreement to subject-verb agreement when the form is misleading.

The Álamo 25 building, Wednesday morning. Yesterday there was a residents’ meeting: they voted on a plan to turn the rooftop into a shared garden. Elena Robles, the president, and Julián Méndez, the secretary, are writing the minutes. In minutes you talk about groups and amounts: “people”, “the majority”, “half”, “70 %”. Today you learn when the verb is singular, when it is plural and when both forms are fine.
People want a garden. (In Spanish “gente” is grammatically singular.)
Most of the residents voted in favour. (Both verb forms are correct.)
Elena and Julián are preparing the minutes.
The people in the building are happy with the plan.
Elena and Julián will send the minutes on Friday.
How does a noun that means “a group of people” agree?
People say the rooftop has been neglected.
The residents’ association decided to fix the rooftop.
In the end, the majority voted in favour.
Most people think it is a good idea.
In English you say “people are”, but in Spanish “la gente es”, “la gente está”, “la gente dice”. Adjectives are feminine singular too: “la gente está cansada”.
The audience clapped a lot at the end of the presentation.
Most people prefer plants that are easy to look after.
And if “de los vecinos”, “de los propietarios” comes after it?
Half of the people at the meeting arrived late.
70 % of the owners approved the plan.
Half of the money comes from the association’s fund.
40 % of the residents have lived in the building for more than ten years. Which form is correct?
Half of the budget is for the plants.

In Spain, “tú y Óscar” is “vosotros”: “Tú y Óscar vais”. In Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia, the plural of “tú” is “ustedes”: “Tú y Óscar van”. Both are correct in their variety. With “usted y Rosa”, everyone uses “ustedes”.
Julián and I will talk to the architect on Monday.
Neither the property manager nor the treasurer came to the meeting.
There were a lot of complaints. There have been two meetings. There are going to be changes.
You will hear this plural in many places, but standard Spanish uses the singular.
Each of the owners will pay an extra fee in January.
Rosa and Óscar were worried about the noise of the building work.
There were more people at the meeting than last year.
Which sentence is correct? (The family on the third floor moved in June.)
Which sentence is correct? (Yesterday there were two votes.)
Elena, I’m working on yesterday’s minutes. How many people came in the end?
There were thirty-two people, nearly all the owners. And people were in very good spirits.
And how did the vote on the rooftop garden go?
Very clear. The majority voted in favour: 70 % of the owners said yes.
And the rest? I had the impression that a group of residents complained about the cost.
About the cost and the noise. Rosa and Óscar were worried about the building work.
Understandable: Óscar is one of the people who work from home the most. And the budget?
That’s the problem: neither the property manager nor the treasurer brought the final figures.
Oh dear. So what do I put about the money?
Put that each owner will pay an extra fee and that half of the money comes from the association’s fund.
Perfect. You and I check the minutes on Friday and send them to everyone, OK?
Yes. And write that there’s going to be another meeting in February: people want to see the plans.
How many people came to the meeting?
Why were Rosa and Óscar worried?
What is the problem with the budget?
The meeting approved the plan by a majority.
Half of the rooftop will have herbs: rosemary, mint, basil.
Neither Rosa nor Óscar will be able to come to the February meeting: they are away.
On Saturday, Julián and I will visit the rooftop with you.
On the rooftop there were lots of old boxes that had to be thrown away.
The residents’ association voted in favour.
Neither Elena nor Julián had the keys.
There were few chairs in the room.
The caretaker and the neighbour are happy.
What is the main idea?
What did a group of residents from the first floor ask for?
Why is there no final budget yet?
When will the residents get the minutes?
What is the good news at the end?
the head is singular and there is no plural to agree with
both are correct; the plural is very common
with “yo” → we; with “tú” → vosotros or ustedes
haber does not agree; mixed genders → masculine plural

Before you conjugate, find the head of the subject. A collective noun alone (“la gente”, “la asamblea”): singular. An amount + de + plural (“la mitad de los vecinos”): you can choose. Two subjects: plural, and “yo” beats “tú”. And impersonal haber never agrees: “había treinta personas”.
The audience gave a standing ovation at the end of the concert.
There have been two meetings at the office this morning.
My brother and I play in the same basketball team.
Half of the students passed the exam. What is correct?
My grandmother and grandfather are very happy with their new flat.
A company runs a survey about its canteen. Lucía, from HR, writes the report. Correct her notes: change the subject or the tense and adapt the verb.
Three more cases for learners who want precision: ser + a plural complement (the plural is normal), más de uno (singular) and el resto de + plural (both forms).
Most of the people present were owners; there were only four tenants.
More than one resident complained about the smell of the fertiliser.
The rest of the residents voted by post. What is correct?
The volunteers, each with their watering can, arrived at nine.

You can now report on groups and amounts with the right agreement: “la mayoría votó”, “Elena y yo vamos”, “había treinta personas”. In class 124 you learn not to repeat those subjects: “La mayoría votó a favor; el resto, en contra”. It is the natural next step: once you know what each verb agrees with, you can leave words out without losing the meaning.

Clara Benítez is a translator at Palabra Viva, a small translation agency in Madrid. On Saturday she went to her friend Irene’s wedding in Valencia… and almost didn’t make it. Today, Monday, she tells her colleague Marcos Gil. Telling an anecdote is not just putting verbs in the past: you open the story, set the scene, tell the events in order, create surprise and close with a comment. No new tenses today: you combine the past tenses you know with storytelling markers.
I missed the train. I took another train. I got to the wedding. (correct, but flat)
Guess what happened to me? It turns out I missed the train… Anyway, I made it to the wedding by a miracle.
“¿A que no sabes qué me pasó?” is used to…
“I was having breakfast quietly” is…
When I got to the platform, the train left. (I arrived, and then it left)
When I got to the platform, the train had already left. (it left first)
When Clara opened the door, her neighbour was on the landing looking worried.
Clara got to the station at twenty past nine. The train had left at a quarter past nine.
At the station, Clara spent a good hour waiting for the next train.
How do I start, order, surprise and finish?
Once, on a trip to Seville, I was left without a hotel.
At first we couldn’t find the problem, but after a while we saw that the washing machine was leaking.
So, long story short, I arrived just in time. Thank goodness there was another train.
In a story, “al rato” means “a little later” everywhere. In Mexico it is also very common for the future: “Te llamo al rato” = I’ll call you later today.
We called a taxi from the hotel and after a while it arrived at the door.
We were driving calmly along the motorway and suddenly the car made a really strange noise.
I left my wallet on a park bench. Thank goodness a young man saw it and ran after me with it.
While I was having a shower, someone rang the doorbell.
I was having a shower and suddenly the hot water stopped.
In the end I missed the train. / In the end everything went well.
After an hour, the train finally arrived.
While Clara was unplugging the washing machine, her neighbour was drying the bathroom floor.
After three weeks of rain, the sun finally came out on the wedding day.
I ran along the whole platform, but in the end the train left without me.

“¡Qué fuerte!” is very colloquial and very common in Spain; in Latin America you hear it much less. “¡Qué barbaridad!” is used in both Spain and Latin America, also for something excessive. The others work everywhere.
“And when I opened the door, it was my downstairs neighbour, soaking wet.”
“In the end, Irene’s brother had kept a seat for me.”
When we got to the cinema, the film had already started.
On the metro I realised I didn’t have my wallet.
Morning, Clara! How was Irene’s wedding? You look tired.
Phew! Guess what happened to me? I missed the train to Valencia.
You’re kidding! But you’re always early for everything…
Well, it turns out that on Saturday I got up at seven. I was having breakfast quietly when the doorbell rang: it was my downstairs neighbour. Water was coming through her bathroom ceiling.
How awful! And then what?
At first we couldn’t find the problem, but after a while we saw that my washing machine was leaking. I unplugged it, cleaned everything up and ran out of the house.
Oh dear… And did you get to the station in time?
Not at all! When I got to Atocha, the train had already left. And suddenly I realised I had left the present at home.
No way! So what did you do?
So I bought a ticket for the next train and texted Irene. I got to Valencia at half past twelve, and the ceremony was at one, in a garden outside the city.
And did you make it?
By a miracle. When I walked into the garden, the couple were walking in at that very moment. So, long story short, I made it on time. Thank goodness Irene’s brother had kept a seat for me.
Why did Clara have to go down to her neighbour’s flat?
What did Clara discover at the station?
How did the story end?
On Sunday, while I was reading a book on the train, a man tapped me on the shoulder.
He told me I was in his seat. And it was true! I had misread the carriage number.
I looked for my seat all over the train for twenty minutes. At last I found it: it was in the last carriage.
Marcos reacts to the surprise.
We talked all the way to Madrid. So, long story short, I got home without even opening the book.
When I got to the cinema, the film had already started.
While we were looking for the hotel, it started to rain.
So, long story short, in the end we didn’t sleep at all.
Thank goodness Nuria had an umbrella.
What is the main idea?
What was Irene doing when the problem started?
Who solved the problem?
Why didn’t the florist arrive?
What happened while they were making the bouquets?
the background: what it was like, what was going on
what happened and moves the story on
something that happened before another past event
open, order, surprise, close and listen
A good anecdote has five parts: open it, set the scene, tell the events, create a twist (using the pluperfect for what had already happened) and close it. And the listener reacts.
Nuria was making dinner when her sister called from Porto.
When Marcos got to the bar, his friends had already left.
We were having dinner on the terrace and suddenly it started to hail.
“In the end, the ticket inspector let me get on without a ticket.”
We missed the ferry and there were no hotels with free rooms. So, long story short, we slept in the car.
On Friday, Marcos went to an interview for a translation project. Tell his story by transforming each sentence.

In spoken anecdotes, people very often switch to the present at the most exciting moment so the listener can “see” it: “… and suddenly the doorbell rings. I open the door and it’s my neighbour…”. It adds intensity; in formal writing, keep to the past.

You can now tell a complete anecdote: open it, set the scene, order the events, create a twist, close it and react when someone tells you one. In class 126 you move from what happened to what may happen: comparing hypotheses with puede que, quizás and a lo mejor. It is the natural next step: after telling the facts, you learn to imagine possible explanations.

Natalia Ríos is a graphic designer in Guadalajara. A studio in Monterrey is offering her a job with a higher salary, but she would have to move. At her agency, on the other hand, her boss, Luisa, may make her coordinator in the summer. This afternoon Natalia is having coffee with her friend Sergio to compare the options. Today you learn to think aloud about a decision: what will happen if you choose one option, what you would do, what is likely and which option is better.
If I accept, I’ll earn thirty percent more.
If I were you, I’d talk to Luisa this week.
They may make you coordinator in the summer.
In “Si acepto, ganaré más”, Natalia…
With “Yo que tú, hablaría con Luisa”, Sergio…
Do you see the condition as real, as something that may really happen?
If you accept, you’re going to have a much better salary.
If you stay, you can stay close to your mom.
If I move in March, I’ll have to find an apartment fast.
If you’re not happy with the salary, ask for more.
Are you imagining what your life would be like with one option, without deciding yet?
In Monterrey you’d earn more, but you’d be far from your family.
With that salary I could save up for a trip.
Here you’d have less money but more free time.
If Natalia accepts the offer, she’ll have to look for an apartment.
In Monterrey, Natalia would have a bigger but more expensive apartment.
Are you putting yourself in someone else’s shoes to give advice?
If I were you, I’d ask for the offer in writing.
In your place, I wouldn’t say anything at the agency yet.
It would be better to wait for the answer from Monterrey.
It would be a good idea to visit the city for a weekend.
If I were you, I’d ask for a day to think about it.
It would be better to decide calmly.
How likely is it to happen?
Maybe they’ll pay for my move.
Perhaps Luisa will offer me something better.
The studio may accept hybrid work.
Most likely the studio will want to see you in person.
Are you putting two options side by side?
It’s better to ask now than to regret it later.
On the one hand, the salary is much better; on the other, I don’t know anyone there.
The downside is that apartments there are more expensive.
I’d rather stay a few more months because I love the new project.
Maybe the studio will accept hybrid work.
Most likely Natalia will stay in Guadalajara.

To compare options, combine four things: the real condition (“If you accept, you’ll earn more”), the hypothesis with the conditional (“There you’d be alone”, “If I were you, I’d wait”), the possibility (“They may pay for your move”) and the comparison (“It’s better to wait than to decide in a hurry”).
In your place, I’d put both offers in a list.
If the studio doesn’t accept hybrid work, what are you going to do?
So, tell me. Do you know what you’re going to do about the offer yet?
Not at all. On the one hand, the salary is thirty percent higher; on the other, I’d have to leave my mom, you guys, everything.
And at the agency? What did Luisa tell you?
That they may make me coordinator in the summer. But it isn’t certain.
Look, if I were you, I’d talk to her this week. If she knows you have another offer, maybe she’ll give you a clearer answer.
Yeah, but if I tell her, won’t she think I just want more money?
I don’t think so. It’s normal to compare. Besides, it’s better to ask now than to regret it a year from now.
You’re right. What if I ask the studio to let me work from here? It would be ideal: one week a month there and the rest at home.
Most likely they’ll want to see you at the office at first, but you’ve got nothing to lose. If they say no, you still have both options.
The good thing is that I don’t have to answer until the fifteenth.
Then, in your place, I’d make a list of the pros and cons of each option. And at the weekend you could go to Monterrey to get to know the city.
Good idea. Maybe I’ll go on Saturday. And you’re coming with me!
What is the advantage of the Monterrey offer?
What does Sergio advise her first?
Until when does Natalia have to answer?
If the studio pays for my move, I’m going in March.
With a higher salary, Natalia could help her mom more.
If I were you, I wouldn’t sign anything until I had the offer in writing.
Luisa may take the news badly.
It’s better to decide calmly than to decide in a hurry.
If I were you, I’d talk to Luisa tomorrow.
If you accept, you’ll have to look for an apartment.
Most likely I’ll stay here.
It’s better to wait than to decide today.
Why does Sergio leave the message?
What problem does Sergio see in the Monterrey option?
What does he advise her to ask Luisa?
According to Sergio, what is most likely with working from Guadalajara?
What does Sergio suggest for Saturday?
the consequence of a real option
you imagine an option or put yourself in someone’s place
how likely it is
you set the options side by side and choose

Never “si” + conditional: “si aceptas”, not “si aceptarías”. The conditional goes in the other clause or on its own: “Allí ganarías más”, “Yo que tú, esperaría”. And for advice with “que”, for now: “Es mejor que esperes”; “sería mejor que esperaras” comes at B2.
If I have time tomorrow, I’ll call you.
If I were you, I’d wait a bit longer.
Maybe we’ll move to the coast next year.
Most likely the bank won’t give you the loan.
It’s better to rent first than to buy without knowing the neighbourhood.
Rocío and her partner, Hugo, live in an apartment in downtown Querétaro. They are thinking of buying a house with a garden outside the city. Help them think it through.

At B2 (classes 128 and 131) you learn the imperfect subjunctive, but you can already recognise it. “Si” + imperfect subjunctive + conditional presents an unlikely or imaginary hypothesis: “If they offer me more money, I’ll stay” (real: it may happen) / “If they offered me more money, I’d stay” (I see it as unlikely). “Si yo fuera tú” = if I were you, like “yo que tú”. And “sería mejor que esperaras” is the general form after “sería mejor que”. For now you only need to understand them.
Which sentence presents the condition as less likely?
“Si yo fuera tú, hablaría con Luisa” means…
“If I had more time, I’d learn to play the guitar.” Does the person have time now?

You can now think aloud about a decision: what will happen if you choose an option, what you would do in someone else’s place, what is likely and which option is better. In class 127 you take the next step: defending your decision with arguments, concessions (“Although it’s expensive, I’d choose it for its location”) and a clear conclusion. It is the natural next step: you already compare options; now you learn to persuade.

The town council is giving the Las Palmeras public library some extra money this year, but it is only enough for one project. Marta Lozano, the director, calls a team meeting. Diego Paredes wants a digital workshop for older people; Carmen Vega wants to renovate the children’s room; Rubén Soto wants to open on Saturday afternoons. There is no new grammar today: you combine what you already know (giving opinions, judging, reasoning, conceding, proposing) to defend an idea and make a group decision.
I think the digital workshop is the best option. (what you defend, stated first)
Many older people can’t do official paperwork online; besides, they come to the library almost every day.
It’s true that it’s the most expensive project, but it reaches more people.
That’s why I propose that we choose the workshop.
Diego says: “It’s true that it costs a lot, but laptops last for years.” Here Diego…
Where does the thesis usually go?
“That’s why I propose that we vote on Friday.” This sentence is…
Are you asserting something, or are you denying it, judging it or asking for it?
I think the workshop is useful for a lot of people.
I don’t think the children’s room needs so many changes.
It’s important for older people to learn how to book a doctor’s appointment online.
It’s clear that the money isn’t enough for everything.
I don’t think ten laptops are enough.
It’s clear that the children need a better space.
I think it’s a good idea for Rubén to check the Saturday timetable.
Are you giving a cause, drawing a consequence or adding another argument?
As the money is only enough for one project, we have to choose.
Students have nowhere to study, since we close at two on Saturdays.
The study room is empty in the afternoon, so we can use it for the workshop.
The laptops will be useful for older people and even for students.
“Como…, así que…” expresses the same relation twice: pick one. And before a word beginning with an “i” sound, “y” becomes “e”: “e incluso”.
As Rubén works on Saturday mornings, he knows that day’s users well.
The laptops can be useful for students too; besides, the library’s wifi is very good.
Nobody uses the study room in the afternoon, so we could use it for the workshop.
Do you acknowledge what the other person says before you answer?
Although it’s the most expensive project, I’d choose it because it’s so useful.
You’re right that the children’s room is old, but it can still be used.
The workshop runs all year; the renovation, on the other hand, is finished in two weeks.
The problem isn’t the money, but the staff for Saturdays.
Although it’s the most expensive project, I would choose it.
“You’re right that the workshop is useful, but…” What is the speaker doing?
Carmen is speaking and Diego wants to say something. What is more polite?
Are you proposing something to the group, or saying what will happen with an option?
I propose that we vote on Friday.
If we choose the workshop, we’ll have to buy ten laptops.
If we don’t decide before the end of the month, we lose the money.
I’d choose the workshop, but we could do storytelling sessions with volunteers.
If we choose the workshop, Diego will teach the first classes.
I suggest that everyone send their proposal in writing.
A general idea: “It’s necessary to listen to the whole team.”
Which sentence is correct? (I don’t think the workshop is too expensive.)
Which sentence is correct? (As there’s little money, we must choose carefully.)
Which sentence is correct? (I’m sure it will work.)
Right, let’s start. As the money is only enough for one project, today we have to choose one. Diego, will you start?
Yes. I think the digital workshop is the best option. Many older people don’t know how to book a doctor’s appointment online; besides, they come to the library almost every day.
Can I say something? You’re right that it’s a real problem, but the workshop takes almost all the money.
Sorry, let me finish. Although it’s the most expensive project, I’d choose it: laptops last for years and even students can use them.
Thank you, Diego. Carmen, what do you think?

I don’t see it that way. I don’t think that many older people will come every week. In the children’s room, on the other hand, there are thirty children every afternoon, so we need new shelves and more space.
If I may… For me, the problem isn’t the rooms but the opening hours. Students have nowhere to study, since we close at two on Saturdays.
That’s a good point, but opening on Saturdays means paying overtime all year round.
Here’s an idea: if we choose the workshop, I can teach the classes on Saturday afternoons, and that way the library is open that afternoon.
I partly agree with you. But it’s important that the children get something this year too.
What if we organise storytelling sessions with volunteers? It’s cheap and the children love it.
Sounds good. So I propose that everyone writes a short proposal and we vote on it on Friday.
Why does the team have to choose?
What argument does Carmen give against the workshop?
What does Diego offer in response to Rubén’s idea?
Rubén: “I think lots of students will come on Saturdays if we open.”
Carmen: “I don’t think the workshop is the most urgent thing this year.”
Marta: “It’s clear there isn’t money for all three projects.”
Diego: “It’s essential that older people learn to use online banking safely.”
Carmen: “It’s true that the room works quite well, but the shelves are broken.”
I don’t think it’s the best option.
Although it’s expensive, I would choose it.
If we vote today, we’ll start in January.
It’s important that everyone gives their opinion.
What is the main idea?
Why won’t Carmen be there on Friday?
What made her change her mind?
What does Carmen concede about the workshop?
What does she ask for at the end?
assert → indicative; deny or judge → subjunctive
one relation, one connector
acknowledge the other side, then answer
a clear proposal, real consequences

Before choosing the form, ask yourself what you are doing. Asserting (creo que, es verdad que, aunque): indicative. Denying, judging or proposing (no creo que, es importante que, propongo que): subjunctive. With a real-condition “si”: present. And a complete argument has four parts: thesis, arguments, counterargument and conclusion.
I don’t think the meeting will be very long.
I think Marta has the best solution.
Although the venue is small, we’re going to have the party there.
The budget is limited, so we have to choose.
If we decide today, the project starts in January.
Four flatmates have some shared money and must decide: a new sofa or a washing machine? Write their sentences with the given structure.

If the library sends its proposal to the council in writing, the register goes up. “Dado que” (given that) gives the cause; “no obstante” (nevertheless) introduces a contrast; “por consiguiente” (consequently) draws the conclusion; “en nuestra opinión” states a group’s thesis. And a B2 preview: “aunque” + subjunctive means “even if”: whatever happens, the decision does not change.
Given that the budget is limited, we are applying for a single project.
The workshop has a high cost. Nevertheless, it provides a service to more than a hundred people.
Recognition only: “Even if the council doesn’t give us more money, we’ll open on Saturdays.” What does it mean?

You can now defend a proposal in a group: you assert with the indicative, deny, judge and propose with the present subjunctive, and reason with connectors. But after the vote you’ll want to tell people what happened: “Marta proposed that we vote on Friday”, “Carmen didn’t think so many older people would come.” Those forms are the imperfect subjunctive. In class 128 you learn to form them (-ra and -se) so you can take everything you know into the past.

Bogotá, La Lámpara theatre company. Last night «La casa del río» opened and the audience gave it a standing ovation. This morning the actress Valeria Rincón is having breakfast with her sister Natalia and telling her about two months of rehearsals with a very demanding director, Ernesto Salas. Today you learn to report what someone asked for, wanted or felt in the past.
Present main verb → present subjunctive: the request is described from inside the rehearsal period.
Past main verb → imperfect subjunctive: the requested action is seen from that past moment.
Same mechanism with a feeling: the verb of emotion is in the past, so the event that caused it goes into the imperfect subjunctive.
The tense of the main verb sets the tense of the subjunctive.
Which main verb fits an imperfect subjunctive after it?
When the main verb expresses influence (asking, ordering, forbidding, advising), wish or emotion and is in a past tense, the verb after «que» goes into the imperfect subjunctive.
My boss asked me to call her before five: a request.
As a child, my father wanted me to study medicine: a wish about someone else.
Marta was not allowed to leave hospital before Monday: who forbade it does not matter.
I was glad you called me on my birthday: a feeling about a past event.
Ernesto demanded silence during rehearsals.
Camilo was worried that the lights might not work in time.
Diego hoped the audience would get the jokes in the second act.
If the person who wants or feels is the same person who acts, Spanish uses the infinitive, in the past as in the present.
I wanted to go to the rehearsal (I want, I go), but they didn’t let me.
I was glad to see you in the third row (I am glad, I see).
With causative and permission verbs, the person who acts can be a pronoun followed by an infinitive.
The same content with «que» + imperfect subjunctive: both versions are correct.
With pedir, querer or esperar and a different subject, use «que». «Me pidió salir» means something else: he asked me for permission to go out himself.
Valeria didn’t want to perform without her sister in the audience.
Which sentence means Ernesto made me stay?
The producer allowed us to use the stage on Mondays.
To give the purpose of a past action, use para que + imperfect subjunctive when someone else is the subject; para + infinitive when the subject is the same.
Ernesto dimmed the lights so that the audience would look only at the letter.
We rehearsed on Sundays to be ready for opening night: same subject, para + infinitive.
Lucía wrote to tell me she was at the theatre door.
Lucía wrote asking me to wait for her at the theatre door.
Camilo moved the spotlight so that Valeria’s face could be seen better.

Both endings are correct and mean the same here. The -ra form is the most frequent everywhere. In spoken Latin American Spanish -se is rare; in Spain it is heard more often, although -ra still predominates there too. In formal writing -se appears across the Spanish-speaking world.
Both the request and the call are in the past: only the imperfect subjunctive works.
The call has not happened yet, so the present subjunctive is possible and very common, especially in Latin America. The imperfect is also correct.
Which sentence is NOT correct?
Today is Friday: which forms are possible for a rehearsal on Sunday?
What is the difference?
They dimmed the lights so that the audience would look at the letter.
My mother was surprised that they gave me the part.
What an opening, Valeria! I loved it when the audience stood up at the end.
And I was so glad you came. I know you were on shift at the hospital.
I swapped with a colleague. Hey, was Ernesto really that demanding in rehearsals?
Very. He’d ask us to be there at seven sharp, and he banned phones in the auditorium.
And the letter scene? You were amazing.
He made me do that scene twenty times. He wanted me to say it more slowly so the audience would catch every word.
And you never complained?
Once. I told him I was exhausted and he told me to go home. The next day he brought me honey and lemon for my throat.
How thoughtful! I wanted to go to a rehearsal, but it wasn’t allowed, was it?
No. Ernesto wouldn’t let anyone in, not even the producer.
And what have you got today?
A show at seven. This morning Ernesto asked me to call him before four. And the theatre sent us a very formal email: “The management requested that the dressing rooms be cleared before midnight.”
What did Ernesto do when Valeria said she was exhausted?
Why didn’t Natalia go to any rehearsal?
Why does Valeria say «lo llame»?
Valeria kept a diary during rehearsals. Here are some sentences. What does each express: influence over someone, a wish, a feeling or a purpose?
“On the first day, Ernesto demanded that we know the script by heart.”
“I was worried the tickets wouldn’t sell before opening night.”
“I wanted to go to the dress rehearsal, but I was on call.”
“I turned up the volume so the music could be heard from the back row.”
“Ernesto told Diego to speak louder.”
The director forbade us to leave the theatre.
I was glad you called me.
Ernesto didn’t let us leave before ten.
Why does Ernesto send the message?
What did Ernesto ask the actors in August?
Why was he so demanding, according to him?
What moved him last night?
What did Lucía ask Ernesto to do?
A past verb of influence, wish or emotion takes the imperfect subjunctive after que
Same subject: infinitive, no que
Causative and permission verbs: pronoun + infinitive, or que + subjunctive
Decir, escribir, insistir en: indicative to inform, subjunctive to request; para que + -ra for purpose
-ra and -se are both correct; the present subjunctive is possible if the request is still pending

Ask yourself three questions: is there influence, wish or emotion? (then subjunctive); is it the same person? (then infinitive); is the main verb in the past? (then imperfect subjunctive, unless what was asked is still pending).
My grandmother always wanted us to come for lunch on Sundays.
We were surprised the museum was closed on a Tuesday.
When I was young, I preferred to travel alone.
The doctor told my father to eat less salt.
I left them the keys so they could get in without me.
A cookery school in Quito. Chef Paula Andrade was very strict on the first course. One of her students, Mario, tells a friend about it months later.

Minutes, reports and news use more formal verbs of influence: solicitar que, rogar que, disponer que, instar a alguien a que. There the -se form is more frequent than in conversation. One exception: in polite requests («Quisiera una mesa para dos») only the -ra form works.
Minutes: the chair asked residents to submit their proposals in writing.
News: the ministry urged companies to reduce energy use.
Which sentence does NOT allow the -se form?
Report: during last year’s works, the committee ordered the theatre to close.

You now know that a past main verb takes the imperfect subjunctive, and that the present is possible when the request is still pending. The natural next step is the whole system: how the tenses of the main and subordinate verbs combine in present, past and future.

Nuria Campos is an editor at a small publishing house in Madrid. On Friday they launch Héctor Lima’s first novel at Carmen Vidal’s bookshop. A month ago Carmen wanted the launch to be on a Saturday; today Nuria wants everything ready for Friday. Today you learn to choose the subjunctive tense from the main verb and from when the action happens: the sequence of tenses.
Nuria wants Héctor to come half an hour early: the wish is made now, so the subjunctive stays in the present.
A month ago Carmen wanted the launch to be on a Saturday: the wish belongs to the past, so the subjunctive moves to the imperfect.
Nuria needs Paula to design the posters today.
Last week Héctor asked Nuria to change the date, and she did.
When the main verb speaks from the present (present, future, imperative or present perfect), the subordinate verb goes in the present subjunctive.
I want the launch to be simple.
I’ll tell Paula to change the colour of the title.
Tell Carmen to set out eighty chairs.
This morning I asked them to check the printer’s proofs.
When the main verb is in a past tense or in the conditional, the subordinate verb normally goes in the imperfect subjunctive.
Carmen asked me to send her the poster.
At first, Héctor didn’t want his photo to appear in the book.
Héctor had already asked me to book a table for signing.
I’d like you to read the first chapter.
On Thursday I’ll ask Paula to take the posters to the bookshop.
We’d love lots of readers to come on Friday.
At first Héctor didn’t want the novel to be so long, but then he changed his mind.
I hope you get to Valencia safely (he is still travelling).
I hope you got to Valencia safely (she assumes the trip is over).
I’m glad you came to the meeting yesterday: a present feeling about a finished past event.

The two frames cover most cases, but what really decides is when the action in the subordinate clause takes place. From a present-tense main verb you can refer back to the past: “I don’t think Héctor knew anything about the interview”, “It’s a pity you couldn’t come yesterday”.

If the main verb is in the past and the subordinate action happened even earlier, Spanish uses the pluperfect subjunctive: “It annoyed me that the printer hadn’t warned us about the delay”. You study it in class 133; today you only need to recognise it.
Nuria assumes he has already arrived.
It’s a pity you couldn’t come to the meeting yesterday.
What does “hubieran avisado” express?
Yesterday Carmen asked me to confirm the number of chairs before Thursday: the standard sequence, always correct.
The present subjunctive is possible after a past verb when what was asked is still pending or still true now; it stresses that the request is still open.
A month ago Carmen asked us to postpone the launch, and we put it back a week.
On Monday Héctor told me he’d call as soon as he got to Valencia, and he called on Tuesday night.
In 2023 Nuria hired Paula to design the covers of a poetry series, which came out in June.
Call me when you listen to this message.
Right, Héctor, four days to go. Carmen called me yesterday and asked us to confirm how many people we expect.
And what did you tell her?
To set out about eighty chairs. She hasn’t settled it yet, so I’m writing to her again today.
Eighty? My previous editor wanted launches to be small every time, so that nobody would see empty chairs.
Well, I’d rather the room were full. By the way, the local radio station has asked you to do an interview on Thursday.
An interview? I’d love to, but I’d like them to send me the questions beforehand.
I’ll tell them, though I doubt they’ll send them: it’s a live programme. I will ask them to let you read an extract, though.
OK. And I hope Paula has finished the poster by now. Last Friday she told me she’d have it ready as soon as she got the photo.
She finished it yesterday. I’m glad you went for the harbour photo in the end; nobody liked the other one.
And what do you want me to do on Friday?
Get there at half past six, so we can test the microphone. And I’d like you to read the first chapter aloud.
The whole thing? Then tell Carmen to keep a glass of water on the table for me.
What did Carmen ask Nuria?
What would Héctor like before the interview?
What does Nuria want Héctor to do on Friday?
Please send us the books before Wednesday.
We are sorry the order went out late last week.
Check the poster before printing it, so there are no typos.
In 2019 they demanded that I cut a hundred pages from the novel, and I did.
It would suit us if the radio aired the interview before Friday.
I wanted the cover to be blue.
I’ll tell her to bring the posters.
She passes on other people’s requests and says what she wants him to do.
What did Carmen ask Nuria to do?
What does Héctor have to do before Thursday?
What time does Héctor have to arrive on Friday?
What would Nuria love?
the main verb speaks from now: present subjunctive
past or conditional main verb: imperfect subjunctive, also after cuando and para que
from a present verb you can look back: perfect or imperfect subjunctive
a past request still open now may take the present; the imperfect is always safe

First look at the main verb: present, future, imperative or present perfect → venga; past or conditional → viniera. Then ask when the action happens: something already done, seen from now, takes haya venido or viniera; a past request that is still open can also take the present. And remember: a real past event after cuando stays in the indicative.
When I was a child, my parents didn’t let me go out after ten.
I’ll give you the book back as soon as I finish it.
It would be great if we spent the holidays together this summer.
I hope you’ve received it by now.
In January my boss asked me to prepare the report, and I handed it in in February.
Lorena moved house last month. Now she tells what she was asked and what she wants. Change the frame and adjust the subjunctive.
For strong students or spare time: decide when the present subjunctive is possible after a past verb, and recognise the register.
News report: the mayor asked residents to save water all summer.
A request from 1995, about that summer only.
In a formal email, which form fits?
It hurt me that you hadn’t called: which came first?

You can now choose between “quiero que vengas” and “me gustaría que vinieras” from the main verb and the timing. In class 131 you use the same imperfect subjunctive in a new way: in the if-clause, to imagine the present: “If I had time, I’d travel more”. It is the natural next step: the imperfect subjunctive stops following a past verb and starts building hypotheses.

Irene Salas, an architect, is hosting her Architecture class reunion in Bogotá tonight, fifteen years after graduation. Daniel arrives late because he missed his flight; Felipe lives in Montreal and cannot come. Everyone talks about past choices and how life would look today. You already know present and past hypotheses; today you mix them: the condition in one time frame, the result in another.
A present hypothesis: he lives abroad now, so he isn’t at the party now.
A past hypothesis: both the condition and the result belong to this morning.
A mixed conditional: a decision taken ten years ago, a consequence visible tonight.
If Irene had more free time now, she would play the piano again.
If Daniel had checked his bag the night before, he wouldn’t have had to go back home for his ID card.
Use this when you imagine a different past and describe the present it would have produced: the if-clause looks back, the result clause describes today.
If Felipe hadn’t taken that job, he would be living in Bogotá now.
If Lucía hadn’t dropped out, she would be an architect like us today.
If we had booked the big room, we wouldn’t be so cramped now.
If you had listened to me, you’d already be resting at the hotel: a reproach.
Lucía opened her bakery in 2015. If she hadn’t, she would work at an architecture firm today.
If Irene had accepted the Berlin scholarship, she would speak perfect German now.
Use this when the condition is a lasting trait or a current situation, true now and also back then, and the result is a past event that would have turned out differently.
If Daniel were a more organised person, he wouldn’t have missed the flight this morning.
If Irene didn’t live so far from the centre, she would have got here earlier to set up the room.
If I could cook, I would have made tonight’s dinner myself.
If Felipe didn’t have two small children, he would have flown to Bogotá for the reunion.
The cause is who Daniel is, then and now: a general criticism.
The cause is one past moment (last night), so it sounds less like a judgement of his personality.
Daniel is very absent-minded. If he weren’t, he wouldn’t have left his ID card at home.
If Irene didn’t speak English, she wouldn’t have won the Toronto project last year.
If I hadn’t met Irene in first year, we wouldn’t be friends now.
If Daniel weren’t so stubborn, he would have set the alarm last night, as I told him.
De + perfect infinitive works like an if-clause with hubiera; it is compact and slightly more careful in tone, common in writing and in educated speech.
Had I known, I would have brought the photos from our university days.
Had he stayed in Bogotá, Felipe would be here today.
If he hadn’t missed his flight, Daniel would have made it to lunch.

In casual speech, especially in Spain, people say “Si lo sé, no vengo” (literally “If I know, I don’t come”) to mean “Had I known, I wouldn’t have come”: a half-joking complaint. Recognise it; you don’t need to produce it.
What does “De haberlo sabido, habría venido antes” mean?
Which sentence does NOT suit a formal report?
If you had listened to me when I told you to travel yesterday, you’d be rested now.
If Lucía weren’t so brave, she would never have opened it.
Daniel, at last! We thought you weren’t coming.
I missed the seven o’clock flight: I left my ID card at home. If I weren’t so scatterbrained, I wouldn’t have missed it.
I told you: if you’d listened to me and travelled yesterday, you wouldn’t be exhausted now.
All right, all right, don’t tell me off. What about Felipe? Isn’t he coming?
No, he’s still in Montreal. He says that if he hadn’t taken that job he’d be here today, but he has no regrets.
Fair enough. Had he stayed in Bogotá, he’d still be in that grey office he hated so much.
And you? Do you regret anything?
A little, yes. I got into journalism very late. If I’d started at twenty, I’d have more contacts now.
Me, sometimes, about the piano. If I’d stayed at the conservatoire, maybe I’d be giving concerts. But if I were more disciplined, I wouldn’t have given it up, would I?
Look, here comes Lucía with a huge cake. Had I known, I wouldn’t have eaten on the plane.
Hi, everyone! If someone had told me at twenty that I’d end up baking cakes, I wouldn’t have believed it.
Well, if you hadn’t dropped out, we wouldn’t be eating the best cake in Bogotá right now.
Why did Daniel miss his flight?
What does Daniel think of Felipe’s decision?
What does Irene say about the piano?
If I hadn’t done that set-design course, I’d be designing buildings today.
If he weren’t, he wouldn’t have put up with three years of building work.
If Daniel had spent last night in Bogotá, he wouldn’t be so sleepy now.
If I didn’t speak Portuguese, the company wouldn’t have sent me to São Paulo in 2019.
If I had studied Architecture at another university, I wouldn’t know anyone at this table now.
I’d be living in Berlin now if I had accepted the scholarship.
If I were more punctual, I wouldn’t have missed the train.
Had I known, I would have come earlier.
He misses the party but has no regrets about his life abroad.
What would not have happened if Felipe had stayed in Bogotá?
Why didn’t he buy his ticket in September?
What would he have done had he known the audio would be played to everyone?
What does Felipe reproach Daniel for?
a different past produces a different present: regrets, relief, “what if”
a lasting trait explains a past event: useful for self-criticism and gentle reproaches
habría and hubiera are both standard in the main clause; the imperfect indicative is colloquial
a compact, slightly more careful if-clause; pronouns attach to haber

Ask two questions: is the condition a past event or a lasting trait or situation? Is the result about today or about something that already happened? Time markers help: ahora, hoy, todavía point to the simple conditional; anoche, esta mañana, a date point to the compound one. And never use the conditional right after si.
If I hadn’t missed the night bus, I’d be at home asleep now.
If my sister weren’t so generous, she wouldn’t have lent me her car last summer.
If we had planted the lemon tree three years ago, it would already be producing lemons.
Had we known they closed at eight, we would have arrived earlier.
If I were taller, I would have played on the school basketball team.
Marisa is a nurse and her brother Óscar is looking for work. They talk about what happened and how things would be today. Write the hypotheses.
For strong students or spare time: recognise the register of each form and choose the right one for the situation.
A friend at a dull party says “Si lo sé, no vengo”: what does it express?
Where does this sentence with “te llevaba” fit?
In a formal complaint letter, which form fits?
What does “de ser cierto” correspond to?

You can now mix time frames in conditionals: a past condition with a present result, and a present trait with a past result. In class 136 you use the same imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive after como si to compare with something unreal: “He talks as if he were the boss”, “She looked at me as if she had never seen me”. It is the natural next step: the same forms and time logic, now for comparisons.

Irene Salas runs a small theatre company in Bogotá. In two weeks they open “Primer día”, a comedy about Clara’s first day at an office. In rehearsals Irene gives directions like “Talk as if you owned the company” or “Come in as if you’d had an argument with someone”. Today you learn to compare the way someone behaves with an imagined situation: como si + imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.
Marcos isn’t the director: the comparison is imaginary and refers to the same moment as “habla”.
Lucía saw no ghost: the imagined event would have happened before she came in.
Marcos doesn’t know his lines yet, but he says them as if he knew them by heart.
Did Lucía actually see a ghost?
Use the imperfect subjunctive when the imagined situation holds at the same time as the main action: it describes a state or a manner, not an earlier event.
Don Ernesto signs papers as if he were in a great hurry.
Clara looks at the office as if it were a maze.
Marcos moves around the stage as if he were at home.
Rosa looks after us as if we were her children.
Use the pluperfect subjunctive when the imagined event would have happened before the main action: it explains a result you can see now or saw then.
Lucía arrived out of breath, as if she had run all the way from home.
Daniel keeps yawning as if he hadn’t slept all night.
Marcos talks about the play as if he had written it himself.
Daniel’s clothes are covered in dust, as if he had built the whole set on his own.
Rosa runs the dressing room as if it were an army barracks.
Irene smiles as if she already knew the opening would be a success.

Ask yourself whether the imagined situation holds at the same time as the main action (imperfect) or would have happened before it (pluperfect). That is why even a present-tense main verb takes “hubiera”: “He looks at me as if I had done something to him”.
On Friday we’ll greet the audience as if we had known them all our lives.
Marcos looks at me as if I had said something to him before rehearsal.
A real, known manner: Irene already told him how to do it. Como + indicative.
An imagined manner: it’s not an ordinary Monday in the play, but he should act as if it were.
A colloquial exclamation rejecting a reaction as over the top: “It’s not as if it were that hard!”
A colloquial exclamation, used on its own, that rejects someone’s behaviour: “You act as if…, but that’s not the case”. Same tenses as como si.
Anyone would think he was a millionaire!
Don’t shout at me. You’re not my boss!
Why that face? Anyone would think you’d seen a ghost!
“Igual que si” and “lo mismo que si” work like “como si” (just as if). “Como si nada” is a set phrase: as if nothing had happened. “Hacer como si” means to pretend: “I pretended I hadn’t seen him”.
Lucía, set the chairs the way Rosa set them at the last rehearsal.
It’s not as if you were a film star!
The lighting technician turned up an hour late and said hello as if nothing had happened.
Which sentence is correct?
Let’s stop for a moment. Marcos, don Ernesto is the boss, but you’re playing him as if he were a soap-opera villain.
Am I overdoing it? I wanted him to come across as tough.
Tough, yes; ridiculous, no. Talk to Clara as if you had no time for her: you check your watch, you sign papers…
And me? A while ago you said I came in as if I’d run a marathon.
Exactly. Clara is nervous, but she isn’t rushing in. Come in the way you did at the first rehearsal: slowly, looking all around.
Oh, right, as if she were looking for someone she knew.
Hey, Irene, and why does Clara look at me as if I’d done something to her? It’s her first day.
Because in the previous scene don Ernesto moves her desk without warning. She looks at him just as if he had insulted her.
Well, it’s no big deal. It’s not as if I’d fired her!
Ha ha, save that line for the show. Again from the entrance. Marcos, you keep signing papers as if nothing were going on when she says hello.
OK. And if I get a line wrong, I carry on as if nothing had happened, right?
That’s it. On opening night nobody will notice a thing. From the beginning!
What problem does Irene see in Marcos’s acting?
How should Lucía come in?
Why does Clara give don Ernesto a dirty look?
When the phone rings, answer as if you were expecting bad news.
Lucía knows the script so well she recites it as if she had written it herself.
Pour the coffee the way Rosa showed you: slowly and quietly.
Daniel complains his scene is short. It’s not as if he were the lead!
That day the audience clapped as if they had just seen the best play of the year.
He talks as if he knew everything.
She looked at me as if she had seen a ghost.
She gives her notes on the rehearsal and reminds them of tomorrow’s schedule.
What does Irene say about Lucía’s acting?
What does Marcos need to change?
What must everyone do when the lights go out?
What does Irene tell Daniel about the lift scene?
an imagined situation at the same time as the main action
an imagined event before the main action, even after a present verb
a colloquial exclamation rejecting an overreaction; avoid it in formal writing
a real, known manner takes como + indicative

After como si there are only two tenses, whatever the main verb: the imperfect for something imagined at the same time, the pluperfect for something imagined before. Never the indicative, the present or perfect subjunctive, or the conditional. For a real manner, use como + indicative.
My neighbour parks as if the street were his.
He arrived at the meeting soaked, as if he had walked in the rain for an hour.
Make the rice the way the recipe says, without changing anything.
It’s not as if it were made of gold!
For years my boss treated me as if I were new at the company.
Sunday lunch at Sara’s family home. Turn each observation into a comparison with como si or a protest with ¡Ni que…!
For strong students or spare time: como si with a future idea, “¡Como si…!” on its own as an ironic exclamation, igual que si, and register.
He said goodbye as if he were never coming back.
As if I had nothing else to do!
They welcomed us just as if we were family.
Which sentence suits a review in a magazine?

You can now compare with something imagined. In class 137, “aunque” also makes you choose the mood: indicative for a fact you accept, subjunctive for one you don’t confirm or that doesn’t matter to you. It’s the natural next step: you keep choosing between fact and hypothesis, now to talk about obstacles.

Lola Robles runs the bakery her father opened forty years ago. A coffee-shop chain wants to buy it, and her son Rubén, who keeps the accounts, thinks they should consider it. Lola is clear: “No matter how much you insist, I’m not selling.” In class 137 you conceded with “aunque”; today you learn connectors that concede more forcefully or in a different register.
A fact presented as information: sales really have fallen, yet the business still makes a profit.
No matter how much they offer: any amount, still no. The concession is pushed to the maximum.
However good the offer is: the intensity falls on an adjective.
Lola means that no amount of insisting will change her mind.
Which sentence states the obstacle as a fact?

“A pesar de que” works like “aunque” but sounds a little more emphatic: it stresses that the obstacle exists and still does not stop the result. With the indicative you put the obstacle on the table as a fact.
Although the chain has twenty shops, it wants ours.
Even though we open at six, there is always someone waiting.
Lola kept kneading by hand, even though her father had given her a machine.
A possibility: nobody knows whether flour will go up; either way, prices stay the same. “Aunque” is more frequent here, but this is correct.
A fact already on the table: Lola does not deny it, she just treats it as irrelevant to her decision.
Without “que”, “a pesar de” takes a noun or, with the same subject, an infinitive. In formal writing you will also see “pese a que”, which means the same as “a pesar de que”.
Although the chain already has two coffee shops in the area, it also wants the bakery.
Even if electricity gets more expensive next year, we are not closing.

These are intensive concessions: “however much…, it makes no difference”. The subjunctive is the usual choice, both for a possibility and for a known fact you dismiss. The indicative appears when you report a real fact, typically something repeated or past: “Por más que lo intento, no me sale” (however hard I try — and I do — it doesn’t work).
However many times you ask me, I am not signing.
We won’t change the recipe, however much the chain insists.
Try as I might (and I really do), I can’t get up at four without an alarm.
However much they pressed him, my father never agreed to replace the oven: a real past fact.
However much flour we order, we always run short in December.
However early Rubén gets up, his mother is already kneading.
However much I knead the dough, it never turns out like my father’s.

“Si bien” concedes a real fact, always with the indicative, typical of reports and formal emails. “Aun cuando” is a formal “even if” with the subjunctive, or a formal “even though” with the indicative. “Aun + gerund” compresses a concession into one phrase: “aun sabiéndolo” = even though he knew it.
While the premises are small, the bakery has loyal customers.
Even if the chain improves its offer, the answer will be the same.
Even though sales fell in March, the quarter closed in profit (a real fact: indicative).
Even though she knew the oven was old, Lola refused to replace it.
Although the oven is forty years old, it still works.
Even if the chain rejects our proposal, we will keep selling in the shop.
In front, with a comma, the concession sets up the result. After the main clause it sounds like a comeback or an afterthought. Never add “pero” before the result.
Rubén is writing a report for the bank: which sentence fits best?
However cheap the chain’s croissants are, they don’t taste like ours.
Lola still kneads by hand, even though she knows the machine is faster.
Mum, the man from the chain called again. They’re raising their offer once more.
However much they raise it, I’m not selling. Your grandfather opened this bakery.
I know. But even though we work twelve hours a day, we’ve earned less this year.
Granted, we’ve earned less, but we haven’t lost money. Nieves said so.
And the oven? No matter how often we fix it, it breaks down every two months.
Old as it may be, that oven makes the best bread in the neighbourhood.
Mum, however nostalgic you feel, numbers are numbers.
Well, I want to carry on, even knowing what it costs us. Isn’t there another way out?
Maybe: we don’t sell them the bakery, but we sell them bread every morning. Even if they pay us little per loaf, it’s a steady income.
Now that I like better. Chain or no chain, if they respect our recipe, we can talk.
I’ll call Nieves tomorrow. And we order the new oven this year, however hard it is for you to say goodbye to the old one.
I’m not saying goodbye to the old one: I’ll put it in the shop window.
Why doesn’t Lola want to sell?
What is wrong with the oven?
What solution does Rubén suggest?
However much flour goes up, we won’t raise the price of bread this month.
Although the shop is small, there is room for a breakfast table.
However early we open, there is always a queue at the door.
However many offers they send us, the recipe is not for sale.
While the premises need refurbishing, the bakery has loyal customers.
Lola opens at six, however tired she is.
However much money they offer us, we are not selling.
Although the oven is old, the bread comes out perfect.
She gives Lola her professional view on the offer, the contract and the oven.
How is the bakery doing financially?
What does Nieves dislike about the contract?
What does she think about selling bread to the chain?
What does she recommend doing with the oven?
a real obstacle you state as fact; por más que + indicative for something real and repeated
no amount changes the result; also a pesar de que + subjunctive for a possibility
mucho agrees with the noun; muy goes with adjectives and adverbs, usually with the subjunctive
formal register: si bien only with the indicative; aun cuando = even if / even though
