Ask yourself three questions. Fact or possibility? A fact you state takes the indicative; a possibility or a dismissed fact takes the subjunctive. Quantity or quality? With a verb or noun use “por mucho (que)”; with an adjective or adverb, “por muy… que”. Which register? In a formal email, “si bien”, “aun cuando” and “aun + gerund”. And never put “pero” before the result.
However fast you run, you won’t catch the eight o’clock train.
Although the exam was hard, I passed with a good mark.
However patient he is, my neighbour can no longer stand the building noise.
Even if it rains on Saturday, the wedding will be in the garden.
Even at ninety, my grandmother still cooks for the whole family.
Marina is training for her third marathon. Her coach uses sentences with “aunque”. Rephrase them with today’s connectors.

For strong students or spare time: two special-register concessions. “Así + subjunctive” (“así me lo pidan de rodillas” = even if they beg me on their knees) is literary or emphatic, and in some Latin American countries it is also heard in conversation. “Mal que me pese” is a fixed phrase meaning “much as I hate to admit it”; the pronoun changes with the person.
What does “así” mean here?
Which form follows concessive “así”?
What does Lola express?
Much as management may dislike it, the figures are clear.

You can now hold your ground with “por mucho que insistas” or “aun cuando suban los precios”: the subjunctive marks what is not yet real. In class 139 you apply the same logic to time: “when we have the new oven”, “before the offer arrives”, “as soon as I know”. It is the natural next step: from a possible obstacle to a moment that is still uncertain.

Inés Calvo runs a small theatre company in Madrid. In September it starts its first tour of Mexico. The set is held at customs, the work permits haven’t arrived and the second venue hasn’t signed: everything depends on things that haven’t happened yet. In class 098 you talked about a future moment from now; today you look at that uncertain future from a point in the past, add new connectors and use infinitive constructions.
Seen from today, the arrival is still pending, so the verb after the connector goes in the present subjunctive.
When Rodrigo spoke in March, the arrival was still ahead of him: the same uncertain future, shifted into the past, takes the imperfect subjunctive.
You are reporting what actually happened, so the connector takes the indicative.
When Rodrigo said it, had the ship arrived?
Which sentence reports a real event?
When you report a plan, promise or instruction made in the past, the time clause moves from the present to the imperfect subjunctive, just as the main verb moves from the future to the conditional.
The customs agent said they would release the set once we paid the duties.
Lola asked us not to buy the tickets until we had the permits.
We decided to wait at the theatre until the technicians left (their leaving was still ahead).
Inés wanted to leave Madrid before the holidays started.
Rodrigo promised he would send the posters as soon as the theatre confirmed the date.
Lola got to the rehearsal and waited at the door until Inés turned up with the keys.
Last year we agreed we wouldn’t open the play until the costumes were ready.
These connectors stress that one thing follows straight after another. They follow the same rule as cuando: subjunctive for a future moment, indicative for facts and habits.
As soon as we have the permits, we’ll buy the tickets.
Once the set is up, we’ll rehearse with the lights.
The moment I hear anything about the second venue, I’ll write to you.
As soon as the show ended, the audience stood up (a past fact: indicative).
Siempre que can also set a condition, like “as long as” or “provided that”, and then it always takes the subjunctive. Ask yourself whether it means “every time” or “only if”.
Once customs releases the set, we’ll send it to Guadalajara.
Every time Lola goes on tour, she takes her own pillow.
What does siempre que mean here?
Two things really happening at the same time take the indicative.
A stretch of time that is still ahead takes the subjunctive.
Here mientras sets a condition (as long as / provided that), and it always takes the subjunctive.
In present-day Spanish mientras que mainly contrasts two facts (“whereas”) and takes the indicative. For time or condition, plain mientras is the usual choice.
What does mientras express here?
Rodrigo works with big theatres, whereas Inés prefers small venues.
Antes de que always takes the subjunctive, even when you narrate a real past event: in a past narrative it simply moves to the imperfect subjunctive.
In Bogotá we put the set up before they opened the venue.
Inés left the theatre before the meeting ended (it did end, but later).

In “hasta que no tengamos”, the second no adds no negative meaning: it means exactly “until we have”. This expletive negation is very common, especially after a negative main clause, and the RAE grammar accepts it; very careful writing often leaves it out.
The technician turned off the lights before the actors left the stage.
On reading the theatre’s letter, Inés smiled.
What does this sentence mean?
The theatre manager assured us she’d return the deposit once we left the venue clean.
Straight after the dress rehearsal, the whole company went out for dinner.
Rodrigo, any news about the ship? In March you told me you’d let me know as soon as it reached Veracruz.
It got in on Monday, but it’s still at customs. As soon as they release it, we’ll send it to Guadalajara by truck.
And will it get there in time? Remember Bogotá: the producer swore everything would be set up before we arrived, and we ended up building it ourselves at three in the morning.
Not this time. Once it’s in the theatre, my crew will put it up in two days while you rehearse in the small room.
Great. And the work permits? I don’t want to buy the tickets until we have them.
Makes sense. They told me they’d issue them when the paperwork was complete, and it is now. The moment they send them, I’ll forward you the email.
Great. Another thing: Lola asks me the same thing every time we talk: will we have time to rest?
Of course. Straight after landing, we’ll take you to the hotel and you’ll have the afternoon off. And whenever you want to go out for dinner, let me know and I’ll come with you.
What luxury. And the theatre in Mexico City?
That’s moving more slowly. Until they confirm the date, I can’t announce anything.
Fine. After what we went through in Bogotá, I’d rather take it slowly. But I want to see the theatre before the hotel when I get to Guadalajara.
I thought you’d say that. I’ll call you as soon as I hear anything about the second venue.
What had Rodrigo promised Inés in March?
What happened on the Bogotá tour?
When will Inés buy the tickets?
The producer assured us the set would be up before we arrived.
As soon as I get the permits, I’ll forward them to you.
Every time the company goes on tour, I take my own pillow.
Rodrigo said he’d send the truck once customs released the set.
The moment I landed at Guadalajara airport, I switched on my phone and saw ten messages from Inés.
He said he would let us know as soon as the ship arrived.
As soon as she landed, Lola called her mother.
Once we have the permits, we’ll buy the tickets.
He gives an update on the set, the permits and the second venue, and asks for the flight times.
What had the customs agent said?
What will Rodrigo do the moment he hangs up?
Why isn’t he announcing the Mexico City shows yet?
What does Rodrigo want to do for Lola?
What does Inés have to send Rodrigo?
an uncertain future seen from now, or a condition with mientras / siempre que: present subjunctive
a future seen from a past moment, and antes de que in any past narrative: imperfect subjunctive
real events and habits stay in the indicative
with the same subject, these infinitive phrases replace a full time clause in any tense

Ask where the moment is viewed from. Still future from today: present subjunctive. Future from a past moment: imperfect subjunctive. A fact or a habit: indicative. And two fixed rules: antes de que always takes the subjunctive; nada más and al take the infinitive.
My boss promised he’d give me a raise as soon as I finished the project.
Yesterday we left home before it started to rain.
Whenever you need help with the move, call me.
On hearing the news, María called the whole family.
I’ll lend you the car as long as you return it with a full tank.
Andrea moved into a new flat in the spring. Now she tells how it went. Change the viewpoint or the structure.
For strong students or spare time: three uses you will meet in the press and in fiction, plus a connector with two meanings.
News report: after the theatre closed in 2019, the neighbourhood changed completely.
Once the set had been released, the truck left for Guadalajara.
What does apenas mean in each sentence?
In a very formal report, which version do many writers prefer?

You can now place an uncertain moment from today or from the past. In class 140 you apply the same logic to another family of clauses: those expressing purpose, or an action that does not happen (“so that they know”, “she left without anyone seeing her”). It is the natural next step: the connector changes, but the subjunctive and the sequence of tenses work the same way.

Amparo Lozano has run the Santa Rosa public library for thirty-one years and retires this Friday. Her team is preparing a surprise farewell. Irene, who is organising it, has done this before: last year they played music in Fermín’s office so he wouldn’t hear anything, and carried everything up without him seeing them. Today you learn to state a purpose in past contexts and in formal and colloquial registers, and to say what does not happen or what you want to prevent.
A plan for Friday: the main verb looks forward, so the purpose clause takes the present subjunctive.
Everything happened and is over: a past main verb pulls the purpose clause into the imperfect subjunctive.
On Tuesday Irene hid the invitations so that Amparo wouldn’t see them.
Raúl, close the tribute programme so that Amparo doesn’t see it on the screen.
Is the main verb in a past tense or in the conditional? Then the purpose clause usually moves to the imperfect subjunctive, just as with quería que (class 130).
Don Julián took Amparo to the archive so that she wouldn’t go up to the hall.
We printed the programme in large type so that older guests could read it.
A past verb, but the goal is still open (tomorrow), so the present is possible here; «revisaras» would also be correct.
Are you writing a report, an application or a formal account? These connectors raise the register; the subject rule is the same as with para.
The association paid for the video so that the neighbourhood would keep a record of Amparo’s work (formal, written register).
We arrived two hours early in order to set up the hall: same subject, so the infinitive.
We have been saving since January with the farewell in mind: a goal further ahead that shapes what we do now.
In 2019 the library extended its opening hours so that students could prepare for their exams.
The team met on Monday in order to organise the tribute.
We opened a shared account with December’s party in mind.
Do you want to say what does not happen while something else does? Same subject: sin + infinitive. Another subject: sin que + subjunctive, never the indicative.
We prepared everything without Amparo finding out a thing.
Raúl carried the chairs up without making a sound: he carried, he made no noise.
Explain it to Beatriz tactfully, in a way that doesn’t offend her.
Are you doing something as a precaution, to avoid a risk? «No vaya a ser que» is like “in case” or “just in case”, but it names the danger you want to avoid. It is very common in speech.
Hide the cake in the kitchen, in case she sees it.
Switch your phone off during the surprise, in case it rings.
Raúl kept an eye on the stairs in case Amparo came up too early (past frame).
After «sin que», Spanish naturally uses negative words: «sin que nadie lo supiera» means that nobody knew. «Alguien» sounds odd here.
Irene left the office without saying anything to anyone.
They bought the present without Amparo suspecting anything.
Close the door to the hall, in case someone comes in.
We arranged the chairs in a semicircle so that everyone could see the screen: the way we did it, with that aim.
Amparo arrived early, so we had to improvise: a real result, not an aim.
Giving an order and then the purpose? In colloquial speech «que» + subjunctive after an imperative means “so that”. With the indicative, «que» gives a reason instead.
Come closer, so everyone can see you in the photo.
Hand me the list so I can check it before printing it.
Keep your voice down, Amparo is in the office: «que» + indicative gives the reason.
Put the microphone in the middle so that everyone can hear you.
The power went out during the video, so we played it twice.
Hurry, Amparo is already coming up the stairs.
Beatriz left the meeting without anyone thanking her.
Irene sent the emails from home so that Amparo wouldn’t see anything.
Irene, have you got a minute? It’s about Friday.
Shh… Come back here, so she can’t hear us. And shut the door, in case someone walks in.
Done. How do we manage it on Friday so that she doesn’t notice? Amparo notices everything.
At five, don Julián is going to ask her to help him with some boxes in the archive, so that she doesn’t go up to the hall until six.
And how do we carry the chairs up without her seeing us?
Up the back stairs. Last year, for Fermín’s retirement, that’s how we did it: we carried everything up without a sound and put the radio on in his office so he wouldn’t hear anything.
Clever! And how do we set out the chairs?
In a semicircle, so that everyone can see the screen. We’re showing a video with messages from long-time readers.
And who’s paying for the video? And the present?

In March we wrote to the Friends of the Library association so that they would pay for the video, and they agreed. And since January we’ve been saving a little every month with a view to buying her something special.
Great. By the way, Beatriz is a bit upset because she isn’t giving a speech.
Oh, right. You explain it to her, tactfully, without offending her. And on Friday come at four to help me with everything, OK?
Why is don Julián going to ask Amparo for help?
What did they do last year so that Fermín wouldn’t hear anything?
What does Raúl have to do about Beatriz?
Keep the invitations in your drawer so that Amparo doesn’t see them.
That year we gave him a trip so that he could visit his daughter in Oaxaca.
Tomorrow I’ll arrive at three in order to hang the decorations before the guests arrive.
Don Julián kept Amparo busy in the archive without her noticing anything odd.
Put the camera behind the books in case Amparo sees it as she comes in.
We prepared everything without her finding out.
Keep your voice down, in case Amparo hears us.
We wrote to them so that they would record a message.
Why does Irene send the audio message?
Why did don Julián take Amparo to the archive?
Why did Raúl stay on the stairs?
Why did they record the speech?
What does Irene want Mónica to do when she gets back?
one subject: the infinitive, in present and past alike
another subject: subjunctive, present or imperfect according to the main verb
what does not happen, or the risk you want to prevent: always subjunctive
the mood decides: subjunctive for an aim, indicative for a real result or a reason

Three questions: same subject? Use the infinitive. Another subject? Use que + subjunctive, with the main verb choosing vea or viera. Aim or fact? De manera que and que after an imperative take the subjunctive for an aim and the indicative for a result or a reason.
My grandmother always slipped me money without my parents knowing.
Write my number down on paper, in case your battery dies.
In 2020 the company shortened the working day so that employees could look after their children.
Run, the last bus is leaving.
I left the meeting without saying goodbye because I was in a real hurry.
Elena’s friends threw her a party for her fortieth birthday. Join the sentences or shift the time frame.

For strong students or spare time: after ir / venir, a purpose with another subject can also be «a que» + subjunctive; the past precaution is «no fuera a ser que»; and each connector has its own register.
Yesterday I came to the office for you to sign my contract, but you weren’t there.
We locked the hall in case anyone came in.
Official report: the timetable was reorganised with a view to helping staff balance work and family.
“He did it without anyone asking him”: what does it mean?

You can now say what something was done for and what people wanted to avoid. In class 141 you use the same imperfect subjunctive to describe how something is done by comparing it with something unreal: “as if nothing had happened”. It is the natural next step: from «sin que» and «de manera que», which already talk about manner, to imaginary comparisons.

Marina Robles is restoring her grandmother’s old house in the centre of Querétaro. Rodrigo Paz runs the building work and Julia Ferrer, the designer, chooses colours and materials. Some things are done the way Marina said, others will be done however she likes, and almost everything costs more than she thought. Today you learn to say how something is done and to compare reality with what you expected, what you imagine or what is not real.
Rodrigo painted the front the way Marina told him: the manner is a real, known instruction, so the indicative.
We’ll lay the tiles however you like: the manner is still open, any way Marina chooses, so the subjunctive.
Last week the builders laid the floor exactly as the plan showed.
Arrange the living-room furniture whatever way suits you best.
Use the indicative when the manner is real and identifiable: an instruction already given, a method you know, the way something usually happens.
We restored the beams the way the carpenter explained to us.
According to what Rodrigo told me, the kitchen will be ready in May.
They left the courtyard exactly as it was in Grandma’s day.
I always make coffee the way my grandmother did.
Use the subjunctive when the manner is not yet known or is left open: “whatever way…”, “depending on what…”. It is the same logic as relative clauses with an unknown antecedent.
Arrange the kitchen however you like.
We’ll change the design depending on what the architect tells us.
We’ll do the bathroom exactly as Julia draws it (she hasn’t drawn it yet).
Hang the pictures whichever way you think looks best.
You choose the window colour. We’ll paint them however you say.
Yesterday Julia put the lamp together exactly as the instructions said.
Rodrigo asked Marina to arrange the furniture however she preferred.

When the second part of a comparison is a clause with a verb (what you thought, expected, were told), Spanish uses de lo que, not que. Indicative for a real expectation or amount; subjunctive for an open or imagined one.
The kitchen is more expensive than I thought.
The builders work better than I expected.
Don’t buy more paint than you need (the amount isn’t known yet).
It’s going to look lovelier than you could ever imagine.
Two things are compared directly (this house, mine): más… que.
The comparison is with an idea expressed by a verb (how it looked): más… de lo que.
A compact, slightly formal option: more than planned, than expected, than necessary.
The final budget was much higher than we calculated in January.
Rodrigo is more patient than his business partner.
They haven’t measured the bathroom yet: don’t order more tiles than you’ll need.

In class 136 you saw como si with the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. Today you extend the idea: a comparison with something unreal can also use igual que si, lo mismo que si, tanto como si or más que si, always with the same subjunctive tenses.
The second term is a supposition that is not true. Imperfect subjunctive for a situation imagined at the same time; pluperfect subjunctive for one imagined before.
Rodrigo looks after the house just as if it were his own.
After carrying out all the old furniture, Marina was as tired as if she had run a marathon.
When she saw the finished kitchen, she was more moved than if someone had given her a car.
Rodrigo told her about the burst pipe as if nothing had happened.
The neighbour gives the builders orders just as if she were the owner.
Marina was as happy as if she had won the lottery.
In the end, the paint cost less than planned.
Place the lamps depending on what the light in each room is like.
Come in, Marina. Look at the beams: we cleaned them and left them exactly as they were.
How lovely! They look better than I expected. And the kitchen?
That’s the tricky part. When we opened the wall we found an old pipe, so the kitchen is going to cost more than we worked out in January.
How much more? I don’t want to spend more money than I have.
About twenty thousand pesos. Still, we changed it in a single day, without the neighbours being left without water.
Thank goodness. And the windows? I still don’t know what colour to paint them.
We’ll paint them however you prefer. And we’ll lay the courtyard floor according to what Julia decides: she has the samples.
According to my mother, the windows used to be green. I’d like them to look just as if nobody had ever touched them.
Old green, then. And don’t worry about the dust: we clean everything the way the restorer showed us.
Thank you, Rodrigo. You look after this house as if it were yours.
It reminds me of my grandparents’ house. You’ll see: it’s going to look lovelier than you can possibly imagine.
Why is the kitchen going to cost more?
Who decides on the courtyard floor?
How does Marina want the windows to look?
Put the lamps in exactly as the plan I left on the table shows.
For the bathroom, choose the washbasin however you see fit: I trust your taste.
Today we finished the roof earlier than planned.
The neighbour talks about the work as if she were paying the bills.
Rodrigo had told Marina to arrange the furniture however she wanted.
Do it however you think best.
The building work is more expensive than I thought.
They left it exactly as it was.
He reports on the week and leaves her a decision to make.
How did the courtyard floor turn out?
Why are they going to finish later?
What does Rodrigo say about the window colour?
How does the neighbour behave, according to Rodrigo?
a real, known manner or source of information: indicative
an open, future or “any” manner: subjunctive (imperfect in a past frame); sin que always subjunctive
de lo que before a clause; indicative for a real expectation, subjunctive for an open or imagined amount
comparison with something untrue: imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, never indicative or conditional

Ask whether the manner or amount already exists: then the indicative. If it is open or imagined: the subjunctive. If you compare with something unreal: imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. And before a verb, never “más que pensaba”: always más de lo que pensaba.
You can pay whichever way is easiest for you: by card or in cash.
The exam was much easier than we had been told.
My brother hugged me as if he hadn’t seen me for years.
I made the soup exactly as my mother explained on the phone.
My daughter already reads faster than I do.
Teresa and Hugo held a small wedding in some friends’ garden. Now Teresa says how it went. Use the structure each sentence asks for.
For strong students or spare time: other ways to compare with the unreal depending on register, and two nuances of comparatives with amounts.
A colloquial exclamation: “Anyone would think this was a hotel!”
Cual si is a literary equivalent of como si.
No… más que means “only”; no… más de sets an upper limit.
A formal, hypothetical expectation: “than one might expect”.

You can now say how something is done and compare with what you expected or imagined. In class 142 you return to relative clauses, now with a preposition in front: “the architect I told you about”, “the builder I work with”. It is the natural next step: de lo que and del que are already relatives inside a comparison; now you learn to link ideas precisely with preposition + relative.

Valdelirio, a town in Mexico, is preparing the tenth edition of its literature festival. Lorena, the coordinator, writes the printed programme; Héctor, a volunteer, handles social media and a radio spot. Lorena needs sentences that introduce each guest and, in the same breath, something that belongs to them. Today you learn «cuyo», the Spanish «whose».
Two separate sentences: the possessive «sus» says whose books they are. Perfectly natural, especially in speech.
«Cuyos» links the two ideas and takes the place of «sus»: it is a relative and a possessive at the same time, like English «whose».
Rubén is a poet whose first book sold out in a month.
What idea does «cuyo» always express?
«Cuyo» agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows it (the thing possessed), never with the possessor. English «whose» never changes, so this is the point to watch.
Feminine possessor, masculine possessed noun: «cuyo» follows «padre».
A town whose streets fill with books in October: possession also works with places and things.
Plural possessor, singular possessed noun: «cuyo», not «cuyos».
Masculine plural possessor, feminine singular noun: «cuya».
Nuria is an illustrator whose drawings every child in town knows.
Rubén is a poet whose voice the whole town recognises on the radio.
The Ruiz sisters, whose bookshop opened in 1980, will sell books in the square.
If the original sentence has a preposition (in the square, for the project, about the book), it moves to the front of the whole «cuyo + noun» group, just as with «en el que» or «con quien».
Valdelirio is the town in whose square the fair is held: the fair is held IN the square.
Nuria works FOR the publisher’s catalogue.
We talked ABOUT her novels yesterday.
Personal «a»: I met his daughter, so «a cuya hija».
It is the school with whose teachers he learned to read.
It is the town through whose streets he walks every afternoon.
Amparo is the author whose latest novel they talked about on the radio.
Programmes, press, reports, speeches: «cuyo» is what readers expect. Commas mark an explanatory clause, as in English.
In everyday conversation «cuyo» is rare: people usually split the idea into two sentences with «su».
«Que su» is heard in informal speech in many places, but the norm rejects it: avoid it, especially in writing.

The Spanish Royal Academy and the Association of Academies advise against «que su» instead of «cuyo». It is common in casual speech, but it sounds careless in public or written language. Speaking, you have plenty of correct options; in formal writing, use «cuyo».
Héctor texts a friend: tomorrow an author is coming whose novels I have all read.
Which sentence suits the printed programme best?
Chatting with friends: I live in a house with a huge patio.
Neutral: fine in speech and in writing.
A formal written variant you met in class 112: press releases, reports, academic texts. In conversation it sounds stiff.
Whose scarf is this? Someone left it on the chair.
Lorena: I don’t know whose car that is in front of the library.
Press release: a 1910 letter will be shown, whose addressee is unknown.
It is the bookshop whose owner organises the festival.
They are the neighbours whose children we invited to the workshop.
Lorena, I’ve read the draft. I love how you introduce Amparo: “a novelist whose stories are read all over the world.”
Thanks. It’s a printed text and I wanted a careful tone. How would you put it on social media?
More direct: “Amparo Ledesma is coming, an author I’ve read every single novel by.”
Perfect for social media. And Rubén’s profile? I wrote: “the poet of whose first book three editions sold out.”
It’s clear, but on the radio I’d say: “Rubén’s coming, that his first book sold out three times.”
You hear that a lot, but it isn’t standard, and on air it sounds sloppy. If you don’t want «cuyo», use two sentences: “Rubén Echeverría is coming. His first book sold out three times.”
OK, two sentences. And the publisher? You wrote “Marea Alta, for whose catalogue Nuria works.”
Yes, Nuria illustrates all their children’s books. Does it sound odd to you?
A little. Shouldn’t it be «cuya», since «editorial» is feminine?
No, «cuyo» looks forward: it agrees with «catálogo». Same as in “the Plaza de la Fuente, under whose arcades we’ll set up the bookstalls.”
Got it. Last question: in the press release you wrote “a manuscript of which only two copies survive.” Is that the same thing?
It’s like «del que», only more formal. It works in a press release; in a message to a friend it would sound really odd.
What does Lorena suggest for the radio if Héctor doesn’t want to use «cuyo»?
Why does Lorena write «para cuyo catálogo»?
What does Lorena think of «del cual»?
Héctor has collected sentences from several drafts. Which are correct and formal, which are correct and conversational, and which are not standard Spanish?
“Inés Carrasco, whose travel pieces a Guadalajara paper runs every week, will sign books on Saturday.”
“The old station, on whose platforms the second-hand book market will be set up, opens at ten.”
“Thanks to the Ortega family, without whose support this festival would not exist.”
“Tomorrow I’m meeting Amparo, the writer whose novel I lent you.”
“Excuse me, do you know whose backpack this is?”
She is a novelist whose characters seem real.
We visited the town in whose square Rubén gave a reading.
He is an author I know every book by: the spoken alternative.
What is the radio piece about?
What will there be under the arcades of the square?
What do we learn about Rubén’s first book?
Why do so many local children know Nuria?
What links the publisher to Valdelirio?
«Cuyo» agrees with the possessed noun that follows it, never with the possessor; no article after it
The preposition the verb needs goes in front of the «cuyo» group
In conversation people rephrase; «que su» is common but non-standard
«Del cual» is a formal variant of «del que»; to ask who owns something, use «de quién»

Before you write «cuyo», look at the noun that follows (it decides the form), find the preposition in the original sentence, and think about register: «cuyo» in careful texts, something simpler in conversation.
It is a restaurant whose chef won a national award.
I met a painter whose works are shown in three museums.
She is the teacher thanks to whose advice I passed the exam.
Whose keys are these? — I think they’re Marta’s.
Report: the committee reviewed the contract, two of whose clauses will be amended.
A regional museum in Zacatecas. Gabriela Sosa, a curator, is writing the labels for a new room. She has her ideas in separate sentences and needs to join them in careful written Spanish.

Three more uses in written Spanish. «En cuyo caso» is a fixed formula meaning «in which case». Before two coordinated nouns, «cuyo» agrees with the first one. And outside fixed formulas like that one, «cuyo» always expresses possession or belonging; when there is no possession, use another relative (el cual, que).
Notice: entry is free until the venue is full, in which case the doors will close.
Contract: the author, whose rights and obligations are set out in the annex, signs this document.
Which sentence is correct?
Academic text: three novels are analysed, whose authors were born in the same decade.

You can now link a noun to what belongs to it with «cuyo», and you know «del cual» as a formal variant. The natural next step is relatives that refer not to a noun but to a whole idea: «lo cual», «lo que», «aquello que».

Elena and Raúl Duarte are siblings who run Casa Robledal, a rural guesthouse in the sierra de Albarracín. This weekend they hosted a group of twenty hikers, and on Saturday morning the boiler broke down. In class 113 you used lo que for a thing with no name. Today you go further: lo que and lo cual can also refer back to a whole sentence, like “and that”, the way English uses “which” after a comma.
What guests value most is the silence: lo que contains its own antecedent and means “the thing that”.
The boiler broke down, which left us without hot water: here lo que sums up the whole previous clause.
What complicated dinner? After the comma, lo que points back to the whole event.
Raúl made what the hikers asked for.
After a full statement, a comma plus lo que or lo cual adds a comment or a consequence about the whole fact, much like English “which” in “He was late, which annoyed us”.
The technician didn’t come until midday, which forced us to heat water in pots.
Gonzalo didn’t complain once, which says a lot about him.
The house is forty minutes from the village, which some people see as an advantage.
It rained all night, which left the paths full of mud.
We replaced the boiler, which was twenty years old.

The neuter relative can also follow a preposition. This lets you chain consequences and reactions without starting a new sentence. The preposition depends on the meaning or on the verb that follows (responder a, avisar de).
When there is no antecedent and the verb needs a preposition (estar de acuerdo con, hablar de, pensar en), the preposition goes in front of lo que. Lo cual is impossible here.
Raúl doesn’t agree with what the review says.
That’s exactly what I wanted to talk to you about.
It was very windy at the top, so the group came back earlier than planned.
Elena asked Gonzalo whether they would come back, to which he replied yes.
With indicative, lo que refers to something specific and known; with subjunctive, it means “whatever”: anything at all, not yet decided. This is the same choice you made with relatives in class 100.
For breakfast, order whatever you like: there’s bread, fruit and eggs.
Raúl bought everything Gonzalo asked him for.
Whatever you decide about the boiler will be fine with me.
Lo + adjective or adverb + que + verb stresses the degree, like English “how tired they were”. Unlike lo bueno, here the adjective agrees with the noun it describes.
You can’t imagine how tired the hikers were when they arrived.
I was surprised by how well everyone took it.
You’ll see how lovely the sierra looks in October.
The good thing is that dinner turned out perfectly: lo bueno names an aspect and never changes form.
You’ve no idea how good the migas were: here the adjective agrees with the noun because it describes it.
When you finish the hike, do whatever you feel like: pool, nap or nothing.
You’ve no idea how worried Elena was on Saturday.
Aquello que / aquello de point to an idea that is distant in time or memory, or sound more formal than lo que. Eso de que + a statement quotes a claim, often with some doubt or irony.
What the technician told us two years ago was true.
You know, that old saying: buy cheap, buy twice.
This idea that there’s nothing to do in the sierra is a cliché.
Do you remember that idea of selling the house? Good thing we didn’t.
I don’t buy this idea that customers only read the bad reviews.
What I liked most about the weekend was Saturday’s dinner.
Gonzalo offered to do the washing-up, which we didn’t expect at all.
Well, they’ve gone. What a weekend! On Saturday the boiler broke down, which left us without hot water just as they were coming back from the hike.
And the technician wasn’t answering the phone, so we had to heat water in pots for twenty people.
You’ve no idea how stressed I got. I thought they were going to leave for somewhere else.
Well, you saw how well they took it. Gonzalo said he’d been through worse in the mountains.
Yes, but Marta Iglesias has posted a three-star review, which brings our average down quite a bit.
And what does she say? That the house is ugly?
No, that the house is lovely and dinner was delicious, but that on Saturday there was no hot water until eleven, so she couldn’t shower before leaving.
She has a point. Remember that plan to replace the boiler before winter? We said it two years ago.
And what the technician told us back then: that its days were numbered. We didn’t listen.
Right, I’ll answer the review. I’ll apologise, explain everything that happened and offer her a discount.
Good. And don’t buy the idea that one bad review sinks a business: people read the replies too.
I know. You deal with the quotes for the boiler and choose whatever you like, as long as it’s reliable. And that’s exactly what I wanted to talk to you about: we’re going to need a loan.
Why did they have to heat water in pots?
What does Marta criticise in her review?
What do the siblings have to do now?
Saturday’s hike lasted nine hours, so the hikers arrived exhausted.
Gonzalo asked to have dinner at nine, which suited us perfectly.
Help yourself to whatever you like from the fridge by the entrance.
Raúl always remembers that idea of opening a restaurant in the house, though they never did.
The boiler broke down, which worried us.
You’ve no idea how hard it is to find a technician.
Choose whatever you like from the menu.
It rained all night, so we cancelled the hike.
The review issue has been sorted out; now they need to decide on the new boiler.
What did Marta do after reading Elena’s reply?
Why does the boiler have to be replaced before December?
Why isn’t Elena convinced by the cheapest quote?
What does Elena ask Raúl to do?
comments on or draws a consequence from the whole previous clause; always after a comma
the thing that / whatever; lo cual is impossible here
ideas distant in time, formal, or quoted with some doubt
stresses degree; unlike lo bueno, the adjective agrees with its noun

Ask what “lo” points to. Everything you have just said? Comma + lo que / lo cual (or with a preposition: por lo que, con lo cual). Nothing before? Only lo que (“Pide lo que quieras”). A distant or quoted idea? Aquello que / aquello de / eso de que. Stressing how much? Lo + adjective + que, with agreement.
The train left an hour late, so I was late for the interview.
I haven’t told anyone what you told me yesterday.
They’ve put our rent up without warning, which we think is outrageous.
What photos! I love seeing how grown-up your kids are.
I don’t buy this idea that afternoon coffee keeps everyone awake.
Irene has just moved into a shared flat and is telling a friend about it. Help her join her sentences and stress what matters.

An extra step, if you have time. Lo que also appears in comparisons with a clause (“It costs more than we expected”), in formal writing to express purpose (“…, para lo cual necesitamos…”) and in exclamations of complaint: “¡Con lo que hemos trabajado!” = after all the work we’ve put in.
The new boiler costs more than we expected.
We want to replace the boiler before December, for which we have applied for a loan.
What does Elena mean?
In a set of rules: guests may request whatever they consider necessary at reception.

You can now refer back to whole facts (“…, lo cual nos dejó sin agua”), talk about unnamed ideas (“Pide lo que quieras”) and distant ones (“aquello de…”). In class 145 you take “lo que + subjunctive” further: cualquiera que and dondequiera que, for people and places you do not know. It is the natural next step: from “do whatever you like” to “wherever you go” and “whoever comes”.

Rocío Medina coordinates a volunteer tree-planting day in the hills. At the registration table, Lidia has put up a sign: “Anyone who comes must register.” Rocío does not know who will come: it could be anyone. Today you learn to talk about people, places and things you cannot identify, and to say that something holds whatever happens.
Rocío can see him: a real, identified person, so the relative clause is in the indicative.
Nobody knows who will come: the sign is about any person at all, so the verb is in the subjunctive.
The sentence covers every possible person, not one specific person.
Rocío points at someone she can see, so the indicative is needed.
These words refer to any person, place or thing whatsoever. When the clause looks ahead (rules, plans, instructions, possibilities), the verb goes in the subjunctive.
Anyone who has gloves can start digging.
Any tree you plant needs water during the first month.
Whoever has taken my spade, please give it back to me.
Wherever you are, send me your location if you get lost.
Whoever has taken my gloves, please give them back.
Why is it “cualquier” and not “cualquiera” here?

Lo que sea, donde sea, cuando sea, quien sea and como sea are everyday ways of saying anything, anywhere, any time, anyone, anyhow. They are much more common in speech than quienquiera or dondequiera.
I’ll help with anything at all: carrying plants, watering, digging.
Call me any time; my phone is on.
Leave your rucksack wherever you like: nobody will touch it.
Repeating the same subjunctive verb around a relative word means “no matter what / where / how”: whatever the option, the main sentence still holds. It works like “aunque + subjunctive”.
Whatever happens, we start at nine.
Whatever the forecast says, we are going up the hill.
Wherever you go, don’t leave the group.
Whatever the weather, the day goes ahead.

With two alternatives Spanish uses a similar pattern: “rain or shine, we leave”, “like it or not, you have to sign”. With “cual” the verb and the pronoun agree in number: sea cual sea el resultado, sean cuales sean los resultados.
Whatever you say to him, Ignacio won’t change his mind.
I can help with anything: carrying, watering or planting.
What does “vayas donde vayas” mean?
The person exists and you know who she is: indicative.
You are looking for someone, but you do not know whether such a person exists.
You deny that such a person exists: subjunctive.
Nobody in the association knows how to prune holm oaks.
Ignacio hasn’t decided yet: tomorrow we will plant wherever he tells us.
Yesterday we planted where Ignacio told us.
One way or another, tomorrow we plant the hundred trees.
A group is coming from Ireland: we need a volunteer who speaks English.
Hi, Rocío. I’m Gabriel, the new one. Lidia told me that anyone coming for the first time has to talk to you.
Welcome! First you sign at her table, then we give you gloves and a hoe. Whatever tool you use, leave it in the boxes by the entrance when you finish.
And where are we going to plant? Is there a marked area?
We’ll plant wherever Ignacio, the forest ranger, tells us. He decides every morning, depending on the state of the soil.
I’ve heard he is very strict.
He is, but nobody knows these hills like he does. Whatever he says, do as he tells you.
Got it. By the way, the forecast says it may rain in the afternoon. Is the day called off?
No: whatever happens, we start at nine. Besides, with a bit of rain the soil is softer.
Great. And is there anyone who could give me a lift back to town? I came by bus.
Lidia, who lives in the centre, leaves at four. Anything you need, just tell her or me.
Thanks. And if needed, I’ll help with anything: carrying seedlings, watering…
Perfect. One thing, though: wherever you go, always take water and your whistle. The weather changes very quickly up here.
Who decides where they plant?
What happens if it rains?
How will Gabriel get back to town?
Any volunteer who arrives after nine must wait at the table.
Leave your rucksack wherever you like; we’ll fetch it later.
I don’t know anyone who plants as fast as she does.
Whatever you see, don’t pull up any small plants.
Whatever the weather, Rocío was always the first to arrive.
Nobody knows the hills better.
Anyone who arrives late must let Lidia know.
She goes through the rules and practical arrangements for the next day.
What must first-timers do?
What about the rain?
Why will they plant wherever Ignacio says this time?
What does Rocío need?
Rocío addresses the whole group with ustedes, as is normal throughout Latin America. In Spain, among friends, people would use vosotros.
any person, place or thing, not identified: subjunctive
no matter what, where or how: the main sentence still holds
it does not exist, or you do not know if it exists: subjunctive
the speaker knows exactly who or what: indicative

Always ask: can I identify it, or could it be anyone or anything? Anyone, not yet known, sought or non-existent → subjunctive. Real and known → indicative. In the repeated pattern, the same subjunctive verb twice. And remember: cualquier before a noun, cualquiera on its own.
“Whatever you do, do it well,” my grandmother used to say.
Nobody in my office knows how to fix the printer.
The technician who came yesterday fixed it in five minutes.
Anyone who wants to sign up can do so online.
When I was little, wherever I went, my dog followed me.
Teresa is organising a free concert in a park and is writing the rules for the audience and the volunteers. Help her write them with today’s structures.
For strong students or spare time: formal forms you will meet in official texts, and a case where the indicative is also possible.
Official notice: whatever the reasons, applications must be submitted by the 30th.
In formal writing, “comoquiera que” can mean “since, given that”.
Wherever she went, people recognised her: a real, habitual past.
Among friends, which sentence sounds most natural?

You can now talk about what is not yet known: “we’ll do whatever Ignacio says”, “whatever he says, listen to him”. In class 146 you take the next step: reporting what someone actually said, asked or ordered. It is the natural progression from possible words to another person’s real words.

Words like hoy, mañana, aquí, este, venir and traer point to the speaker’s own time and place (linguists call them deictic words). When Pablo reports Lucía’s call two days later and from another city, he has to re-aim each of them from where he stands.
Lucía speaks from her Tuesday in Oaxaca: “tomorrow” is Wednesday and “here” is Oaxaca.
On Thursday, Lucía’s “tomorrow” (Wednesday) has become “yesterday”, her “Friday” is now “tomorrow”, and Oaxaca is “there”, so coming becomes going.
Why does Pablo turn “mañana” into “ayer”?
Why does Pablo say “go there” and not “come here”?
When did the other person speak, and when are you reporting it?
A month later, “today” must be anchored to that day: ese día.
Pasado mañana becomes “two days later” once the date is far behind.
“Now” becomes “at that moment” or “then”: the situation belongs to the past.
“Next week” becomes “the following week” when seen from much later.
The same “mañana” can end up as mañana, hoy, ayer or al día siguiente, depending on when you report it. Don’t convert words mechanically: work out which day it was and name it from your own today.
Lucía said they were filming at the workshop today.
Sonia told me that she lived in Puebla at the time.
Are you in the place that was being talked about?
From Mexico City, Oaxaca is “there”.
This room becomes that room once you are no longer in it.
Aquel adds distance in time: it suits memories.

Both allí and allá are correct everywhere. In much of Latin America allá is the usual choice in speech; in Spain allí is more common for a specific place, while allá tends to suggest direction or vaguer distance. Ahí points to a place near your listener or just mentioned.
Raúl says it is raining a lot there.
She told me that loom belonged to her grandmother.
Who spoke, to whom, and who are you telling?
Mi becomes su; add “la de ella” if su could be misread.
Te, said to you, becomes me when you report it.
Talking to Sonia herself, “her idea” becomes “your idea”.
Does the movement go towards where you are now?
Lucía is at the destination, so she uses venir and traer.
Pablo is not there yet: ir and llevar.
Once Pablo is in Oaxaca, the destination is “here” again: venir and traer.
English “I’m coming” moves towards the listener, but Spanish normally uses ir for that: “¡Ya voy!”. In many places “ya vengo” means “I’ll be right back”.
Sonia asked me to take her a rug.
She said she would wait for me in the square.
Raúl asked if he should bring us the cables.
Same day, same place: keep hoy and aquí. Shifting them would sound as if Sonia meant another day and another place.
Different day, different place: now the shift is needed.
Which version fits now, in the same room?
Lucía told us to come whenever we wanted.
She told me they were going to the concert that night.
Have you heard from Lucía? I’ve been texting her since Tuesday and she doesn’t answer.
She called me on Tuesday night. She said they had filmed at the market that day and that the next day it was the weaving workshop’s turn.
So, yesterday. And how are things over there?
Fine, but she said it was terribly hot there and that at that moment they were in a village with almost no signal.
That’s why she isn’t answering. And what does she want us to do?
She asked us to go there on Friday, that is, tomorrow, and to take the new batteries.
Are they for Raúl’s camera?
No, for hers. She said her big camera hadn’t been charging properly since Monday.
Got it. And where are we meeting?
She said she’d wait for us at that café on the square, the one with the terrace. Oh, and she asked me to tell you that your market idea works brilliantly.
Great! And she hasn’t written to you since then?
Yes, a little while ago. She says they finally have a signal today and that she’ll see us in the square tomorrow.
Why wasn’t Lucía answering Sonia’s messages?
When are Pablo and Sonia travelling to Oaxaca?
Who are the new batteries for?
Doña Elvira told me that room was the oldest one.
Raúl said he would arrive in Oaxaca two days later.
Lucía asked me to go and take the spare microphone.
Lucía asked me to come and bring the spare microphone.
Sonia says she can’t talk now and will call me this afternoon.
Doña Elvira told us they were opening the museum the following week.
She said she would wait for us there the next day.
He asked me to take the batteries to Oaxaca.
She explained that at that moment they had no signal.
Why does Lucía send the voice message?
Why didn’t they film the archive on Wednesday?
When does the rug fair start?
What does Pablo have to do?
Why does Lucía say “come” and “bring” at the end?
Recalculate from your own day; naming the actual day is clearest.
If you are no longer there, that place is now far from you.
Adjust every pronoun and possessive to the new conversation.
If you are at the destination, venir and traer stay.

Don’t translate words: recalculate references. Ask yourself which day that “today” is for you, whether you are in that “here”, and who “you” is now. Same day and same place? Change nothing: over-shifting is just as confusing.
He said he wasn’t coming to the office on Tuesday.
She says everything is really expensive there.
He said he would bring me the ladder on Saturday.
Lucía told me she lived in that neighbourhood at the time.
Sonia said she would send me the script this afternoon.
A month ago your friend Valeria called you from Cartagena to invite you to her wedding. Today, in your own city, you tell your partner about the call: recalculate time, place, people and movement.

Chronicles, biographies and news reports tell events from far away in time. Besides ese día and al día siguiente, they often use la víspera (the day before, especially before a special date), a la mañana siguiente (the next morning), dos días más tarde, en aquel momento and en aquel entonces (back then).
Chronicle: the mayor arrived the day before the fair.
Biography: back then nobody knew her work.

You can now report messages from another day and another place with the references correctly adjusted. Class 148 takes you further into the language of chronicles and news: the passive with ser + participle (“the archive was opened the next day”), which puts the focus on what happened rather than on who did it. It is the natural next step, because informative texts combine both tools.

Valparaíso, Chile. In the newsroom of El Mirador, a local digital paper, the editor, a new reporter and the copy editor are preparing Monday’s edition. The big story: after eight months of works, the Las Gaviotas funicular is running again. The same fact appears in four different texts, and each one tells it differently.
Which version names the doer? Only the ser passive includes an agent with por.
In everyday speech, a 3rd person plural verb with no subject means “someone”, not a specific group.

Spanish hides the doer when it is unknown, obvious, irrelevant or “people in general”. When the doer is known and relevant, the active is the most direct choice; ser + participle keeps the thing as the topic and still names the doer, typically in writing.
Active: the town council is the topic and the doer.
Ser passive: the funicular is the topic; the doer comes at the end, as new information.
Passive se: what was done matters; the workers are obvious.
Impersonal se: anyone, people in general.
In a recipe the doer is irrelevant, so passive se is the natural form.
When the doer is the news, name it: ser + participle + por, or the active.
Passive se: the noun is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it, before or after the verb. This includes people “in general”, with no personal a (se necesitan guías).
Rooms to rent for students. (Chile: pieza = room, arrendar = to rent.)
The old photographs will be digitised this month.
Guides with English needed for the summer: any guides, so no a.

Impersonal se: there is no subject at all, so the verb is always 3rd person singular. This happens with intransitive verbs, with ser and estar, with personal a + people, and with an infinitive or a que-clause.
A hundred residents were interviewed: personal a, so singular.
We are looking for the specific residents who worked there.
When you’re a journalist, you never fully switch off.
Personal a means there is no subject: singular verb.
Any photographers, no personal a: they are the subject, so plural.

The ser passive belongs to writing: news, reports, history. The participle agrees with the subject. It allows por + agent. In the present tense, for habits or ongoing actions, it sounds forced, and in conversation people prefer the active or se.
The works were funded with regional money.
Typical of historical writing.
In casual speech the 3rd person plural active is natural; the ser passive sounds like a news report.
With an agent in formal writing: ser + participle agreeing with the subject.

Signs in many areas, in Spain and Latin America, show a singular verb with a plural noun, because writers feel it as impersonal. It is common, but the academic norm recommends agreement, and careful writing always uses it.
The noun is the subject: plural agreement, as the norm recommends.
Personal a → impersonal se, singular.
Ignacio, I read your piece on the funicular. It’s well written, but the headline sounds like corner-shop chat.
The thing is, I wasn’t sure who had done it. The town council or the construction company?
The council paid for it, and that’s news. In the first paragraph write that it was reopened by the council after eight months of works.
And for the headline, something short. The who goes in the article.
Great. Another question: in the feature I wrote “Se entrevistaron a cien vecinos”. Is that right?
Nearly. With that a, the verb doesn’t agree. But in your archive notice, “old photographs wanted”, the plural is perfect.
And highlight the conclusion: almost everyone says life on the hill is better since the funicular started running.
Noted. This one came in for the classifieds. Shall I publish it as it is?
That’s how many signs put it, but in the paper we correct it. The norm recommends agreement.
And your grandmother’s recipe, Rosa? Shall I write it with usted commands?
Better with se, as in cookbooks.
One last thing: no “se reabrió por la municipalidad”. If you want the who, use the active, and that’s it.
Why doesn’t Valentina like the headline? It sounds too colloquial.
What is the conclusion of the survey feature?
How does Rosa want the recipe written?
Headlines need brevity: passive se without an agent.
The doer must appear: ser passive with por.
Recipes use passive se, agreeing with the noun.
Personal a plus a que-clause: impersonal singular.
Casual speech: the 3rd person plural active.
Old photographs of the funicular wanted.
A hundred residents of the hill were interviewed.
The viewpoint was restored by the town council.
What does the bulletin contain?
Who reopened the funicular?
What was done during the works?
How many people were interviewed for the feature?
What does the paper ask listeners for?
Active: the doer matters; in speech, the 3rd person plural means “someone”.
Ser passive: written, formal; it can name the doer with por.
Passive se: the verb agrees with the noun; no agent with por.
Impersonal se: always singular, never plural with personal a.
Three questions: does the doer matter? Is there a noun without personal a? Is there nothing to agree with? Then choose by text type.
“Red flags are put up on the region’s beaches when the sea is rough.”
“Forty families from the port were interviewed for the study.”
“When you’re young, everything seems possible.”
Report: “The agreement was signed by both unions.”
Careful notice: “Flats with parking to rent.”
Cartagena, Colombia. Lucía Méndez is writing a history museum’s annual report. Her colleague’s notes are written with “we”, but the report must be impersonal.

Three details of official texts: se les + verb when addressing people; modal + infinitive + plural noun, where agreement is preferred in careful writing although the singular is also found; and por phrases that express manner, not a doer, which are fine with se.
Notice: “Passengers are informed that the funicular will close at eleven.”
With a modal + infinitive + plural noun, careful writing prefers agreement.
Por unanimidad expresses manner, not a doer, so it is fine with se.
Passive se hides who made the mistakes: the topic of the next class.

You can now choose between naming the doer and hiding it depending on the text. The natural next step is the se that presents events as accidents and softens responsibility: “the glass broke on me”, “we forgot”.

Spanish has three ways to tell the same mishap: you can say you did it, say it happened to you, or say it simply happened. The choice is not only grammatical: it shows how much responsibility you take.
Camilo is the subject: he presents himself as the one who did it, which can even suggest he did it on purpose.
The tray is the subject and Camilo is the person it happened to: he was involved, but it was not intentional.
No person appears at all: just the event. Useful for neutral facts, but it can sound like hiding.
Which version says it was accidental but still shows Camilo was involved?
In «Se me cayó la bandeja», what is the subject of the verb?
Ask what broke, fell or was forgotten: that thing is the subject, so the verb agrees with it, not with the person. The pronoun says who it happened to.
Cables is plural, so the verb is plural. Felipe appears twice: a Felipe and le.
One thing ran out (el hielo): singular. Nos says it happened to the team.
Les for the waiters (mozos, the usual word in Peru), plural verb for the napkins.
With an infinitive (mandar), the verb stays singular.
Te: it happened to you. Telling someone they dropped something is a typical use.
Sorry, I left the batteries in the storeroom.
I forgot to confirm the time with the DJ.
Camilo broke two glasses (by accident).
The pronoun already tells you whose thing it is, so Spanish uses the article: se me rompió el celular means my phone. Adding mi sounds redundant.
My phone broke just before the event: el, not mi.
Natalia’s dress got a red wine stain: le already says it is hers.

For a device that stops working, regions prefer different verbs (malograrse in Peru, dañarse in Colombia and Venezuela, descomponerse in Mexico and Central America, estropearse in Spain), all with the same structure. Se me quedó for leaving something behind is used everywhere.
I lost my wallet on the bus.
In the meeting, a solution for the ice occurred to me.

The accidental se presents what happened as unintended. That makes excuses and apologies sound kinder, but if the problem came from a decision or real carelessness, it can sound like avoiding the blame.
Accidental se + apology + repair: the usual professional formula.
The shortage came from a decision (how much to order), so the team owns it.
Without any person, the speaker disappears from the story: in this context it sounds like hiding.
The speaker is the subject: the most direct way to admit it.
Still the speaker as subject, and very common in conversation. Note the de.
The birthday is the subject, as if it slipped out of my head: the softest version.

The structure only works with verbs for things that can happen on their own (break, fall, get lost, get deleted, run out). Verbs that need someone acting, like escribir or mandar, cannot be used this way: say escribí mal or mandé.
Camilo chose not to order more ice to save money. What should he say?
The guests left their coats in the cloakroom.
Well, the client was happy, but I want to go over what went wrong. Felipe, what happened with the microphones?
It was my fault. I left the cables in the storeroom and had to go back by taxi.
And the playlist? The DJ says he never got it.
That one got deleted from my phone, I don’t know how. But Natalia sorted it out.
Yes, I had the idea of using the playlist from last week’s wedding. Nobody noticed a thing.
Good thinking. Camilo, what about the glasses?
One of the waiters dropped a tray next to the stage. Six of the hotel’s glasses broke.
And the ice? At eleven people were asking for it and there wasn’t any.
Well, we ran out. These things happen.
No, Camilo, that didn’t just “happen”. We ordered half of what we needed. In the email to the client we’ll say exactly that.
Fair enough. And I have a confession: I let slip the surprise video in front of the manager.
Natalia! Luckily he forgot about it straight away: when he saw the video, he was just as moved.
What problem did Felipe have with the microphones?
Why doesn’t Paula accept «se nos acabó el hielo»?
What did Natalia do by accident?
Last night I locked my keys in the car.
The guests forgot the time of the last bus.
Sorry, I forgot to send you the quote.
Excuse me, did you drop something?
During dinner I came up with two ideas for the next event.
We were chatting and the empanadas burned in the oven.
Camilo dropped the tray.
We ran out of napkins at ten.
I forgot to call the supplier.
Why is Paula calling?
Why did the manager’s speech start late?
What happens about the broken glasses?
How does Paula present the ice problem?
What idea did Natalia have?
The thing is the subject: one thing or an infinitive takes a singular verb, several things a plural one.
Le stays even with a + person, and the pronoun already shows whose thing it is.
For decisions and clear carelessness, own it with an active verb.
Just the event: fine for reporting, evasive if you did it.

First the form: the verb agrees with the thing. Then the intention: the accidental se softens blame but does not erase it. Use it for genuine accidents, add an apology and a fix, and own your decisions with an active verb.
Sorry, I left the photocopies in the printer.
My neighbours’ cat got out and we looked for it all afternoon.
Which answer sounds professional?
How was the move? Fine, although we lost two boxes of books.
Which version takes the most responsibility?
You spent a weekend in a holiday flat in Cusco. Before leaving, you write a note to the owner about what happened: use the accidental se for real accidents.

The same pattern appears in very common set phrases: se me hizo tarde (I lost track of time), se me pasó (it slipped my mind), se me fue la mano (I overdid it), and the colloquial se me fue el santo al cielo (I completely forgot what I was doing). In formal writing, a noun phrase such as por un descuido nuestro often sounds more professional.
The soup is far too salty: I overdid the salt.
Sorry I’m late, I was reading and lost track of time.
Formal email: through an oversight on our part, we didn’t send you the invoice on time.

You can now tell mishaps with se me olvidó and know when to own them with olvidé or me olvidé de. That de is no accident: many verbs require a fixed preposition (olvidarse de, confiar en, depender de). Class 151 works on those verbs, the natural next step for precise apologies and explanations.

Guadalajara, Estudio Cobalto, a small architecture firm. Its director, Irene Garza, has just turned down the biggest contract of the year: a hotel by Lake Chapala. On Friday the architects Rodrigo and Paula talk about nothing else. Today you learn to put a fact at the start of a sentence in order to comment on it.
New information, simply stated: indicative.
Everyone already knows; now the fact is the subject of a comment, so it goes into the subjunctive.
A bare «que» can also open the sentence; «el hecho de que» stresses that we are talking about something that really happened.
The whole clause is the subject of the verb.
Plain indicative informs; the other two comment on something already known.

When a clause with «el hecho de que» or «que» opens the sentence, it presents a known fact that the rest of the sentence comments on. The normal mood is the subjunctive, in the tense that matches the main verb.
The fact that the client isn’t answering emails worries me: a present fact, commented on.
It’s strange that you don’t know yet: a bare «que» opening the sentence.
Samuel staying until ten shows his commitment: even «demostrar» takes the subjunctive here.
A project being expensive doesn’t mean it is good: «no significa que» also takes the subjunctive.
The fact is a known topic under comment. After evaluations and emotions this is the expected choice: use it when in doubt.
The speaker asserts the fact as true information. Less frequent, never compulsory: the subjunctive would also be correct.
With verbs of knowing or certainty, a fronted «que» clause can be in the indicative, and «lo» picks it up again after it. The fact is not being evaluated, just taken as true.
It’s exhausting that the client changes the plans every week.
It annoyed me that nobody warned us.
Neighbours complaining doesn’t mean the project is bad.
«Lo de que» and «eso de que» pick up something that has been said. If it is a piece of news or a rumour, the indicative; if it is a proposal (something someone wants to happen), the subjunctive.
Is it true they’re closing the Monterrey office? A rumour, taken up as information.
That idea that architects never sleep is a myth: «eso de que» shows some distance.
The proposal for us to work from home on Fridays has been approved: a proposal, so subjunctive.
«Que» stands for the noun itself (I read the news): a relative clause, no «de».
The clause says what the news is: «de» is required. Leaving it out is «queísmo».
We run the risk of the project being delayed by a year.
I get the feeling the client didn’t read the report.
Is it true that Paula is moving to Mérida?

Adding an unnecessary «de» is avoided in careful Spanish everywhere. Dropping a required one is very common in everyday speech in many regions, but careful writing keeps it. A few verbs accept both: avisar, advertir, dudar.
I’m convinced Irene is right.
The client will probably come back next year.
She explained to us that the deadline was impossible.

With the same subject, use the infinitive instead of «que» + subjunctive. If the action happened before the main verb, use the compound infinitive: haber + past participle. Pronouns attach to «haber».
I’m glad I met you at the conference: I am glad now, we met before.
I’m sorry I didn’t call earlier (same subject) · I’m sorry they didn’t call you (different subject).
The compound gerund presents an earlier action and belongs mainly to formal writing. In conversation people say «después de terminar» or «cuando terminó».
I’m sorry you’re ill.
I’m glad I did that course last year.
Samuel says nothing, but I sense he is worried.
It hurt me that you didn’t let me know.
I’m glad I tried.
Have you heard? Irene turned down the Chapala hotel contract.
Yes, Samuel told me. The fact that she turned it down really surprises me: it was the project of the year.
Me too. Irene saying no to a client like that is really unusual.
And is it true the client wanted to build on part of the wetland?
So it seems. And did you hear that story about the firm having money problems?
Yes, but I don’t believe it. I’m sure Irene thought it through.
Me too. But I sense the team is nervous. Samuel didn’t even have lunch today.
That’s understandable. He’s an intern and he’s worried they might not renew his contract.
Poor guy. I’m sorry I didn’t say anything to him this morning; he looked very serious.
Hey, and the news that we’re among the finalists for the library? That’s good, isn’t it?
Great! Although Irene insists we don’t say anything yet.
Makes sense. And honestly, I’m glad I chose this firm: nobody here will do just anything for money.
Why is Rodrigo surprised by Irene’s decision?
What does Rodrigo think of the rumour about money problems?
Why the indicative after «siento que»?
That night the firm’s group chat is full of comments. Which mood does each sentence need: subjunctive (evaluated, possible or requested) or indicative (asserted, perceived or reported as news)?
“The client not sending the plans on time delayed the whole job.”
“I heard a rumour that Irene was going to sell the firm.”
“It’s not normal for Samuel to get tired so quickly; he works too much.”
“I’m sorry I didn’t go to your presentation.”
“Rodrigo insists the mistake was the client’s, not ours.”
The fact that she didn’t call worried me.
I’m sure we’ll manage it.
I’m sorry I didn’t let you know earlier.
Why does Irene send the message?
What does Irene say about the firm’s money problems?
What did she find unacceptable?
Why didn’t she explain earlier?
What does she ask the team to do?
A fact placed first and commented on: normally subjunctive; the main verb agrees in the singular
When content is reported or asserted (news, rumours, impressions), the indicative
Nouns of possibility, risk, fear and hope take the subjunctive
No «de» where the verb doesn’t take it; keep it where the verb, adjective or noun requires it
Sentir, entender, decir, insistir change meaning with the mood; haber + participle for an earlier action with the same subject

Ask yourself: am I asserting or reporting a fact (indicative), or commenting on it, evaluating it, wishing for it or seeing it as only possible (subjunctive)? And before writing «que», try the «eso» test: is «de» needed?
It’s a shame your brother isn’t coming to the wedding.
At the airport we got the news that the flight was cancelled.
I’m convinced we can do it.
I’m so sorry you had to cancel your trip.
I’m glad I took this course: it was really useful.
Valparaíso, Chile. The council has closed a neighbourhood’s main street to traffic on Sundays. Carmen, who runs a bookshop there, talks it over with her neighbours.

Three finer points. «El que» can replace «el hecho de que» at the start of a sentence. With verbs of knowing or proving, a fronted «que» clause can be in the indicative and is picked up again by «lo». And reports and minutes use the compound gerund.
Report: having reviewed the documents, the committee approved the project.
Which forms are possible?
Which sentence means the same?
That the project is viable, the engineers proved it.

Today you saw that the subjunctive appears when a fact is not asserted but commented on or treated as the topic. Class 153 applies the same logic to causes: when you deny one cause in order to give the real one, it takes the subjunctive.

Marina Robles has coordinated the routes of the Los Alerces hiking club for six years. On Sunday she announced she is stepping down at the end of the month, and a rumour is going round that she argued with Óscar, the new president. She wants to set the record straight: she is leaving, but not because of a fight; the real reason is her father. Today you learn to reject a false reason and give the true one, to rule out an interpretation with «no es que…, es que…», and to pick a causal connector that fits the register and the position in the sentence.
The «no» denies the action: she is not coming, and the indicative gives the real reason.
The «no» denies only the reason: she is leaving, but anger is not why. The rejected reason takes the subjunctive.
Marina is stepping down, but not because she has problems with Óscar.
“I’m not going on Saturday’s hike because I have to work.” Is Marina going?

Is the action real, but someone has the wrong idea about why? Reject that reason with «no porque» + subjunctive and give the true one with «sino porque» + indicative. The subjunctive signals that you do not assert the rejected reason.
I’m stepping down not because anyone is making me, but because I want to.
I kept quiet at the meeting. I didn’t do it out of fear, but out of respect: she did keep quiet; fear is the rejected reason (past frame, so tuviera).
I’m leaving the post not out of tiredness, but for my family’s sake: with nouns, «no por…, sino por…».

In speech you will sometimes hear the indicative after «no porque» when «sino porque» follows. The subjunctive is the recommended form, especially in writing: it makes it clear that you are not asserting that reason and that the action did happen.
Esteban stays on as treasurer, not because he likes numbers, but because nobody else wants the job.
Last year Marina organised the lakes route, not because Óscar asked her to, but because she was excited about it.
I kept quiet at the meeting, not out of fear, but out of respect.

Do you want to rule out what the other person might think? «No es que» rejects an interpretation, so it always takes the subjunctive; then give the real explanation with «es que» (colloquial) or «sino que» (more careful). It is also a very common way to soften a refusal.
It’s not that I don’t want to carry on; I just can’t.
It’s not that I’m angry with Óscar; the thing is, I need time for my father («sino que» is a little more careful than «es que»).
Pilar, it’s not that I didn’t believe you, it’s just that the story struck me as odd (past frame: creyera).
You give a reason or an excuse, in a conversational tone.
First you rule out what the other person might think, then you explain.
It’s not that the route is difficult; it’s just very long.
“Marina, are you angry?” “No, it’s not that I’m angry; I’m just tired.”
It’s not that I didn’t want to go to last Saturday’s dinner; I already had plans.

Only porque (and por) can be negated or put in focus: not because, only because, precisely because, above all because. Como, ya que and puesto que present a reason as a given, so they cannot be denied or highlighted this way.
“Óscar didn’t change the fee because the members voted against it.” Did he change it?
“Óscar changed the fee, but not because the members complained.” Did he change it?
Marina is giving up the coordination because she has no free time at weekends.

Adding the reason for an order or a piece of advice in conversation? Use «que» + indicative after it. With the subjunctive, «que» would express purpose instead (class 140). And when the subject is the same, por + infinitive gives the cause; the compound infinitive stresses that the cause came first.
Take your raincoat, it’s going to rain: a reason added to advice, typical of everyday speech.
I’m so tired, I’ve been walking for six hours! «Que» can also explain an exclamation.
They congratulated Esteban for having found the shortcut: same subject, cause before the result.
As the mountain hut was closed, we slept in the village.
Club notice: owing to the storm forecast, Sunday’s hike is cancelled.
Take plenty of water, there are no fountains up there.
Pilar signed up for the long route, not because she was fit, but to keep her sister company.
As he already knew the path, Esteban led the way.
Marina, have you got a minute? Someone told me something and I can’t quite believe it.
The Óscar thing? I can imagine. Pilar is telling everyone I’m quitting as coordinator because I had a row with him at the meeting.
And is it true? You looked very serious that day.
Look, I don’t agree with him about the fee, I won’t lie to you. But I didn’t argue with anyone. I kept quiet, yes, but not out of fear; out of respect.
So why are you stepping down? Are you tired of the club?
It’s not that I’m tired of it, quite the opposite. I just can’t do everything. As my father has been living alone since March, from November I’m going to spend weekends with him.
Oh, I had no idea. And why didn’t you say so on Sunday?
Because I didn’t want to turn the hike into a drama. Besides, since it was the members’ meeting that elected me, the fair thing is to explain it to everyone at once, in writing.
Sounds right. Oh, and the lakes route… People say you cancelled it because you hadn’t booked the mountain hut.
Not at all! I cancelled it because of the storms; the hut had been booked since January. And if Sunday’s hike went well, it was thanks to you and your GPS.
All right, all right… Then write that message soon, because people are already talking.
I’ll write it tonight. I’m giving up the coordination, but not because I don’t like the club; it’s because my father comes first now.
Why did Marina keep quiet at the meeting?
Why is Marina stepping down as coordinator?
Why was the lakes route cancelled?
I’m staying in the WhatsApp group, but not because I want to keep organising things.
We are proposing a higher fee not because we want to make money, but because the insurance has gone up.
When I told people, it’s not that I meant any harm; that’s just how it was told to me.
As the bus leaves at seven, we’re meeting in the square at half past six.
The hike up Mirador peak is postponed owing to the poor condition of the trail.
It’s not that I don’t want to; I just can’t.
I kept quiet, but not because I was afraid.
Wrap up warm, it’s cold up there.
Why does Marina send the voice message?
Why did she keep quiet at the meeting?
Does she enjoy organising the hikes?
Why is Esteban taking over as coordinator?
What does Marina recommend for Saturday?
the action happens; you reject the reason, in the subjunctive (present or past by frame)
the true reason, introduced with sino after the denial
rule out what others might think, then explain; also softens a refusal
como goes first; ya que and dado que are more careful; que after an order is spoken Spanish

Ask yourself: does the action happen? If it does and you reject a reason, use no porque + subjunctive, then sino porque + indicative. If the action does not happen, use no + verb + porque + indicative. To rule out an interpretation, use no es que + subjunctive. Then choose the connector by position and register.
I moved to the countryside, not because I hated the city, but because I needed silence.
It’s not that the restaurant is bad; it’s just too far from where we live.
As there were no tickets left, we stayed at home.
The flight was delayed owing to fog.
Call your mother, she’s been waiting all afternoon.
Daniel is closing the restaurant he opened in his neighbourhood fifteen years ago, and the neighbours have their own theories. Help him explain himself.

For strong students or spare time: a rejected reason that happened before a past event takes the pluperfect subjunctive. Very formal texts use «en vista de que» and «habida cuenta de que», close to «dado que». Watch out: «como» + subjunctive is not causal but conditional, often a warning. And «porque sí» means “just because”, refusing to give a reason.
