Óscar resigned in June, not because he had been criticised at the meeting, but because he was moving to another city.
Board report: in view of the fact that membership has grown, the insurance policy will be extended.
“If you’re not here by seven, we’re leaving without you.” What does «como» mean here?
“Why did you change the route?” “Just because.” What does the answer mean?

You can now reject a false reason and give the real one. Class 154 looks at the relationship from the other side: the consequence, especially when it comes from something intense, as in “it rained so much that we cancelled the route”. It is the natural next step: from cause to consequence.

Lucía Herrera left her office job in Medellín to open a sourdough bakery with her business partner, Daniel Ospina. Before the opening she is doing a workshop with Rosa Montoya, a master baker with thirty years in the trade. Rosa explains almost everything in proportions: the longer the dough ferments, the more flavour it has; the sooner they open, the better. Today you learn to say that two things rise or fall together.
Correct, but it simply links a condition to a result.
Both things grow together, step by step, on a sliding scale, like English “the longer…, the more…”.
The more water you put in the dough, the more open the crumb.
The more you knead, the more elastic the dough becomes.

Use cuanto más / menos…, más / menos… when one quantity changes in step with another, like English “the more…, the more…”. Neither part takes an article, nothing links them but a comma, and the subject normally follows the verb.
The more Lucía kneads, the smoother the dough gets.
The colder the kitchen, the more slowly the bread rises.
The less the dough is handled while it rests, the better it ferments.
The less Daniel sleeps, the worse he does the accounts.
The longer the dough ferments, the more flavour it has.
The busier Daniel is, the later he answers his messages.
When más or menos is followed by a noun, cuanto agrees with that noun in gender and number: cuanto, cuanta, cuantos, cuantas. Before a verb, an adjective or an adverb, cuanto never changes.
The more hours the dough ferments, the tangier the bread tastes.
The more water the dough has, the harder it is to shape.
The more customers come in, the more bread we have to bake.
The less time the dough rests, the denser the crumb.
The more online orders we get, the more flour we need.
The bigger the oven, the more bread fits in each batch.
The more yeast you add, the faster the dough rises.
Something generally true or already experienced: indicative.
It refers to something future and not yet real: present subjunctive, exactly as after cuando.

The cuanto clause behaves like a time clause with cuando: when it points to the future, it takes the subjunctive, never the future tense. The second part usually goes in the future, in the present, or is simply mejor / peor.
The earlier you get here tomorrow, the better: the oven takes an hour to heat up.
The more neighbours come to the opening, the more bread we’ll give away.
The less you touch the dough tonight, the better it will ferment.
The more you practise shaping the loaves, the faster you’ll get.
The earlier you light the oven, the less stressed you’ll be.
As a rule, the more hours the dough spends in the fridge, the more flavour it has.
Last year, the more Lucía worked at the office, the less she liked it.

In many Latin American countries, especially in speech, mientras más…, más… is very common; it is also heard in some parts of Spain, though less. It is a widespread, legitimate variant, but mientras never agrees with the noun, and formal writing prefers cuanto más.
One thing changes because the other one does: two linked variables.
A single thing keeps rising or falling over time: more and more, fewer and fewer, better and better.
Since they opened, more and more customers have been coming in the morning.
The more orders we have, the happier we are.
Morning, Lucía. Feel this dough: it’s been in the fridge for eighteen hours. The more hours it ferments, the tangier and deeper the flavour.
It smells amazing. But at home my dough barely rises. Could it be the temperature?
Definitely. The colder the kitchen, the more slowly the starter works. That’s not bad: you just have to give it more time.
Right. And when I knead by hand, it sticks to my fingers more and more.
Because you handle it too much. The less you touch it at the start, the better. Wet your hands and be patient.
I’ll try. Another thing: Daniel wants to open in three weeks. He says the sooner we open, the sooner we’ll get back what we’ve invested.
He’s right, but don’t rush. The more loaves you bake now, in the trial runs, the more confident you’ll feel on day one.
That’s what my mum says: “The more you practise, the more you learn.”
That’s how we say it here, yes. And don’t make twenty kinds of bread: the simpler the menu at the start, the less bread gets thrown away.
So, three breads and nothing else. And what if loads of people come on the first day?
The more the merrier! And if the bread runs out before noon, don’t worry: people come back earlier and earlier.
Why does Lucía’s dough hardly rise at home?
What does Rosa think about opening soon?
What does Rosa advise about the menu?
Sourdough bread: the slower the process, the easier it is to digest.
The sooner you put the dough in the fridge tonight, the more time it’ll have to ferment.
The more almojábanas (Colombian cheese rolls) we sell, the less white bread people ask for.
The more tired I am, the worse I shape the loaves.
When I started out, the more loaves I made, the more mistakes I discovered.
The more you practise, the better your bread turns out.
The more hours it ferments, the more flavour it has.
The sooner the orders arrive, the better.
She answers Lucía’s questions about the first week.
Why is Lucía’s bread so sour?
What used to happen at Rosa’s bakery when the bread sold out early?
What does she advise about production?
Why does Rosa want to know how many customers Lucía had on Saturday?
a general or habitual link between two changes: indicative; no article, no que
future or hypothetical: present subjunctive, never the future tense; imperfect subjunctive in a past frame
cuanto agrees with a following noun; before a verb, adjective or adverb it is invariable; cuanto mayor, cuanto antes (no más)
mientras más is a widespread Latin American variant (invariable); cada vez más describes one thing changing over time

“The more…, the more…” is never lo más or el más in Spanish: it is cuanto más…, más… If a noun follows más or menos, cuanto agrees with it. And check the time reference: general or past, indicative; future, subjunctive.
The greater the risk, the bigger the potential gain.
The more people sign the letter, the more weight it will carry.
The sooner you give me an answer, the sooner I can book.
The more I read about the subject, the less I understand.
As the years go by, my grandmother hears less and less.
Elena Ruiz conducts a neighbourhood choir and is preparing the Christmas concert. Transform what she says using the structure each sentence asks for.
For strong students or spare time: formal variants of the structure and a preview of C1.
Tanto más in the second part is a formal, emphatic option; the meaning stays the same.
Tanto más… cuanto que means “all the more… because / since”: formal written register.
A medida que links two processes developing side by side, like English “as”.
Tanto mejor means “so much the better”.

You can now link two changes with cuanto más…, más…, make cuanto agree with nouns and choose the mood for general or future situations. Class 156 covers connectors of concession and objection, such as no obstante: the natural next step, because arguing well means not only showing how one thing grows with another, but also acknowledging a problem and holding your position despite it.

The La Alameda neighbourhood association meets this evening. The council wants to close calle del Mercado to traffic for a one-year trial. Adela chairs, Lucía is in favour and Hugo, who owns the hardware shop, has doubts. So far you have conceded inside one sentence; today you link whole sentences and paragraphs, and learn to object in a debate without shutting the conversation down.
Two complete sentences: the connector comes after the full stop and announces a contrast.
Hugo accepts the proposal, then adds a condition he considers essential: “that said…”.
A single sentence: the concession depends on the main clause, as in class 138.
Hugo accepts the proposal and adds a condition.
Which connector links two independent sentences?

These connectors do not subordinate: they link two complete sentences, each with its own verb, and can open the second one or sit in the middle between commas. Sin embargo and no obstante mark contrast (however, nevertheless). Aun así, con todo and así y todo insist that the result stands despite what was said. De todas formas (de todos modos, de todas maneras) plays the previous point down: whatever the case, what follows holds.
The closure is only a trial. However, many shopkeepers are already worried.
The proposal does, however, have a weak point: parking. In mid-position, between commas, it sounds formal and written.
Hugo will lose customers who come by car. Even so, he signs the petition.
I don’t know if the street will look nice. Either way, it’s worth a try.
“Pero” can combine with “aun así”, which reinforces it. “Pero sin embargo”, however, says the same thing twice and is best avoided: choose one. “Y, sin embargo” is fine: “He knew, and yet he did it.”
The majority voted for the closure. Nevertheless, the association will request a report on deliveries.
Lucía knows there will be protests. Even so, she is going to defend the proposal.
I don’t know if I’ll make it to the meeting. Either way, I’ll email you my ideas.

Ahora bien accepts what has been said and announces something important that limits it, an objection or a condition (that said…); it is common in argument, spoken or written. Eso sí adds a point that balances or limits what came before, often a condition; it is very common in speech. Aunque, placed after the main clause, can mean “but”: it adds a reservation, takes the indicative and cannot be moved to the front.
I’m in favour of the closure. That said, delivery lorries must be able to get in before ten.
I’ll lend you the wheelbarrow; just make sure you bring it back before Saturday.
It’s a good idea, though I’m not sure customers will understand it: a reservation added at the end.
Concessive: the obstacle does not stop the result; it can go before or after the main clause.
Adversative: it works like “but”, adds a reservation, takes the indicative and always comes second.
I’m fine with closing the street. That said, I want to know where residents will park.
I’ll leave you the key; just lock up properly when you leave.
Which word can replace “aunque” here?

You already know si bien and aun cuando (class 138). Pese a works like a pesar de and is typical of formal and journalistic writing: pese a + noun or infinitive, pese a que + indicative (a fact) or subjunctive (as with a pesar de que). Y eso que is colloquial: it comes after the main clause, takes the indicative and adds a fact that should have changed the outcome, often with surprise or complaint (“and that’s even though…”).
Despite the protests, the council is keeping the trial: newspaper style.
Although the closure is temporary, some shops are already seeing fewer sales.
Hugo voted against it, and that’s even though his daughter cycles everywhere: colloquial, slightly surprised.
Even if the figures are good, the council will review the measure in a year’s time.
Nobody from the council came, even though we had asked in writing.
Despite the rain, hundreds of residents stroll along calle del Mercado.
In a debate, a flat “no” shuts the conversation down. Speakers usually concede first and object afterwards. These formulas vary in register and in strength.
Formal meeting: which objection fits best?
You’re right that the street will be safer, but older people need the bus.
You may be right, but I’d rather wait and see the figures.
The project is useful; however, it comes too late.
They voted against it, even though the report was clear.
Right, let’s start. The council wants to close calle del Mercado to traffic for a year. However, before deciding anything, it wants to hear from residents.
I’m in favour. In the morning there’s so much traffic that children can’t walk to school on their own, and it’s only two streets away.
Sure, but what about deliveries? My stock comes by lorry three times a week.
You’re right that it’s a problem. That said, there could be loading hours, as in other neighbourhoods.
Maybe, but many of my customers drive in from other areas. If they can’t park, they’ll go to the shopping centre.
According to the council, shops in other cities sold more once streets were pedestrianised. All the same, every neighbourhood is different.
Look, I’m not saying it’s a bad idea. I’ve been here thirty years and the noise is unbearable. But a whole year is a long time for a trial.
A year may seem long, but with less time you can’t see the results.
All right… I’ll vote for it. But I want the association to request the loading hours in writing.
That seems fair. We’ll put it in the minutes, though the final say lies with the council.
Thanks, Hugo. I know it’s harder for you than for anyone.
You know me: I complain a lot. Either way, if it isn’t working in six months, I’ll be back at the meeting to complain.
What worries Hugo?
What condition does Hugo set for his vote?
What will Hugo do if the trial isn’t working in six months?
The closure has reduced noise. Nevertheless, shops are asking for support during the first months.
It rained all morning. Even so, the fair on calle del Mercado was packed.
I don’t know if the proposal will go through. Either way, I’m voting for it.
I’ll help you set up the stall; I do have to leave at eight, though.
There have been complaints about deliveries and some access problems. All in all, the outcome is positive.
The idea is good; that said, the deadline is tight.
Hugo voted in favour, even though he had doubts.
The street will be closed; ambulances will be able to get through, though.
It summarises the assembly’s vote on closing the street.
What are the shopkeepers afraid of?
What does the council say about other cities?
What did Hugo Medina ask for?
What does the council promise?
contrast between two sentences; no obstante is more formal; never “pero sin embargo”
the result stands despite what was said; de todas formas plays the previous point down
you accept and then add a condition or an objection; choose the formula by register
one sentence with the concession inside: pese a is formal, y eso que is colloquial and comes second

Ask yourself three questions. One sentence or two? Two sentences need a connector with a full stop or semicolon before it and a comma after; one sentence takes si bien, pese a que, aunque or y eso que. What do you want to do? Contrast, keep the result, play the point down or add a condition. Where are you? In a report, no obstante, con todo, si bien, pese a; in conversation, ya, pero; eso sí; y eso que.
The flight left late. Even so, we got to the wedding on time.
Your order is ready. However, delivery will be delayed by two days due to the transport strike.
He overslept, even though he had set three alarms.
You can use my studio at the weekend; just water the plants.
The hotel is beautiful, though the breakfast leaves a lot to be desired.
At a design company, the team is debating a four-day week. Ana jots down quick notes; you turn them into the formal minutes of the meeting.

For strong students or spare time: the same argument changes shape with register. And a preview: in conversation people also concede with the future tense, “Será muy práctico, pero…” meaning “it may well be practical, but…”. You will study it in class 161; for now, just recognise it.
Make it formal.
What does “será” express here?
Make it conversational.

You can now concede and object across sentences. In class 157 you learn to describe precisely how things end up after a change: “the street was left closed”, “residents are worried”, “a shop affected by the works”. It is the natural next step: in the same debates and reports, after arguing you need to describe results.

You already know estar + participle for states (la ventana está abierta). Spanish has other verbs that present an action through its result: quedar tells how a situation ended up, tener presents the result as something you now have ready. Today you learn the whole family and when the participle agrees.
The action itself, as a perfect tense. The participle never agrees after haber.
The result as something Marina now has in hand, ready to use; the participle agrees with the object, like an adjective.
How a situation ended up, often without anyone intending it; the participle agrees with the subject.
Why “tiene escritas” and not “tiene escrito”?
Which sentence simply reports the action?
What have you already got done and ready?
The booking is done and secured: tener presents it as a result Hugo has in hand.
The subject of tener does not have to be the one who did the job.
Tengo pensado = I’m planning to; tengo entendido = I understand / I’ve heard. Both are fixed and invariable.
A reproach: “I’ve told you again and again”. It sounds annoyed, so use it with care.
How much have you done so far?
Five read so far, three to go: the task is not finished.
The count so far; sales are still open.
Time + gerund measures how long; participle + amount measures how much is done.
We’ve sold three hundred tickets so far.
I’m planning to go to Santiago on Monday.

With dejar, someone leaves something in a state; with quedar, the thing simply ends up that way, with no one in the picture. That makes quedar a tactful way to report a problem without blaming anyone.
Before leaving, Ignacio left all the stage lights switched off.
After the audience’s question, the author fell silent for a moment.

He leído reports the action; tengo leído presents the result you can use now (you know the contract). Tener also needs a direct object: with llegar, ir or dormir only haber is possible. Compound tenses in general Spanish are always built with haber.
The director has already arrived at the hotel.
We have rented four hundred chairs for the audience.
Does the adjective describe someone affected by the action, or someone who does it?
Leída describes a well-read person; un libro muy leído is a widely read book.
Atrevido means bold or daring: it describes the one who dares, not something dared.
Ser callado is a personality trait (quiet); estar callado describes the moment (silent).
Ser cansado = tiring; estar cansado = tired.
This morning I woke up at five because of the noise from the port.
Hugo knows a great deal about sound: he is quite an expert.
I’ve got the author files checked.
How are we doing, Marina? You’ve got me worried with all this silence.
Better than it looks. I’ve got almost all the interviews lined up, and we’ve sold three hundred tickets so far.
Three hundred already? And the programmes? Have they printed them?
Yes, they’re printed. I picked them up this morning and left them stored in the storeroom.
Great. I’ve got the big tent up, but the small one ended up crooked in the wind.
We’ll fix it tomorrow. Listen, did you talk to Claudia Rey?
Yes. She’s arriving on Saturday, not Friday. I’ve already left word at the hotel.
Thank goodness. I’m planning to open the festival with her novel. It’s daring, but it’s very well written.
She’s very well read; the talk is going to be great. And you? You look tired.
Exhausted. Last night I fell asleep in the office with my laptop on top of me.
Well, you’ll be well prepared on Saturday: you’ve got everything done. Go home early.
I hear you haven’t slept much this week either, have you?
Are ticket sales over?
What is the problem with the tents?
What does Hugo mean by “es muy leída”?
I’ve checked seven chapters so far; I have five left.
Before leaving for Santiago, Lorena left the instructions written down on the table.
The volunteers have handed out all the posters around the neighbourhood.
I understand the mayor will come to the opening, but it isn’t confirmed.
For the cocktail party, the cook has already fried two hundred empanadas.
The volunteers are going in very well prepared: they took a course last month.
We’ve sold almost five hundred tickets so far.
I left word at the hotel reception.
The author fell silent for a moment.
Why does Marina leave the message?
How many tickets have been sold?
What did Marina do about Claudia Rey’s change of date?
Why is Marina feeling tired?
What you have ready, what you have done so far, how you left something. The participle agrees with the object.
How something ended up, or how someone is. The participle agrees with the subject.
The action. Never agrees. Tener cannot replace it: he llegado, never tengo llegado.
Only imprimir, freír and proveer have two participles valid with haber; some participle-adjectives take on a new, active meaning.

Look at the verb in front. After haber, the participle ends in -o, full stop. After tener, llevar and dejar, it behaves like an adjective of the object; after quedar(se), ir and andar (and estar), like an adjective of the subject. Then choose by meaning: the action, the result you hold, progress so far, how you left it, or how it ended up.
The printer has printed the certificates for us a day late.
Someone left the storeroom door open all night.
Of the twenty invited authors, we’ve already got eighteen confirmed.
My grandmother is very well read: she has read almost all the classics.
For the radio interview, Ignacio was wearing a suit.

Your friend Gonzalo is finishing his PhD thesis and his supervisor asks how it is going. Rewrite his notes with result verbs: llevar for progress, tener for what is ready, quedarse for what happened to him.

In ceremonies, queda + participle performs the act as it is said (“I hereby declare the festival open”). Signs and rules use it too. In reports, una vez + participle, or the participle alone, presents one action as completed before the next; it agrees with its noun. This is formal, mostly written Spanish.
The mayor, opening the event: “I declare the festival open.”
Sign on the dock: “Vehicles are not allowed during the festival.”

You can now present results with tener, llevar, dejar and quedar plus a participle. Class 158 moves on to infinitive periphrases for obligation and inference: tener que, deber, deber de, haber que (“she must be tired”, “she must hand in the report”). It is the natural next step, because the same verb changes meaning with what follows it: tengo escritas (a result) versus tengo que escribir (an obligation).

Irene Salvat has just bought a 1950s apartment and is renovating it with her architect, Hugo Lema. On site, two things happen at once: there are obligations (permits, hours, quotes) and there are clues that force you to draw conclusions. In class 080 you used hay que, tener que and deber to oblige and advise. Today you will see that some of those same verb phrases also express deduction, and you will learn new ones: deber de, haber de and venir a.
A duty: a rule they must follow before knocking down any wall.
A guess based on a clue: “he must have been a musician”. Irene does not know for sure.
A confident deduction: the evidence is so clear that Hugo is almost certain.
Irene is guessing from the sheet music, not stating a known fact.
Which sentence expresses an obligation?

The standard keeps two meanings apart: “deber + infinitive” for obligation (what is required or right) and “deber de + infinitive” for supposition (what is probably true). It works in every tense: “debía de tener” = he probably had; “debió de olvidarse” = she probably forgot.
Neighbours must respect the building-work hours: a rule.
These tiles must be about seventy years old: an estimate from what she sees.
The lady on the fifth floor must have heard the noise, because she came down to ask.
The technician hasn’t come: he must have run into a problem on another job (an inference about the past, with “haber” + participle).

According to the RAE-ASALE guide to usage: for obligation, educated usage requires “deber” without “de”; “deber de” with that meaning is common in speech but advised against. For supposition, “deber de” is recommended, although “deber” alone is also accepted. Practical rule: add “de” only when you are guessing, and you will always be correct.
There must have been damp here for years: Hugo is inferring from what he sees.
Owners must notify the building management of any work: a rule.

“Tener que” is not only about obligation. With verbs like ser, estar, haber or venir, it can express a conclusion you are almost sure of: “tiene que estar en casa” = she must be at home (the light is on). “Tenía que ser él” means “of course it was him”: what was to be expected.
With this smell, there has to be a leak behind the tiles: Hugo is nearly certain.
There’s a light on on the fourth floor: the Paredes family must be home.
The lift broken on moving day? Of course it had to be today (resigned irony).
Hugo is not sure at all: which sentence fits his doubt?
Someone knocks at eight sharp, as every day: it has to be Hugo.

“Haber de + infinitive” expresses obligation or necessity in a formal or written register: regulations, official instructions, literature. In everyday speech in Spain and many countries, people say “tener que”. In Mexico and parts of Central America, however, it is very common in conversation to make a guess: “ha de estar en su casa” = he must be at home.
Building work is to be carried out Monday to Friday, nine to six: the wording of a regulation.
The owner must give the start date in writing.
You should know that this building is almost a hundred years old: solemn or literary.
Mexican Spanish: “The technician must be on his way by now” (a guess).
When they bought the building, all the windows had to be replaced.
Building waste is to be removed before six: regulation style.

“Venir a + infinitive” gives an approximate figure (“viene a costar unos tres mil” = it comes to about three thousand) or says what something amounts to (“viene a ser lo mismo” = it amounts to the same thing). It sounds natural with costar, tener, durar, medir, ser and decir.
Fixing the ceiling comes to about three thousand.
The living room is about the same size as the kitchen and hallway put together.
Repairing the pipe or replacing it amounts to the same cost.
Direct: a clear necessity, close to an order.
The conditional turns the obligation into a recommendation.
Impersonal and soft: you suggest it without pointing at anyone. Very useful with clients and neighbours.

“Tener que” usually presents a necessity imposed by circumstances; “deber” sounds like a moral duty or a rule. In the affirmative they are very close, but in the negative remember class 080: “no tienes que” = it is not necessary; “no debes” = it is not right.
The full renovation should take about four months.
The pipes for the whole building ought to be checked, don’t you think?
There must be about forty boxes in the basement.
To bring materials in, the lift will have to be left on the ground floor.
Look at that stain on the ceiling. It has to be coming from upstairs: none of your pipes run through here.
From señor Paredes? I haven’t seen him for a week. He’s probably staying at his daughter’s.
Either way, we’ll have to let the building manager know before touching anything.
All right. And this wall? I’d love to knock it down to get more light.
Impossible, it’s forty centimetres thick: it’s definitely load-bearing. And under the building rules, work must be done on weekdays, nine to six.
Then I’ll have to change the plan. And what about fixing the ceiling?
It depends on what we find, but it comes to about three thousand.
Look at this cupboard: it’s full of old sheet music. The previous owner must have been a musician.
Or his wife. I wouldn’t throw them away: they probably matter to the family. You should keep them in a box.
The thing is, when I signed, the apartment had to be emptied in two days and nobody checked the cupboards.
Well, someone ought to call the estate agency to track down the family.
Why does Hugo think the stain comes from upstairs?
Why can’t Irene knock the wall down?
What does Hugo advise about the sheet music?
This wall must be over seventy years old.
Last year, to replace the boiler, three quotes had to be requested.
Residents are to remove their bicycles from the courtyard before Monday.
Replacing all the windows comes to roughly six thousand.
You should get another quote before signing.
The tiles must be seventy years old.
The fourth-floor neighbours will have to be told.
The work takes about three months.
She explains the likely cause of the stain and reminds Irene of the rules for building work.
Where does Ximena think the stain comes from?
Why isn’t señor Paredes answering?
Who pays for the repair?
What does Ximena suggest?
obligation: deber without “de”; haber de is formal; haber que is impersonal and always singular
inference: deber de = probably; tener que = almost certainly; debe de haber stays singular
an approximate figure or what something amounts to; never with exact numbers
the conditional turns an obligation into tactful advice; habría que does not point at anyone

First ask yourself: am I obliging or guessing? To oblige: deber without “de”, tener que or, in formal writing, haber de; for everyone, hay que (always singular). To guess: deber de (probable) or tener que (almost certain). For a rough figure: venir a. And to advise tactfully, use the conditional: deberías, tendrías que, habría que.
María hasn’t come to the meeting; she must be ill, because she never misses one.
Last winter, because of the snow, the office had to close for three days.
The train journey takes about five hours.
Candidates are to bring their ID document.
She has to be still at the office: the evidence is clear.
Óscar is organising a mountain hike for his club. Rephrase his notes with today’s verb phrases.

For strong students or spare time. 1. Since “deber” without “de” is also accepted for guessing, “Debe estar en la obra” can be an obligation or a guess; context decides, and in careful writing “de” removes the doubt. 2. In the past, “Debió de llamar” = he probably called, while “Debiste llamarme” or “Deberías haberme llamado” is a reproach. 3. “Venir a decir” sums up the gist of a message: “Vino a decir que no” = basically, he said no.
What does the sentence mean?
What is Irene expressing?
In a report, which version makes it clear you are only estimating?
What does “vino a decir” mean here?

You can now use verb phrases to oblige, infer and approximate. In class 159 you work on another group: verb phrases that show how an action unfolds, whether it progresses gradually, builds up or reaches a result (“the work is gradually progressing”, “I’ve got three rooms painted so far”). It is the natural next step: from your attitude to the action to the way it develops.

Marina and Daniel left their city jobs and bought a stone house in a mountain village to turn it into a small rural guesthouse. Marina tells a friend: “We’ve been renovating the house for eight months. We’re getting there little by little, but the builder has been holding up the work since March, and a neighbour is going round the village saying we’ll never open.” You already know how to say when an action starts or ends (classes 106–109). Today you look inside the action: how long it has lasted, how it develops and since when it keeps happening.
We’ve been renovating the house for eight months (and we still are).
We’re making progress little by little.
Ernesto has been holding up the work since March (again and again).
A neighbour is going around saying we won’t open.
“Llevamos ocho meses reformando la casa” means…
The neighbour “anda diciendo” they won’t open. What nuance does it have?
How long has something that started in the past been going on? Or how long has it not happened?
Daniel has been looking for some old hinges all morning.
We’ve been asking for permission to replace the roof since September.
The house had been without an owner for thirty years when they bought it.
Daniel has been looking for hinges all morning and still can’t find them.
Marina hasn’t slept well for two weeks.
They lived in Lima from 2015 to 2018: they spent three years living there.
Is the process moving forward step by step? Or does it come from a point in the past up to today?
With every coat of paint, the walls are getting whiter.
I’ve been telling you for months: we need another builder.
The price of timber has been going up since last year.
Is someone doing something here and there, on and off or without a clear direction, and are you telling it informally?
Ernesto is going around telling people the delay is the rain’s fault.
Daniel is on the lookout for a plumber who can come on a Saturday.
The walls were black; now, with every coat of paint, they’re gradually getting their colour back.
“The price of timber viene subiendo since last year” means…
—What are you looking for round here, Daniel? —Some old hinges.

A long story also has moments: something starts suddenly, happens again, is about to happen or ends in an unexpected way. You saw these periphrases in classes 106, 108 and 109. Here you combine them with llevar, ir, venir and andar.
When she saw the finished roof, Marina burst into tears of joy.
On Saturday water came in again through the same crack.
At first they didn’t like the house at all, but they ended up buying it.
—Did you tell Ernesto about the roof? —Yes, I’ve been telling him for weeks.
Which sentence is correct?
What a wonderful house, Marina! And where’s Daniel?
He went down to the village. He’s been looking for hinges for the shutters all morning.
It looks like the work is almost finished, doesn’t it?
Not at all! We’ve been renovating for eight months and the kitchen still isn’t done. Still, we’re getting there: every week we finish something.
And the builder? You told me there were problems.
Ernesto has been holding up the work since March: he always has something more urgent. And on top of that, a neighbour is going round the village saying we’ll never open.
That’s so unfair! And how are you coping?
Not great. I haven’t slept properly for two weeks. On Tuesday, when water came in through the roof again, I burst into tears in front of Ernesto.
That’s understandable. But look on the bright side: the bedrooms are turning out beautifully.
That’s what everyone says. To be honest, I’m tempted to call another firm for the kitchen.
Do it. My brother waited a year for a builder like Ernesto and ended up doing the kitchen himself.
Well, I’m not ruling it out. In fact, we’re about to agree a quote with a builder from the valley.
Why isn’t Daniel at the house?
What problem has the work had since March?
What is Marina thinking of doing?
—How long have you been living in the house? —Eight months, since September.
“Stone houses gradually deteriorate with the damp if nobody looks after them.”
“Ernesto has been promising the kitchen since December and still hasn’t started it.”
“I’ve heard Ernesto is going around saying you don’t pay him.”
“Since Sonia arrived, I haven’t woken up at four for three nights.”
I haven’t seen Ernesto for a week.
The bedrooms are turning out better and better.
I’ve been telling you for months.
Marina’s episode is mainly about…
How long have they been renovating?
What happened with the windows?
How did Marina react when she saw them fitted?
What did doña Remedios do?

Marina says “the windows we had been waiting for since January”. Venir + gerund in the imperfect looks from one point in the past (January) to a later past moment (Tuesday, when they arrived). With llevar the idea would be the same, but told as accumulated time: “we had been waiting for them for three months”.
time built up to now (or to a past point); never in the preterite
gradual progress; from a point in the past, often insistently
informal: here and there, often critical
sudden start, repetition, imminence, outcome

With the gerund you look at the action from inside: “llevar” counts the time, “ir” the progress, “venir” the path from the past and “andar” the informal coming and going. None of them takes a preposition. For what does not happen: llevar + time + “sin” + infinitive. And the phases (echarse a, volver a, estar a punto de) take a preposition + infinitive.
I’ve been waiting for the bus for half an hour and none have come.
Since the crisis, the newspaper’s readership has been falling.
My grandmother hasn’t left the village for a year.
With practice, I’m gradually losing my fear of public speaking.
When the clown fell over, the children burst out laughing.
Paula Ríos is training for her first half marathon. Transform what her coach says.

“Llevar” + past participle counts what has been done so far, with more still to do: “We’ve painted six of the eight rooms so far.” The participle agrees with the object. “Venir a” + infinitive is not “venir” + gerund: it means roughly, or in essence: “The renovation costs about the same as a small flat.” In the news, “venir” + gerund is very common: “Unemployment has been falling for three quarters.” And in many parts of Latin America, “estar por” + infinitive means “to be about to”: “The train is about to leave.”
“As of today we have fitted forty of the sixty planned windows.”
“Basically, the film is saying it’s never too late to start.”
“Hurry, the bus is about to leave.”
“Rents have been rising steadily since 2021.”
“—What about Carlos? —He’s looking for a job: he can’t stand his boss any more.”

You can now look at an action from inside: how long you’ve been at it, how it is progressing and how long it has been happening. In class 160 you look at it from the future, already finished: “By August we’ll have opened”, and you learn to make guesses about the past: “Ernesto must have had another emergency.” It is the natural next step: from a process under way to its end in the future.

Clara and Héctor Soler are emptying the flat of their grandmother Amparo, who has moved in with their mother. Their cousin Iván was due at six and hasn’t turned up. “He’ll be on the metro,” says Clara. You already know this use: the future here is not about tomorrow but a guess about now. Today you take the B2 step: guessing about what has just happened and about the past, and using these forms to concede a point.
A fact: Héctor has checked the time.
A guess about the present: “it must be about half past six”. No future time is involved.
Same meaning, built with the present and an adverb.
When, according to Clara, is Iván on the metro?
Which sentence states a fact rather than a guess?

Start from the sentence you would say if you knew the fact. To turn it into a guess, move the verb one step “forward”: present → simple future, present perfect → future perfect, imperfect or preterite → conditional, pluperfect → conditional perfect. The time you are talking about does not change, only your certainty.
The doorman will be having lunch: the porter’s lodge is closed (guess about now).
Iván isn’t answering. He must have left his phone at home (guess about something that has just happened).
When grandma bought the flat, she must have been about thirty (guess about the past).
The neighbours must be having building work done.
The doorman must have opened it this morning.
In this photo grandma must have been about twenty.

The conditional, besides hypotheses and politeness, expresses a guess about the past. “Serían las ocho cuando llegó” means “it must have been about eight when he arrived”. It is especially frequent with ser, estar, tener, haber and with ages, times and quantities.
It must have been about ten when Iván called last night; I was already having dinner.
There must have been over a hundred guests at that party.
The letter has no stamp: someone must have delivered it by hand.
A past fact and a likely explanation: “she must have been nervous”.
An imagined situation (“in her place, I would be nervous too”), not a guess about what happened.
What does it mean?
Last night Iván didn’t answer the phone. He must have been asleep.

Two more uses. In questions, the future and the conditional express wondering: you ask yourself, without expecting anyone to know (“¿Dónde estará?” = I wonder where he is). In statements followed by “pero”, they concede a point you don’t argue with in order to stress the opposite: “Será muy listo, pero no escucha” = he may well be clever, but he doesn’t listen.
Where can the storeroom key be? (I wonder.)
Who might the boy in the photo have been?
The flat may be old, but it gets lovely light.
Grandpa may not have had much money, but the family never went without.

In “Será antiguo, pero tiene luz” there is no real doubt: the speaker accepts the flat is old and downplays it. It equals “It’s true it’s old, but…”. That is why it is almost always followed by “pero” or “sin embargo”.
Does Héctor doubt that Iván is friendly?
Where might he have written these letters from?

“Deber de + infinitive” expresses a guess; “deber + infinitive” expresses obligation. Educated usage also accepts “deber” without “de” for guesses, but advises against “deber de” for obligation: it would sound like a guess, not an instruction.

In much of Latin America, everyday speech uses the simple future little for future plans and prefers “voy a + infinitive”. But the future of probability is alive everywhere: “¿Qué hora será?”, “Estará en camino”.
Which sentence is NOT a guess?
Grandma may have kept that photo on purpose.
When he met her, grandpa must have been working at the port.
The box is very heavy. There must be books inside.
It’s almost seven and still no sign of Iván. Where can he be?
He’ll be waiting for the bus. On Saturdays it only comes every half hour.
Or he’s forgotten it was today. Anyway, look what was in the wardrobe.
What a photo! Grandma must have been about twenty here. And this boy in uniform? Who could he have been?
On the back it says “For Amparo, with love. R.” Grandpa’s name was Julio, so it isn’t him.
He must have been a boyfriend from before she met grandpa. She kept that quiet!
He may have been very handsome, but look how serious he looks.
And judging by the bag, it must have been a postman’s uniform. There are more letters from him, all from the port.
They must have written to each other for years. And why would grandma have kept them here, between the sheets?
So that grandpa wouldn’t see them, I suppose.
(The doorbell rings.) At last! That’ll be Iván.
Well, he’d better get ready: this story is going to take a while.
Does Clara know why Iván is late?
Why do they think the young man was a postman?
What does Héctor think of the young man?
He must be at home.
Back then the street probably wasn’t paved yet.
The neighbours must have gone out to work.
Grandma may have been very shy as a young woman, but she wrote to a postman.
He must be in the lift, with no signal.
It must have been about ten when Iván arrived.
The flat may be small, but it gets a lot of light.
He passes on what the neighbour remembers and suggests asking grandma.
Who was the young man, according to the neighbour?
How old would grandma have been then?
Why didn’t grandma’s father like Ramón?
Where is Rosario’s wedding photo?
a guess about the present; in questions, wondering
a guess about something that has just happened and explains the present
a guess about a past moment; habría + participle for something earlier still (C1)
you accept a point in order to stress the opposite: no real doubt
Think of the sentence you would say if you knew, and move the verb one tense forward. If you’d rather not change the verb, use “debe de”, “a lo mejor” + indicative or “puede que” + subjunctive.
Who can that be at this time of night?
The museum was closed when we arrived; it must have been past six.
The neighbour must have watered the plants.
This restaurant may be expensive, but the food is wonderful.
The meeting may start later than planned.
Monday morning at an office. Nadia finds strange things on her desk and tries to explain them. Transform her sentences.

For strong students or spare time. “Habría + past participle” is a guess about something earlier than another past moment: “she would already have met grandpa” = she had probably already met him. You will study it in depth at C1. And a very common exclamation: “¡Será posible!” is not a guess; it shows annoyance or disbelief.
What does it express?
Which sentence is a guess about something earlier than another past moment?

You can now guess, wonder and concede by shifting the verb: “serían las ocho”, “habrá salido”, “será antiguo, pero…”. In class 162 you switch tools: instead of the verb, you work on the noun. You learn to pack ideas into noun phrases (“Iván’s late arrival”, “the discovery of the letters”), a key skill in B2 texts such as reports, news items or the post you have just written.

Marta Ríos manages an apartment building. On Saturday a pipe burst on the fifth floor, in the flat of Luis, who was away, and the water got into the kitchen of Ana, the fourth-floor neighbour. On Monday Daniel Ferrer, the caretaker, tells Marta everything. At B1 you already put the topic first. Today’s B2 step: deciding when the pronoun is compulsory, when it is advisable and when it does not appear at all.
Neutral order: the object follows the verb and is not repeated.
Ana is the topic, something already known and contrasted with Luis; the pronoun picks her up again.
“Eso mismo” is not the topic but what Daniel stresses (“that’s exactly what I told him”). No pronoun.
Did Daniel call Luis?
Why is there no “lo”?

When a definite direct object (with an article, a demonstrative, a possessive or a name) comes before the verb as the topic, a clitic must pick it up: “Ese libro ya lo leí”; “*Ese libro ya leí” is not normal Spanish. A fronted indirect object almost always takes le / les too. When you contrast two topics, the second one often goes without the verb: “a Luis, no”.
I’ve already signed the technician’s quote; the painting one, not yet (two contrasted topics).
I left the third-floor neighbours a note in their mailbox (fronted indirect object).
We cut off the water at ten; the electricity, no.
I’ve already sent the photos of the damage to the insurer.
“Did you let the chairwoman and the technician know?” “The chairwoman, yes; the technician, no.”

With the indirect object after the verb, adding le / les is grammatically optional but extremely frequent, and it is the advisable choice in speech: “Le di el regalo a Juan”. With gustar-type verbs (gustar, doler, parecer, pasar, quedar) it is always there. Leaving it out sounds more formal or written: “Entregó el premio al ganador”.
I gave Ana the insurance phone number that very Saturday (le + a Ana: the usual pattern).
We asked the neighbours for patience during the work (plural: les).
The same thing always happens to Luis (pasar: the pronoun is always there).

In conversation, both in Spain and Latin America, people very often use “le” with a plural indirect object. The norm recommends agreement, especially in writing: “Les di las llaves a mis vecinos”. In a formal email or minutes, always use “les”.
In a formal notice: “We remind all owners that the meeting is on Tuesday.”
Which sentence is the most natural in conversation?

A tonic pronoun (a mí, a ti, a ella, a usted…) as an object never appears on its own: the clitic is compulsory. “Me lo dijo a mí” is right; “*Lo dijo a mí” is not. It adds contrast (to me, not to others) or makes “le / se” clear (a ella, a usted). This is not a faulty redundancy: “a mí me” is perfectly correct Spanish.
The technician explained it to me, not to Daniel (contrast).
The spare key belonged to his sister, so I gave it back to her (“a ella” makes “se” clear).
People say the work is expensive, but I don’t think so (contrast with what others say).
With creer, pensar or opinar, the person is the subject: “yo”.
“Parecer” works like “gustar”: “a mí me parece”. Never “*Yo me parece”.

With several recipients, “se” stays the same and “lo” agrees with the thing: “Se lo dije a ellos”. In colloquial speech across much of Latin America, “Ya se los dije” is very common, with the -s marking several people. It is widespread, but the RAE does not accept it in formal writing: there, write “se lo dije a ustedes”.
“The technician didn’t talk to Ana: he told me.”
“We informed the owners of the agreement on Monday.”

Not everything placed before the verb is a topic. When the fronted element is the focus (the part you stress, correct or insist on), it carries the main stress, the verb follows straight away, the subject goes after the verb, and there is no clitic: “ESO te dije yo” (that is exactly what I told you). Typical focus words: eso, eso mismo, algo, nada, poco, and amounts of time.
That’s exactly what I was thinking: the pipe was forty years old.
Fernando must know something: he came to check it twice (indefinite focus + future of probability).
We’ve been asking for a new pipe for three whole years (the amount is stressed).
“See, Marta? That’s exactly what I told Daniel.”
In which sentence is “eso” a topic, not a focus?
I gave the spare key back to Luis’s sister.
Which sentence is correct?
Morning, Daniel. What happened on Saturday? Nobody told me until last night.
Sorry, Marta, it all happened very fast. The leak came from the fifth floor, from Luis’s place. Ana I called straight away, because water was dripping into her kitchen; Luis, no: he was away.
And how did you get into his flat? Who had a key?
His sister has a spare, so I asked her for it and she was here in twenty minutes.
Well done. And did you give Ana the insurance phone number?
Yes, I gave it to both of them, her and her husband. And I left the third-floor people a note in their mailbox.
Great. What I don’t understand is why nobody checked that pipe earlier.
That’s exactly what I told the technician in March: that it was old.
Well, I have no record of that. Did you put it in writing?
No, I only mentioned it to him. But Fernando must know something: he came to look at it twice.
OK. I’ll write the residents a notice today, and you prepare the insurance report, all right?
Agreed. And who’s going to tell Luis? He still doesn’t know anything.
Why didn’t Daniel call Luis?
Who has a spare key to Luis’s flat?
How do they share out the tasks?
I’ve already paid the technician’s invoice.
I sent the chairwoman the report yesterday.
They didn’t give it to my husband: they gave it to me.
“We’ve been asking for it for three years, Marta.”
I think the quote is expensive, but Luis doesn’t.
They checked the lift yesterday; the door, they didn’t.
She explained it to me, not to Daniel.
That’s exactly what I told the chairwoman.
She thanks her, asks for the quote and suggests a topic for the meeting.
Who did the technician give the quote to?
What does Ana ask Marta to do?
What happened with the third-floor neighbours?
What state is Ana’s kitchen in?
How long have the residents been asking for the pipe to be replaced?

In Colombia “usted” is very common, even between neighbours who know each other well. Notice “la” (= you, Marta), “agradecérselo también a usted” and “¿Me lo podría mandar a mí?”: the tonic pronoun clarifies and contrasts, always with its clitic.
a known object placed first must be picked up by a clitic; a second contrasted topic can drop the verb
a tonic pronoun as an object always comes with its clitic: contrast or clarity, not faulty redundancy
optional in theory, but the natural choice in speech; in writing, make it agree: les
a stressed, highlighted element in front takes no clitic, and the subject follows the verb

Ask yourself what comes first. A known topic needs its pronoun; a stressed focus takes none. After the verb, the indirect object almost always takes le / les, and tonic pronouns always take their clitic. In writing: “les” for plurals and “se lo… a ustedes”.
I’ve already seen that film twice.
“And the tickets?” “I gave them to my sister.”
“Did you enjoy the concert?” “I did; my partner, not so much.”
“See? That’s exactly what I told you this morning.”
In formal minutes: “We explained the problem to the residents on Monday.”
Irene is getting married in June and goes over what’s already done with her mother. Transform her sentences.

For strong students or spare time. 1. With “todo” as the object, doubling is the most natural choice: “Lo sabe todo”, “Se lo comió todo”; fronted, “Todo lo sabe”. 2. The topic can also come at the end, after a pause, as an afterthought: “Ya lo leí, ese libro”; the pronoun anticipates it (more on this at C1). 3. Register: in conversation you will hear “le” for plurals and, in much of Latin America, “se los dije”; in formal writing, “les” and “se lo”.
“My grandmother knows everything: who’s getting married, who’s moving, who’s job-hunting.”
What is the speaker doing?
In a formal email you would write…
In the residents’ meeting minutes, which sentence follows the norm?

You can now decide when the pronoun is compulsory, advisable or impossible, and adapt it to register: “les” and “se lo” in a notice, “le” and “se los” in casual speech in many places. In class 164 you keep working on register: how to request, instruct and keep a polite distance (“Could you send it to me?”, “We kindly ask you to…”), exactly what texts like Marta’s notice need.

In the Las Acacias building the front door is left open almost every night. Lucía Medina, who chairs the residents’ association, needs people to close it. But she doesn’t talk the same way to her son, to a neighbour, to the building manager or on a sign. You already know the imperative, the polite conditional and the imperfect subjunctive: today you arrange them on a scale, from a direct order to the most distant request, and learn to choose according to the relationship and the situation.
A plain imperative: closeness and authority. Within the family it is not rude in Spanish.
A question in the conditional leaves the other person room to say no: it sounds like a favour, not an order.
Usted, the conditional and the imperfect subjunctive together: the most distant, formal option, typical of emails and letters.
Impersonal: the request is addressed to nobody in particular, so nobody feels singled out.
Which sentence shows most clearly that Lucía has authority over the person?
Why does the sign avoid a direct plural command?

Spanish grammar has three main tools for softening a request: ask instead of ordering; move the verb away from the present (conditional, polite imperfect, quisiera), which creates distance much as English does with “could” or “I was wondering”; and remove the person (se, infinitive). The more tools you combine, the more distance you create.
Can you pass me the minutes of the last meeting? (A present-tense question: the everyday request between equals.)
I wanted to ask you a favour, Mr Salas. (The imperfect here refers to now: it only adds politeness.)
Punctuality is appreciated. (Impersonal: typical of notices.)

“Por favor” always works. “Anda” coaxes warmly (“come on, help me”). “¿Eh?” insists in a friendly way. “¿Quieres?” after an imperative can sound impatient, depending on intonation, much like English “will you?”.
Both are questions: what makes the first one more polite?
Which request fits a dinner between close friends?

With “importar”, an infinitive means the person you are talking to does the action (“¿Te importaría cerrar?” = would you mind closing?). “Que + subjunctive” means someone else does it, often you yourself: you are asking for permission (“¿Te importaría que cerrara?” = would you mind if I closed?). After a conditional (importaría, gustaría, agradecería, quisiera), the subjunctive goes into the imperfect.
Would you mind signing here, Mr Salas? (He signs.)
Would you mind if I opened the window? It’s very hot. (I open it: asking permission.)
I would like the residents to vote today.
Who puts the music on?
I would be grateful if you could confirm the date of the repair.

The present with an explicit subject sounds authoritarian (“Tú te vas ahora mismo” = you are going right now); without one it gives neutral directions or recipe steps. The infinitive is the form of signs and written instructions; “¡A + infinitive!” is a colloquial order to a child or a group, or a call (“¡A comer!” = food’s ready). “¡Que + subjunctive!” repeats an order that has been ignored, with impatience. “Haz el favor de…” usually sounds impatient too.
You sit down there and don’t move until I’ve finished. (Present with “tú”: an authoritarian order.)
Do not leave bicycles in the entrance hall. (Infinitive on a sign.)
I told you to come down! Come down! (Repeating an ignored order.)
With an explicit subject, in a conflict: no discussion allowed.
No subject, no conflict: neutral directions, like “you come out of the lift and turn left”.
Fill in all fields in capital letters.
Third time: “Bruno, turn the TV off!”

Usted does not signal the same distance everywhere. In Costa Rica it is very common, also among friends and in the family; in many Colombian families parents and children, or partners, use it affectionately. In Spain tú is very widespread, even in shops or with young strangers. When unsure with an adult stranger, start with usted and let them offer tú.
What is “pasame”?
In Lima, to a group of young neighbours: “Close the door when you leave, please.”
I would like the manager to come to the next meeting.
Which sentence is correct but too blunt for a stranger?
Good evening, everyone. If you’re all happy, let’s begin. Mr Salas, would you mind reading the first item?
With pleasure. The front door: several residents complain that it’s left open at night. I wanted to suggest a sign: “Please close the door when entering and leaving.”
Fine, but we’re missing the bikes issue: you can hardly get through any more. Lucía, pass me the list and I’ll write it down.
Here you go. And about the bikes, Mr Salas, I’d like you to get us a quote for putting racks in the courtyard.
Of course. For that I’d be grateful if you could send me the courtyard measurements this week.
Excuse me, Lucía, could you repeat the part about the noise? I got here late.
Of course, Mariela. It’s item two. The proposal for the noticeboard says: “From 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., respect your neighbours’ rest.”
(Coming down the stairs with a ball.) Mum, can I play in the courtyard for a bit?
Not now. You’re going upstairs to study: you’ve got an exam tomorrow.
But Mum, just ten minutes…
Bruno, I said upstairs. And the ball stays at home. Off you go and study!
(Laughing.) That reminds me of my mum in San José: “You go to your room right now.” Back home usted is used a lot, in the family too.
Why does Mariela use usted with Lucía?
What does Ernesto need in order to get the quote?
How does Lucía’s tone with Bruno change?
In the lift with an elderly stranger: which request fits?
Two friends carrying chairs: which sentence fits best?
Which text belongs on a sign?
Would you mind if I put a plant by the door?
I wanted to know when you can come and check the lift.
Would you mind if I opened the window?
I would be grateful if you could let me know the result.
Please do not leave bicycles in the entrance hall.
He follows up on the meeting and asks Lucía for several things.
What does he ask her to do with the sign?
What does he need before Friday?
How does he want to deal with the noise problem?
Until what time is Ernesto at the office?
closeness, authority or impatience; softened with por favor, anda, ¿eh?
a question leaves the other person room to refuse; the conditional adds distance
the verb moves away from the present; after a conditional, imperfect subjunctive
signs and written rules: addressed to nobody in particular

Before asking, decide who you are talking to and how big the request is. Then choose a tool: ask, move the verb away from the present, or remove the person. And keep the grammar straight: infinitive when the other person acts, “que” + imperfect subjunctive after a conditional.
I’d like to see that jacket in a medium.
Would you mind if I left my suitcase here for a moment?
Shower before entering the water.
Third time: “Laura, turn the TV off!”
We would be grateful if you could return the signed invoice.
Sara’s first week at a new office. Her first drafts are too direct, so she adjusts them to each person. Transform her sentences.

For strong students or spare time. Business letters, official notices and public announcements use formulas you rarely hear in conversation: “Les rogamos que…” (we kindly ask you to…), “¿Sería tan amable de…?” (would you be so kind as to…?), “Sírvase + infinitive” (please…, very formal, almost only in administrative texts) and the impersonal future “Se agradecerá…” (… will be appreciated). Companies also speak in the plural: “Le informamos de que…”.
What is the company doing?
Where would you expect to read this?
Which request is the most formal?

You can now adjust the distance when you ask or tell someone to do something, from “¡Que subas!” to “Le agradecería que me informara”. In class 165 you move on to longer texts: you learn the connectors that organise an explanation and those that let you refute an argument politely. It is the other half of formal register: after asking well, arguing well.

The adult-education college in Arenales holds the final of its debate league on Saturday; the motion is “Public museums should be free”. Valeria and Rubén argue for it and Clara coaches them. Each speaker has three minutes, and without structure the judges get lost. Today you build a complete exposition and learn to refute the other side.
The ideas are there, but the listener can’t tell cause from consequence or where the reasoning is going.
The connectors tell the listener what role each idea plays: first point, consequence, conclusion.
The opposing claim is quoted, rejected and answered with evidence.
Here “de ahí que” presents what follows as a result of the price.
It emphatically rejects a claim someone has made: “that couldn’t be further from the truth”.

Ordering connectors build the map of a speech: en primer lugar… en segundo lugar… por último; para empezar… a continuación (next, in a talk)… para terminar; por un lado… por otro (lado) to present two sides or two aspects. Adding connectors stack arguments: además (neutral), asimismo (formal, written), es más (the next point is even stronger), incluso (the most surprising item) and encima (colloquial, often a complaint).
First, public museums are paid for with taxes. Finally, culture shouldn’t depend on how much money you have.
On the one hand, free entry draws visitors; on the other, the museum loses income: two sides of the issue.
The opening hours are short. What’s more, the museum is closed on Mondays: a stronger point follows.
The exhibition drew all kinds of visitors, even people who had never set foot in a museum.
Ticket sales cover a small part of the budget. In addition, donations increase when entry is free.
They’ve raised the price, cut the opening hours and, on top of that, closed the café.
First I’ll explain the problem. Next, I’ll present our proposal.

Por ejemplo introduces a case; es el caso de + noun points to a real example of what you just said; pongamos por caso sets up a hypothetical one. Es decir explains the same idea in other words; o sea does the same in conversation; en otras palabras sounds more careful; mejor dicho corrects what you have just said (or rather). Según, de acuerdo con and como señala attribute an idea or a figure to a source: the speaker does not take full responsibility for it.
Some cities have already scrapped entry fees; Valdemora is a case in point, where visits doubled.
Take, say, a family of four: with tickets and transport, an afternoon at the museum costs almost fifty euros.
About a hundred people attended, or rather, a hundred and twenty: the speaker corrects the figure.
According to the council’s report, only one family in three visits the museum: the figure belongs to the report.
“Según” takes no “de” and uses subject pronouns: según tú, según ella. “De acuerdo con el informe” means “according to the report”; “estar de acuerdo con alguien” means “to agree with someone”.
The debate starts at six, or rather, at half past six: they’ve just changed it.
Entry is free for over-65s; in other words, retired people don’t pay.
According to the museum director, visitor numbers have risen by twenty per cent.

You already know así que and por lo tanto (class 116). Por consiguiente is the formal equivalent. De ahí que also introduces a consequence, but presents it as something explained by what came before, and in careful Spanish it takes the subjunctive: present subjunctive in a present frame, imperfect subjunctive in a past one. De ahí + noun is a short form: “De ahí su éxito”. To close: en resumen sums up, en definitiva gives the final verdict, en conclusión is the formal closing of a speech or essay, and “total, que…” wraps up a story in conversation.
Tickets cover only twelve per cent of costs; consequently, free entry would not ruin the museum: formal.
The museum closes at six, which is why so few working people visit it: present frame, present subjunctive.
Last year they raised the price, hence the fifteen per cent drop in visits: past frame, imperfect subjunctive.
In short, a museum that not everyone can visit is not fully public: the final verdict.
The consequence is stated as new information: indicative.
The consequence is presented as explained by what came before: subjunctive.
The museum has no lift, which is why many older people can’t get up to the second floor.
Last year the exhibition was free, hence the long queues.
Clara made us run through the speech five times. Long story short, I got home at midnight.

No es cierto / no es verdad que deny a specific claim and take the subjunctive (compare es cierto que + indicative). Al contrario follows a negated idea and asserts the opposite. Más bien replaces an idea with a more accurate one, often cautiously. Lejos de + infinitive says the result is the opposite of what was expected; the infinitive shares the subject of the main clause. En absoluto means “not at all”, never “absolutely”. Nada más lejos de la realidad rejects a claim emphatically, right after quoting it.
It isn’t true that young people don’t go to museums: last year they were half the visitors.
Free entry is not an expense; on the contrary, it’s an investment in the neighbourhood.
Far from emptying the galleries, free entry filled them with new visitors.
The problem isn’t really the price; it’s more the opening hours.
It isn’t true that free entry scares off paying visitors.
Far from cutting income, free entry increased donations.
—Do you think culture is a luxury? —Not at all. It’s a right.
The galleries have no heating, which is why so few visitors come in winter.
The museum isn’t empty; on the contrary, you have to queue on Sundays.
Valeria, you start. Three minutes, and the judges must always know which part of the speech you’re in.
We argue that public museums should be free, for three reasons. First, they belong to everyone: they’re funded by taxes; in other words, we’ve already paid for them.
Second, the price keeps many families away. According to the council survey, one in three has never visited the museum.
For example, a family of four pays almost forty euros for an afternoon. And on top of that, the museum closes at six, just as people finish work.
Careful, Rubén: “encima” sounds like an after-dinner grumble. In the final, say “es más” or “asimismo”.
Got it. And the rebuttal? The other team will say people don’t value what’s free.
Then you refute it with data: “It isn’t true that people value a free museum less: on free Sundays, the average visit lasts just as long.”
And I’ll add: “Far from devaluing the museum, free entry fills it with new visitors.” Or rather, with people who had never walked through the door.
And if they call it a waste of money: “It’s not a waste; on the contrary, every visitor spends money in the café, the shop and the neighbourhood.”
Very good. Remember too that ticket sales cover only a small part of the budget, which is why free entry isn’t as expensive as it looks.
And how do I finish? With “En conclusión”?
That’s correct and formal. “En definitiva” also works and sounds a bit more natural when speaking. What you can’t say is “total”: that’s for telling your friends a story.
Why does Clara correct Rubén?
Which argument does Valeria expect from the other team?
According to Clara, why is free entry not as expensive as it seems?
The museum closes at six. In addition, it’s closed on Mondays.
Tickets are expensive for many households, which is why so many families never go to the museum.
They say young people aren’t interested in art. That couldn’t be further from the truth: last year half the visitors were under thirty.
The final is on Saturday, or rather, on Sunday: they changed it this morning.
According to the museum’s report, donations grew by thirty per cent in the year of free entry.
Far from losing visitors, the museum gained new ones.
It isn’t true that art is a luxury.
The opening hours are very short, which is why few working people can go.
He argues that entry to public museums should not be free.
How many arguments does he announce?
According to Gonzalo, who pays if entry is free?
What does the report he cites say about free-entry days?
What example does he give to deny that the price keeps families away?
they map the speech and stack arguments; asimismo is formal, encima is colloquial
mejor dicho corrects, es decir explains; según takes no “de”
de ahí que takes the subjunctive; total, que… only in conversation
al contrario follows a negated idea; en absoluto means “not at all”

A good speech has a map: the listener knows where each argument starts, where each figure comes from and when you reach the conclusion. When refuting, quote the opposing idea, reject it and prove your point. And watch the mood: de ahí que and no es cierto que take the subjunctive.
The train arrived two hours late, which is why we missed the meeting.
They say remote work lowers productivity. That couldn’t be further from the truth: in our team it has gone up.
My brother lives in Lima, or rather, on the outskirts of Lima.
We have redesigned our website. We have also updated our rates.
It isn’t true that the new timetable harms customers.
Sandra works for a logistics company and on Monday she presents a remote-work plan to management. Her notes are too informal: you turn them into sentences for the presentation.

For strong students or spare time: the same argument changes shape with register. And two previews: de ahí + noun (“hence its success”) and a saber, which introduces a list spelling out what was just mentioned (“namely”); you will study it in class 189. For now, just recognise them.
Make it formal.
Which sentence uses “a saber” (namely) correctly?
Which sentence is correct?

You can now build a structured exposition and refute an argument. Class 166 is the B2 synthesis: you combine these connectors with concession, cause, the subjunctive and formal register to debate, explain and write a complete text. It is the natural way to round off the level.

In Monteluz, the old railway station has been closed since 2009. The council bought it two years ago and two projects have made the shortlist: a library with a youth centre, and a hotel. This is the B2 review class: you learn no new rules; instead, you practise choosing among the tools you already have to debate, explain and write a formal text on a single topic.
A passive sentence: the focus is the building and the event, not who closed it.
Which sentence reports what someone else said?

One reminder covers the whole area. If you assert something as true (creo que, es verdad que, aunque + new fact), use the indicative. If you deny it, reject it as the real reason, evaluate it, or play it down, use the subjunctive. “Por mucho que” is almost always followed by the subjunctive, especially for something that hasn’t happened.
I believe the library will attract lots of people, but I don’t think it will open before 2028: assertion vs denial.
It’s not that I’m against the hotel; it’s that I prefer a public space. The rejected reason takes the subjunctive, the real one the indicative.
However much they insist, I’m not going to change my mind.
You present the fact as information the listener may not have.
The fact is known or merely possible, and it doesn’t change your conclusion: you play it down.
I don’t think the hotel will create so many jobs.
It’s not that I don’t want tourism; it’s that the town needs something else.

Choose each half separately. The condition: imperfect subjunctive for the present (si tuviéramos), pluperfect subjunctive for the past (si hubiéramos tenido). The result: simple conditional for now (estaría), conditional perfect for then (habría estado). Mixing them is normal when a past cause has a present effect.
If we had the money, we would open the library this very year (present, unreal).
If it had been restored in 2010, a lot of money would have been saved (past, unreal).
If it had been restored in 2010, it wouldn’t be in ruins today (past cause, present effect).
Even if the works were delayed, the library would still open in spring: a hypothetical concession.
If someone had fixed it, water wouldn’t be getting in now.
If the council had a bigger budget, it would hire two librarians.

Formal texts hide the agent when it is unknown, obvious or irrelevant. Ser + participle (the participle agrees) is typical of reports and minutes; passive se agrees with the noun; impersonal se stays singular, especially before personal “a”. Relatives make the text dense and precise: preposition + el que / el cual, cuyo (agreeing with what is owned) and lo cual for a whole idea.
The project was submitted by the association in March: typical of minutes and news.
It is a building whose façade is listed, which makes the work more expensive.
The room where the youth council meets is tiny.
All the proposals were heard at the session.
A resident spoke whose grandmother used to sell tickets at the station.

Reporting in the past moves tenses back (será → sería, he hablado → había hablado) and recalculates words like hoy or aquí from your own time and place; a reported request takes the subjunctive (pidió que + imperfect subjunctive). To guess, move the verb one tense forward: hay → habrá (now), ha llegado → habrá llegado (just now), había → habría (back then).
Marta assured everyone that the committee would study both projects.
She asked us to send in our proposals in writing.
The first proposals will have arrived by now; yesterday there must have been about thirty.

Sin embargo / no obstante mark formal contrast; ahora bien accepts a point and adds a condition; en cambio sets two positions side by side; por lo tanto draws a conclusion; es decir clarifies. Use a full stop or semicolon before and a comma after, and never “pero sin embargo”.
Sergio said they would open the hotel in two years.
It must have been about ten when the last resident left.
It’s a decision on which the future of the neighbourhood depends.
The signatures were handed in at the registry yesterday.

Good evening. As you know, the station was closed in 2009 and the council bought it two years ago. Since then three projects have been submitted; today we are debating the two finalists. Ms Robles, you have the floor.
Thank you. I’ll be brief: I don’t think Monteluz needs another hotel. It needs a place where young people can study and meet.
With all due respect, it’s not that I’m against the library; it’s that the council has no money to run it. If the building had been restored fifteen years ago, it wouldn’t be in ruins today.
But however many tourists the hotel brings, it doesn’t solve anything for young people. There are forty of us on the youth council and we don’t have a single room.
And we’re not alone: our association, whose members are nearly all local residents, has collected two thousand signatures.
Two thousand signatures don’t pay for building work. Lovely as the library idea may be, someone will have to pay the heating bill. My project, on the other hand, creates thirty jobs.
In March the councillor promised us she would listen to young people before deciding. All we’re asking is that she keeps her word.
And I will. That said, let me remind you that, according to the technical report, the full refurbishment would cost about two and a half million.
We know. That’s why we’re proposing to do it in phases, which halves the cost in the first year.
It may be cheaper at first, but in the long run it costs the same.
Very well. Both proposals will be examined by the technical committee and the decision will be announced in June. Thank you all for coming.
(Quietly, to Elena.) There must be over a hundred people here, right? They didn’t expect this.
Why doesn’t Sergio support the library, in his own words?
What does Daniela remind the councillor of?
How does Elena respond to the cost problem?
I believe a hotel will create stable jobs for the area.
However many tourists the hotel brings, the neighbourhood will still have no library.
If someone had restored it in 2010, it would be a useful building today.
More than forty questions were asked at the session.
A resident spoke whose father had been the stationmaster.
The councillor asked the audience to wait their turn to speak.
They must be setting up the room for the next meeting.
It’s not that we’re against it; it’s that there isn’t enough data.
If it had been restored earlier, it wouldn’t be in ruins today.
It’s a building whose façade is listed.
She sums up the session, gives her view and encourages listeners to take part.
How many people attended, according to Daniela?
What does Daniela think of the jobs argument?
What did the councillor ask the audience to do?
What can listeners do until the thirtieth?
assert with the indicative; deny, rule out or play down with the subjunctive
choose the time of the condition and the time of the result separately; mixed conditionals are normal
hide the agent and join ideas precisely: the backbone of formal writing
report what others said or asked, and guess what you don’t know

At B2, conjugating correctly is no longer enough: you have to choose. Before each sentence, ask yourself what you want to do. The intention decides the structure, and the structure decides the mood and tense.
I don’t think the proposal is clear enough.
If they had told us earlier, we would be ready now.
The new regulations were approved by the board yesterday.
The director asked us to hand in the reports before Friday.
It’s a town whose streets flood every autumn.
A school board is debating whether to ban mobile phones for the whole school day. Rosa, the secretary, has to turn what was said into formal minutes. Transform her notes.

For strong students or spare time. At C1 your tools get sharper: “de + perfect infinitive” replaces a past condition; “habría + past participle” guesses about something earlier than another past moment; and tense agreement in the subjunctive gets more complex (ha pedido que enviemos vs pidió que enviáramos).
What does it mean?
What does it express?
What changes between the two sentences?

You have finished B2: you can debate, concede, imagine, report facts and quote others while choosing the right structure.
