The first step of C1 picks up something you have seen many times today: which subjunctive tense follows “pidió que”, “no creo que” or “aunque” when the main verb is past, present or conditional. In class 167 you learn to control that agreement in long, complex sentences.

In the newsroom of “La Plaza”, a local online paper, there is a rumour: the city government will close the Central Market in January because a technical report found problems with the roof. Gonzalo Rey wants to publish it right away; Mercedes Arias, the editor, is not so sure. You already know the basic rules. At C1 you go further: the mood depends not only on the word before it but on your stance. Are you asserting it, questioning it, passing on what others say, or taking it as given and reacting to it?
Gonzalo presents the closure as true: he is committing to it.
Mercedes does not commit herself: the closure is left open to doubt.
For her the closure is a fact, but she is not reporting it, she is reacting to it. Subjunctive does not mean “false”.
Does the stallholder doubt the closure?
Who commits more to the news?

In questions and negative commands with opinion verbs both moods can appear. The indicative is the neutral choice in questions; the subjunctive lets your doubt show. With “¿No crees que…?” you are really giving your own opinion and asking for agreement. With “No pienses / No creas que…” you reject an idea you attribute to the listener.
Do you think they’ll close it? (open question) / Do you really think they’ll close it? (you doubt it)
Don’t you think it’s too early to publish it? (= I think it is.)
Don’t think I’m saying this to annoy you. (I reject the idea you might have.)
Don’t imagine it’s that easy to confirm a source.
What does Mercedes think?
What does the reader’s question reveal?

With verbs like saber, darse cuenta de, enterarse de or olvidar, the content is a fact the speaker takes for granted. Negating the verb does not negate the fact (“I didn’t know the report was public” still means it is public), so the indicative is the normal choice. With emotion verbs and “el hecho de que”, the fact is also true, but you are evaluating it, so the subjunctive is used.
I didn’t know the report was already public. (It is.)
I didn’t notice the recorder was off. (It was.)
I’m surprised nobody read it earlier. (A fact, evaluated.)
The fact that the report is public doesn’t change anything yet.
Has Alba read the report?
Choose the sentence where the speaker does not commit to the content.
You pass on someone else’s claim as a claim. It does not say whether you believe it.
A “que” clause at the start is being evaluated, and “no significa que” denies the conclusion: both in the subjunctive.
What does it mean?
You assert the fact as information: “although the report is worrying…”.
You grant the point without debating it: it is not what matters. Class 170 goes deeper.
Which sentence shows the most distance on the speaker’s part?
Maybe the councillor will reply today.
I find it regrettable that some media outlets published the rumour as fact.
It’s clear the roof has problems.
Mercedes, I’ve got the headline: “Central Market closes in January”. Shall we put it on the website?
Hold on. Don’t you think it’s a bit early? Nobody has confirmed it.
The stallholders themselves are saying it: they say the technical report recommends closing the building.
I’ve read the report, and it doesn’t say it has to close in January. It talks about repairing the roof “in the coming months”.
Sure, but they’ll probably close it before summer. Nobody fixes a roof with the stalls open.
You may be right. But until they confirm it, it’s a hypothesis, not a headline.
I understand why the stallholders are nervous. And from what a councillor told me yesterday, I gather they are already looking for temporary premises.
So the closure is certain, right?
Not necessarily. The fact that they’re looking for premises doesn’t mean they’ll close in January. Perhaps they’ll do it in stages.
Okay. Don’t think I’m after an easy headline, eh? I didn’t know Alba had the report.
I know, don’t worry. We’ll run “City government considering closing the Central Market”, and in the text we separate what we know from what may happen.
Maybe we’ll get an official answer today. I’ll call the councillor.
What exactly does the report say, according to Alba?
Why doesn’t Mercedes want the first headline?
What does Alba know from a councillor?
I can confirm that the report has been public since yesterday, although there is still no decision.
Maybe the government is holding a press conference this afternoon. Does anyone know anything?
Which version shows the most doubt?
I didn’t notice the recorder was off until the end of the interview.
It hurts me that people think the market is no longer any use.
I didn’t know the report was public. (It is.)
I understand why the stallholders are worried.
The market may close in spring.
Maybe the councillor will call us today.
What is the main idea?
What does Mercedes present as a solid fact?
What does the councillor think?
What does Mercedes regret?
What does she promise the listeners?
the speaker asserts something or passes on someone else’s claim
negating saber or darse cuenta does not deny the fact
doubt, possibility, or a fact you react to rather than report
the mood selects the meaning of the verb: noting vs sympathising or regretting

Before choosing the mood, ask yourself what you are doing with the content. Asserting it, passing it on or taking it as given: indicative. Doubting it, denying it, seeing it as merely possible or reacting to it: subjunctive. Where both moods are possible, the choice is not right or wrong: it fine-tunes your stance.
I bet the bus is late again; it’s already quarter past nine.
I’ve just found out your brother is in town.
I’m sorry you had to wait so long at the doctor’s.
My sister told me to take an umbrella because it’s going to rain.
A video having a million views doesn’t mean it’s true.
Another rumour is going round the language school in your neighbourhood: it is moving to another building. Rewrite each sentence with the stance given.

For strong students or spare time. Three uses typical of more careful speech: “no niego que” takes either mood (the indicative concedes the point more openly); “yo nunca dije que + subjunctive” denies that you ever claimed something; and the fixed phrase “que yo sepa” (as far as I know) is always in the subjunctive.
Which one more clearly admits the other person is right?
Gonzalo defends himself: “I never said the closure was certain.” What is he doing?
As far as I know, nobody has confirmed the date.

You now use mood to show your stance towards what you say: asserting it, passing it on, doubting it or evaluating it. In class 169 you apply the same logic to relative clauses: “Buscamos un local que tiene patio” (a specific place you know exists) versus “Buscamos un local que tenga patio” (any place that meets the condition). It is the natural next step: mood keeps showing what you take as real and what you do not.

Every year the Valdeluz public library runs a short-story prize. The rules are written months before any text arrives, so they talk about people and stories nobody knows yet: “Anyone with questions can write to the secretary.” Today the jury has to choose the winner. In this class you fine-tune something you already know: the mood of a relative clause depends on whether you identify the referent or speak of whoever fits the description.
Three specific stories that really exist: the speaker can point at them.
Any story that may arrive late in the future: no specific text, and perhaps there will be none.
Describes how things are actually done here, presented as an established fact.
The subjunctive presents the stories as not identified: whichever, if any.
The indicative refers to a real, identified group of stories.

At C1 the key point is that “el que”, “quien”, “lo que”, “todo el que” or “cuanto” can take either mood. The subjunctive says: I am not picking out a real referent, I mean whoever or whatever turns out to fit.
Whoever wins will present their book at the October fair.
Anyone who wants to attend the ceremony has to book a seat.
All texts submitted, however many, will be read by all three jury members (formal).
Whoever confirms attendance before Friday will receive the invitation by email.
“Whatever title you like; you’re the secretary.”
“Everything said from now on will be recorded in the minutes.”
A proverb defines a type of person as a timeless truth; its wording is fixed, always indicative.
Both are correct: the indicative refers to a real class of people, the subjunctive to anyone who might know her.
Looks ahead to a possible case (invitation, rule, plan): only the subjunctive works.

In proverbs the relative clause stays in the indicative even when the main verb is future, because they define a type of person rather than a future case: “Quien bien te quiere te hará llorar” (those who truly love you will make you cry). Change the mood and it no longer sounds like the proverb.
Proverb: forewarned is forearmed (lit. he who warns is no traitor).
“Anyone who wants to come is welcome; there’s room for everyone.”
In general statements in the present both moods are possible; only the nuance changes.

“Eres la única persona que me entiende” says something about a real person in front of you. “La única persona que me entienda…” talks about someone you cannot identify and who may not exist. Same adjective; what changes is what you know about the referent.
With superlatives both moods are possible: the subjunctive emphasises the judgement.
“It’s the first time I’ve been on a jury.”
They haven’t voted yet: the only story that goes through will be the one that convinces all three.
You deny that such a place exists: subjunctive.
The story exists and you know which one; you only deny having read it.
A rhetorical question expecting “nobody”: it questions whether such a person exists.
“I don’t know of any publisher that publishes single short stories.”
The story exists and is identified; the negation does not affect it.
“Is there anyone in this room who has never dreamed of writing a book?”
Any participant who submits more than one story will be disqualified.
Proverb: grasp all, lose all (lit. who embraces much, squeezes little).
Before we vote, a practical matter: three stories came in after the deadline. What do I do with the ones that arrived on Monday?
The rules are clear: “Stories arriving after the 30th will be excluded.” I’m sorry for them, but they go back.
A shame. Right, back to business. For me, “La casa del faro” is the best story I’ve read in this round.
Well, I’m going with “Agua de marzo”. It’s the best thing I’ve read in years, and I’m not exaggerating.
And “Los inquilinos”? The ending is very polished.
It’s well written, but there’s nothing in it that surprises me. Anyone who has read the classics of the genre already knows that ending.
And if there’s a tie between you and Rodrigo? What do I put in the minutes?
You’ll put whatever we decide, of course. But first I want to win Rodrigo over.
Go ahead. Mind you, whichever story wins gets published as a book, so it has to hold up in print.
“Agua de marzo” can take that and more: nobody who reads it will forget it. No objections? Silence means consent.
I’m not silent: I consent. It has a voice I haven’t found in any other text.
Noted. And it’s the first time the prize has been decided unanimously.
What happens to the three late stories?
Why does “Los inquilinos” fail to convince Rodrigo?
How does the vote end?
Stories exceeding three thousand words will be excluded.
Anyone who wishes to receive feedback from the jury must tick the box.
I’ve left the stories that came in late on the table, in case you want to look at them.
I’ve been on juries for twenty years and I can’t remember a year with so many entries.
Whichever author wins will have to present the book at the October fair.
Anyone who needs more time should ask for it in writing.
There isn’t a single story that has fully convinced me.
It’s the best ending I have ever read (emphatic).
Anyone who arrives late will wait outside.
What is the main purpose of Elena’s talk?
What will happen to late entries?
What does she say about this year’s late entries?
Which new feature is she most excited about?
Why does she quote the proverb?
a real referent you can point to
whoever, whatever, if any: rules, plans, invitations
existence denied or questioned; a “no” about a known referent is not enough
they define a type of person; their mood never changes
both correct: stating or emphasising; “la primera vez que” takes the indicative

The word does not choose the mood: “el que”, “quien”, “lo que” or “único” take either. What decides is what you know about the referent: if you can identify it, indicative; if it is whoever, whatever, or may not exist, subjunctive. Proverbs are the fixed exception, and with superlatives you choose between stating and emphasising.
Employees who wish to work from home on Fridays must give a week’s notice.
Yesterday I finally met the neighbour who lives on the third floor.
There’s no pharmacy in this area that’s open at night.
Proverb: he who laughs last laughs best.
It’s the first time I’ve come to this city and I already love it.
The Valdeluz cultural centre runs a traditional cooking contest. This year’s is over; now you write next year’s rules based on what happened.
For strong students or spare time: relative clauses you will meet in legal texts, official notices and careful prose.
Relative “cuanto” means “everything that”, in a formal register.
An old legal form (future subjunctive): today you would write “pague”.
Which is the correct formal version for a notice?
With superlatives both moods are correct; the nuance changes.

You now choose the mood according to what you know about the referent. In class 170 you apply the same logic to concession: “aunque es” versus “aunque sea”, where the subjunctive can even take up a known fact in order to play it down. It is the natural next step: mood as a tool for how you present information.

Inés Valdés runs a small theatre company about to open “La fábrica”, a play about the closure of the city’s old textile mill. The council’s Culture office offers the main theatre for the opening on one condition: cut the final monologue, in which an old mill worker accuses the authorities of the time. When the producer reminds her that the council is paying, Inés replies with a subjunctive: she grants the fact and denies it any weight. Today mood and tense become tools for arguing.
The indicative presents the concession as news: the journalist did not know the council lends the theatre.
The subjunctive takes up a fact already on the table and dismisses it: “fine, so what?”. It sounds like a comeback.
The imperfect subjunctive pushes the case into the unlikely; the main clause goes into the conditional.
The pluperfect subjunctive rewrites the past: it did not happen, and even if it had, the outcome would be the same.
She accepts the fact but refuses to let it count in the argument; the subjunctive here is not doubt.
Which sentence talks about something that did not happen?

Grammars call this the “polemical” subjunctive. The fact is true and both speakers know it, so the subjunctive is not about doubt: it signals that you are not offering information but picking up the other person’s argument in order to discard it. With the indicative the same fact is asserted or brought to the listener’s attention. Both are correct; what changes is the move you make.
Julián’s argument is repeated almost word for word and set aside: a typical polemical subjunctive.
Inés grants the length the director mentioned and denies that it matters.
Said to someone who has not seen the play: the shortness of the scene is presented as information.
The fact is asserted: you put it in the foreground and still draw the line.
Your friend offers “he’s my boss” as an excuse; you accept it and take its force away.
Even if she does know half the city’s theatre people, she is not going to decide our script.
Although the dress rehearsal is closed to the public, you are welcome to come.

The further you move down the ladder, the further from reality the concession is. The present subjunctive covers what may happen (or a known fact you dismiss); the imperfect subjunctive, what you see as unlikely or what is unreal now, with a conditional in the main clause; the pluperfect subjunctive, a past that did not happen, with a conditional perfect (or a simple conditional for a present effect).
An unlikely offer: even then, not a single line would go.
Unreal in the present: they do not have a theatre of their own.
A past that did not happen: they refused, and accepting would not have helped.
Past condition, present effect: the main clause can use the simple conditional.

“Incluso si” and the less frequent “aun si” mean “even if”. They take the tenses of “si”: present indicative for an open case, imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive for a hypothetical one, and never the present subjunctive.
Even if we were offered a ten-country tour, we would not change the ending.
Even if the insurance report arrives late, we will rehearse at the mill.

Reduplicated concessives repeat the same subjunctive verb (“digan lo que digan”, whatever they say) or add “o no” (“quieras o no”, like it or not). In the past the verb moves to the imperfect subjunctive. “Por + adjective + que” without “muy” is a more polished variant of “por muy… que”. And “por más que” takes the indicative when you report something that really happened.
Whatever they say at the council, the monologue stays.
Like it or not, the opening is on the 14th.
Uncomfortable as the scene may be, it is necessary: more polished than “por muy incómoda”.
After the verb, “como sea” means “one way or another, at any cost”.
Try as we might (and we really did), we could not get another date at the main theatre: a real past fact in the indicative.
The company opened in May, whatever the critics said.
However far away you live, you have to come to the opening.

“Así + subjunctive” means “even if”: “I won’t cut it, even if they pay me three times as much”. It is emphatic, common in everyday speech in parts of Latin America and literary elsewhere. With the indicative, “así” goes back to meaning “this way”: “¡Y así me pagan!” is “and this is how they repay me!”.
What does “así” mean here?
Carmen spoke at the meeting even though she knew she would be fired.
Even if we had asked the Teatro del Puerto for help, we would not have made it in time.
Whatever they do, Inés is not cutting the monologue.
I’ve just talked to Sonia Paredes. She won’t budge: if we want the main theatre, Carmen’s monologue has to go.
Right. Well, it may be the only big theatre in town, but I’m not cutting it.
Wait, there’s something you don’t know: although the tour is almost settled, three theatres will only confirm it if we open at the main theatre.
Seriously? I didn’t know that. Even so, however much we need the tour, without that monologue it’s a different play.
I know, and even knowing that, I had to tell you. Besides, however hard I tried to explain, Paredes wouldn’t read the whole script.
Of course: even if she’d read it, she’d have asked for the same thing. It’s not the scene that bothers her; it’s what it says.
And what if they offered us another council venue? Even if it were smaller, it would save the tour.
Look, whatever the council says, the monologue stays. I’m not cutting it, not even if they offer me the main theatre free for a whole year.
OK, OK. What if we open in the old mill? The building has no seats, but the acoustics are superb.
I love it! It’s where it all happened. And even if it rains, we can perform in the main hall.
Like it or not, we’ll have to tell the press. And Paredes.
Invite her to the front row. Let her hear the whole monologue, whether she likes it or not.
What new information does Julián give Inés?
According to Inés, what really bothers the Culture director?
What do they decide in the end?
Although the play is about a mill, it is really about a family.
Sure, it may be harsh, but it is the best scene in the play.
Even if they offered us three times as much, we would not sell the rights to the play.
Even if she had read the script, she would have asked for the cut anyway.
Even if they take away our funding, we will open in May.
Long as it may seem, the monologue lasts only four minutes.
Whatever they say, the monologue stays.
Even though she knew, the director kept quiet.
Even if they had asked us, we would not have cut anything.
She has reservations about the play, yet calls it the opening of the season.
Who was in the audience?
What surprised her during the monologue?
What weakness does she find in the play?
What advice does she give listeners?
the indicative presents the concession as information; “y eso que” works the same way, after the main clause
the polemical subjunctive: you grant a fact both speakers know and deny it any weight in the argument
the further from reality, the further down the tense ladder; “incluso si” never takes the present subjunctive
closing formulas: no option, amount or degree changes the outcome; concessive “así” is emphatic and partly regional

Before choosing the mood, ask yourself what you are doing with the fact. Reporting it: indicative. Picking it up to dismiss it: present subjunctive. Imagining it as unlikely or unreal: imperfect subjunctive. Rewriting the past: pluperfect. “Aunque es” and “aunque sea” can both be right about the same fact; what changes is the move you make.
He may be your brother, but he can’t use your car without asking.
Even if they paid me double, I would not work on Sundays.
Even if it rains tomorrow, the match will go ahead.
Whatever they say, I am not moving.
Even if I had known earlier, I could not have helped you.
Rocío coaches a local football team. After a tough season she talks to her players. Rephrase what she says with today’s structures.

For strong students or spare time. When you report in the past what someone said, the concession follows the sequence of tenses: the present subjunctive becomes imperfect subjunctive. Here “aunque lloviera” is not an unlikely case, just the reported version of “aunque llueva”. The same shift applies to the polemical subjunctive and to reduplicated concessives.
Julián said that even if they lost the funding, they would do the tour.
Inés said that, director or not, Paredes could not censor a script.
Marta repeated that, whatever they said, she would do the monologue.

You can now use the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive to say that nothing would change the outcome. In class 171 you take the same tense ladder into hypotheses: remote conditions, counterfactual pasts and rhetorical “who would have thought!”. It is the natural next step: from a concession that imagines another world to a hypothesis that uses it to persuade.

Nuria runs production for a summer theatre festival in a mountain village near Madrid. Tonight’s open-air premiere is threatened by storms, and the lead actress’s flight from Mexico City is late. You already handle the basic si-clauses; today you widen the toolkit: other conditional connectors, remote hypotheses, and counterfactual phrases that people use in conversation to complain, warn or push back.
An open, realistic condition: Nuria treats rain as a genuine possibility and states the plan.
Same future event, but the speaker distances herself from it: less likely, or simply imagined.
Llegar a pushes the event further away: “if it ever came to that”, “if, by some chance, it actually rained”.
Gabriel thinks the delay is very unlikely but has a backup plan.
Nuria sees the storm as very likely: which form fits her plan?

Si is neutral. These connectors say what kind of condition you mean: a contingency plan, an exception, a requirement, a bare minimum, or a warning. All of them take the subjunctive when they introduce a condition.
Should the power go out, there are torches under every row: a contingency plan.
We start at ten unless there’s a queue at the entrance: an exception.
The town hall lends us the chairs provided we return them on Monday: a requirement.
Valeria would act on any stage as long as they let her open tonight: the one thing that matters to her.
Adela’s volunteers will stay to the end, except in one case.
The councillor offers a fallback: which mood follows en caso de que?
With the indicative it is temporal: “whenever, every time”.
With the subjunctive it is usually a condition, “provided that”. (It can also mean “whenever” about the future: Siempre que vengas, tendrás entrada.)
With the indicative, como gives a reason: “since, because”.
With the subjunctive it is a condition with a warning or threat: “if he doesn’t turn up, (watch out)…”. Very common in speech.
With the indicative, salvo que means “except for the fact that” and reports something real; with the subjunctive it means “unless” and introduces a possible exception.
Nuria jokingly warns Valeria. Which connector takes the subjunctive here?
What does siempre que + indicative mean here?
In an if-clause, llegar a + infinitive means “if it actually came to that, if by any chance”. In the present it can also refer to the past in colloquial speech: Si llego a saberlo… = had I known.
If you happen to see Valeria before I do, tell her I’m waiting in the dressing room.
If the show ever had to be called off, we would refund the tickets.
Colloquial: had I known the flight would be late, I’d have brought her over on Thursday.
Gabriel complains after a long rehearsal in the sun. What does he mean?
Which version suits a written report?

¡Ni que…! is an exclamation meaning “anyone would think…!”, “it’s not as if…!”: it rejects an assumption that the situation implies. It takes the imperfect subjunctive (same time) or the pluperfect (earlier).
Twelve more spotlights? Anyone would think we were putting on a rock concert!
Look at your face! Anyone would think you’d seen a ghost in the dressing room!
Valeria protests: anyone would think she had only learnt her lines yesterday.
Gabriel gives advice: which form follows yo en tu lugar?
Mateo lends his torch on one condition.
Thanks to Adela’s tarpaulin, the costumes stayed dry.
Nuria, have you seen the forecast? There’s a forty per cent chance of a storm tonight.
I have. If it rains, we move the show to the sports hall; I’ve already sorted it with the councillor.
And he’s just letting us have it, no strings attached?
As long as we leave it as we found it, yes. Unless there’s a basketball game, of course.
A game on a Saturday at ten at night? Anyone would think it was the league final!
Go on, laugh. If it actually starts raining halfway through the second act, I don’t know what we’ll do with two hundred people in the square.
Relax. Adela has twenty volunteers ready. If it weren’t for them, I’d be more nervous than you.
What worries me is Valeria: her flight is delayed. If she isn’t here by eight, we won’t get a lighting rehearsal.
If I were you, I’d call her now. And if she were delayed even further, I’d ask the driver to wait for her at the terminal.
I already have. It would have been better to bring her over on Thursday, like you said. And the sound technician doesn’t arrive until six… Had I known, I’d never have agreed to move the premiere.
Come on, it’ll be fine. I’ll help with whatever you need, as long as you stop looking at the sky every five minutes.
On what condition does the councillor lend the sports hall?
Why does Gabriel laugh at the idea of a basketball game?
What does Nuria regret?
The councillor sets a requirement for using the sports hall.
Her volunteers would do anything to see the play for free.
If the generator should fail, use the spare one in the van.
Nuria refuses: anyone would think they had an opera budget.
Her colleague advises her to see a doctor first.
If I were you, I wouldn’t sign that contract.
I’ll wait for you in the square, provided it doesn’t rain.
If it hadn’t been for Adela, we would have got lost.
She sets out the storm plan and thanks him.
What does Nuria admit about Valeria’s travel plans?
What happens if it rains before the interval?
In what case would they leave the square after the interval?
What condition does the councillor set?
What annoys Nuria?
unlike si, these connectors always take the subjunctive and specify the kind of condition
with the indicative they report facts (every time, because, except that); with the subjunctive they set conditions or warnings
the further from the present tense, the more remote the speaker presents the event
conversational formulas: the present for an unreal past (mainly Spain), and exclamations that reject an assumption
advice formulas take the conditional; quisiera and hubiera + participle are standard in the main clause, the -se forms are not

Ask three things. What kind of condition is it? Then use the matching connector and the subjunctive. How likely do I think it is? Choose si + present, si + imperfect subjunctive or si llegara a. Am I chatting or writing formally? Keep the rhetorical present for friends.
I’ll lend you my beach flat as long as you water my plants.
If you leave the door open again, the cat will get out: a warning.
Sleep at the office? It’s not as if they paid me double!
If it hadn’t been for the GPS, we’d have got lost in the forest.
It’s almost impossible, but if I ever won the lottery, I’d buy a house on the coast.
Lorena is organising her sister’s wedding at a country estate in late August. Her friend Pablo helps and gives advice. Write their sentences.
For strong students or spare time: politeness nuances, indicative uses and a structure you will study in class 172.
What changes between quisiera and quiero here?
What does salvo que mean with the indicative?
Which is the most formal version?
How do como si and ¡ni que…! differ?
What does de llover correspond to?

You can now set precise conditions with connectors and the subjunctive, grade probability and recognise conversational counterfactuals. In class 172 you compress the condition into a non-finite form: de + infinitive and the gerund. It is the natural next step: the same conditional logic in a more compact, careful register.

An Ibero-American libraries congress opens in Valparaíso tomorrow. The organisers keep expressing conditions without «si»: reduced forms with an infinitive, a gerund or a fixed phrase. You will learn to understand them, produce them and spot when the full si-clause is the better choice.
The full if-clause: neutral, clear, valid everywhere.
More compact and more careful in tone; typical of written texts and formal speech.
The standard formula for notices, rules and instructions.
“De seguir así” works like an if-clause, not a concession or a cause.
“En caso de + noun” belongs to written instructions and notices.

De + infinitive replaces a si-clause. The simple infinitive covers both real conditions (si + present) and hypotheses about now (si + imperfect subjunctive); the main verb tells you which. The perfect infinitive (de haber + participle) looks back at a past that did not happen.
If registrations keep up like this, we’ll need more volunteers: a real, open possibility.
If we had a bigger budget, we would invite speakers from Brazil: a hypothesis about now.
Had we booked in March, we would have got the big auditorium: a past that did not happen.
If we hadn’t signed with the usual printer, we would have the badges today: a past cause with a present result.
If Raúl knew the truth, he wouldn’t be so calm.
Had we spotted the sound problem earlier, we would have fixed it in time.

Without an expressed subject, the infinitive is read as sharing the subject of the main clause. If the subjects differ, put the subject after the infinitive; if that sounds forced or ambiguous, keep the si-clause.
If Raúl arrives late, he’ll miss the last bus: one subject, Raúl.
If the flight is delayed, Raúl will pick the speakers up: two subjects, the second one placed after the infinitive.
If I were you, I’d change the order of the panels: a careful, slightly formal version of «yo que tú».
If you arrive late, Carmen will be annoyed: «de llegar tarde» would mean Carmen is the one arriving late, so «si» is clearer.
Who is late, according to the sentence?
If she confirms, we’ll include her in the panel: which version is standard?

A gerund placed before the main clause can work as a condition, but only when the main clause points to the future, to a hypothesis or to something generally true. With a past event, the same gerund reads as means, time or cause.
If you follow the green arrows, you’ll reach room B in two minutes: typical of instructions.
If they worked in pairs, the volunteers would deal with people twice as fast.
If you book with the congress code, the hotel works out cheaper: a general condition with an impersonal result.
Future result: the gerund sets a condition.
Past event: the gerund means “as/when she was leaving”, not “if”.
In which sentence does the gerund act as a condition?
“Visto así” means “seen this way”, a fixed conditional formula.

Formal texts love de + infinitive, en caso de and instruction gerunds. Speech prefers si, though de ser así, de haberlo sabido, con + infinitive and yo que tú are common. When in doubt, a plain si-clause never sounds wrong.
Should there be any changes to the programme, we will announce them on the screens.
If you don’t sign up before twelve, you can’t eat in the congress canteen.
Had we known the wifi would fail, we would have printed the slides.
Which sentence says it most clearly and naturally?
Carmen, shall we go over the guide? The printer closes at six.
Let’s do it. First: what did you write about Thursday’s dinner if it rains?
“In case of rain, dinner will be held in the Pacific room.” And below: “If you are unable to attend, please let the secretariat know.”
Very formal, but perfect for a guide. Bad news: the badges won’t arrive until nine tonight.
At nine? Had I known, I’d have ordered them from the university printer. At this rate we’ll open the congress without badges.
Relax. If I leave at eight, I’ll be back before ten with all the boxes.
And the volunteers? If they don’t know the building, they’ll send people to the wrong rooms.
Giving them the map this afternoon will do. And if necessary, we’ll do a walk-through tomorrow at half past seven.
If I were you, I’d do it today: tomorrow we won’t have a minute to spare.
You’re right. Come to think of it, a walk-through today will save us a lot of scares tomorrow.
One last thing: shall I write “should the badges arrive late, they will be handed out in the lobby”?
Better not: the guide is for attendees, they don’t need to know. If I were you, I’d leave it out.
What happens to Thursday’s dinner if it rains?
Why is Carmen worried?
What does Raúl advise Carmen to do?
Should you have any problems with the wifi, please go to the information desk.
Had he confirmed, Dr Rivas would have been on this morning’s panel.
If you read the programme carefully, you’ll see there’s a gap at four.
Without showing your badge, you won’t be able to enter the auditorium.
Judging by the queues, the eleven o’clock break is too short.
If it weren’t for Raúl, we wouldn’t have badges today.
If you follow these instructions, you won’t have any problems.
In case of fire, do not use the lift.
Practical instructions for tomorrow, plus thanks to Raúl.
Which door should volunteers use if they arrive after eight?
Where will the reception desk be if it rains?
What must they not do without checking the list first?
What would Carmen have done had she known about the supplier?
the infinitive has no tense of its own: the main verb tells you whether the condition is real, hypothetical or past
an unexpressed subject is read as the main-clause subject; a different one goes after the infinitive, or you keep si
the gerund is conditional only before a future, hypothetical or general result; participle formulas are fixed
en caso de for notices, sin for negative conditions, con for minimal ones; en caso de que takes the subjunctive

Before dropping si, ask three questions: is it really a condition? Is the subject shared, or can I place it after the infinitive without ambiguity? Does the register call for it? Reduced forms bring precision to formal writing; si and yo que tú sound more natural in conversation.
If the train leaves on time, we’ll arrive before lunch.
Had I read the small print, I wouldn’t have signed that contract.
If you practise a little every day, you’ll speak fluently by June.
Which sentence cannot be reduced to de + infinitive?
Should you have any problem with your booking, call reception.
Ester Robles leads a hiking group in the Andes and is writing the mountain hut rules. Reduce her conditions.
For strong students or spare time: the same constructions can express concession or time, or appear in literary conditionals.
“Con ser tan experta” here means “expert as she is”: a concession.
“A no ser por” is a slightly more formal “de no ser por”: “if it hadn’t been for”.
With a past event, the gerund means “as we were coming down”.
Which version sounds most natural in a casual voice message?

You can now express conditions precisely and choose the form by subject and register. Class 173 takes the next step: showing how certain you are and where your information comes from (apparently, it seems, maybe, it is possible that…). Conditions and hypotheses share that territory of what is not yet certain, so it is the natural next step.

Monday, 9 a.m., in the newsroom of a local online paper. Since the weekend a rumour has been going round: the hundred-year-old Teatro Olimpia is said to be closing and the building being sold to a hotel group. The editor asks the reporter the two questions this class teaches you to answer through grammar: how sure are you, and where does the information come from?
A checked fact: no marker at all. Plain indicative is the strongest statement Spanish has.
An inference drawn from visible evidence: “it’s clear they aren’t planning…”, “they obviously aren’t…”.
Reported information: “apparently”, “reportedly”. The speaker passes it on without vouching for it.
Only the bare statement is certain: the rest is an inference and a piece of hearsay.
Which sentence passes on what someone else said?

A bare statement is the most certain one. Adding “seguro que” or “sin duda” reveals that this is your own conclusion, however firm, not a checked fact. And “seguramente” means “probably”, not “surely / certainly”.
Gabriel is holding the official letter. Which sentence best reflects what he knows?
I doubt the councillor will confirm anything before the council meeting.

Spanish has several ways of saying that information comes from your own inference. “Tener que + infinitive” is the most confident deduction (“it has to be”), “deber de + infinitive” a solid one, the future a conjecture. “Se ve que”, “por lo que veo” and “a juzgar por…” explicitly point to the evidence; “parece que” works both for inference and for hearsay.
Two architects are measuring the foyer: they’re obviously planning a refit.
From what I can see, nobody has updated the website since October.
Her office door is locked: the councillor must have gone out.
Only the director has that key. It has to have been him.
“There has to be someone inside”: the evidence leaves no sensible alternative.
“There must be someone inside”: a solid conclusion, still open to another explanation.
“They’re clearly rehearsing”: the conclusion is presented as obvious from what can be seen.
Gabriel sees costume boxes at the theatre door. Which sentence signals that he infers it from what he sees?
What does “tener que” express here?

Reportative markers pass information on while making clear that you are not its source: “al parecer”, “según parece”, “parece ser que” (apparently, reportedly), “por lo visto” (from what I hear), “dicen que / se dice que / se comenta que” (people say). “Se supone que” presents what is said or expected, and often hints that reality may not match. All take the indicative.
Apparently the actors found out from a union message.
It seems the offer came in September.
The theatre was supposed to reopen in September, but it’s still closed.
As far as I know, nobody has signed anything. · By all appearances, there’s no hurry either.
It’s hard to believe nobody has told the theatre company.
What does it imply?

In news writing the conditional marks information the paper has not confirmed and attributes to a source: “El ministro habría dimitido” = reportedly, the minister has resigned. The simple conditional covers present facts (estaría negociando), the compound one past facts (habría dimitido). It is not the writer’s guess, unlike the conditional of probability from class 161 (“serían las ocho”), and it is not a hypothesis (“would have resigned if…”).
According to party sources, the minister resigned this morning (unconfirmed).
According to the regional press, the deal has reportedly been closed since Friday.
The hotel group is said to have offered about three million, according to the same source.
Someone else’s unconfirmed claim: “has reportedly been approved”.
The speaker’s own estimate: “it must have been about nine”.
An unreal situation: “it wouldn’t have closed”.

Very common in the press on both sides of the Atlantic. Academic grammar describes it as the conditional of rumour or unconfirmed information, but several newspaper style guides advise against it as a gallicism that leaves unclear who stands behind the claim. A clearer option is to attribute and use the indicative. In conversation, “al parecer, ha dimitido” is far more natural.
Headline: “The mayor has reportedly accepted the offer.” What does it mean?
According to an anonymous source, the hotel group already has the plans for the new hotel (unconfirmed).
I don’t think the councillor has all the information.
Which sentence is correct?
Gabriel, the Olimpia story is already in every messaging group. What have we got?
Not much that’s confirmed. Apparently the council wants to sell the building to a hotel group.
“Apparently” isn’t a source. Who says so?
A sound technician at the theatre. And according to someone at the council, the sale has reportedly been closed, but they won’t give their name.
So for now it’s a rumour. And the culture councillor?
She isn’t answering. I went to her office and it was locked: she must have gone out; apparently she went to a meeting elsewhere.
And anything you’ve seen yourself?
Yes: the website has no shows after December, and this morning two architects were measuring the foyer. They’re clearly preparing something.
Now that’s something. There has to be a file in the register. As far as I know, a sale like that has to go through the full council.
Most likely they’ll take it to the December meeting.
Maybe, but I doubt the councillor will confirm it before then. So carefully: what we’ve checked, in the indicative; what we’re told, with its source.
And do we run “Olimpia reportedly to close in January” as the headline?
What has Gabriel checked himself?
Why isn’t “por lo visto” enough for Lucía?
What does Lucía think the councillor will do?
Most likely the councillor will appear at a press conference tomorrow.
There’s no doubt the building needs refurbishing: the foyer ceiling has been leaking for years.
As far as I know, the sale hasn’t been approved yet: it isn’t in any minutes.
The stage lights are still on at midnight: some company must be rehearsing.
“Apparently the hotel group has already bought the bar next door.”
As far as I know, nobody has signed anything yet.
The theatre obviously isn’t selling tickets any more.
According to union sources, the staff have reportedly received an offer.
She keeps the confirmed closure apart from the unconfirmed sale.
What is confirmed, according to the station?
How does she present the hotel group’s offer?
What has councillor Ibarra done?
What does she consider unlikely?
how sure you are: each step of the scale has its mood
your own inference from a clue, or the limits of what you know
you pass the information on without vouching for it
news register for unconfirmed, attributed facts; style guides often advise against it

Ask yourself two questions: how much do I know, and how do I know it? Then pick the marker. The mood depends on the marker, not on how sure you feel: “lo más probable es que” takes the subjunctive, “seguramente” the indicative.
The museum is unlikely to open on Sunday afternoons.
Apparently the flight is two hours late: a passenger in the queue told me.
The floor is wet and smells of bleach: they’ve obviously just cleaned.
Headline: “Company reportedly to cut two hundred jobs, according to the union.”
It’s hard to believe there are still people who don’t recycle.

At a software company there are rumours of a merger. Natalia, from the communications team, is revising the internal newsletter draft so that confirmed facts and hearsay are clearly separated. Transform her sentences.

For strong students or spare time. Three more reportative markers. “Supuestamente” distances the speaker and often hints at doubt. “Presuntamente / presunto” belong to legal and news language: they avoid treating as proven what no court has yet decided. And in informal speech in many Latin American countries, such as Mexico or Colombia, “dizque” means “so they say”, often with doubt or irony.
Why “presunto” (alleged)?
What does the speaker express?
Which sentence puts most distance between the speaker and the claim?

You can now grade certainty and signal your source, and you have seen that “habría dimitido” can be a press rumour. In class 174 you focus on the conditional perfect to guess about events before another past moment, to estimate (“there must have been about twenty people”), and to tell that guess apart from hypotheses and rumours.

Friday, 11 p.m., in the middle of a storm. Three friends reach the mountain cabin they have rented: the door is open, the key box is empty, there are still embers in the fireplace, two half-drunk coffees and an unfinished note. The owner had promised the house would be clean by six. Next morning everyone tries to reconstruct what had happened before they arrived: that is today’s grammar.
A fact: they had already left. The pluperfect states it as known.
A guess about that earlier past: “they must have already left”, “they’d probably gone by then”.
An unreal result: “we would have seen them” (but we didn’t).
“When we arrived, the fire must have already gone out.” What does the speaker actually know?
Which sentence describes something that did NOT happen?

To turn a known fact into a guess, Spanish moves the verb one step: present → simple future, present perfect → future perfect, imperfect or preterite → simple conditional, pluperfect → conditional perfect. The new piece at C1 is the last one: “habría + participle” for a guess about something that happened before another past moment.
By eleven, the village shop would probably have closed already.
When we found the note, who could have started writing it? (wondering about an earlier past)
There must have been about twenty people in the village bar that night (simple conditional of impersonal “haber”).
Someone must have driven by here this morning already.
When we arrived at eleven, the other guests must have left a good while before.

Besides guessing, the conditional perfect describes a past result that never happened (“I wouldn’t have done it”), what someone said would be finished by a past deadline (reported speech of the future perfect), a polite or softened wish about the past (“we would have preferred…”), and a concession (“they may well have been in a hurry, but…”). In the press it can also mark an unconfirmed report, which you saw in class 173.
With a little more light we would have seen the fallen tree. · I wouldn’t have done it.
Rosario said she would have cleaned the cabin by six (her words: «Para las seis habré limpiado»).
We would have preferred you to let us know before we set off (a polite complaint).
They may well have been in a hurry, I won’t argue with that, but they left the door open.
“The plumber assured us he would have replaced the pipe by Monday.” Which use is this?
“I would have gone to the dinner, but my phone died and I couldn’t find the address.” Did the speaker go?

Only when the meaning is counterfactual (something that did not happen) can “hubiera + participle” replace “habría + participle” in the main clause: both are correct and both are common. With the other uses (guessing, reported future, concession, rumour) only “habría” works. The “-se” form “hubiese” belongs in the if-clause; in the main clause careful usage avoids it.
If we had known about the tree, we would have driven up the other road.
The same meaning: “hubiera” in the main clause is equally correct and very frequent in speech on both sides of the Atlantic.

After conditional “si” (if), never a conditional. After “si” meaning “whether” in an indirect question, the conditional is perfectly correct: “I don’t know whether she would have come up.” “Si habría” in an if-clause is heard in some areas, such as northern Spain, but standard usage rejects it.
Which sentence is wrong in standard Spanish?
By the time we finally found the spare key, someone must have used up the hot water.
An open reproach: “you didn’t tell us and you should have.” Can sound harsh in a formal relationship.
A softened complaint framed as an unfulfilled wish: “we would have preferred you to let us know.”
“We would have liked to know earlier, though we understand”: the complaint is barely felt.

Like the future (“Será muy listo, pero…”), the conditional perfect can concede a likely past fact only to say it doesn’t change things: “Habría estudiado mucho, pero suspendió” = granted, he may have studied hard, but he failed. Fixed companions: “no lo discuto”, “no digo que no”, “de acuerdo”, followed by “pero”.
The caretaker may well have cleaned the stairs on Monday, I’m not saying he didn’t, but by Saturday they were covered in mud.
The driver may have done that road a hundred times, but that night he got lost.
“They may have had their reasons, but leaving the door open isn’t right.” What is Bruno doing?
I would have liked you to tell me yourself, not your sister.
Which sentence is correct?
They must have gone back to the city already.
Celia texted me something about an open door. What happened last night?
We got here at eleven, in the storm, and the door was open. Rosario had told me she would have cleaned by six and would leave the key in the box.
Well, no key and no cleaning. The previous guests must have left already, but not long before: there were still embers in the fireplace.
And what time did they leave?
No idea. Around nine, maybe. There were two half-drunk cups of coffee.
And an unfinished note: “Thanks for everything, Rosario. We’re leaving early because…” They must have had some urgent call.
Or they’d heard the weather forecast and didn’t want to get stuck.
Could be. They may have been in a hurry, fine, but closing a door takes a second.
I certainly wouldn’t have left it open. And what does Rosario say?
She isn’t answering. This morning I left her a very polite message: “We would have preferred you to let us know.”
And if we had left at four, as I kept saying, we would have arrived in daylight.
Anyway, never mind. By the way, I wonder who left these muddy boots by the door?
What do the friends know for sure?
What had Rosario promised?
Why does Darío say “habrá dejado” rather than “habría dejado”?
When we went in, someone must have switched it on shortly before.
Right now Rosario isn’t answering: she’s probably on the road with the workmen.
They said they would have brought the firewood by Wednesday.
If I were you, I wouldn’t have booked without reading the small print.
When we arrived, the guests must have already left.
Rosario said she would have cleaned the cabin by six.
The guests may have been in a hurry, but they didn’t close the door.
She reconstructs the night, apologises and offers something in return.
According to Rosario, when did the other guests leave?
What does Rosario think happened to the key?
Why didn’t she clean the cabin as promised?
What does Rosario offer?
a guess, one tense “forward”: “habría + participle” for before another past moment
something that did not happen; “hubiera” is equally correct in this use only
what someone said would be done by a deadline, reported later
softening a complaint; granting a likely fact and setting it aside

Find the reference point first: now → “habrá”; a past moment → “habría”. Then check the use: only for unreal events can “habría” become “hubiera”. And after conditional “si”, always “hubiera / hubiese”, never “habría”.
When the teacher came in, the students must have already finished the exam.
If you had told me in time, I would have helped you move.
The construction company promised it would have finished the bridge by March.
“He may well have studied hard, but he failed.” What does the speaker mean?
My sister isn’t answering: she must have left her phone in the car.
An archaeologist is writing up the dig of a two-thousand-year-old house by a river, abandoned in a hurry. Rewrite her notes with the right use of the conditional perfect.

For strong students or spare time. More ways of looking back at a past that didn’t happen. “¡Me lo hubieras dicho!” (you should have told me!) is a common reproach everywhere. “¡Haberlo dicho!” with the infinitive is colloquial and very frequent in Spain. “Podrías habérmelo dicho” is more neutral. “¡Quién lo hubiera dicho!” is no reproach at all: “who would have thought it!”
“You should have woken me!” What does Irene express?
What does “¡Quién lo hubiera dicho!” express here?
Which version suits a formal email best?

You can now place an event in time and say how much you know about it: a guess, something that never happened, or what someone had foreseen. Class 175 looks at actions from the inside: how long they last, whether they start, continue, end or repeat. It is the natural next step for telling the past with all its nuances.

It’s closing night at a regional newspaper. A young reporter has his first front page, and the style editor’s corrections are mostly about gerunds: some express manner, others time or cause, and two of them are uses that the norm advises against. You’ll learn to read those meanings and decide when a gerund is the best choice.
Manner: the gerund sits right after the verb and describes how the action was done.
Time: placed first and followed by a comma, it frames the main event as happening at the same time.
Cause: the gerund gives the reason for a real fact, much like «como» + a finite verb.
A gerund in front of a real, past fact usually reads as its cause.
Which gerund tells you HOW something was done?

A gerund inside the predicate, with no pause, usually answers “how?” or “by what means?”. A gerund placed in front and set off by a comma builds a frame for the whole sentence: when, why, under what condition, or despite what. The gerund has no tense or person of its own, so the context decides.
Ramiro got the shot by climbing a ladder: means, how he managed it.
Óscar answered the editor’s questions with a smile: manner.
As he was leaving the town hall, Óscar got Lucía’s call: a time frame.
If we speak plainly, we’ll understand each other better: a condition, because the result lies in the future.
Óscar got the interview by insisting for weeks: what is the gerund doing?
Which gerund sets a time frame?

The same front gerund can be read in three ways. Before a real fact it gives the cause; before a future, conditional or command it sets a condition (you saw this in class 172); with aun or incluso it becomes concessive: “even though”.
Since she lives downtown, Lucía doesn’t need a car: cause.
If he lived downtown, Óscar wouldn’t need a car: condition, signalled by the conditional.
Even though he lives downtown, Ramiro drives everywhere: concession.
Even earning less, Óscar prefers local journalism: incluso works like aun.
In front, the gerund takes the subject of the main clause: I was the one walking.
After a perception verb and its object, the usual reading is that Luis was walking; if you mean yourself, move the gerund to the front.
A future result turns the gerund into a condition.
Aun without an accent means “even”: a concession.

Without an expressed subject, the gerund shares the subject of the main clause. If it has its own subject, that subject goes after the gerund, never before it. For a clearly earlier action, use the compound gerund: habiendo + past participle.
With me there, nobody dared criticise the headline: the gerund has its own subject, placed after it.
With ten minutes to go before the deadline, a breaking story came in.
Having read all three versions, Lucía chose the shortest one: a finished, earlier action.
Having checked with the editor-in-chief, Óscar changed the headline.
While I was away, they shut down the culture section: where does the subject go?
Having checked the text three times, Óscar sent it off calmly.

Two uses are common in the press and in official texts, but the RAE advises against them. The gerund should not report an event that happens clearly later (use y + finite verb), and it should not describe a noun the way a relative clause does (use que + finite verb). The second is often a calque of English -ing.
Five hours separate the two events: a gerund can’t carry that later event, so use y + verb.
The gerund is classifying the box, which is the job of a relative clause.
Typical of official prose and advised against: «que regula».
In job ads, the relative clause takes the subjunctive because the person is not yet identified.
Which sentence follows the norm?
Why does this sentence need correcting?

A participle (or adjective) set off at the start describes the subject and agrees with it. Like the gerund, it is read through context: a state that explains the action (often cause), a condition, or with aun / aunque a concession.
Tired, Lucía went to bed: her state explains why.
Worried about the headline, Óscar called the editor-in-chief: a cause.
Properly edited, the story would have made the front page: a condition, shown by the conditional perfect.
Exhausted as they were, the photographers stayed until the end: a concession.
Convinced, the editor-in-chief decided to change the front page.
What does the participle tell you here?
Lucía, have you got my story? It’s my first front page and I’m a bundle of nerves.
I’m reading it. Let me start with the good part: “Residents came in applauding.” You can picture it.
And the first paragraph? “The market closed for works in March, reopening its doors yesterday.”
Not there. Six months pass between the two events, and a gerund can’t report what comes later. Write “closed in March and reopened yesterday”.
OK. And the bit about the mayor? “Walking through the aisles, she greeted the stallholders.”
Perfect: both things happen at once. What I’d change is “a stall selling flowers”: better with a relative clause, «que vende».
Sorry, Lucía. Front-page caption: “Stallholders celebrating the reopening.” Shall I leave it?
Leave it: in a caption that describes the scene, the gerund is accepted. What I’d never write is “Photo showing the market”.
I thought so, but having seen your corrections last week, I’d rather ask.
Same here. Even knowing you’ll check it, I’m scared of getting it wrong.
Relax. With me on duty, not a single typo gets through. Mind you, I’m off at ten: worn out as I am, I can’t even see the commas any more.
Then I’ll give it one last read. If I work fast, you’ll have it in ten minutes.
Why does Lucía correct the first paragraph?
What does Lucía decide about Ramiro’s caption?
Why is Lucía leaving at ten?
The interviewee answered with a smile, without looking at her notes.
With the editor-in-chief at the meeting, nobody dared to criticise the front page.
Even though it knew the story was false, the website published it.
If he spent one more hour on it, Óscar would finish the feature.
The paper ran the interview on Monday and printed a correction on Wednesday.
Even though she knew, the councillor said nothing.
The residents came into the market singing.
With me there, nobody criticised the front page.
Several valid readings, plus two uses to avoid.
What does «siendo festivo» express in Lucía’s example?
What does the concessive example mean?
Why is the market sentence wrong?
Which exceptions does Lucía accept?
What is Lucía’s final tip?
inside the predicate, the gerund tells you how or by what means
in front, the gerund frames the sentence; the main clause decides between cause and condition, and aun or incluso make it concessive
a gerund’s own subject goes after it; the compound gerund marks an earlier action
don’t use a gerund for a clearly later event or to classify a noun
a fronted participle agrees with the subject and is read through context, like the gerund

Ask three questions about every gerund. When does it happen: at the same time, before or after? Does it modify a verb or a noun? Who performs it? If all three answers are clear, context will do the rest.
If you lived downtown, you wouldn’t need a car.
I’m looking for an apartment with a terrace.
The train left late and reached Mérida at midnight.
Exhausted after the deadline, Lucía went straight home.
Clara Fuentes is writing the wall labels for an exhibition on a 19th-century painter. Correct or transform her sentences.
For strong students or spare time: ambiguity with perception verbs, the consequence gerund, legal language and gerunds that organise discourse.
With perception verbs, the gerund after the object usually describes the object.
Consequence gerunds are a grey area: widely used, but y + verb is the safe choice.
In legal language, «considerando que» introduces the grounds for a decision.
«Hablando de…» works like “speaking of…”: a fixed discourse link.

You can now read gerunds and participles through context and avoid the uses the norm advises against. Class 177 goes one step further: participles with their own noun (absolute constructions) and how to shorten subordinate clauses in formal writing. It applies today’s logic to participles with their own subject.

Formal written Spanish rarely strings together clause after clause with cuando. It condenses them: a participle agreeing with its own noun (an absolute construction), an infinitive after tras or al, or simply a noun. Today you learn to reduce clauses in these three ways, to expand them back, and to recognise when reduction does not work.
Fully explicit: tense, person and the link word are all there. This is the normal choice in speech.
Compact and formal: the participle agrees with its noun and presents the action as completed before the main one.
The action turned into a noun: the densest option, typical of reports and news writing.
What does the sentence tell you about the order of events?
Where would you expect this sentence?
Which action was already over when the rest happened?
The meeting was over before the visit: a typical sequence in minutes and reports.
Revisadas agrees with las cuentas (feminine plural), not with la junta.
Una vez makes the time reading explicit; with a future main verb it means “once the agreement has been signed”.
The agent can be kept with por, as in the passive.
Once the minutes had been read, the secretary closed the session.
Which absolute construction is not possible?
Una vez is followed straight by the participle; una vez que needs a finite verb, in the subjunctive when it refers to the future. Blending the two (*una vez que firmado) is a common mistake.
What does the sentence mean?
Once the shelves have been installed, we’ll bring the books.
Formal and written; the noun of the absolute need not match the main subject.
Neutral register: fine both in a report and in conversation.
Stresses immediacy; especially common in Spain.
After studying the plans, the architect approved the design.
Because the permits did not arrive, the reopening was delayed by a week.

An absolute construction carries no tense or mood, so expanding it forces you to choose. A past main clause gives a past indicative; a future one requires the subjunctive after cuando (cuando concluyan). A causal reading becomes como + indicative.
Which reduction keeps the meaning?
Expand the absolute construction.
Given the results, the committee renewed the contract.
Rodrigo, the report has everything, but three paragraphs in a row begin with “when it was approved”, “when it was signed”, “when it was finished”…
Well, that’s how I tell it. What do you suggest?
Condense it. Instead of “when the project was approved”, write: “With the project approved, the mayor’s office opened the tender.”
Fine. And the second one? “When the contract was signed, work began.”
To avoid another participle: “After the signing of the contract, work began.”
And can I write “The team having worked all summer, the roof was finished”?
That doesn’t work: trabajar is an activity with no result you can present that way. Better: “After working all summer, the team finished the roof.”
Got it. Here’s another: “As the funds had run out, we requested an extension.”
“The funds exhausted, an extension was requested.” Careful: agotados is plural because of los fondos.
And the ending? I’ve got “when the furniture is installed, we’ll open”.
“Once the furniture is installed, the library will open to the public.” That said, the rest is very good.
Thanks. I’ll send it to Beatriz when I get in tomorrow; given how this has gone, I’d rather reread it tonight.
What is wrong with Rodrigo’s draft?
Why does Paula reject that sentence?
With the year’s accounts approved, the board moved on to the second item on the agenda.
Once the registration period has closed, no more applications will be accepted.
Once the shelves are up, we’ll start putting the books in place.
As soon as the reopening was announced, the library’s phone didn’t stop ringing.
After reviewing the technical report, the mayor’s office authorised the reopening.
Once the contracts are signed, work will begin.
After the budget was approved, the tender was opened.
When the time comes, the mayor’s office will make a decision.
What is the news item about?
Why didn’t the work stop in March?
What will the history students do?
What changes in the opening hours?
What does the station recommend at the end?
An action completed beforehand. The participle agrees with its own noun. Only transitive or change-of-state verbs.
Use it for activity verbs and when the subject is shared; al + infinitive can take its own subject.
The most compact option; durante covers actions still in progress.
When expanding, you must choose the tense, the mood and the link word again.

Three questions before you condense: is the action finished beforehand, is the verb transitive or a change-of-state verb, and can the link word go without losing the meaning? Three yeses: a participle agreeing with its noun. Otherwise, tras + infinitive, a noun, or the ordinary clause.
With the introductions made, the moderator gave the floor to the first speaker.
Which sentence is not correct?
Once your application has been sent, you will receive a confirmation email.
The meeting was tense. That said, a reasonable agreement was reached.
Lucía Peña, secretary of a residents’ association, has to turn her notes into the official minutes. Help her condense each note into the formal style of minutes.

With aun, the absolute construction becomes concessive (“even with the work finished…”). Administrative and legal rulings open with absolutes such as vistos los informes (“having examined the reports”). Two well-known proverbs are absolutes too: remove the cause and the problem goes away; every law has its loophole.
Even with the budget approved, the mayor’s signature was missing, so work did not start.
Municipal ruling: “Having examined the technical reports, the reopening of the building is authorised.”

You can now condense clauses with participles, infinitives and nouns. Class 178 focuses on the infinitive: whose is the unexpressed subject (te prometí llamarte: I call; te permito salir: you go out), when you need que + a finite verb instead, and how to avoid ambiguity. It follows naturally: today you saw that tras + infinitive works when the subjects match; next you learn exactly when they do.

A notebook has gone missing from a foundation’s archive in Valencia. The people reconstructing what happened use many infinitives with no visible person. Today you learn to work out who performs each infinitive, and when Spanish needs «que» and a conjugated verb instead.
One subject for both verbs: Spanish uses the infinitive, exactly like English “wants to check”.
Two subjects: Spanish cannot say «quiere Marcos revisar»; it needs que + subjunctive (English “wants Marcos to check”).
Verbs of permission, prohibition and obligation let the infinitive take the object (le = Marcos) as its subject.
Nadia needs to consult the original notebook for her thesis.
For now, Elena would rather Nadia worked with the photocopies.

The main verb decides who performs the infinitive. With wanting, trying, promising or claiming verbs it is the main subject; with verbs of influence, causatives and perception it is the object; with gustar-type verbs it is the dative; after an impersonal expression it is “anyone”. If none of these fits, use que + a conjugated verb.
Same pattern, opposite readings: with prometer I come back; with permitir he or she comes back.
With advice verbs both options are correct and mean the same; the que-clause sounds a little more explicit.
The person who is obliged or forbidden is the one who signs or enters.
With costar, the dative (me) is the one who understands; after an impersonal phrase, the subject is anyone.
Who is going to return the key?
Same structure, different verb: who returns the key now?

After ver, oír, sentir or notar, the person or thing you perceive is the object of the main verb and the subject of the infinitive. The infinitive presents the whole event; the gerund shows it in progress; que + indicative reports a fact you noticed or found out.
Rafael heard someone crying on the stairs: the infinitive presents the event as something he perceived.
Marcos saw her come out of the workshop with a folder: la is both the object of ver and the subject of salir.
In the small hours the guard heard the store door open: with things, the pronominal infinitive (abrirse) is common.
From the window, Elena saw the restorers arrive.
Which meaning does the infinitive version express?

The simple infinitive and gerund are simultaneous with the main verb or later than it. To present an action as already completed, use haber + participle (infinitive) or habiendo + participle (gerund). Pronouns attach to haber or habiendo.
Sorry for being late: the lateness is already over. «Siento llegar tarde» is what you say as you walk in.
Denying a past act needs the compound form; the simple one turns it into a habit or a promise.
The porter was dismissed for having lied: por + compound infinitive gives an earlier cause.
Having finished the inventory, Elena called a meeting: typical of reports and formal narration.
Rafael admits he didn’t write down the time of entry on Saturday.
Having signed the contract, the restorer started work.

After a preposition (al, antes de, por, sin…) the infinitive can carry its own subject, placed after the verb. It is correct and common with al + infinitive; with antes de or para, que + subjunctive is usually more natural.
When Marcos opened the box, we saw it was empty: the infinitive has its own subject, placed after it.
Before you arrived, we had already called the guard. Both versions are correct; the que-version is the more frequent one.
Your having said it in front of everyone was the right move: a nominal infinitive clause with its own subject.
When I arrived, the room was already closed.
The constant ringing of the phone bothers me: what kind of form is it?
I advise you to rest a little.
I am sending you the map so that you can find your way.
Morning. Sorry I’m late: the tram got stuck on the bridge. What’s going on? It’s strangely quiet.
The 1887 notebook isn’t in its box. Marcos has just opened it and it’s empty.
And I remember locking the cupboard on Friday at seven, before switching off the lights. Elena, you saw me lock it.
I did. The odd thing is something else: Rafael, the guard, says he heard the store door open on Saturday.
On Saturday? But they don’t let anyone in at weekends.
Not without authorisation. But this Saturday the board let the restorers work, and with boxes coming and going for the exhibition, who knows.
That’s why, Nadia, I’d rather you didn’t mention anything to the other researchers yet.
Of course, I won’t say a word. But just so I understand: did anyone take the notebook out of the store last week?
Well… yes. On Thursday Clara, the restorer, asked me to let her photograph a few pages in the workshop.
And you let her take it without writing it in the log?
Only for an hour, and she brought it back that same afternoon. Having seen her put it in the cupboard, I didn’t check again.
Well, now we know where to start. Nadia, come with me to the workshop. Marcos, I need you to go through Clara’s photos and Saturday’s log.
Why is Nadia late?
Who was in the archive on Saturday?
What mistake does Marcos admit?
I wanted to photograph the pages before setting up the exhibition.
The board makes us sign for every document that leaves the store.
Clara insists she didn’t take the notebook out of the workshop all week.
Rafael says he heard someone go up the service stairs.
When Elena got to the workshop, Clara already had the photos on screen.
Elena made all of us sign the log.
Nadia states that she did not see anyone in the store.
Having gone through the photos, Clara found the clue.
The notebook turned up in the wrong box, and the procedure will change.
Where was the notebook?
How did Nadia find it?
What did Rafael hear on Saturday?
What changes in the procedure?
with wanting, promising and claiming verbs, the main subject performs the infinitive; another subject needs que
with influence, causative and perception verbs, the object is also the subject of the infinitive
an infinitive’s own subject goes after it; «para yo entender» is regional and colloquial
the compound forms present the action as completed before the main verb; habiendo is formal

For every infinitive ask two questions. Who does it? The main verb decides: the subject, the object, or anyone; if none fits, use que + a conjugated verb. When? Simultaneous or later takes the simple form; earlier takes haber + participle.
The neighbours denied making any noise that night.
My parents never let me go on holiday on my own.
From the balcony we watched the parade go by.
I hope to have finished my thesis before the summer.
When the guests arrived, the music started.
Lucía Pardo, a secondary-school teacher, is writing up notes on a class trip to the botanical garden. Make them more compact.
For strong students or spare time: the infinitive in formal prose, a verb that misleads, and sentences that can be misread.
“I believe I have understood the problem”: a correct, formal choice.
Who is leaving early?
Why might this sentence be misread?
Some infinitives have become full nouns and can be plural.

You can now tell who performs each infinitive and place earlier actions with haber and habiendo. Class 179 keeps building long, precise sentences, this time with relative pronouns: cuyo, el cual, lo cual. It is the natural next step for writing reports and careful texts that stay clear.

Gabriel, a local historian, has written the history of the textile mill the town grew up around. He based it on hours of recorded interviews, and it shows: some sentences work in speech but not in a book. His editor, Adriana, is revising it with him. This class takes you to C1 relative syntax: choosing the exact relative after a preposition, knowing when «el cual» fits, using «cuyo» inside long sentences and highlighting information with cleft sentences.
After short prepositions, «el que» is the everyday choice; «el cual» sounds more formal.
After longer prepositions and prepositional phrases, careful prose prefers «el cual»; with «según» it is almost the only option.
Without a preposition, «el cual» only appears in a non-restrictive clause between commas; in speech you would use «que».
Long prepositions need article + relative, and «según» almost always takes «el cual».
In everyday speech, plain «que» is the usual choice in a non-restrictive clause.

After a preposition you need an article: el que or el cual (both agree with the antecedent). «El cual» is stressed and can bear the weight of two-syllable prepositions and longer phrases, so careful writing prefers it there. These are preferences, not strict rules — except that a long preposition can never be followed by bare «que».
The table on which the 1933 agreement was signed stands in the entrance.
Leonor opened a school thanks to which hundreds of children learned to read.
It was a collective effort without which the building would not have been rebuilt.
The building burned down, as a result of which the company announced its closure (lo cual = the whole event).
The workers’ estate was the neighbourhood around which village life revolved.
Which option is wrong? «Desde que» means «since» (time), not «from which».
The boiler failed, after which the dye house burned down in minutes.
Restrictive: only the workers who lived there paid it. Without a preposition, only «que» is possible.
Non-restrictive: all the workers lived there; the clause just adds information. «Que», «quienes» or «los cuales» are possible.

«Que» does not show gender or number, so the sentence is ambiguous. «La cual» points to the daughter, «el cual» to the foreman. Because it carries its own article and stress, «el cual» can also refer back to a noun that is several words away.
A non-restrictive clause applies to the whole group.
«El cual» agrees with «el nieto» and rules out Rosario as the antecedent.
Restrictive clause without a preposition: only «que».

You already know «cuyo». At C1 it moves inside long sentences: the preposition goes before the whole «cuyo + noun» group, including personal «a» (a cuyo padre). To talk about part of a group, use a quantifier + «de los cuales / de las cuales» (de los que is also possible).
Rosario, in whose house I found the photos, is ninety-four.
She is the teacher whose father I interviewed in 2019 (personal «a» before cuyo).
Two hundred families worked there, most of whom lived by the river.
«Tener miedo a» → «al que». Doubling with «le» is fine; bare «que» + «le» is not.
«Cuyo» agrees with the possessed noun, «archivo».
Partitive: number + «de las cuales», with no extra «de ellas».
It was the weavers who asked for the school, not the management.
It was in the old warehouse that Gabriel found the first rulebook.
1978 is the year in which the mill closed for good.
«A friend whose house flooded»: careful writing uses «cuya».
That is how the estate got running water.
Gabriel, I love the chapter, but some sentences sound like a recorded interview. Look: “Rosario, that her mother started at the mill at fourteen, showed me the photos.”
Yes, that’s how she said it. Shall I put “Rosario, whose mother started at the mill at fourteen…”?
Exactly. And here: “the weaver that they gave her the medal”. You hear it a lot, but in a book it grates.
So, “the weaver to whom they gave the medal”. Anything else?
