Yes: “I interviewed the foreman’s daughter, who lived by the river.” Who lived there, her or her father?
Him, the foreman. Then I’ll write «el cual vivía junto al río» and the doubt is gone.
Perfect. Now the commas: “The workers who lived on the estate paid a token rent.” Did all of them live there?
No. I spoke to twelve families, four of which lived there; the rest walked in from Valdecañas. So, no commas.
Good point. In the fire section you have two very short sentences: “A report survives. According to that report, the fire started in the boiler.”
I’ll join them: “A report survives according to which the fire started in the boiler.” And then: “The company announced the closure, as a result of which the workers organised themselves in shifts.”
Very good. And the ending is weak: “The workers rebuilt the building.” It’s the key idea of the chapter; make it stand out.
“It was the workers who rebuilt it, and it was then that the mill came to belong to everyone.” And I’ll close with the warehouse: “That is where the town’s books are launched today.”
Why are some sentences unsuitable for the book?
Who lived by the river?
What happened after the closure was announced?
The 1905 rulebook survives, under which weavers were not allowed to talk during their shift.
The looms, which arrived from England in 1898, are still in the main hall.
This is the Albarracín family, with whose money the school was built.
It was the mothers on the estate who set up the nursery.
1932 was the year the dye house burned down.
It was then that the workers decided to rebuild the building.
That is the reason why the mill closed.
What is the main purpose of his talk?
Where did most of the families live?
What did Leonor do?
What did he find at Rosario’s house?
What does he think of Rosario’s saying?
After long prepositions and phrases, prefer «el cual»; never bare «que» after them
Without a preposition «el cual» needs commas; its gender and number remove ambiguity
Careful writing avoids «que su» and resumptive pronouns, common as they are in speech
In cleft sentences «ser» agrees, and the relative matches what you highlight: person, place, time or manner

Before writing a long relative clause, ask three questions: which preposition does the original sentence need? (long → el cual); am I selecting or adding? (no commas / commas; «el cual» without a preposition only with commas); what do I want to highlight? (cleft sentence). And when you turn speech into writing, change «que su» and «que le» into «cuyo» and «al que».
The council passed a rule under which bars must close at one.
That is the bridge under which the goods train used to pass.
I met a writer whose novels have been translated into twelve languages.
It was my grandparents who bought the village house.
We invited forty people, ten of whom came with children.
Another town is refurbishing its public library and asks you for a short text for its website. Your notes are in short sentences: combine them or put them in focus.
For strong students or spare time: cleft sentences where the highlighted element has a preposition, and agreement points even native speakers hesitate over.
Careful writing repeats the preposition: «Fue con Rosario con quien…». Bare «que» is common in speech in much of Latin America but avoided in careful prose.
Careful prose prefers «es por eso por lo que»; «es por eso que» is very widespread, especially in Latin America.
With «quien», third person is the recommended agreement; «quien lo redacté» is also heard and accepted.
«La cual» agrees with «carta», the distant antecedent, and rules out the bank and its manager.

You now know that the verb’s preposition travels in front of the relative, and that casual speech sometimes drops it. In class 180 you continue with prepositions required by verbs, now before the conjunction «que»: «me acuerdo de que» versus queísmo, and «pienso que» versus dequeísmo. It is the natural next step: the same educated norm, in another type of clause.

Bogotá, Cuaderno Urbano, a small local news site. Daniela has interviewed the founder of a community library, and before publication the head of copy-editing goes through the piece with her. The trouble is a handful of «que»: some are missing a «de», others have one too many.
«Pensar» meaning «to hold an opinion» takes a direct object: no preposition.
«Acordarse» is always followed by «de» (acordarse de algo), and that «de» stays in front of «que».
Some verbs accept both constructions, so both are correct with «que» too.
Teresa remembers that the first book was donated by a neighbour.
Teresa thinks the neighbourhood needs more cultural spaces.

A «que» clause fills the slot of a noun phrase. If the verb, adjective or noun that governs it needs a preposition before a noun («me acuerdo de la fecha»), it needs the same preposition before «que». If it doesn’t, adding one is wrong.
Same preposition with a noun and with a clause.
«Insistir» takes «en», so the clause keeps «en».
«Opinar» takes a direct object: no preposition.
Daniela realised the recorder wasn’t working.
It’s obvious that the residents want the library.
The volunteers trust the local council will renew the agreement.
With these expressions the «que» clause is the grammatical subject, and subjects never take a preposition. Turning the sentence round makes this easy to see.
Which sentence follows the careful norm? «Comentar» takes a direct object.
As readers get to know the project, more donations will arrive.
It worries me that the premises are so small: the clause is the subject.
A direct object or a subject clause: no preposition.
The pronominal verb or the adjective governs «de», and the clause keeps it.
Teresa is convinced the neighbourhood will stand up for the library.
Even though it was raining, over a hundred residents came to the opening.
Teresa stressed that the library isn’t only for children.

Both are heard in everyday speech across Spain and Latin America, including among educated speakers. Dropping the preposition is widespread and barely noticed in speech; adding an extra «de» tends to be more stigmatised. The academies recommend avoiding both in careful usage, and that is the only standard tested here.
Is it correct? «Avisar» accepts both patterns.
Rereading the text, Lucía noticed the photographer’s name was missing.
The residents agreed they would paint the premises in June.
Which sentence follows the careful norm? I’m sure they will publish it.
Which sentence follows the careful norm? She told us she couldn’t come.
Daniela, I’ve read the interview with Teresa. I love it, but I noticed a few «que» we should check before it goes out.
In Teresa’s quotes? I think we should respect the way she speaks.
In the direct quotes, yes. If she said it that way, we leave it: it’s her voice.
So the problem is in the part I wrote?
Exactly. In the outlet’s own voice, «insistir» needs «en».
Oops, that’s true. And «she was sure the local council would back her»?
Same thing: «sure of that». But in the headline you wrote «es seguro de que»…
There the «de» is extra! «That is certain»: no preposition.
Perfect. The rest is fine: «avisar» works with or without «de», and so does «antes (de) que».
What a relief. I’m glad you spotted it and not the readers.
Don’t worry: it’s clearly your best interview. And the fact that Teresa speaks the way she does gives the quotes real force.
Then I’ll fix my part and make sure Óscar gets the final version before noon.
What do they do with Teresa’s direct quotes?
Where does Daniela have an extra «de»?
Why doesn’t Lucía correct it?
These sentences come from Daniela’s own part of the article, the outlet’s voice. Sort them: is a preposition missing, is there an extra «de», or is the sentence already fine?
The founder said she was convinced the project would succeed.
Teresa told us the children come every afternoon.
Even though the funds arrive late, the library has never closed.
Looking at the front page, Óscar noticed the photo was upside down.
Which forms are correct? «Avisar» accepts both.
There’s no doubt you’re right.
I’m glad you came: the clause is the subject, so no «de».
The point is for everyone to take part.
What is the main message of the capsule?
What happened in the newsroom this week?
What trick does Lucía suggest?
Which cases are not worth worrying about?
What does she say about everyday speech?
When the governing word takes a preposition, the «que» clause keeps it; dropping it is «queísmo»
Verbs with a direct object and subject clauses take no preposition; adding «de» is «dequeísmo»
A few verbs and connectors accept both; don’t correct them
When the meaning changes, so does the construction

Before each «que», swap it for «eso» or ask the question. If you get «de eso / en eso» or «¿de qué? / ¿en qué?», keep the preposition; if you get plain «eso», there is none. Both phenomena are common in conversation; the careful norm is for writing and public speaking.
I’m glad you’ve found a job.
The train will probably be late.
When I went in, I noticed someone had moved the furniture.
The important thing now is that we all agree.
We are aware that there is a lot left to do.
Seville, Spain. Marina, secretary of a residents’ association, is writing up the minutes of the last meeting. Her notes were jotted down quickly, the way people spoke.

Four cases that trip up even educated speakers: «cabe destacar que» vs «cabe la posibilidad de que»; a relative «que» after a noun vs a content clause; «resultar de» meaning «to stem from», which is correct; and «informar», where Latin American usage also accepts the form without «de».
It is worth noting that visits doubled.
Which sentence is right? A relative clause, not a content clause.
Is it correct? Here «resultar de» means «to stem from».
What does the norm say about this official notice?

Today you saw how the verb’s pattern decides whether a preposition comes before «que», and how spontaneous speech differs from the careful norm. Class 181 applies the same approach to object pronouns: the verb decides whether the object is direct or indirect (lo, la or le), and there too legitimate regional varieties coexist with uses avoided in careful writing.

A Madrid publisher is preparing two editions, one for Spain and one for Mexico, of a novel set in a Castilian village. The copy editor and the Mexican editor go over the pronouns. Carmen says “le vi” and Paula says “lo vi”: both are correct. But the grandmother in the novel says “la dije”, and that is a different matter. Today’s C1 step: knowing which variation the norm accepts, which it rejects and where each one is heard.
The etymological system: “lo” for a masculine direct object. Correct and usual everywhere.
“Le” for a male person as direct object, in the singular: common in central and northern Spain and accepted by the Academy.
“Decir” takes an indirect object, so it must be “le dije”. Using “la” here is laísmo, which the norm rejects.
According to the academic norm, this sentence is…
What is wrong with this sentence?

The pronouns keep the Latin case distinction: lo, la, los, las for the direct object (they also mark gender), le, les for the indirect object (no gender). Neuter “lo” refers to an idea or a whole clause. This system is the general one in the Spanish-speaking world and the one every editor applies in neutral texts. The key is the function, not whether the referent is a person or a thing.
Direct objects: “la” for Rosario, “lo” for her brother.
Indirect object: what they told is the news; the grandmother is the recipient, so “le”, whatever her gender.
Neuter “lo” sums up a whole clause.
Etymological system: “I phoned Rosario yesterday.”
“I wrote my aunts a postcard from Segovia.”

Leísmo is using le(s) for a direct object. Only one kind is accepted by the norm: a male person in the singular (“A Juan le vi ayer”), very common in central and northern Spain, educated speech and literature included. The plural (“les vi”) is less widespread and not recommended; with women (“a Ana le vi”) or with things (“el libro no le encuentro”) it is not accepted. The courtesy “le” with usted, for men and women alike, is very widespread, even in areas without leísmo, and accepted.
Accepted leísmo: a man, singular. “Lo esperamos” is equally correct.
Courtesy “le” with usted: very widespread and accepted, also when talking to a woman.
The classic letter closing: “le” of courtesy, whoever the reader is.

Person leísmo is common in central and northern Spain. Andalusia, the Canary Islands and almost all of Latin America mainly use the etymological system. A Mexican reader understands “le vi” but hears it as Spanish from Spain; a reader from Madrid accepts “lo vi” without blinking. So for a pan-Hispanic text, lo / la is the safest choice.
Which sentence does the norm NOT accept?
A receptionist to a guest: “Shall I take your bags up to the room?”

Laísmo is using la(s) for a feminine indirect object (“*La dije que viniera”); loísmo is using lo(s) for a masculine one (“*Lo di un golpe”). Neither is accepted by the educated norm. Laísmo is typical of speech in central Castile, Madrid included, and is socially stigmatised; loísmo is much rarer and is perceived as rural or uneducated. With decir, dar, pedir, regalar, doler or gustar, the person is always “le”.
Laísmo corrected: she receives the scarf, so “le”.
Loísmo corrected: with “doler” the person is always indirect.
Plural laísmo: what she asked for is help; the neighbours are the indirect object.
In a character’s mouth, laísmo is a deliberate portrait of how she speaks; editors normally keep it.
The narrator follows the educated norm, so here laísmo is corrected.
In the narration: “They gave the postman a tip.”
Why doesn’t Carmen correct “la dije” in a dialogue?

Some verbs allow both cases without any leísmo involved. Llamar by phone takes a direct object (la llamé); llamar meaning “to call someone a name” allows both (la / le llamaban “la Maestra”). Avisar a alguien de algo takes lo / la; avisar algo a alguien takes le. With feeling verbs (molestar, asustar, preocupar), a thing that causes a state usually goes with le (le molesta el ruido), while a person acting on purpose makes the verb fully transitive: lo / la.
“Llamar” meaning to give someone a name: both constructions are correct, even with a woman.
Avisar a alguien DE algo (la) / avisar algo A alguien (le): note the “de” goes with “la”.
A noise that bothers her: “le”. A colleague teasing her on purpose: “la”.
“Let Paula know the meeting is at ten.”
“Storms frighten my brother.”
Which sentence follows the educated norm?
The “lo” in this sentence is…
Hi, Paula. I saw Gonzalo at a book launch yesterday and he asked me how the two editions are going.
Great! I saw him at the Guadalajara book fair. Listen, in chapter three the narrator writes “la dio un beso a su madre”. Are you correcting that?
Yes, in the narration it becomes “le dio un beso”. But in the dialogues the grandmother says “la dije que no saliera”, and I leave that alone: that’s how people talk in her village.
Of course, it’s the character’s voice. And when the narrator writes “a su hermano le esperaba en la estación”?
That’s person leísmo, masculine singular. The Academy accepts it and it’s very common in Castile, so it stays in our edition.
In Mexico, though, it sounds very Spanish. In ours I’d put “lo esperaba”.
Fine by me. What I’m changing in both is “a los nietos les despertaba” and “el candil no le encontraba”.
Yes, the plural and the object: “los despertaba”, “no lo encontraba”. And the priest? He says to the grandmother, “¿Le acompaño, señora?”
That one stays in both: it’s the courtesy “le” with usted. It’s very widespread, even where there is no leísmo, and the norm accepts it.
Perfect. Last question: “al abuelo le llamaban el Sabio”. I’d have written “lo llamaban”.
Both are fine: with “llamar” meaning to give someone a name, they alternate. And “le molestaba el viento” stays as it is too.
Great. I’ll send you my notes this afternoon and pass them on to Gonzalo too.
What does Carmen do with the grandmother’s laísmos?
What does Paula change only in the Mexican edition?
Which cases are corrected in both editions?
They found her aunt Engracia asleep by the stove.
She asked the neighbour for salt and some matches.
He couldn’t find the notary’s papers anywhere.
She told the doctor the truth about the wound.
She always woke her grandchildren with a song.
I told my grandmother to come (indirect object: le).
Shall I walk you to the door, madam? (courtesy “le”).
Storms frighten the boy (a thing causing a state: le).
She explains her changes, what she keeps and asks about one case.
What does Paula do with “a su hermano le esperaba”?
What does she suggest for the grandmother’s laísmos?
Why doesn’t she change “¿Le acompaño, señora?”?
What does she ask Carmen?

Paula means a single PDF but says “se los mandé”: the -s shows there are several recipients. As you saw in class 163, this is very common in conversation in Mexico and much of Latin America, but formal writing has “se lo mandé a los dos”.
the general system: the function decides, and only the direct object marks gender
the only accepted leísmo, plus the very widespread courtesy le with usted
rejected by the educated norm; in a character’s dialogue it may be kept as a portrait of their speech
some verbs genuinely allow both cases, depending on construction or meaning

First ask about function: direct or indirect? Then about the norm: the etymological system works everywhere; masculine singular person leísmo and courtesy le are accepted; laísmo, loísmo and other leísmos are not. Finally, about context: in a dialogue, the character’s voice may come first.
I saw my boss (a woman) on the underground yesterday.
Which forms does the norm accept?
“What did you tell your parents?” “The truth.”
Which forms are correct?
Pablo’s knee has hurt since the match.
Elena works at a language school in Valladolid and checks the messages a colleague is about to send to management. Rewrite them following the educated norm.

For strong students or spare time. In impersonal sentences with “se”, a person object varies too. With a male referent both forms are used: “se le considera” prevails in Spain, “se lo considera” is common in much of Latin America. With a female referent, “se la” is the most general choice. Remember that the “se” in “se lo dije” is a different one: it is “le” before “lo”.
“The new head is considered very demanding.” The most general form is…
In a Madrid newspaper: “The new director seems very pleased with the project.”
What do you tell Paula?

You can now choose between lo, la and le by function, recognise accepted leísmo and explain why laísmo and loísmo are rejected. In class 182 you move on to the most versatile pronoun in Spanish, se: middle se, reflexive se and the ethical dative, where once again function decides the form.

Se is one of the busiest words in Spanish. It can mean the action falls on the subject, that two people do it to each other, that something happens with no agent, that the verb itself changes meaning, or simply that the speaker is emotionally involved. Translators cannot render it with one English word.
Gabriel subtitled «La puerta del garaje se abrió sola» as «The garage door opened itself». What is wrong?
In «No te me pongas nervioso», who is getting nervous?

In a reflexive sentence the subject does the action to itself; in a reciprocal one, a plural subject does it to each other. Both are real objects of the verb, so you can test them by adding a sí mismo or el uno al otro.
Reflexive: she does her own make-up. English usually drops «herself».
Indirect reflexive: the hands are his, so Spanish uses las, not sus.
Reciprocal: each helps the other.
El uno al otro removes any doubt: they blame each other, not themselves.
English rarely needs himself or herself for everyday grooming; keep it for emphasis or contrast. Reciprocals, on the other hand, nearly always need each other.
Which test confirms that the sentence is reciprocal?
Which is the natural form? (Julián brushes his teeth.)

Many verbs have two versions: a causative one with an agent (someone opens the door) and a middle one where the thing just changes (the door opens). The middle se is not reflexive: the door does not open «itself». It also covers emotions: something angers you, or you get angry.
A change of state with a natural cause, no agent.
Emotional middle: the ending angered her. Enojarse is usual in Latin America; enfadarse in Spain.
The windows steamed up: nobody did it on purpose.
Sola fits; an agent with por does not. With an agent, use the active voice: el portero abrió la puerta.
The agent is named because it matters.
An implicit agent acted on purpose: hence para el público is possible.
No agent at all: the change just happens to the door.
In which sentence is se a middle se?
The news worried doña Rosario. → Doña Rosario got worried at the news.
Some verbs only exist with se: quejarse, arrepentirse, atreverse, jactarse. Here se is not an object and has no separate meaning: it is part of the verb, like the particle in English give up.
Quejarse has no non-pronominal version with this meaning.
Atreverse a + infinitive: to dare to.
Lorena and the client agreed to change the delivery date.
They asked me to sign without reading the contract, but I refused.

With verbs of consuming or taking in (eat, drink, read, learn, watch), a pronoun that matches the subject stresses that the action was completed, often with a hint of enjoyment or excess, like English eat up, drink down, read through. It needs a delimited object: a specific amount, not just «buñuelos» or «water».
Three coffees, all of them: delimited, so the aspectual se fits. Tinto is black coffee in Colombia.
Saberse: to know thoroughly, by heart.
Café with no determiner is an open amount, so no se.
Te refers to the subject (you): eat it all up.
Me is the speaker, who is not eating: she is emotionally invested. It cannot be doubled with a mí.
Me is the person affected by what happened, and it can be doubled: a mí se me enfermó la gata.

The ethical dative is a me or te that plays no part in the action: it shows that the speaker (or the listener) is emotionally involved, much like English on me in don’t go quiet on me. It is colloquial, it cannot be doubled with a mí, and it comes after te in the cluster: te me, never me te.
Don’t go all dramatic on me: Lorena is involved, not dramatic.
A classic: the child does not eat «for me»; the parent shows concern.
Dative of interest: the speaker is affected, so a mí is possible. Enfermarse is usual in Latin America; in Spain, enfermar or ponerse enfermo.
Which sentence is incorrect?
In «No te me vayas sin despedirte», what is me?

Some verbs sit in two boxes: enojarse is both middle and pronominal, and irse adds the idea of leaving a place to ir. Grammars describe a continuum. What matters is knowing what the pronoun adds and whether it can be removed.
Rosario: «I told Sara a thousand times». What is se?
Gabriel, I went through your episode. You’re doing really well, but you translated nearly every se as himself.
Isn’t that the usual thing? Don Hernando se afeita, so I put shaves himself.
That one’s fine, though shaves is enough. The problem is the garage: the door opens by itself and you wrote opens itself.
I see, nobody opens anything there. And Julián and Sara? They’ve been writing to each other since he left for Medellín.
Each other, of course. Now, the mother: Julián ate up all the buñuelos! It isn’t just ate.
Polished off? So the se tells you there wasn’t a single one left.
Exactly. And that’s why she wouldn’t just say se comió buñuelos. Then comes my favourite line: don’t go all dramatic on me.
That me threw me. Rosario isn’t the one getting dramatic…
No, it’s the mother putting herself into the sentence. Take it out and the order is the same, but you lose the affection and the impatience.
And don Hernando on the sofa? I put he slept.
But he fell asleep in the middle of the match. And when the grandmother says te pareces a tu abuelo, it isn’t you seem: it’s you look like.
Right, tomorrow I’ll go over every se one by one. And if I can’t remember one of the tests, I’ll ask you.
What is Gabriel’s general mistake?
Why wouldn’t Rosario just say «se comió buñuelos»?
According to Lorena, what is lost without the me?
She was so tired she fell asleep on the bus without realizing.
Gabriel and Lorena agreed to review the episode together at nine.
If you leave the butter in the sun, it melts straight away.
They offered her more money, but she refused to work on Sundays.
On the flight to Lima, Sara read the whole novel in three hours.
Gabriel came up with a brilliant solution for the final subtitle.
Don’t go getting nervous on me, Julián.
The garage door opened by itself.
Sara read the whole script in one night.
Why does Rosario leave the message?
What happened to the cat?
Why didn’t don Hernando go with her?
Why was Rosario stuck outside for half an hour?
What does she ask Julián about the buñuelos?
The pronoun is a real object: test with a sí mismo or el uno al otro.
Something changes with no agent; add me / le and you get the accidental se.
Se changes the meaning or is part of the verb: learn it with its preposition.
Completeness, often with enjoyment; it needs a delimited object.
Ethical: emotional involvement, never doubled with a mí. Interest: someone affected, a mí possible.
Faced with a se, do not look for a translation: run a test. Each value passes a different one, and knowing which tells you both what the sentence means and how to render it.
During the storm the power went out in the whole neighbourhood.
My cousins call each other every week since they live in different countries.
After running, Sara drank a whole bottle of water.
Which sentence contains an ethical dative?
In «La olla se quemó», which test shows the se is middle?
Lorena gives Gabriel a new job: a nature documentary. The source script is stiff, so he rewrites some lines with the right se before subtitling them.

Values combine: in no te me comas toda la torta, te is aspectual and me ethical. The ethical dative is colloquial and stays out of formal writing. News prefers murió or falleció; se murió is more colloquial and usually refers to natural or expected deaths. There is also regional variation: enfermarse in Latin America versus enfermar in Spain, devolverse meaning «go back» in Colombia and other areas, tardarse in Mexico.
In «No te me comas toda la torta», what do te and me do?
Newspaper headline: which version fits best?
Formal email to a worried client: which sentence fits?

Today you completed the map of the se that tells what happens to the subject or who is involved. Class 183 takes the next step: choosing between the ser passive, the passive se, impersonal forms and word order depending on which information you want to foreground in a text.

Valle Alto, Mexico. In the hospital’s communications office, the head of department is editing the first press release by a new press officer who used to translate English press releases. The news is good, but his text is full of ser passives and keeps jumping from one subject to another. You already know the forms; today is about choosing between them.
Five passives in a row, an agent that adds nothing and a calque of “it is expected that”. It is understandable, but it reads like a translation.
The new wing is the topic and stays the subject; each sentence ends with the new information.
Lorena keeps one topic as the subject and puts the news at the end of each sentence.
A por-phrase agent is only worth including when it tells the reader something new.

In a neutral Spanish sentence, what the reader already knows (the topic, tema) comes first and the new information (rema) comes last, where it receives the main stress. Choosing between active and passive is often a way of putting the topic in subject position, so that the text keeps talking about the same thing.
The wing is already known; the designers are the news, so they go last, after por.
Now the architects are the topic: active voice, with the building as the new information.
Three verbs, three different constructions, one constant topic: the wing.
Three different subjects in three sentences: grammatical, but the reader has to reorganise the information each time.
The wing stays the subject and does not even need repeating; the agents are the new information, so the passive with por is justified.
The scanner is already the topic, so the passive keeps it as subject and leaves the donor, the news, at the end.
Now the foundation is the topic, so the active keeps it as the (implicit) subject.

Most Spanish passives have no agent. Include a por-phrase only when the doer is new and relevant information; if it is obvious (doctors operate, councils approve budgets), leave it out and use the space for something useful.
Informative agent: nobody would have guessed it.
No agent: of course doctors and nurses did it. The time is the news.

The ser passive is correct and has its place, but many newspaper style guides warn against overusing it, as often happens in news translated from English. Warning signs: chains of passives, “it was announced by…”, “is required / is recommended”, and “it is expected that”, which Spanish says with se.
With verbs like anunciar + que-clause, Spanish uses the active; the passive version is a calque.
Patients writing a protocol is unexpected, so the agent is worth mentioning.

With pronominal verbs, impersonal se is impossible, since Spanish cannot stack two se. Uno or una is the way to generalise, and it usually includes the speaker; a woman speaking from her own experience often says una.
A pronominal verb rules out se; una generalises and includes the speaker herself.
An impersonal 3rd person plural says nothing about number; it just hides the doer and leaves out the speaker.

With people as the subject, a plural passive se is easily read as reflexive (“they moved themselves”) or reciprocal (“each other”). That is why careful Spanish uses impersonal se + a, or the ser passive, when people receive the action. In the press, “se mataron” is the classic trap: in everyday speech matarse often means “to die in an accident”.
Reflexive: they moved themselves.
Impersonal se + a: someone moved them. No ambiguity.
Reciprocal: they congratulated each other.
Ser passive: the clearest choice in a news report.
Impersonal se + a removes the reflexive reading; the plural versions could mean they assessed themselves.
Se mataron is ambiguous; news writing prefers murieron or a passive that states what happened.
Es requerido is an English calque; a Spanish notice says se ruega, hay que or, in Mexico, favor de.
La gente takes singular agreement.
Rodrigo, the press release has everything, but it starts with “It was announced by the management that…”. It sounds translated.
The template I was given was in English and I copied it almost word for word.
It shows. If the story is the new wing, make it the subject from the first line.
And the architects? I wrote “The project was designed by architects”.
“By architects” tells nobody anything. But the fact that the university team did it is news.
Sorry to interrupt. Are you going to mention the transfer? It says here that the patients “se trasladarán” on Sunday.
Yes, what’s wrong with that?
It sounds as if they’re going to move beds by themselves. Use impersonal se with a, or the ser passive.
She’s right. And in the notice for families, no “is required”: use hay que.
What about the paediatric ward? It isn’t finished yet.
Then: “the opening of the paediatric ward is scheduled for March”. And to finish, “the wing is expected to halve waiting times”.
Now I get what they used to tell me at the agency: you translate so fast that you don’t notice Spanish works differently.
Why did Rodrigo write so many ser passives?
What problem does the doctor see in the phrase about the transfer?
Which agent does Lorena keep, and why?
The machine is the known topic; the passive keeps it as subject and puts the donor, the news, last.
In conversation the impersonal 3rd person plural is natural; the ser passive sounds like a news report.
Hay que expresses a general obligation; es requerido is a calque.
Academic writing favours a nominalisation as subject: the process without a doer.
Pronominal verb, and Lorena includes herself: una.
The wing is expected to cut waiting times: the natural Spanish for “it is expected that”.
You never know when you might need an ambulance: generic uno, which includes the speaker.
The paediatric ward was paid for by a neighbourhood fundraiser: an agent worth mentioning.
What is the news item about?
Who designed the building?
What happened during the night?
When will the paediatric ward open?
What do people going to the emergency department have to bring?
Known information first, new information last; choose the voice that keeps the topic as subject across sentences.
The ser passive is legitimate, but only add por when the doer is news, and avoid chains of passives; estar + participle describes the result.
Se is the default for leaving out the doer; with people, use se + a or the ser passive to avoid a reflexive reading.
Choose by who is included (the speaker, the listener, others) and by register, from chat to official reports.

Three questions: what is my text about (make it the subject)? Is the doer news (if not, drop por)? Who am I talking to (choose the register)? And one alarm bell: if it sounds translated, it probably is.
The bridge stays the subject and the new information is the time; “by workers” adds nothing.
Museum sign: “Photography without flash is allowed.”
“Eighty volunteers were selected for the study.”
A doctor speaking from experience: “Over the years, you learn not to take work home.”
Council report: “The opening of the new market is planned for January.”
Zaragoza, Spain. Lucía Cano works in a city council press office and receives three sentences from an intern that need a different construction.

Academic Spanish presents the researcher’s actions with se, with the “modest” we (even with a single author) or with an inanimate subject (“this study analyses”), which is widespread though some manuals see it as influenced by English. For ongoing processes, “está siendo + participle” is grammatical, but many style guides prefer se + progressive.
Traditional academic style: se, not the ser passive in the present nor colloquial uno.
For an ongoing process, se + progressive is the safest choice.
The author says “we” even when writing alone, to avoid foregrounding themselves.

Today you chose the voice to keep the topic as subject and the news at the end. The natural next step is doing the same by changing word order without changing the voice, and learning to put one element in the spotlight.

Sonia Arce is directing a documentary on the hundredth anniversary of the Mercado Norte, and Julián Ortega is writing the script. Two weeks before the premiere they go through the voice-over line by line. The facts are right, but the text doesn’t flow: the problem is the order. Today you learn how Spanish packages information: the topic (what is already known) first, the rheme (what is new) last, and several ways of highlighting.
Everything is new, so Spanish uses the neutral order: subject, verb, object.
The photos are already known (“las”), so the new piece, Laura, goes last, where Spanish puts new information.
A correction: “it was Laura who found them, not Julián”. A cleft sentence singles her out against someone else.
Asked “Who found the photos?”, which answer sounds most natural?
What is this sentence doing?

Spanish word order is flexible because it follows information, not just grammar. The topic (what you are talking about, already known) tends to come first; the rheme (the new information) tends to come last, where the main stress falls. In a text, the rheme of one sentence often becomes the topic of the next, and that chain is what makes a paragraph flow.
The market is the topic (we are looking at it on screen); the date is the new part, so it goes last.
The rheme of the first sentence (the grandmother) becomes the topic of the second: a smooth chain.
The known part is taken up by “lo”; the answer, the new subject, closes the sentence.
Which sentence continues the text best?
Asked when the documentary premieres, which answer is the most natural?

With verbs that introduce something into the scene (llegar, aparecer, surgir, ocurrir, existir, faltar, sobrar, quedar) and when the whole sentence is news, the natural order is verb + subject: “Llegó el tren”, “Faltan dos sillas”, “Ha llamado tu madre”. With gustar-type verbs the subject (the thing liked) usually follows too. If the subject is already the topic, it goes first: “El tren llegó tarde”.
Two chairs are missing for the test-screening audience (faltar presents what is missing).
Rafael called: he says he has found more photos (news: the whole sentence is new).
In 1931 the first flower stalls appeared (aparecer introduces them into the story).
The residents are worried about the building noise (preocupar works like gustar).
We were already talking about Rafael; the sentence tells us something new about him.
Announcing an arrival: it’s all news, so the subject follows the verb.

In Caribbean Spanish (Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Cuba and other coastal areas) it is common not to invert when the subject is a pronoun, especially “tú”: “¿Qué tú quieres?”. It is a regional feature, normal there, not a mistake; with a full noun it is much less usual. General Spanish says “¿Qué quieres (tú)?”.
“Oh no, two spotlights are missing.”
“What does Laura think of the new ending?” “That it’s too long.”

You met fronted focus at B2 (lesson 163: “ESO te dije yo”). At C1 you use it to correct or contrast: the highlighted element comes first with strong stress, the verb follows straight away and the subject, if expressed, goes after the verb. No pronoun picks it up. It is very expressive: frequent in conversation, used sparingly in formal writing.
“Rafael is eighty.” “Eighty-FOUR, and he remembers everything.” The fronted number corrects the other speaker.
Little money did the stallholders make in the forties: the amount is stressed and the subject follows the verb.
That’s exactly what I wanted to tell you: the ending is too long.
Two known topics, set off by a pause and picked up by “se” and “lo”: “As for Laura, I wouldn’t tell her that.” Class 185 covers this in depth.
“That” is singled out against everything else: strong stress, no “lo”, subject after the verb.

Focus adverbs go right before the element they highlight, and moving them changes the meaning. “Solo” (normally written without an accent) restricts; “incluso” and “hasta” extend to something unexpected; “precisamente” and “justamente” mean “exactly that”; “también” adds. If adverb + focus comes first, the subject moves after the verb.
Only Laura has seen the 1931 photos: nobody else has.
Laura has seen only the 1931 photos, not the ones from other years.
Even the mayor came to the test screening (hasta = incluso: something unexpected).
That is exactly why we want to end with Rafael.
“Did you make a lot from your first documentary?” “Not at all! I made very little from it.”
Which sentence means that nobody but Laura saw the photos?

Cleft sentences split the message in two: a relative clause presented as known or assumed (“I need something”) and the focus, linked by “ser”. The pseudo-cleft puts the focus at the end, like a rheme: “Lo que necesito es tiempo”. The cleft puts it straight after “ser”, with stronger contrast: “Es tiempo lo que necesito (not money)”. The relative depends on the focus: quien / el que for people, donde for places, cuando for time, como for manner, lo que for things and ideas.
What’s missing is one voice that ties all the stories together.
It was in 1962 that the fire destroyed half the market (time focus → cuando).
It’s Rafael who remembers those years best (person focus → quien).
Where you can see the change is in the 1931 photos (place → donde; the preposition “en” is repeated).
What the documentary needs is more accounts from stallholders.
It was in 2010 that they renovated the market roof.
Which sentence is correct? (It was the residents who rebuilt the market.)
“Who edited the trailer?” “Julián did.”
Julián, I’ve read the new version. What I’m not convinced by is the opening.
Why? It starts with a clear fact: “In 1925, the architect Ramiro Gil completed the Mercado Norte.”
That’s exactly where the problem lies. On screen we see the market, not the architect. Better like this: “The Mercado Norte opened its doors in 1925”, and the architect later.
Fine. And the part about the fire? I’ve written that the fire brigade arrived within ten minutes, according to the paper at the time.
That works. And in the interviews, who tells the story of the fire, Rafael or his sister?
Rafael tells it. His sister only talks about the reopening.
Perfect. Listen, two photos are missing from the 1931 sequence. Have you got them?
No, Laura has them. By the way, it was she who found them in the city archive, not me. I want her in the credits.
Of course. And we’re dedicating the film to her as well, right? But I wouldn’t tell Laura that yet: let it be a surprise.
That’s just what I was thinking. And the ending? Even Rafael says it’s too long.
He’s right. What we need is thirty seconds less and a line that sticks in people’s minds.
Not much time you’re giving me for that… Anyway, I’ll send you another version tomorrow.
Why does Sonia want to change the first line?
Who found the 1931 photos?
What don’t they want to tell Laura yet?
“Who wrote the script?” “Julián Ortega did.”
“Who likes the new ending more?” “Sonia does.”
“What’s left to finish the edit?” “The credits and the music.”
“No, Laura: it was you who found them.”
Rafael: “It’s a HUNDRED years old, it turns a hundred and one next year.”
What we need is two more weeks.
It was in this square that the first stall opened.
Only Laura knows where the photos are.
She sums up what worked and what didn’t, and plans the next few days.
What did people like most?
What problem was there?
Who is arriving tomorrow at ten?
Why does Laura have to appear in the credits?

Notice how Sonia organises her message: each block starts with what the team already knows and ends with the news. She uses pseudo-clefts to take stock (“What people liked most was…”, “What didn’t work was…”) and addresses the team as “ustedes”, as everywhere in Latin America.
Known information first, new information last; chaining rheme to topic makes a text flow
Verbs that present something put the subject after them; a fronted contrastive focus forces the subject after the verb
Clefts single out one element; “ser” agrees in number, person and tense, and the relative matches the focus
Focus adverbs go right before what they highlight; moving them changes the meaning

Before ordering, ask yourself what your listener already knows: that goes first, and the news goes last. To highlight or correct, you have three tools: a fronted focus with the verb straight after it, a cleft sentence, or a focus adverb. In wh-questions and exclamations, the subject follows the verb.
“Who recommended this book to you?” “My teacher did.”
What I miss most about my country is the summer festivals.
“It cost you forty euros, didn’t it?” “No way! It cost me EIGHTY.”
Which sentence says nobody expected your grandmother to come?
It was in Lima that I met my partner.
Nerea is preparing the audio guide for a science museum. Her sentences are correct, but they don’t follow what the visitor sees. Rewrite them.

For strong students or spare time. 1. “Es por eso que…” and “Fue así que…” are very common, especially in Latin America, and appear in educated usage too; in very careful writing many prefer “Por eso…”, “Es por eso por lo que…” or “Fue así como…”. 2. Both “Fui yo quien lo hizo” and “Fui yo quien lo hice” are correct. 3. “Lo que pasa es que…” is a fixed pseudo-cleft that introduces an explanation or an excuse. 4. A topic with a pause and a pronoun is dislocation: class 185.
In the final report for a foundation, which option do many editors choose?
Is “Fui yo quien lo propuse” correct?
What is “lo que pasa es que” used for?
In careful writing: “That was how we got the permit.”

You can now order information from known to new, put the subject after the verb when it is the news, and highlight with a focus, an adverb or a cleft. In class 185 you study the other side of word order in depth: the topic placed before or after the sentence with a pause and picked up by a pronoun (“That book, I’ve already read it”).

Elena Robles’s translation agency moves on Monday. It is Friday and the office is full of boxes. Diego asks her about everything, and she answers the way we all do when many topics are open: she names the topic first and then comments on it (“The keys? I’ve got them”). Today you learn to place a topic at the start or end of a sentence and to decide whether a pronoun picks it up.
Plain statement: everything is new and nothing is singled out.
The keys are already under discussion, so they open the sentence after a pause and “las” picks them up again.
A correction: one set of keys is contrasted with another, stressed, with no pronoun and the subject after the verb (lesson 184).
“What about the old printer?” Which answer sounds most natural?
What is this sentence doing?

Left dislocation moves a known element to the front as the topic, followed by a pause (often a comma in writing). If that element is a direct or indirect object, an unstressed pronoun that agrees with it picks it up inside the sentence, and with a definite direct object that pronoun is compulsory: “Ese libro lo leí”, never “*Ese libro leí” (unless it is a stressed focus). A whole clause or an attribute is picked up by neuter “lo”. The personal “a” stays: “A Valeria, la llamo yo”.
That contract: we signed it in 2014. The pronoun is required with a fronted definite object.
The clients: we’ll send them the new address on Monday (indirect object → les).
That the new premises are smaller, everyone knows already: neuter “lo” takes up the whole clause.
Expensive, it certainly is; but it’s next to the metro (neuter “lo” takes up an attribute).
The meeting-room furniture: we’re giving it to a school.
That we were moving in October, the landlord already knew.

Spanish has no unstressed pronoun for most prepositional phrases (unlike French “en” and “y” or Italian “ne” and “ci”), so a fronted topic with “de”, “con”, “en”, “para” or “por” is simply left without one: “De eso, no quiero hablar”; “En Madrid, trabajé diez años”. A bare noun (no article) is normally not picked up by a pronoun either: “Cajas, tenemos muchas”. Only the personal or dative “a” brings a clitic with it.
About the deposit, I don’t want to talk until Monday (no pronoun: “hablar de”).
As for the landlord, I’ve already spoken to him myself (“hablar con”: no pronoun).
In these premises, we spent twelve years (a place: no pronoun).
Boxes, we’ve got plenty; what we’re short of is tape (bare noun: no pronoun).
We are talking about those keys: normal intonation, a pause after the topic and a pronoun.
A correction: heavy stress on “esas”, no pause, no “las”, subject after the verb. With “a” + person (A ELENA le di las llaves), “le” often stays even in focus.
About our former secretary, I haven’t heard anything since.
In the new neighbourhood, there’s everything.

“En cuanto a”, “respecto a / con respecto a”, “por lo que respecta a” and “en lo que se refiere a” announce a new topic, typical of meetings, emails and reports. Because they introduce the topic from outside the sentence, the sentence itself carries its own pronoun or preposition: “En cuanto a la editorial, no le digas nada”. In conversation, the topic can also be set out on its own, with no preposition, and linked by a pronoun or a word inside: “Mi jefe, no me fío de ese hombre”. That “hanging topic” is colloquial; in writing, use the full preposition or “en cuanto a”.
As far as deadlines are concerned, we are keeping them as they are.
As regards the hospital, Valeria has already spoken to them (formal).
The landlord… I don’t trust him an inch: a hanging topic, picked up by “de él”.
My sister, nobody can talk her round: the link is “a esa… la” (colloquial).

In emails and reports, “en cuanto a / respecto a” announce the topic; in meetings, also “por lo que respecta a”. Among friends, a bare topic works (“The move? Don’t even mention it”). Avoid the hanging topic in formal writing: keep the preposition or use “en cuanto a”.
In a report: “As for the moving costs, the company will cover them.”
“My neighbour, I don’t trust him.” What completes this hanging topic?

In speech, the topic can also come at the end, after a pause, as an afterthought that makes clear what you meant. The pronoun appears first and the noun phrase comes later: “Ya lo sé, lo de la reunión”. A right-dislocated object must be announced by its pronoun (“Ya lo hemos firmado, el contrato”); a right-dislocated subject needs no pronoun, because the verb already agrees with it (“Me lo dijo ayer, tu padre”). It is very common in conversation and rare in formal writing.
I know, about the meeting: Diego told me.
Your father told me yesterday: that you’re moving to Valencia. The subject comes at the end, with no pronoun for it.
We haven’t said anything to the publisher yet: “le” anticipates “a la editorial”.

In River Plate Spanish (Argentina and Uruguay) doubling a definite personal direct object with “a” is very common, with no pause and in educated speech too: “Lo vi a Juan”. It is a regional feature, not a mistake. Most varieties say “Vi a Juan”. With a stressed pronoun, doubling is compulsory everywhere: “Lo vi a él”.
“Who has the contract for the new premises?” “I have it, the contract.”
A translator from Montevideo says “Ayer la vi a Lucía en el centro”. What is it?
Which sentence is correct? (The table at the entrance: we gave it to Diego.)
Which is correct? (The removal people: I’ll talk to them.)
Elena, before I forget: who has the keys to the new premises?
The keys? I’ve got them. Gonzalo, the landlord, gave them to me yesterday.
And the storeroom ones? Have you got those as well?
No, no. It’s the GARAGE keys I’ve got. The storeroom ones, Valeria has.
OK. And the old printer? It weighs a ton.
The printer, we’re selling. There’s a student who’s interested. Boxes, we’ve got more than enough.
By the way, Gonzalo has written to me again about the deposit.
Ugh. About the deposit, better not to say anything until Monday. That man, I don’t trust him an inch.
Another thing: the hospital wants the report on Wednesday, not Friday.
I know, about the hospital. That it’s going to be a tough week, we all know.
Shall I email the clients with the new address?
Yes, but don’t say anything to the publisher yet: I’ll call them myself. As for the rest, a short email will do.
Who has the storeroom keys?
What are they doing with the old printer?
Why shouldn’t Diego email the publisher?
“And the projector?” “The projector, I’ll take in my car.”
“What about the invoices?” “We’ll talk about the invoices on Monday.”
“Did you know Rosa is retiring in December?” “Yes, I know, about Rosa.”
“No, it’s the MAILBOX keys I’ve got, not the street-door ones.”
That the new premises get less light, we knew when we signed.
The invoices, I’ll sign tomorrow.
The suppliers, we’ll write to on Monday.
I know, about the deposit.
She runs through her tasks and asks them to send the glossary and keep quiet about the deposit.
What will Valeria do on Monday?
What does she ask them to send the publisher?
Where are the September invoices?
What mustn’t they do with the landlord?

Valeria is from Buenos Aires. Notice “la llamé a Carolina”: doubling a personal direct object is very common in Argentina and Uruguay, while other areas say “llamé a Carolina”. “Los extraño” means “I miss you all”. Her whole message is organised by topics: each block names the topic first and then comments on it.
A fronted known object is picked up by an agreeing pronoun (compulsory with definite direct objects); prepositional and bare topics take none
Topic markers announce a new point in formal registers; the hanging topic is colloquial and needs a link inside the sentence
An afterthought topic: the pronoun comes first and the noun phrase follows a pause
A stressed contrastive focus takes no direct-object pronoun and puts the subject after the verb

Ask yourself three things. Am I correcting something with heavy stress? Then it’s a focus: no pronoun. Is it a known object with an article, demonstrative or name? Then it’s a topic: pause plus an agreeing pronoun. Does it carry de, con, en, para…? Then no pronoun. “Lo vi a Juan” is normal in the River Plate area; most varieties say “Vi a Juan”.
That film, I’ve already seen twice.
About the party, I don’t remember a thing.
Your parents: have you told them about the trip yet?
“Is your boss nice?” “Nice, she is; patient, not so much.”
“Did you buy the wholemeal bread?” “No: it was the CORN bread I bought, not the wholemeal.”
Inés is organising her sister’s wedding and goes through the list with the bride’s father. Her sentences are neutral; he prefers to talk topic by topic. Rewrite them.

For strong students or spare time. 1. Several topics can be stacked, each with its own pronoun: “My brother, the car: I don’t lend it to him”. 2. With an article the topic is specific and takes a pronoun; without one it is generic and usually takes none. 3. Left dislocation with a pronoun fits any register; afterthought and hanging topics belong to speech; reports prefer “en cuanto a” or neutral order. 4. An “a” that marks a place, not an object, brings no pronoun.
My sister, the flat: I’d never rent it to her.
“Are you patient with children?” “Patience, I haven’t got much.”
In a report for management, which option is most suitable?
“Lima, I go back to every summer.”

You can now place a topic at the start or end, decide whether a pronoun picks it up, and tell a topic from a focus. Position and pronouns shape what the listener understands. Class 186 takes the next step: sentences that can mean two things because of their order or what a pronoun refers to, and how to remove that ambiguity.

Irene Ferrer runs Tres Orillas, a translation cooperative. Yesterday the team discussed two commissions: one from a publisher in Quito and one from a museum in Valparaíso. Gonzalo, the editor, wrote the minutes. They are correct, but every noun and every verb is repeated. Irene rewrites them on one principle: what has already been said is recovered, not repeated, as long as the reader knows what is being recovered.
Everything is clear, but the text is heavy: the same verbs and nouns come back again and again for no reason.
The commas stand for missing verbs, “la segunda / la primera” point back to the proposals in order, and “tampoco” recovers a whole negative clause.
In “Irene takes the second proposal; Nuria, the first”, what does the comma after “Nuria” signal?
“The second” proposal is…

You already drop a noun after an article plus an adjective, “de” or “que” (lesson 124: la verde, la de Ana, el mío). At C1, watch the words that change shape once the noun is gone: un, algún, ningún become uno, alguno, ninguno; primer and tercer become primero and tercero; short possessives become long ones with the article; and the “el” of “el agua” goes back to “la”. Demonstratives, numerals and “otro” stay as they are.
This glossary is out of date; we need a new one. (“un nuevo” is not possible without the noun.)
Of the five essays, Nuria has translated three; the other two arrive in April. Order: otros + numeral.
“Which dictionary should I use?” “The one I told you about: the art-terms one.”
The first chapter is ready; the third one isn’t yet.
This dictionary is no use to me. Have you got a better one?
The translation area is on the ground floor; the layout one, on the first.

When two clauses share the verb, the second can shrink to the subject plus a polarity word: también (agreeing with a positive), tampoco (agreeing with a negative), sí / no (contrast). “Sí que” adds emphasis to a contrastive yes. If more than one element is left and only the verb is missing, a comma marks the gap: “Ana estudia Derecho y Pablo, Medicina”. The missing verb is recovered with its own agreement (acepto → acepta). After modal verbs like poder or querer you can drop the infinitive, but Spanish has no all-purpose “do” and never stops at “haber”: “Have you finished?” is answered “Sí (ya he terminado)”, not “*Sí, he”.
Irene translates from Portuguese; Nuria, from English. The comma stands for “traduce”.
Hugo hasn’t read the contract, but Nuria certainly has: “sí que” stresses the contrast.
“Can you check the catalogue today?” “I can, but I’d rather do it tomorrow.” The infinitive is understood.
“I love the cover design.” “So do I.” With gustar-type verbs the person goes with “a”.
“I haven’t had time to read the contract.” “Neither have I. Let’s read it together tomorrow.”
Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

“Que sí” and “que no” stand for a whole clause that has just been said. They follow verbs of opinion (creer, pensar, suponer), hope and fear (esperar, temer), appearance (parecer) and saying (decir, contestar): “Will the museum sign?” “Creo que sí” = I think it will. Without “que” you can only use an adverb: “Quizá sí”, “A lo mejor no”. “No creo” is also a very common short answer.
“Will the publisher be on time?” “It looks like it won’t: they still haven’t sent the texts.”
“Is Hugo free in March?” “He told me he was.”
“Will we have to redo the glossary?” “I’m afraid so.”

“Lo” can replace the complement of ser, estar and parecer: an adjective, a noun or a phrase. It is neuter and never changes, even when the complement is feminine or plural: “¿Estás cansada? Sí, lo estoy”. It sounds emphatic or somewhat formal; in conversation people also just say “Sí, mucho”. “Hacerlo” replaces an action already mentioned (a verb with its complements), especially in writing, conditionals and contrasts: “Quien quiera participar puede hacerlo hasta el lunes”. It only works for deliberate actions, not for states or verbs like saber, ser or gustar.
“Is the March deadline realistic?” “It is, if we start this week.”
“Does that machine translation look reliable?” “It looks it, but it needs checking.”
Hugo had to confirm in writing. If he hasn’t done so already, he will today.

In a short answer Spanish repeats the verb or just says “sí”: “Did you send the minutes?” “Sí, ya la envié.” “Sí, lo hice” is possible but sounds translated from English. “Hacerlo” shines elsewhere: in conditionals, contrasts and formal instructions.
“Are you ready for the meeting?” “Yes, we are.”
Nuria knows Portuguese and so does Hugo.
“Is Hugo coming to the dinner?” “He’s told me he is.”

In writing, “este / esta” points to the last thing mentioned (the nearest), “aquel / aquella” to the earlier one (further back); demonstratives are normally written without an accent. “El primero”, “el segundo”, “este último” are clearer than este / aquel when there are several candidates. “Dicho / dicha” (without an article) and “tal” + noun belong to administrative, legal and academic texts. “Respectivamente” pairs two parallel lists in order.
“Este” = the museum (last mentioned); “aquella” = the publisher (mentioned first). Gender helps too.
Gonzalo suggested two dates, one in March and one in May; the second is more realistic.
The publisher is asking for a 20 % discount. Such a request forces us to revise the budget (formal).
Irene will coordinate the catalogue and Nuria the essays: “respectivamente” pairs the lists in order.

The Diccionario panhispánico de dudas advises against using “el mismo / la misma” as a mere stand-in for a pronoun, possessive or demonstrative, a habit of bureaucratic and journalistic prose. Use su, lo, él, este instead. “Mismo” is fine when it means “the same”: “We work on the same project”.
Who is laying out the catalogue?
In formal minutes, which version is better?
Does Gonzalo appreciate Nuria more than Irene does, or more than he appreciates Irene? The ellipsis leaves two possible gaps.
The “a” makes Irene the person being appreciated.
The verb is restored, so there is no doubt left.
Which version makes it clear that it was Gonzalo who came back?
Irene means she talked about Nuria’s proposal. Which version leaves no doubt?
We have two proposals: the publisher in Quito’s, five essays for March, and the Valparaíso museum’s, the catalogue and audio guides for an exhibition.
I’d start with the first one: it’s the one with the tightest deadline.
And is it realistic? March is just around the corner.
It is, if we start this week. Mind you, I can’t check anything in March: I’ve got the book fair.
Neither can I, at least for the first fortnight. But Hugo can: he has the whole month free.
Has Hugo confirmed that he’s free in March?
He said he was, though not in writing. If he hasn’t already, he will today.
Perfect. That settles who does what. Gonzalo, put it down like this: I take the second one; she takes the first.
Fine by me. But the publisher’s glossary is ten years old; we need a new one.
The one we made for the ceramics exhibition could be a starting point.
And for the minutes: the publisher pays at thirty days; the museum, at sixty. And the latter doesn’t pay anything in advance.
Put it all in, but without as much repetition as last month’s, which nobody could get through.
Who is taking on the Quito essays?
Who can work in March?
What worries Irene about the minutes?
We need a dictionary of legal terms. Do you know a good one?
Room 3 is taken; we’ll use the one at the back.
Of the five essays, the first is short; the other four are very long.
“Which contract do I sign?” “The one I sent you yesterday, not Monday’s.”
This chapter has no notes; the third one has over forty.
Irene takes the second one; Nuria, the first.
If he hasn’t done it already, he’ll do it tomorrow.
The essays and the catalogue will be delivered in March and May respectively.
She updates him on both commissions, the glossary and Hugo, and asks for something in the minutes.
Which deadline does the museum accept?
Which glossary will Nuria start from?
What do Irene and Nuria disagree about?
What does Nuria ask Gonzalo to do in the minutes?

Notice how Nuria speaks: she never repeats “plazo”, “glosario” or “dice”. She uses verbal ellipsis to contrast opinions and an echo question to get ahead of Gonzalo: “Am I tired? I am.” In speech, the ellipsis comma becomes a short pause.
The determiner stays and the noun is understood; shortened forms recover their full shape
Polarity words and a comma stand for the missing verb; “que sí / que no” stand for a whole clause
“Lo” replaces a quality and never changes; “hacerlo” replaces deliberate actions only
Signposts that point back in a text; avoid “el mismo” as a mere pronoun

Leaving things out works when the reader can recover them effortlessly. Before you drop something, ask how many candidates there are. One: drop it or point back. Several in order: use “el primero”, “este último” or “respectivamente”. Two possible readings: add the missing marker or repeat the noun.
This chair is really uncomfortable. Isn’t there a better one?
“I’m not going to the work dinner.” “Neither am I. I’d rather stay at home.”
“Is the exam hard?” “It is, but you can pass it.”
My sister lives in Lima and my brother in Montevideo.
Which version does the DPD prefer?
Lola is writing up the residents’ meeting of her building. Her draft repeats far too much. Help her edit it without losing information.

For strong students or spare time. 1. “Sendos, sendas” means “one each”: “Irene y Nuria firmaron sendos contratos” = each signed one. It does not mean “both”. 2. “Hacer lo propio” means “to do the same” and belongs to journalism and formal writing. 3. “Ello” picks up a whole idea or situation, never a person or a concrete object: “por ello”, “de ello”.
What does “sendos premios” mean here?
In a press release: “The publisher accepted the deadline and the museum did likewise.”
In which sentence is “ello” used correctly?
Formal report: two editors are mentioned and you mean the second one: “The latter proposed postponing the signing.”

You can now leave out what the reader can recover and point back with lo, hacerlo, este último or “tal petición”. In class 188 you take the next step: packing whole ideas into a noun that also evaluates them (“The lack of coordination caused delays”; “This decision…”), the key tool of dense, formal writing.

Valencia, Spain. A citizens’ transport watchdog is preparing its annual report on bus line 7. The coordinator is editing a chapter by an analyst who writes the way he talks: long clauses chained with “because”, “and also”, “so”. The data are good, but the reader gets lost. Today you learn to condense clauses into noun phrases, and to know when not to.
Four finite verbs and three connectors: fine in speech, heavy in a report, where the reader wants the causes and effects at a glance.
One main verb: causes and effects have become nouns, and the causal link is carried by the verb provocar instead of como… por eso.
The verb has become a noun, and what went up is now introduced by de.
When you nominalise, a verb such as provocar takes over the job the connector used to do.

When a verb becomes a noun, the rest of the clause is rebuilt around it: the subject or object is introduced by de (or becomes su), an adverb becomes an adjective, a negation becomes la falta de or la ausencia de, and the connector (como, por eso) is replaced by a verb linking two noun phrases: provocar, causar, explicar, traducirse en, deberse a.
Negation becomes la falta de: the anchor pattern for reports.
The adverb rápidamente becomes the adjective rápida, placed before the noun.
The connector porque disappears; deberse a links the effect to its cause.
Revisar becomes la revisión, the object takes de, and the adverbial phrase can stay.
Negation is nominalised with la falta de, and deberse a links effect and cause.

The suffix is fixed word by word, so you cannot apply it freely. Some verbs even have two nouns with different meanings: apertura is the act of opening (an inauguration), abertura is a physical gap. When in doubt, check a dictionary.
Cumplir gives el cumplimiento; un cumplido is a compliment.
A physical gap is una abertura; apertura is the act of opening.

Some nouns name a fact neutrally (el gasto, el retraso, la decisión); others name it and judge it at the same time (el despilfarro, una chapuza, un acierto). They are powerful because the opinion is packed into the noun and taken for granted rather than argued. That is why they belong in opinion pieces, editorials and conversation, and why a neutral report avoids them or attributes them to someone.
Same fact; the second version also passes judgement.
Un acierto: a decision you consider right.
La torpeza de + infinitive: a clumsy, tactless decision.
Neuter lo + adjective + de: the aspect of the matter you single out and evaluate.
Measurable facts. Even negative nouns like sobrecoste are neutral here: they state a figure, not a verdict.
A signed opinion piece: the verdict is packed into the nouns.

Lo + adjective turns a quality into “the aspect of something that has that quality”. Lo is neuter, never el. With ser, the verb agrees with a plural complement: lo importante son los datos is correct.
El gasto only names the fact; the other two judge it.
Neuter lo + adjective: the positive side of the measure.

Spanish generalises with an article, unlike English (“Patience is a virtue”, “Users value punctuality”). El + singular names the type as a whole; los + plural speaks about its members in general; un + singular describes what any member is or should be, typical of definitions and norms, but it cannot go with predicates about the whole type, such as be invented, become extinct or be abundant. Abstract and mass nouns in general statements also take the article.
The bus as a type of transport.
Users in general; in English there is no article here.
Un: what any good report should do.
Abstract noun in a general statement: article required.
An abstract noun as subject needs the article.
A kind-level predicate rejects generic un; that sentence can only mean one specific computer.
Four ways to break a chain of de: bring back a verb, use a relational adjective (urbano instead of de la ciudad), switch to another preposition (sobre, para, entre), or use a possessive.
Two empty verbs in a row; one plain verb is enough.
De can stand for the subject or the object of the underlying verb.
Raúl, the data are all there, but some sentences run to six lines. Instead of a chain of clauses, put the causes and the effect into noun phrases.
OK. But in the methods section I went to the other extreme: “we proceeded to the carrying-out of a survey”.
That’s padding. The verb is enough: “We surveyed 1,200 users in March.”
And the bus lane? In my column I wrote that the works are a botch and a waste of public money.
In the column, go ahead: it’s opinion and you sign it. In the report, no; there we give the cost overrun and let readers judge.
Understood. And the night line? I think it was a success.
So do I, but the report proves it with a figure.
Another thing. In the summary I wrote “Users value punctuality”. Is that wrong?
It reads like a headline. In running text you need the articles; in a headline the bare noun is fine.
And this one? A chain of four de-phrases about checking deadlines.
Four de-phrases in a row: nobody gets to the end. Bring the verbs back.
You’re right. Although the serious part is still that nobody has explained the delay.
Why does Elena keep chapuza out of the report?
How does the report show that the night line works?
When does Elena accept a bare noun as subject?
The fare rise was approved in December.
Residents complain about how clean the platforms are.
The opening of the new station is scheduled for May.
The report highlights how punctual the night line is.
The single ticket has gone up by twenty cents.
Closing the bridge forced three lines to be rerouted: a nominal cause linked by a verb.
What stands out in the study is the absence of complaints.
A good public service tells people about its delays: generic un for what any member should do.
What does Raúl do in his column?
According to the report, what explains the fall in passengers?
What does Raúl see as the serious part?
What does Raúl call clumsy?
What does he praise?
Turn the clause into a noun phrase and let a linking verb (provocar, explicar, deberse a) carry the relation. The suffix is fixed word by word.
Evaluative nouns name and judge at the same time: right for opinion pieces, out of place in a neutral report unless attributed.
Go back to a verb when the noun adds padding, builds a chain of de or hides who is responsible.
Spanish generalises with the article, even with abstract nouns; bare nouns go after the verb, in headlines and lists, and in classifying phrases.
Three questions before nominalising: am I gaining clarity or just words? Is it still clear who did what? Am I reporting or judging? And to generalise, use the article.
Report: “A lack of coordination between the two departments delayed payments.”
A measurable fact, with no verdict, suits a technical report.
“Trust is the basis of any public service.”
“There are tourists at the station waiting for the first train.”
Empty verb plus nominalisation: the plain verb is enough.
Medellín, Colombia. Mónica coordinates a university library’s annual report and gets three sentences from an intern that need rewriting.

Two more evaluative devices, common in speech and opinion columns. Lo + adjective + que stresses intensity, and the adjective agrees with the noun even though lo is neuter. The epithet pattern (el bueno de Raúl, un desastre de obra) judges someone or something already known.
Lo stays neuter; the adjective agrees with the noun.
El bueno de + name does not compare or pick anyone out; it shows the speaker’s warmth towards someone already known.
Un desastre de reforma judges; the others just classify.

Today you packed information into noun phrases and saw that a dense text sometimes needs unpacking. The natural next step is reformulating without losing the thread, with es decir, a saber or mejor dicho.

The Valdelobos reservoir is at 32% and the drought plan is in force. Héctor, a hydrologist, gives a public talk on Thursday; his slides are rigorous but full of jargon, and Nuria, the communication officer, helps him make them clear. In class 165 you met es decir and mejor dicho as one tool among many; today you study the whole reformulation family: markers that take you back to what you have just said in order to explain it, correct it, play it down or sum it up.
The second part says the same thing more clearly: the first statement still stands.
The second part replaces the first because it is more accurate: the first wording is withdrawn.
What came before stops being decisive: what follows holds whatever the case.
The second part sums up or evaluates everything before it.
With mejor dicho the speaker withdraws the first wording and replaces it.
It sets the doubt aside: we have to save water either way.

Explanatory markers present the second statement as equivalent to the first, only clearer. Es decir is the all-purpose one; esto es is formal and written (don’t confuse it with eso es, “that’s right”); o sea belongs to conversation; en otras palabras and dicho de otro modo usually simplify or translate jargon. A saber is special: it does not paraphrase but spells out the members of something just announced (“three phases, namely: …”), so it needs a list or a specification after it. Vale decir is a formal equivalent of es decir in writing from some American countries.
Consumption is down ten per cent, that is, about two million litres a day: formal, written.
There is a structural water deficit. To put it another way, every year it rains less than we use: jargon translated.
The plan sets out two exceptions, namely hospitals and schools: a saber spells out the “two exceptions”.
“They’re cutting the water off from eight to two tomorrow.” “So, the whole morning without water”: conversational.
Demand exceeds natural recharge; that is, the aquifer loses reserves every year.
The restrictions affect two activities, namely watering gardens and filling pools.
Equivalent to es decir: it pins down what came before. Commas on both sides.
It introduces a consequence, like así que (“so”). No comma after it.
It links nothing: the speaker is just buying time. Very common in casual speech; avoid it in a talk or in writing.

In speech, people often reformulate or conclude with que: “Es decir, que ya hay normas”. That que introduces what the speaker infers, so the verb is indicative, like any statement. Don’t mix it up with decir que + subjunctive for passing on an order: inside es decir, the verb decir no longer reports anything; it is a fixed marker.
“They won’t give us any more water from the transfer.” “So we have to save even more.”
In which sentence is o sea just a filler?

Rectifying markers withdraw the first wording and replace it with a better one. Mejor dicho is neutral and works for facts and for nuance. Más bien offers a more accurate description, often softening or adjusting: “no es prudente, más bien temeroso”; it often follows a negation (no…, sino más bien…). O mejor improves a suggestion or a plan (“call her, or better still, write to her”). Digo is colloquial and fixes a slip of the tongue on the spot (a date, a name, a number). This is the key contrast with es decir: es decir keeps what you said and explains it; mejor dicho takes it back.
Héctor was careful; or rather, overcautious: the first word was too kind.
The meeting wasn’t tense so much as awkward: a more accurate description.
Send Nuria the report, or better still, take it to her in person: an improved plan.
The talk is on Thursday at seven, I mean, at eight: an instant fix of a slip.
There are twenty of us in the building, or rather eighteen: two flats are empty.
We could meet on Monday, or better still, on Tuesday afternoon, when more people are free.

Distancing markers make what was said before irrelevant to the conclusion: whatever the answer to that question or doubt, what follows still holds. En cualquier caso and en todo caso are neutral and frequent in formal speech; de todos modos, de todas formas and de cualquier manera are very common in conversation too. Unlike sin embargo (class 190), they don’t oppose two ideas: they simply stop the previous one from mattering.
It may rain in October or it may not. Either way, the restrictions stay in force until further notice.
I don’t know if many people will come to the talk; we’ll record it anyway.

Recapitulating markers close a stretch of discourse. En resumen sums up; en suma does the same in formal style; en definitiva gives the final verdict. En fin closes a topic and often adds resignation or weariness (“oh well”); it is not por fin (“at last”). Total, que… wraps up a story in conversation. Al fin y al cabo and después de todo introduce the consideration that ultimately settles the matter, often to justify or reassure (“after all”).
Less rain, higher consumption and a depleted aquifer: in sum, a structural problem.
They’ve postponed the treatment plant again. Oh well, we saw it coming: resignation.
Don’t get angry with the technicians; after all, they don’t decide when it rains: the decisive reason.
We’d been waiting three years for the new pipe and at last they’ve installed it.
Some say the drought is temporary and others disagree. Either way, saving water never hurts.
Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
Which sentence is correctly written?
Your slides are rigorous, but what will “structural water deficit” mean to people from the neighbourhood?
That year after year we use more water than falls as rain. To put it another way, it isn’t one bad summer: it’s a deep-rooted problem.
Then say that! And here, where you mention “priority uses”, which are they?
There are three, namely household use, essential services and irrigation. The board approved it on Monday, I mean, on Tuesday.
Another thing: you call the situation “worrying”. I’d say it’s serious, rather. We’re on alert.
You’re right: it’s serious; or rather, it’s the worst in fifteen years. But I don’t want to scare anyone.
Neither scare people nor sugar-coat it. Some neighbours will think we’re exaggerating. Either way, the rules are the same for everyone, and that has to be clear.
And if they ask me about water cuts? I mean, well, none are planned, but I can’t guarantee it either.
Then say it like that, but without the “o sea”. In any case, if there were any, people would get a week’s notice: that’s very reassuring.
OK. And to close? I was thinking of going over the five measures one by one.
Better one sentence: “In sum, small habits, many times a day”. And a final reason: after all, it’s the water that comes out of our taps.
Oh well, looks like I’m redoing half the presentation. Not that I had plans for tonight anyway.
Why is Nuria worried about the second slide?
What does Héctor correct with “digo”?
What does Nuria advise him to do to close the talk?
It takes water straight to the root; in other words, hardly any is lost to evaporation.
The bylaw provides for two kinds of penalty, namely a written warning and a fine for repeat offences.
Last year we used 120 litres per person per day, I mean, 140; sorry.
Maybe, maybe not. Either way, the plan will stay active until it is over fifty per cent.
