I understand, but after all, a pool isn’t an essential use and the water belongs to everyone.
The next day Lucía Ferrer from the local radio goes out to ask residents about the plan. O sea keeps coming up in their answers: classify each use.
The aquifer is depleted; that is, there’s hardly any water left.
It isn’t a ban so much as a recommendation.
There are two exceptions, namely hospitals and schools.
He clearly explains the reservoir situation, the new rules and what each resident can do.
How does Héctor explain the “thirty-two per cent”?
What does he correct with “mejor dicho”?
What does he say about water cuts in homes?
What job does “al fin y al cabo” do at the end?
what you said still stands; a saber only lists the members of a set
what you said is withdrawn and replaced
what came before stops mattering for the conclusion
en fin often sounds resigned and is not por fin, “at last”

Before choosing the marker, ask what you are doing with what you just said: keeping and clarifying it, withdrawing it, setting it aside or summing it up. Then adjust the register: o sea, digo and total belong to conversation; esto es, a saber and en suma to careful writing. And punctuate: a comma after the marker, a colon after a saber.
The flight leaves at seven, or rather at a quarter past: it’s been delayed.
The tenant will cover two costs, namely water and electricity.
I don’t know if I’ll get the job. Either way, the interview was a learning experience.
“They’ve closed the motorway for roadworks.” “So we’re going by the old road.”
Don’t worry so much about the exam; after all, it’s only a placement test.
Elena, a physiotherapist, is preparing an information sheet for her patients. Her notes are either too technical or too casual: you turn them into clear, careful sentences.

For strong students or spare time: three of today’s markers have another very common use. En todo caso can mean “if anything, at most” and scales down what was said. In conversation, total can play something down to justify a decision (“what’s the point anyway”). And a saber followed by a question word doesn’t reformulate at all: it means “who knows”.
Here en todo caso means “at most, if anything”.
Total here means “it’s not worth it anyway”.
A saber + question word means “who knows”.
Make it formal.

You can now go back over what you say to explain, correct, set aside or sum it up. Today’s distancing markers come close to contrast without quite getting there; class 190 takes that step, with connectors that oppose or restrict what was said, and their differences in strength and register.

Elena writes a weekly column in the local paper; this week it is about holiday flats in the old town. Her editor says her arguments are good but her connectors don’t say what she means. You already know how to concede and refute; today you fine-tune four moves: replacing one idea with another, contrasting two realities, restricting what you have just said, and drawing a formal consequence in the right mood.
Both ideas stand: it is legal, and still unfair. “Pero” limits how far the first idea goes.
One idea is denied and another takes its place. “Sino” needs a negation before it.
A fact is acknowledged, but it doesn’t stop the main claim from standing.
We don’t want fewer tourists, but tourists who live alongside the residents: replacement.
I don’t like the measure, but I’ll vote for it: both ideas stand, so “pero”.

Sino always follows a negation and replaces the denied element with the right one: a noun, adjective, adverb or infinitive. When the replacement is a whole clause with a conjugated verb, use sino que. Antes bien is formal and mostly written: after a negated statement, it introduces the idea that is actually true, often the opposite of what was expected. No solo… sino (que) también adds rather than replaces.
The problem isn’t the tourists but the lack of rules: one noun phrase replaces another.
The council doesn’t restrict holiday flats; it bans them: a conjugated verb, so sino que.
The rule doesn’t slow down the local economy; on the contrary, it protects it: formal, written.
Not only are rents going up, but the old shops are closing too: here the second idea adds.
The tax isn’t paid by the tourists but by the owners.
The council hasn’t withdrawn the proposal; it has extended it.
The measure doesn’t drive visitors away; rather, it regulates how they arrive.

En cambio contrasts two realities that are both true (hotels pay, flats don’t); unlike sino, it needs no negation. Por el contrario does the same in a more formal tone, and after a negation it can also correct, like al contrario. Mientras que joins the two realities in one sentence; mientras on its own can also be contrastive, but it may be read as “while (at the same time)”, so in writing mientras que is clearer. Frente a + noun means “as opposed to, compared with”.
Hotels pay a tax per guest; holiday flats, on the other hand, pay nothing.
In the centre rents have risen forty per cent, whereas on the outskirts they have barely changed.
Compared with the thousand holiday flats of ten years ago, there are now over four thousand.
Regulation hasn’t failed; on the contrary, residents’ complaints have halved: here it corrects.
One fact, corrected: the first version is false.
Two true facts set against each other.

Con todo, así y todo and de todas formas acknowledge the previous point and keep your conclusion: “Even so, I support it.” They don’t set two realities side by side; they say the previous argument is not enough to change your position.
There are three thousand residents left in the old town, whereas twenty years ago there were nine thousand.
Unlike the cities that have already regulated, Puerto Alto still has no rules.
I admit the tax is unpopular. Even so, I support it.

Salvo que / excepto que + indicative introduce the one exception to what you have just stated, as a fact. With the subjunctive, salvo que (like a no ser que, class 171) sets a condition: “unless”. Excepto, salvo and menos + noun work like prepositions, but take yo and tú. Solo que adds a snag to something you value (colloquial). Lo que pasa es que and el caso es que bring in the real problem. Más que nada points to the main reason. Si acaso and en todo caso scale a proposal down: “at most, if anything”.
The plan is reasonable, except that it says nothing about people who let a single flat: a fact, indicative.
We’ll vote in favour unless the final text changes: a condition, subjunctive.
I like the proposal; it’s just that it comes too late: the neighbourhood has already changed.
There’s no need for a ban; at most, limit new licences.
I’m writing this column mainly for my elderly neighbours.
The meeting was useful, except that nobody brought concrete figures.
I’ll sign the manifesto unless they change the text.
I’m not asking for the holiday flats to close; at most, that they pay the same as a hotel.

De ahí que (class 165) presents a consequence as explained by what came before and takes the subjunctive in careful Spanish: present in a present frame, imperfect in a past one. De modo que / de manera que / de forma que with the indicative state a real result; with the subjunctive they state a purpose, like para que. The mood alone changes the meaning, so in an op-ed it matters.
Rents have doubled, which is why so many young families are leaving the centre.
Rents doubled, so many families left: a real result, indicative.
Licences must be shared out so that no building has more than two holiday flats: a purpose, subjunctive.
Registration has been compulsory since January, so we now have reliable data.
The register must be published so that any resident can check it.
Last year a hundred new licences were granted, hence the problem got worse.
The report doesn’t blame the tourists but the lack of control.
Everyone in the building voted in favour except me.
Elena, your first paragraph says the opposite of what you think. You wrote “No es un problema de turismo, pero de vivienda”: that “pero” doesn’t work.
You’re right: I’m not adding anything there, I’m replacing. “Not a tourism problem but a housing problem.”
And in the second you say the council has done nothing. That’s no longer true.
True. “The council hasn’t stood still; it has commissioned a study.” And I’ll add a figure: compared with a thousand flats ten years ago, there are now over four thousand.
Good. And the bit about the hotels?
Hotels pay a tax per guest; holiday flats, on the other hand, pay nothing. That’s why the council has no money for inspectors.
You come across as very harsh here. Are you really calling for a ban on all of them?
No. At most, ban new ones in the old town. The existing ones can carry on unless they break the rules.
Then say it like that. Why does this issue matter so much to you?

Mainly because of Mrs Prieto on the third floor: she’s lived in the area for forty years and can no longer afford the rent. I’ll end like this: “Regulating isn’t holding back the economy; rather, it’s sharing out its benefits so that residents can stay.”
Perfect, except that you’re two hundred words over. And the thing is, on Wednesday we close the page at six.
Two hundred… Well, in any case, I’ll send it to you tonight.
What was wrong with Elena’s first paragraph?
What does Elena finally propose about holiday flats?
Why does the issue matter so much to Elena?
Many owners aren’t big companies but families letting a second home.
In the new districts homes are being built, whereas in the centre they are being turned into tourist apartments.
The tourist tax doesn’t drive visitors away; rather, it funds the services they use themselves.
Every group on the council supports the rule except one, which wants more time.
Licences will be granted by lottery so that no owner has an advantage.
It isn’t a tourism problem but a housing problem.
Hotels pay the tax, whereas the flats don’t.
We need to regulate so that residents can stay.
She shares the diagnosis but prefers regulation and enforcement to a ban.
According to Lorena, what does a ban lead to?
Where should the tax money go?
Why is the register the most urgent measure?
Where would Lorena start?
sino needs a negation and replaces; si no is a condition
two true realities side by side; con todo keeps your conclusion
excepto yo; si acaso (at most) is not por si acaso (just in case)
indicative = result; subjunctive = purpose

Before choosing a connector, ask what you are doing with the previous idea: denying and replacing it, setting it against another, limiting it, or drawing a consequence. And watch the mood: salvo que and de modo que change meaning with the subjunctive.
The restaurant’s problem isn’t the price but the quality.
My sister lives in the centre, whereas I live in a village.
The trip went well, except that the train arrived late.
Arrange the chairs so that everyone can see the screen.
I’m not telling you to quit your job; at most, to ask for fewer hours.
Rocío coordinates a language school with two branches and is writing a report for management on a four-day week. Her notes are correct but flat: you turn them into report sentences.

For strong students or spare time. In formal writing, the colloquial snag becomes si bien or ahora bien. Two literary uses of sino: no hacer sino + infinitive means “to do nothing but” (“a ban would only shift the problem”), and nadie sino means “no one but”. Finally, mientras on its own can be temporal or contrastive: context decides.
Make it suitable for an editorial.
What does “no haría sino trasladar” mean? (would do nothing but shift the problem)
What does “nadie sino ella” mean? (no one but her)
In which sentence is “mientras” contrastive rather than temporal?

You can now replace, contrast and restrict ideas precisely. Class 191 teaches hedging: softening a claim without giving it up, with expressions like “to some extent”. It is the natural next step: after qualifying firmly, you learn to qualify cautiously.

Monday morning at a small design studio in Valencia. A junior designer has prepared a website proposal for a rural hotel, and the creative lead has to tell him that some things don’t work. She can say it bluntly or soften it: the content stays the same, but the force of the criticism and its effect on the working relationship change a great deal.
Clear, but it sounds like a verdict on the person. In a Spanish-speaking workplace this can come across as harsh, even between colleagues who trust each other.
It still says that the home page and the copy need changing, so nothing is hidden. The softeners present it as a tentative view and leave room for the other person to reply.

Hedging (atenuación) lowers the force of what you say, not its content. Speakers use it to protect the other person’s face and their own: if the opinion turns out to be wrong or unwelcome, it was only a tentative view. There are four families of tools: limit the claim, lower the force of the words, step back as a speaker, and invite agreement.
Up to a point, the proposal is workable (but not completely).
The home-page video is a bit slow.
It looks as if the menu has too many options.
What does Irene actually think? Hedging changes the force, not the message.
What is hedging mainly for?

Saying “up to a point, the home page works” makes the listener hear the unspoken “…but it has problems”, which is why these phrases are usually followed by “pero”, “aunque” or “ahora bien”. “Digamos” and “por así decirlo” work differently: they hedge the word you chose, flagging it as approximate or a little strong, not the truth of the idea.
“Digamos” flags the word choice, perhaps a polite way of saying “garish”.
Irene only partly agrees. What does she say?

Three ways of making a criticism weigh less. “Un poco” and “algo” go before qualities you see as negative or excessive (a bit long, a bit slow); before positive ones they usually sound odd. Diminutives and “pequeño” shrink the problem (a small detail). Litotes says something by denying its opposite: “no está mal” (it’s good), “no es muy claro” (it’s unclear), “no es precisamente barato” (it’s expensive). “No es que + subjunctive, pero…” rejects a harsh reading before stating the real reservation.
The menu is a bit long and the font slightly small.
There’s just one small thing: the booking phone number is missing.
The new logo is actually rather good (lit. not bad at all).
It’s not that the idea is bad, but it comes too late.
“A bit expensive”: a softened criticism. The price is too high.
“Not very expensive”: “poco” without the article negates the quality. It is a positive comment.
“It isn’t exactly cheap”: it is expensive, said with gentle irony.
Carmen is happy with the quote: the redesign is not expensive for what it includes.
What does “It’s not that the site is slow, but…” mean?

You can step back from your own opinion in three ways. Make it impersonal: “parece que”, “se diría que”, “da la impresión de que”, “uno tiene la sensación de que” (all + indicative) present the criticism as an impression anyone could have. Use the modest conditional or imperfect: “yo diría que” (I’d say), “quería comentarte” (I wanted to mention). Or admit you might be wrong: “a lo mejor me equivoco, pero…”, “no sé si…” (I’m not sure whether), “igual” + indicative, a colloquial “maybe” very common in Spain.
It looks as though nobody has checked the English copy.
You get the feeling the page never ends (“uno” = anyone, but really the speaker).
I wanted to mention something about the budget (the imperfect makes the opening less abrupt).
I’m not sure it’s a good idea to change the logo at this stage (= I think it isn’t).
Maybe we should wait until the client has seen it (colloquial, typical of Spain).

“Igual” meaning “maybe” is colloquial and very common in Spain; like “a lo mejor”, it takes the indicative. In a formal email, prefer “quizá” or “tal vez”. And note that “no sé si…” is often a polite way of saying “I don’t think so”.
Maybe it’s better to remove the video from the home page.
Which sentence presents the criticism as a general impression?

A tag question turns a statement into an invitation to agree: “¿no?”, “¿verdad?”, “¿no te parece?”. A partial concession acknowledges the other person’s point before your reservation: “tienes razón en parte, pero…”, “entiendo lo que dices, pero…”, “puede que tengas razón, pero…”.
The orange is too strong, don’t you think?
You’re partly right, but the client wants to see the rooms as soon as people land on the site.
Clear but abrupt: it can sound like a reproach.
Two or three softeners: polite, and the message still gets through.
Over-hedging: so many softeners that nobody knows what you think. It also sounds insecure.
Irene needs the work by Friday at the latest. Which sentence fits best?
Which sentence acknowledges the other person’s point first?
It’s not that I don’t like the proposal, but I need to think about it.
Which sentence is correct?
Well, you’ve seen it. Be honest: what do you think?
Honestly, it’s pretty good: I love the palette. Now, I’d say the home page is a bit cluttered.
Cluttered? It’s only got six photos…
I know, and they’re lovely. But it looks as if the hotel wants to show everything at once, doesn’t it? Your eye doesn’t know where to go.
You’re partly right. But Carmen asked for the rooms to be visible as soon as you land on the site.
And up to a point that makes sense. I may be wrong, but the rooms would look better on a second page.
And the copy? Her daughter wrote it, you know.
They’re, let’s say, very brochure-like: “an unforgettable paradise”, “a unique experience”… It’s not that they’re badly written, but they could be about any hotel.
I’m not sure Carmen will want to change them. She’s very attached to them.
Then maybe we should suggest it tactfully. In a way, that copy is her way of telling the hotel’s story.
So the home page and the copy have to go.
No, not at all! It’s good work; it just needs lightening a little.
What does Irene really think of the proposal?
Why is Irene so careful about the copy?
What does Óscar really think?
The hotel is a bit far from the village, but the views make up for it.
It’s not that the video is ugly, but it slows the page down.
I may be wrong, but I think Carmen preferred the green.
Which is the softest criticism that still gets the point across?
You’re partly right, but the client insists.
Up to a point, you’re right.
It’s not that it’s expensive, but it’s over budget.
I’d say the video is a bit long.
She is happy overall and asks, gently, for several changes.
What does she think of the home page?
What does she suggest doing with the copy?
What does she think of moving the rooms to a second page?
What does “the price isn’t exactly cheap” mean?
limit how far, in what way or in what words your claim is true
make the criticism weigh less; mind the article: “un poco caro” is not “poco caro”
present the criticism as an impression or a modest opinion
invite agreement and acknowledge the other person’s point before disagreeing

Soften the form, not the substance: the other person must still know what you think and what needs to change. Two or three softeners per criticism are enough; more, and the point gets lost in the fog. Anything they really need to know, like a deadline or a serious error, should be stated plainly.
This restaurant is not expensive: three of us ate for forty euros.
It’s not that I don’t want to help you; I just don’t have time today.
The film wasn’t bad, but I expected more from the ending.
Which answer softens the criticism without losing it?
Maybe it’s better to wait for Monday’s meeting (colloquial, Spain).
Paula, a PhD student, is reviewing a fellow student’s article draft. Her first notes are too blunt. Rewrite her comments so that they stay clear but respectful.

For strong students or spare time. In academic writing hedging is almost compulsory: “cabría pensar que” (one might think), “podría decirse que” (it could be said), “parece razonable suponer que” (it seems reasonable to assume) and “en principio” (in principle) present a conclusion as cautious and open to debate. At the other end, in informal speech in the River Plate region and other parts of South America, “capaz que” often means “maybe”, usually with the indicative.
Which sentence belongs in an academic article?
A friend from Montevideo says this. What does it mean?
Which conclusion sounds most cautious in a thesis?

You can now soften what you say without losing the message. Class 192 does the opposite: intensifying and emphasising with “incluso”, “ni siquiera” or “vaya si”, so your arguments land with full force when the situation calls for it.

A film podcast recorded over a video call between Madrid and Mexico City. The hosts are reviewing a three-hour drama, and the producer finds Irene’s script correct but flat. You already know muy, -ísimo and tan… que; today you learn the resources native speakers use to raise the emotional temperature and to signal what is most, or least, expected.
Everything is true, but nothing stands out: the listener cannot tell what was surprising or how strongly Irene feels.
The degree is presented as something surprising, the scalar words mark what nobody expected, and the final answer is an emphatic yes.
Here hasta means “even”: it places the people with popcorn at the far end of the scale, as the least likely to fall silent.
Vaya si + indicative is an emphatic yes, roughly “and how!” or “it certainly did!”.

Incluso, hasta and aun (no accent) mean “even”: they add the least expected item at the top of an implicit scale. Ni siquiera, or ni + un/una + noun, means “not even”: not even the minimum happened. Like other focus words, they go right before what they highlight. Before the verb, ni siquiera needs no “no”; after the verb, the sentence needs no in front of the verb.
First: even Mateo, of all people, cried. Second: Mateo did several things, and crying was the most surprising one.
Even I understood the ending: hasta is not a preposition here, so it takes yo, not mí.
Not even the minimum: he did not even greet the audience; he did not say a single word.
Aun without an accent means “even”; aún with an accent means “still” or “yet”.
Not even: ni siquiera before the verb, with no extra no.
The particle goes before the highlighted element: incluso Irene means Irene herself, of all people.

Lo + adjective or adverb + que expresses a high degree, presented as something surprising: “how tired I am”, “how well she speaks”. It follows verbs such as saber, imaginar, sorprender or ver, or stands alone as an exclamation. Although lo is neuter, the adjective agrees with its noun (lo cansada, lo largas). The verb stays in the indicative because it states a fact. Lo que + verb works the same way with actions: ¡lo que se ríe! means “how much he laughs”.
Irene, a woman, says cansada: the adjective agrees with her, not with lo.
With an adverb nothing agrees; the verb stays in the indicative.
Plural feminine: the adjective agrees with las escenas.
How much I cried! / Boring, it says? The things you hear! (a fixed phrase of mock indignation)
Lo bueno names an aspect, “the good thing”. The adjective stays masculine singular because it refers to no noun.
Lo buena que means “how good”: it agrees with la película and stresses the degree.

Colloquial Spanish, very frequent in Spain, stresses a quantity with la de + noun + que: “the number of times I’ve told you!”. La cantidad de… que works everywhere. Do not confuse it with lo de, which refers back to a topic.
The adjective agrees with las críticas, even though lo is neuter.
The structure presents a fact, so the verb is indicative.

Sí que before the verb reinforces an affirmation (“that really is cinema”). Vaya si + indicative, often repeating the verb of the question, is a colloquial emphatic yes. Exclamatives add degree: ¡Qué + noun + tan / más + adjective! (both are used; más is especially common in Spain), ¡Cuánto…! for quantity or intensity, and ¡Si (es que)…! or ¡Pero si…! to protest that something is obvious.
An emphatic yes, then sí que to underline that this really is cinema.
Qué + noun + tan / más + adjective; there is no “a”: never *¡Qué una película!
Cuánto with a verb; cuánta agreeing with the noun.
Protest: “But you didn’t look at your watch once!” / “It just never ends!”
Intensity can also be measured by its result: so slow that…, cried so much that… Repeating a noun highlights the “real” or typical thing: a proper film, real coffee.
An emphatic yes that repeats the verb of the question.
Qué + noun + tan + adjective, with no article: the English “a” is not translated.

Each region has favourite intensifiers: re- in Argentina and Uruguay, bien + adjective in Mexico and much of Central America, la mar de and qué… más in Spain. Recognise them all, use your own variety naturally, and avoid mixing them in one text.
A written review in a cultural paper needs a formal intensifier.
De lo más already intensifies; the adjective agrees with noche and takes no other intensifier.
Ni siquiera before the verb, with no extra no.
With gustar the person takes a (a mí); hasta simply goes in front of it.
Recording in three, two… Irene, you start.
Welcome to Butaca doble. Today: almost three hours of lighthouse, wind and family. And I’ll tell you something, Mateo: you have no idea how long it felt to me.
Well, for me it was the other way round. I saw it really early, at the ten o’clock showing, and I didn’t even look at my watch.
Seriously? It is an extremely slow film. The lead goes twenty minutes without saying a single word.
But those silences say a lot. Even the couple next to me, who had come in eating popcorn, went quiet.
I’ll give you that. And the cinematography is really lovely, I admit.
Lovely? What stunning cinematography! Even the waves seem to have a personality.
Sure, sure… but the ending. It just never ends! Three endings, one after another.
And the scene with the grandmother in the lighthouse? Don’t tell me you didn’t cry.
Did I cry! That really is cinema. How I cried in that scene…
I love how well you two argue. But Irene, we still need your score.
A seven. It isn’t perfect, but it is a proper film, the kind they don’t make any more.
What evidence does Mateo give that the film is not boring?
What bothers Irene about the ending?
What is Irene’s final verdict?
Not even the minimum: ni siquiera, with no extra no.
The adjective agrees with Irene.
A fact, so the indicative.
Hasta is not a preposition here, so it takes the subject pronoun yo.
Qué + noun + tan + adjective, without an article.
An emphatic yes that repeats the verb.
You have no idea how nervous I was before the premiere: a woman speaking, so nerviosa.
The lead did not say a single word for twenty minutes: no + verb + ni una.
Did I like the lighthouse scene? I certainly did!
What does Mateo do in his minute?
What does he highlight about the lead actress?
What seems like one more character?
What does he criticise about the music?
How did he feel when he left the cinema?
Incluso, hasta and aun add the least expected item; ni siquiera and ni un(a) deny even the minimum. They go right before what they highlight.
Lo + agreeing adjective or adverb + que + indicative presents a degree as surprising; lo que + verb does the same with actions.
Sí que and vaya si give an emphatic yes; exclamatives express surprise or protest, with no article after qué.
Choose intensifiers by register and region: colloquial bien, la mar de, súper or re-; general or written de lo más and sumamente; and the result clause tan… que.

Two questions before turning up the volume: what do I want to highlight (the unexpected, the bare minimum, or the degree)? And where am I saying it (a voice message or a written review)? Golden rule: if everything is emphatic, nothing stands out.
Hardly anyone came to the book launch, not even the author’s friends.
You’ll be surprised how beautiful her photos are.
Did your boss know? She certainly did!
A newspaper review needs a formal intensifier.
How long I have waited for this moment!
Bogotá, Colombia. Daniela is preparing a toast for her brother Felipe’s wedding. Her first draft is too flat; help her bring it to life.

In conversation intensity can be left unfinished, with intonation doing the work of tan… que, or completed with a bare que + result. ¡Ni que + imperfect subjunctive! rejects someone else’s exaggeration (“as if it were…!”). Con lo + adjective or adverb + que presents a degree as a reason or a contrast (“given how well she acts…”).
Irene rejects Mateo’s exaggeration: “As if it were the best film ever!”
It was so cold on set that nobody could stay on the beach.
Given how well she acts, how can she not have a single award?

Today you learned to turn up the volume on your own statements. The natural next step is saying whose information it is and how far you commit to it, with según, supuestamente or se dice que: controlling other people’s voices as well as your own.

The city wants to build an underground car park under the neighbourhood square. Natalia, secretary of the residents’ association, compares how three outlets report it. The fact is the same; what changes is who answers for it. Every text carries several voices, and grammar shows how far the writer commits to each of them.
“Reconoce” presents the content as true: the source concedes something that goes against its own interest.
Neutral attribution: the claim belongs to the councillor and the paper takes no position on it.
“Pretende que” + indicative reports a claim the writer finds doubtful, roughly “would have us believe”.
With “reconoce”, the paper treats the delay as a fact the councillor has conceded.
Which headline is neutral? “Según” attributes without judging.

“To pretend” is “fingir”. “Pretender + infinitive” means “to aim / intend”; “pretender que + subjunctive” means “to expect someone to do something”, often reproachfully; and in formal writing “pretender que + indicative” means “to claim” something the writer doubts.
The association presents it as wrongdoing: which verb fits?
He first said “the whole square”, then qualified it: only half.

Verbs that pass on a content take the indicative, even when the writer keeps their distance (“pretende que no sabía nada”). Verbs that reject the content, “negar” and “desmentir”, normally take the subjunctive: the content stays outside what is asserted. When a reporting verb is itself negated (“no afirmó que…”), the subjunctive is common too.
The councillor acknowledges that the report arrived late (presented as true).
The councillor denies that the report arrived late (content rejected: subjunctive).
The construction company denies it is going to close the street for a year.
Residents maintain that the square works fine as it is.
A warning that informs: “they warn that the works will take two years”.
A warning that orders: “he told everyone not to enter”.
A claim the writer doubts: “he would have us believe nobody told him”.
“Do you expect me to believe that?”
The council denies that the project costs more than ten million.
The councillor admitted that the public consultation came too late.
“According to you…”: según takes the subject pronoun.
A figure taken from a report: how do you attribute it?

“Supuestamente” (supposedly) attributes the claim to others and usually shows doubt. “Presuntamente / presunto” (allegedly, alleged) belong to legal and news language: they do not express distrust, they respect the presumption of innocence. “El llamado” (the so-called / the plan known as) presents a name someone else gave, neutrally or with a touch of irony. Distancing quotation marks put a word in someone else’s mouth: los «expertos» = the people who call themselves experts.
Supposedly the car park was going to be ready in a year (the speaker doubts it).
The police have identified the alleged author of the graffiti: no court has ruled yet.
The so-called Plaza Viva Plan (the official name) includes two hundred parking spaces.
The council quotes its “experts”, but nobody knows their names (ironic quotation marks).

In Spanish “aparentemente” mostly means “seemingly, on the surface”. For “apparently” in the sense of “I’ve been told”, use “al parecer”, “por lo visto” or “según parece”; “aparentemente” with that meaning often sounds translated.
Rubén echoes what he has just heard, in surprise.
“Apparently (I’ve been told), the works start in March.”
The spokesman denied the council was going to cut down more trees.
Natalia doesn’t want to vouch for something she heard in the street.
Have you seen today’s district paper? According to the headline, the whole neighbourhood backs the car park.
I’ve read it. Look at the verbs: Pilar “assures” readers the car park will save local shops, while we “would have people believe” the square can’t be touched.
We “claim”? So what she says is a fact and what we say is a whim.
Exactly. And they call us “critical residents”, in quotation marks, as if there were only a handful of us.
The councillor, on the other hand, gets kind treatment: “In Llorente’s view, the project is a historic opportunity.”
And nothing about the trees. Yesterday at the meeting he admitted that twelve will have to be cut down, and that’s missing.
Well, he then added that they’ll plant twice as many in other streets.
That’s his claim. In the newsletter we won’t present it as a fact: we’ll write “according to the councillor”, and we’ll see where they plant them.
Fair enough. Oh, and Pilar says to call her before Friday.
I’ll call her this afternoon. She denies the plan harms anyone, and I want to understand why.
For me, the best thing is to include every voice and let each resident draw their own conclusions.
Why is Natalia annoyed? The paper uses friendlier verbs for some voices than for others.
Which fact is missing from the article?
How will the newsletter present the promise to plant twice as many trees?
The association complains that nobody has informed the residents at number 14.
The architect denied that the car park caused problems in nearby buildings.
The construction company claimed that the delay was due to the lack of permits.
Do you expect residents to sign the plan without reading it?
The engineers warned that the ground could subside.
According to the report, the works will take two years.
The association denies that the plan has residents’ support.
In Rubén’s view, the so-called green plan is a mistake.
She sums up the meeting, attributing every position to its source.
What did councillor Llorente acknowledge?
What has Pilar Ferrán said on air?
How does she present the date of the vote?
What do the engineers warn about?
The reporting verb shows what the source does and how far the writer commits; rejecting verbs take the subjunctive.
“Según” attributes facts or opinions (never “según que”, never “según mí”); “para” and “a juicio de” introduce opinions only.
Distance markers pass a claim on without vouching for it; “presunto” is a legal safeguard, not doubt. For “apparently”, prefer “al parecer”.
Echoic “que” repeats what you heard or relays a message; it belongs to speech only.

Before writing a sentence with someone else’s information, ask who answers for it. If you do, state it. If someone else does, attribute it with a verb that describes what they do. If you don’t believe it, mark your distance.
The head teacher denies they are going to close the canteen.
According to the inspectors, the building needs urgent renovation.
The boss admitted the project had been delayed through his fault.
Headline: “Alleged jewellery shop thief arrested”.
You’ve been told the gym closes in August.

For strong students or spare time. “Dizque” is colloquial in several Latin American countries, such as Colombia or Mexico: “so they say”, usually with doubt or irony; before a noun it means “so-called”. “Admitir que + subjunctive” means “to tolerate”, not “to acknowledge”. And when a reporting verb is negated, the subjunctive is common, because the content is not asserted.
“Admitir que” + subjunctive means “to tolerate”.
Colloquial “dizque”: what does the speaker express?
A negated reporting verb: what does the subjunctive convey?

You can now attribute each claim to its voice and choose how far you commit to it. Class 194 takes this to whole texts: weaving direct and indirect quotations into a paragraph, varying reporting verbs instead of repeating “said”, and keeping your distance consistently through an article or report.

Irene Salvat edits the online magazine “Ciudad Abierta”. Mateo, a reporter, has sent her his piece on Thursday’s public meeting about pedestrianising the old town. His facts are solid, but his quotes are not always handled well. Today you learn the mechanics of quoting in writing: when to copy the exact words, how to weave them into your own sentence, how to report statements, questions and requests, how to boil a long speech down, and how to keep your distance from a claim.
Her exact words, introduced by a colon, in quotation marks and with a capital letter. The voice is hers.
Your voice reports what she said: “que”, no quotation marks, and tenses adapted to your report.
Your sentence, with a literal fragment that fits its grammar: the most common technique in the press and in academic writing.
In which version are the words entirely Robles’s, untouched by the reporter?
In this integrated quote, which part is literal?

Quote directly when the exact words matter. A full quote follows a colon and starts with a capital letter. Introductory phrases such as “como señala X” or “en palabras de X” are followed by a comma. An integrated fragment carries no colon and no capital, and it must fit your sentence: same person, compatible tense. If it doesn’t fit, paraphrase in indirect speech instead.
As Castell points out in her report, “the measure would cut traffic in the centre by 40%”: comma after the introducer, lower case because the quote continues the sentence.
In Gil’s words, “nobody is against the plan; what worries us is how it’s done”.
Gil described the timetable as “rushed”: a one-word fragment that slots into the reporter’s sentence.

The RAE recommends angle quotes « » as the first choice, especially in print, and they are standard in the Spanish press. Across much of Latin America and online, double quotes “ ” are more common. Both are correct: be consistent and alternate them for a quote within a quote. Unlike US English, the full stop always goes outside.
Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
You want to quote only the beginning and end of Castell’s sentence. How do you mark the cut?

With a present reporting verb (sostiene, afirma, explica: typical when you discuss a text that is still “speaking”), tenses stay as they were. With a past reporting verb, tenses usually shift into the past. But if the fact is still valid and you, the writer, present it as current, you can keep the present or future. The shifted version keeps the perspective of the moment it was said: neutral in a narrative, and it can leave open whether things have changed.
Present frame: no shift. “Sería” is not a shifted tense here but a hypothesis: the measure doesn’t exist yet.
March is still ahead and the writer presents the date as firm.
Also correct: the report keeps the perspective of the meeting.
A general truth stays in the present.
You report it the same day and treat it as valid: you are vouching for it too. (If Irene had said it last week, “mañana” would no longer fit.)
You keep the perspective of when she said it, without guaranteeing that it still holds: “…but who knows now”.

In fiction and in some feature writing, the narrator renders a character’s thoughts with no reporting verb and no quotation marks, using the narrative tenses but the character’s viewpoint: the question and “tomorrow” belong to Robles, while “iba” and “tendría” are the narrator’s. You only need to recognise it.
Discussing a published report today: Castell argues that the measure would reduce traffic.
A month ago Gil said he was worried; now he supports the plan. Which sentence fits?

Yes/no questions are reported with “si”; other questions keep the question word, with its accent (qué, cuándo, cuánto, por qué). “Quiso saber” and “se preguntó” are more elegant than repeating “preguntó”. Requests and orders take the subjunctive after “que”, normally in the past subjunctive after a past verb. “Ordenar”, “prohibir” and “permitir” also take an infinitive.
A resident asked whether taxis would be allowed in (yes/no question → si).
Another resident wanted to know how much the works would cost (question word kept, with its accent).
Robles asked the shopkeepers to give the plan six months (request → que + subjunctive).
The mayor’s office ordered the street closed during the meeting (ordenar + infinitive).
A shopkeeper wanted to know when the works would start.
Robles asked the residents to be patient.

To summarise, don’t pile up “dijo que… dijo que…”. Choose a verb that names the speech act (announced, defended, admitted, denied, ruled out, warned of, called for) and condense the content into a noun phrase: “the risk of losing customers”, “the extension of the area”. Note the mood: “negar que” and “descartar que” normally take the subjunctive; “reconocer que” and “admitir que” take the indicative.
Gil ruled out outright opposition to the plan but warned of the risk of losing customers: ten minutes of speech in one line.
Robles denied that the plan was improvised (subjunctive) and admitted that the timetable was tight (indicative).
The claim is hers, not yours; “sería” presents the effect as a hypothesis, since the measure hasn’t been applied.
Verbs like “demuestra” or “confirma” commit you, the writer, to the truth of what follows.
The conditional of reported information (class 193): you don’t present it as certain. Some style guides prefer to name the source and avoid it.
Gil spoke for ten minutes about parking and sales. Which summary is most precise?
You want to present Castell’s idea without endorsing it. Which verb do you choose?
Which sentence is right in a written report? (A resident asked whether there would be benches.)
Gil said they felt ignored. Which integrated quote is correct?
Mateo, the facts are fine; the quotes, less so. Here you write that Robles said “we’ll start in March”. Who’s starting, you and me?
I see, I’m mixing her voice with mine. Either I quote her in full or I switch to indirect speech: Robles announced they would start in March on Calle Mayor.
Exactly. And you’ve got a much better quote to open with: “In Robles’s words, ‘pedestrianisation is irreversible’.” With the full stop after the closing quote, OK?
Got it. What about the audience? I wrote that a resident asked whether taxis would be able to get in.
People say it all the time, but in writing “preguntó si” is better. The other one, “wanted to know when the works would start”, is perfect.
I left the bit about the shopkeepers like this: Robles asked them to give the plan six months.
Good. Now, Gil: a ten-minute speech and half your article. Sum it up: Gil ruled out outright opposition but warned of the risk of losing customers.
OK. And Castell? I’ve put that she argues the measure would be effective with good public transport.
Perfect: she’s the one claiming it, not you, and “sería” reminds the reader the measure doesn’t exist yet. If you trim her sentence, mark the cut with an ellipsis in square brackets.
One last question: the banner at the entrance had a spelling mistake. Do I correct it?
No: copy it as it is and warn the reader with “sic” in square brackets, right after the word.
Done. I’ll send it back corrected before twelve.
Why doesn’t “Robles said that ‘we’ll start in March’” work?
What does Mateo do with the banner?
According to Irene, what does “sería” express in the sentence about Castell?
Robles confirmed that the next meeting is on Friday at six.
A cyclist asked whether there would be a cycle lane.
Robles ordered the access points to be checked.
Gil denied that the shopkeepers opposed the plan but demanded guarantees.
The councillor asked the shopkeepers to be patient.
A resident wanted to know when the works would start.
The author argues that the measure would be effective.
It reports the presentation of the plan and how residents, shopkeepers and an expert reacted.
What did Robles say about the emergency services?
What is known about the cost of the works?
What is Ramón Gil’s position?
According to Castell, under what condition would the measure work?

On air you can’t see quotation marks, so the newsreader signals them with “in the councillor’s words”. Notice the tenses too: “announced that it will start” and “assured that they will have access” keep the future because those events are still ahead and the station presents them as firm, while the request takes the past subjunctive.
Exact words in quotation marks; the fragment must fit your sentence; the full stop goes outside; […] marks your cuts and [sic] someone else’s error
A present reporting verb keeps the tenses; after a past one, keep the present if you vouch that it still holds
Yes/no questions with “si”, others with the question word; requests and orders with the subjunctive or, with ordenar or prohibir, the infinitive
Summarise with a verb that names the speech act and a noun; keep your distance with sostiene and the conditional

Before quoting, ask who is speaking in every word of your sentence. Their exact words go in quotation marks with the full stop outside; your voice uses reported speech, with the tense that matches what you are claiming today. To summarise, choose a verb that interprets; to keep your distance, use “sostiene” and the conditional.
She asked me when the street would open.
The officer asked us not to park there.
The author argues that the reform would be effective if applied nationwide.
How do you show that you have cut words from a quote?
Paula Rentería is writing a review of an essay on car-free cities for a university seminar. Her notes are in direct speech; turn them into the register of an academic text.

For strong students or spare time. Some reporting verbs pass on information with the indicative but a request or order with the subjunctive: “dijo que esperábamos” (he told us we were waiting) vs “dijo que esperáramos” (he told us to wait). The same goes for advertir and insistir en. Also, after a past verb, a request that is still pending can take the present subjunctive, common in the press; the past subjunctive is also correct.
Which sentence reports an order?
What did she do?
Which sentence expresses a demand?
Is this sentence correct?

You can now integrate quotes, report statements, questions and requests, and summarise while keeping your distance. Your reports already contain sentences like “About a hundred residents attended” or “Most shopkeepers support the plan”. Class 195 covers agreement in those tricky cases: subjects after the verb, collective nouns and quantifiers.

Inés Carrasco is copy chief at El Mirador, a digital newspaper in Puerto Claro. Daniel Ponce, a local reporter, has written about a residents’ assembly and the city’s transport survey. The facts are fine; the agreement isn’t always. Today you look at the cases where the verb hesitates: does it agree with the grammatical head, with the meaning, or with what comes after it?
“Gente” is a singular collective noun: it refers to many people, but the verb stays singular.
The head is “mayoría” (singular), but the meaning is plural, so the norm accepts both.
With a neuter subject (lo que…) and a plural complement, “ser” agrees with the plural.
Which sentence is correct? (People in the neighbourhood are very angry.)
Which does the norm accept?

A collective noun on its own (gente, público, equipo, comunidad) takes a singular verb. When a noun of quantity or a group word is followed by de + a plural noun (la mayoría de, la mitad de, un grupo de, el resto de, el 30 % de), the verb can agree with the singular head or with the plural meaning: both are standard, and the plural is very common. With ser or estar plus an adjective or noun describing people, the plural sounds most natural.
The audience gave a standing ovation for several minutes (collective alone: singular).
A group of tourists turned up in the middle of the assembly: both singular and plural are correct.
Thirty per cent of voters cast a blank ballot: again, both are correct.
With de + a singular noun (la población), the verb is singular.
With estar + an adjective about the people, the plural is the natural choice.
Seventy per cent of the budget goes on maintenance.
Half of the participants were satisfied with the workshop.

Two subjects joined by y take a plural verb. After the verb, singular agreement with the first noun is also attested (Me gusta el cine y el teatro), especially in speech; the plural is the norm in careful writing. Coordinated infinitives or clauses take the singular, and so can two nouns seen as one single idea. With ni… ni before the verb, use the plural; after the verb, both are possible. With o, both numbers occur: the singular stresses that only one of them will act. Tanto… como takes the plural. A phrase between commas with junto con, además de, al igual que or así como is not part of the subject, so the verb agrees with the first noun.
I like cinema and theatre: plural is the norm; the singular is attested after the verb, especially in speech.
It worries me that they arrive so late: the subject is a whole clause, so the verb is singular even if the clause is plural inside.
Neither the mayor nor the councillor came: before the verb, ni… ni takes the plural.
After the verb, ni… ni accepts singular or plural.
The councillor, together with her team, will present the plan: the phrase between commas doesn’t count, so the verb is singular.
It worries us that the works might be delayed again.
The president, together with two advisers, left the meeting.

When ser links a neuter subject (eso, esto, todo, lo que…) or a singular noun such as problema or causa to a plural noun, the verb agrees with the plural: “Eso son tonterías”, “Todo eran risas”, “El problema son los plazos”. You met “Lo que necesito son vacaciones” in class 184; here it extends to demonstratives, todo and nouns.
Those are unconfirmed rumours: “eso” is neuter, the verb agrees with “rumores”.
At first it was all applause; then the questions came.
The problem is the timetables, not the routes.

Impersonal haber (there is / there are) has no subject: the noun after it is its object, so the verb stays singular in every tense and in periphrases: hubo, había, habrá, ha habido, puede haber, va a haber. Plural forms such as “hubieron problemas” or “habían muchas personas” are very frequent in much of Latin America and in some areas of Spain, but they are not accepted in careful language. Existir, faltar or quedar do have a subject and do agree. Hacer for elapsed time is also invariable: “Hace dos años”.
There were some very tense moments at the assembly: hubo, never “hubieron”.
There may be traffic closures downtown tomorrow: the periphrasis stays singular too.
Several alternatives to the project exist: existir has a subject, so it agrees.
The bike lane was approved two years ago: hace never goes plural.

Plural haber (“habían fiestas”, “hubieron quejas”) and first-person forms (“habíamos veinte” for “there were twenty of us”) are widespread among native speakers in Latin America and in parts of Spain. They are not learner errors, but newspapers, reports and exams always use “había”, “hubo” and “éramos / estábamos veinte”.
According to the local police, there were more than three thousand people at the demonstration.
By the end of the session, it was all congratulations.

With gustar-type verbs, verbs of lack and presence, accidental se (se me olvidaron) and the passive se, the subject usually comes after the verb, and that is exactly where agreement slips: speakers start in the singular before they reach the plural noun. Check what comes after: “Me encantan tus fotos”, “Faltan dos firmas”, “Se venden pisos”. With people introduced by a, the se construction is impersonal and stays singular: “Se busca a los dueños”.
I love your photos of the neighbourhood: the photos are the subject.
Daniel forgot his interview notes (literally, the notes “got forgotten” on him).
Three shop premises are for sale on Calle Mayor.
Wanted: the owners of a lost dog (a + people: impersonal, singular).
On the estate agent’s sign: “Two-bedroom flats for rent.”
Carmen lives in the neighbourhood and includes herself: “We residents are tired of waiting.”
Which sentence is correct in careful writing? (There have been several accidents at that junction.)
Which sentence is correct? (Two signatures are still missing from the minutes.)
Daniel, the piece is really lively, but before it goes out we’re checking agreement. First line: “Habían más de doscientas personas”. That needs to be “había”, singular.
Even though there are two hundred of them? At home I’ve always heard it in the plural.

It’s very common, and not just where you’re from, but in the paper “haber” doesn’t agree: the people aren’t the subject. If you want a plural, change the verb: “more than two hundred people attended”.
OK. And “La mayoría de los vecinos pidieron más autobuses nocturnos”? Is that wrong too?
No, that one’s fine: “pidieron” or “pidió”, both are correct. What doesn’t work is the bit in the third paragraph: “la gente estaban indignados”. It’s “la gente estaba indignada”.
Right. Then I quote Carmen Vidal: “What we’re asking for is buses until one in the morning.” Do I leave it like that?

Perfect: “ser” agrees with the plural. And the line about the council meeting: “La concejala, junto con su equipo, presentarán un plan”. It should be “presentará”: what’s between the commas isn’t the subject.
And if I drop the commas and write “the councillor and her team”?
Then yes, plural. One more thing: “Ni el alcalde ni la concejala acudió”. Before the verb, the normal form is the plural: “acudieron”.
Done. I think the last line is fine: “The bike lane was promised two years ago, and two sections are still missing.”
Spotless. And the closing quote, “We residents are tired of promises”, stays as it is: Carmen includes herself.
Thanks, Inés. I worry that readers will notice these mistakes more than the story itself.
Why does Inés correct “Habían más de doscientas personas”?
Which of Daniel’s sentences needs no change?
Why does Inés keep “Los vecinos estamos cansados”?
According to the technical report, there were serious faults in the sewer system.
What drivers are demanding is more parking spaces.
The opposition is surprised that the council meeting is being held behind closed doors.
The mayor, together with two councillors, opened the new works on Monday.
He is one of the journalists who know the neighbourhood best.
What the residents are asking for is more buses.
It worries me that they arrive so late.
The library closed two years ago.
He covers the transport survey, the residents’ assembly and the new monthly passes.
What do most residents do?
What gets the most criticism?
Who did not go to the assembly?
When will the emergency plan be presented?

Felipe uses news register: full sentences, exact figures and careful agreement. He addresses listeners as “ustedes”, as everywhere in Latin America. Notice that he chooses the singular after “la mayoría de los vecinos” and “el 62 % de los jóvenes”, a very common choice in the press, although the plural would also be correct.
Singular with a collective alone, a clause as subject, a phrase between commas with junto con, and with impersonal haber and hacer
Both numbers are correct after a quantity noun + de + plural, and with ni… ni or o after the verb
Plural with coordinated subjects, ser before a plural complement, and plural subjects placed after the verb
Usted takes the third person; a plural subject can include the speaker; uno de los que prefers the plural

Before you conjugate, ask two things: is there a subject (with haber and time hacer, there isn’t, so always singular), and where is it? If it comes after the verb, find it before choosing singular or plural. And when the head is singular but the meaning is plural, remember that the norm accepts both.
There were several power cuts in the neighbourhood this weekend.
What tires me most about my job is the meetings.
We really liked the photos you sent us.
The coach, like his players, was pleased with the result.
I’ve been living in this city for five years.
Lucía Robles is proofreading a hiking club’s quarterly newsletter before it goes out to members. She finds three agreement mistakes. Correct them.

For strong students or spare time. 1. With a modal + infinitive, both “Se debe revisar los datos” and “Se deben revisar los datos” are accepted. 2. With a plural indirect object after the verb, “les” is recommended; “le dije a mis padres” is very common everywhere but avoided in careful writing. 3. “La mayoría de nosotros piensa / pensamos”: both are correct, and “pensamos” includes the speaker. 4. “Más de un vecino se quejó”: the meaning is plural, but “más de un” takes the singular.
Which does the norm accept? (The results can be checked online.)
In an official report, which option is recommended? (We sent the minutes to all members.)
More than one member complained about the price.
Is this correct? (Most of us think the work is necessary.)

You can now decide agreement in careful writing: collectives and percentages, coordinated subjects, ser with a plural complement, invariable haber and hacer, and subjects after the verb. In class 196 you keep working on word order and force from another angle: questions that expect no answer and complex exclamations, where the subject also tends to follow the verb.

Two days before the final of a university debating tournament. The motion is about closing city centres to private cars. The coach wants her team to stop reading out figures and start persuading, using questions that need no answer and exclamations that carry emotion.
Four accurate statements that the judges hear and forget.
The questions make the listeners supply the answer themselves, which is far more persuasive; the exclamation conveys amazement rather than just reporting a change.
A negative rhetorical question makes a positive claim: who wouldn’t…? means everyone would.
Acaso pushes the question towards an obvious “no”.

A rhetorical question does not request information: it makes a statement, and with the opposite polarity. An affirmative question asserts a negative (Who believes that? = nobody does); a negative question asserts a positive (Who wouldn’t want to live better? = everyone would). Acaso pushes towards an obvious “no”. ¿Cómo no voy a…? means “of course I will”, while ¿Cómo voy a…? means “I can’t possibly”.
Everyone would want one: the negative question asserts a positive.
I haven’t asked you for anything: acaso expects the answer “no”.
Cómo no voy a… = of course I’m going; cómo voy a… = I can’t possibly go.
Para qué + infinitive or verb: there is no point in doing it.
To assert “nobody”, the question is affirmative.
Of course I’m voting: cómo no voy a…
The speaker thinks they know the answer but still asks for confirmation; the voice rises and the other person replies.
Nobody replies: the answer is implied (“for nothing”, “it doesn’t matter”), and the voice usually falls.

On its own, ¿Y qué? dismisses the previous point (“so what?”). Followed by a verb, it is usually a genuine follow-up question (“and what did the judges say?”). In a debate it works, but it sounds confrontational, so back it up with a reason.
The tag ¿verdad? asks for confirmation.
Qué más da means it makes no difference.

In lesson 192 you used qué… tan / más, cuánto and lo… que to intensify. Here is the full system. Cuánto agrees with its noun (cuánta gente, cuántos coches). Cómo + verb exclaims about the intensity or manner of an action (how it’s raining!). Quién + imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish for oneself that seems out of reach (if only I could…); quién + pluperfect subjunctive, especially ¡Quién lo hubiera dicho!, expresses surprise at an outcome nobody expected. The subject goes after the verb.
Qué + noun + tan + adjective, with no article; cuántas agrees with bicis.
Cómo + verb: how much the neighbourhood has changed.
Lo + adjective + que: the adjective agrees (lenta, with la cola).
A wish that feels out of reach (if only I could walk to work!) / surprise at an unexpected outcome (who would have thought it!).
Cuánta agrees with gente (feminine singular).
A wish that seems out of reach takes the imperfect subjunctive.

Opening marks are compulsory and go where the question or exclamation begins, which may be mid-sentence. For a question that is also an exclamation, combine both marks. Rhetorical questions usually fall at the end like statements, tags rise, and exclamatives put strong stress on the exclamative word.
You can’t imagine how glad I am: indirect exclamatives keep the accent.
A wish uses unstressed que, with no accent.
I’ll play the other team: “Closing the centre will ruin the shops.” Valeria, your rebuttal.
Have you ever seen a car buying bread? People do the shopping, and people walk.
Good, but look at the judges, not at me. Pablo: “Lots of people need their car for work.”
Some do, yes. So what? Nobody wants to take the plumber’s van away; we want to get single-occupant cars out of the centre.
Much better. Now, the closing speech. Valeria, start strong.
Who wouldn’t want to step outside and hear birds instead of car horns?
What an opening! What a perfectly rounded line!
It’s good, yes, but no “menudo” in front of the judges. Why risk something so colloquial? And in the question, your voice falls at the end, as in a statement.
Got it. Then I tell them about Bogotá: on Sundays they close whole avenues for bikes. How the city changes on those mornings!
You’re going to nail it, right? Although you look so nervous!
If only I could skip straight to Friday night! In September I didn’t even dare to raise my hand in class.
Who would have thought it! And look at you now, in the final. Tomorrow at five, last rehearsal, right?
How does Pablo answer the argument that people need their cars for work?
Why doesn’t Elena want to hear menudo in the final?
What has changed about Valeria since September?
To assert “nobody”, the rhetorical question is affirmative.
Of course I’m going: cómo no voy a…
If only I had had a coach like that at twenty: exclamative quién, with an accent.
What a pleasant terrace: no article after qué.
So what? Stressed qué, with an accent.
Who wouldn’t want to live without noise? Everyone would.
What a lovely square they’ve made! The subject comes after the verb.
What’s the point of widening the road? (There is none.)
What does Valeria do in her speech?
How does she answer the argument about the shops?
What happened to the high street?
What does her “So what?” mean?
What happens in Bogotá on Sundays?
A rhetorical question states something with reversed polarity: affirmative questions deny, negative questions affirm; acaso leans towards “no”.
Tags such as ¿no? and ¿verdad? ask for real confirmation and expect an answer.
Exclamatives of degree: no article after qué, cuánto agrees with the noun, cómo goes with a verb, and the subject comes after the verb.
Quién + imperfect subjunctive for a wish that seems out of reach, ¡Quién lo hubiera dicho! for surprise; menudo, qué de and si será are colloquial.

Before asking a rhetorical question, check what it actually states: no “no” to mean nobody, with “no” to mean everyone. In writing, accent the exclamative or interrogative word and open the mark where the question begins. One well-placed rhetorical question persuades; ten in a row wear the reader out.
Who hasn’t dreamt of dropping everything? Everyone has.
Have I ever lied to you? (I never have.)
How many people there were in the square!
So what? The debate hasn’t started yet.
If only I could be twenty again!
Lima, Peru. Gabriela is writing a restaurant review for a travel website. Her draft is correct but flat; help her bring it to life with exclamatives and a rhetorical question.

Because a rhetorical question that denies works like a negative sentence, it can contain negative words without no: “Did I ever say anything?” (I said nothing); “Have you ever in your life seen such a queue?” (never). ¿Cómo que…? echoes what someone has just said, with surprise or protest, and is often written with both marks.
Have I said anything against cyclists? (I haven’t.)
Have you ever in your life seen a queue like that?
Both marks open and close symmetrically.

Today you saw that opening marks go where the question or exclamation begins, sometimes mid-sentence. The natural next step is the rest of the punctuation that organises a text: commas, dashes and brackets around asides and clarifications, and punctuation with connectors, so your writing persuades through clarity as well.

A cultural foundation runs reading clubs in neighbourhood libraries. Daniel, the programme coordinator, must hand in the annual report to the board on Friday, and Clara, a copy-editor, says his ideas are clear but his commas aren’t. You already know the connectors from classes 189 and 190; today you learn to punctuate them, along with asides: appositions, clarifications, forms of address, dashes and brackets, following the official RAE-ASALE spelling rules.
The connector is glued to the sentence: the reader can’t see where it begins or ends.
Two commas set the connector apart: the standard punctuation in careful writing.
Dashes separate more than commas and highlight the writer’s comment.
The phrase “la directora del centro” is an aside: it needs a pause, and a comma, on both sides.
Clara is the person being addressed, so her name is set off with a comma.

An aside adds information and interrupts the sentence, so it goes between two commas, or one if it opens or closes the sentence. Forgetting the second comma is the most common slip. An explanatory apposition takes commas; a specifying one, which tells you which person or thing you mean, does not. A vocative, the name of the person you are talking to, is always set off with commas, however short. In a letter, the greeting ends with a colon, not a comma.
Explanatory apposition: it adds information about the town and can be removed.
An aside between subject and verb: two commas are fine, because they open and close the aside.
Inés is the person addressed: a vocative, always set off with a comma.
An explanatory relative clause works like an aside; class 203 goes into this in depth.
With commas, the que-clause adds information about all the members; without commas, it picks out only some of them. Class 203 develops this contrast.
A vocative in the middle needs a comma on each side.
The apposition must be opened and closed; a single comma leaves it half-done.
With commas, the name merely adds information: there is only one sister.

Discourse connectors are always set off by commas: a comma after them at the start, a comma on each side in mid-position. When they link two complete clauses, a semicolon or a full stop goes before them, not a comma. Pero is a conjunction, not a connector: it takes a comma before it but none after it, unless an aside starts right there. Etc. takes a comma before it, and its own full stop closes the sentence.
Mid-position, after the subject: a comma on each side.
Two complete clauses: a semicolon before the connector, a comma after it.
Pero: a comma before it, none after it.
A reformulation inside the sentence: es decir goes between commas.
A comma before etc.; its full stop also ends the sentence, with no extra dots.
A mid-position connector takes a comma on each side.
Between two clauses: a semicolon before sin embargo and a comma after it.
Pero takes a comma before it, not after it.

Commas, dashes and brackets all enclose asides; what changes is how far the aside is set apart. Commas integrate it; dashes set it further apart and draw attention to it, and they are handy when the aside already contains commas; brackets hold marginal information such as dates, acronyms, figures or translations. The Spanish dash (raya) is longer than the hyphen. Opening dashes and brackets touch the next word, closing ones touch the previous word, with a space outside. The closing dash stays even when the aside ends the sentence.
Brackets for an acronym: marginal information the reader will need later.
The aside already contains commas, so dashes keep the sentence readable.
The closing dash stays even at the end of the sentence, before the full stop.
The comma that closes the main aside goes after the closing bracket.
Dashes touch the aside on the inside and have a space on the outside.
An acronym is marginal information, so it goes in brackets.
Keep the closing dash at the end, with the full stop after it.

Subject and verb are never separated by a single comma, however long the subject is: the pause you make when reading aloud is not written. Only an aside between them brings in two commas. In a simple series there is no comma before y: the Oxford comma is an English habit. And the opening ¿ ¡ go exactly where the question or exclamation begins, even mid-sentence.
A long subject, but no comma before the verb.
A simple series: no comma before y.
The question mark opens where the question begins, not at the start of the sentence.
The vocative stays outside the question, followed by a comma.

Spanish has no Oxford comma in simple series, ends letter greetings with a colon rather than a comma, and opens questions and exclamations too. A comma before y is fine when y starts a new clause after the series rather than closing it.
However long the subject, no comma before the verb.
Simple series: no comma before the final y.
The question starts at vendrá, so that is where ¿ goes.
All the clubs in the Estación district close in August: no comma before the verb.
Comma before the name, colon after the greeting.
Daniel, I’ve read the report. The content is very good, but the commas need an afternoon’s work.
I was afraid of that. Where do we start?
Page one. You wrote a comma between the long subject and the verb. It goes.
Fine: no comma there. And the paragraph about the timetable?
There’s a comma missing there: the connector needs one on each side.
And what if I want to stress that it came as a surprise? We all thought it would work.
Then use dashes: they set the comment further apart and draw attention to it.
I like it. On page three I introduce the library director with only one comma.
The first comma is missing: the apposition has to open and close. And the foundation’s acronym is better in brackets.
In the list of activities, do I put a comma before y? In English I would.
Not in Spanish. And you don’t need “etc.” if the list is complete, that is, if nothing is missing.
Thanks for your patience, Clara. I’ll send you the new version tonight.
What does Clara think of the report?
Why does Clara suggest dashes in the timetable paragraph?
What is Daniel unsure about in the list of activities?
Daniel dictated the closing paragraph into his phone and it came out with no punctuation at all. Choose the correctly punctuated version of each sentence.
This year, however, the clubs have grown by thirty per cent.
The aside contains commas, so dashes avoid confusion; they touch the words inside.
The apposition needs both its opening and its closing comma.
The connector between commas; pero with a comma before it only.
The whole form of address is the vocative, so the comma comes after it.
With the comma, the children are being addressed; without it, they would be the meal.
The no answers something else; then the speaker says they do want to go.
With commas, all the members paid and all voted.
With commas, there is only one business partner.
Attendance, however, fell in the summer.
Hugo Lara, the youngest volunteer, runs the youth club.
The Molino club, the oldest in the city, also opens on Saturdays.
She sums up three changes, warns him the deadline has moved and suggests meeting.
What does Clara give as an example of what works well?
What is wrong with the sentence about the volunteers?
What is wrong with the sentence about Rosa Peña?
Why does Clara prefer dashes in the timetable paragraph?
What news does Clara give at the end?
open and close them; always set off a vocative
connectors between commas; pero takes a comma only before it
touching the aside inside; never drop the closing dash
no comma between subject and verb, none before y in a series

Before you add a comma, ask what it does: does it open or close an aside, set off a connector or a vocative, or separate items in a list? If it only marks a pause between subject and verb, leave it out. And whatever opens, whether commas, dashes or brackets, must close.
The results, however, were good.
Thank you for coming, Carmen.
All the students who passed the June exam received the certificate.
The museum, closed since March, reopens tomorrow.
We need bread, cheese and fruit.
Marina, the communications officer at a university hospital, is checking the staff newsletter before it goes out. Choose the version she can publish.
Dr Soto, head of Paediatrics, will present the new protocol.
The car park will be closed in August, so we recommend coming by bus.
The Emergency Department is taking on more staff.

For strong students or spare time. The main sentence’s punctuation goes after the closing dash or bracket. Aunque, porque and así que take no comma after them. A comma before y is fine when y starts a new clause rather than closing the list. Stylistically, dashes highlight a comment, while brackets play it down as a side note.
The main sentence’s comma goes after the closing dash.
No comma after aunque; the comma closes the fronted clause.
The comma before the second y avoids reading “the children” as part of the list.
Dashes highlight the comment; brackets would play it down.

You can now punctuate appositions, vocatives, connectors and asides according to the official rules. Class 198 takes formal writing a step further: impersonal constructions, politeness and precision. It is the natural next step: having polished the shape of your sentences, you now work on their tone and register.

Bogotá. A cultural association is organising its neighbourhood book fair. Felipe, a new assistant, writes well when he messages friends, but his first email to the manager of a sports hall and his first set of minutes land on the coordinator’s desk. You already know the impersonal forms and the politeness scale; today you combine them to write a whole formal text: impersonal, consistently courteous and precise.
Informal tú with someone he has never met, vague catch-all words and a phrase the RAE advises against. Perfectly clear in a chat; too casual and too vague for an institutional email.
Usted kept up throughout (le, su), a polite conditional and exact nouns: the reader knows precisely what is being asked for.
“Tema” is a real word, but here it is a vague catch-all: the reader cannot tell what is actually being requested.
It is a matter of register, not correctness: in a first institutional email, usted is the safe choice.

Formal Spanish avoids “I think we should…”. To recommend or evaluate, it uses impersonal expressions followed by the subjunctive when there is a specific subject, or by the infinitive when nobody in particular is meant. To state or highlight a fact, it uses cabe señalar / destacar que or es evidente que, followed by the indicative. Procede + infinitive is administrative: “it is appropriate / in order to”.
A recommendation with a specific subject: subjunctive.
Valid for anyone: infinitive, no que.
A fact being highlighted, not evaluated: indicative.
Administrative style: “it is not in order to accept it”.
Se ruega + a + person + que + subjunctive; with a bare infinitive: “Se ruega confirmar la asistencia”.
Cabe señalar que introduces a fact, so the indicative follows.
Conviene que evaluates what should happen, so the subjunctive follows.

Formal texts love nouns, but verbs like proceder a, realizar, efectuar or llevar a cabo often add length and nothing else: “proceder a la revisión de” simply means “revisar”. Spanish style guides criticise this padding. Keep the noun only when it carries extra information (an external review) or in fixed formulas of minutes.
Same meaning, half the words.
The simple verb is clearer and more direct.
Here the noun is justified: “external” is information a bare verb could not carry so neatly.
It means “it is appropriate to”. An impersonal resource with real meaning: keep it.
It means “went on to do”. Usually padding: just use the verb.
One meaningful verb plus the concrete detail; the others pile up empty verbs.
No procede + infinitive means “it is not in order to”.

Institutional texts speak as “we” even when one person writes them (plural of modesty or institutional we): consideramos, proponemos. Keep it consistent; do not jump between creo and consideramos. Courtesy tenses (desearía, quería pedirle, le agradeceríamos que + imperfect subjunctive) are already familiar; at C1 the point is to use one well-placed formula, not to stack them.
Institutional we: the association speaks, not Felipe.
The polite imperfect: refers to now, adds distance.
Conditional + imperfect subjunctive: the classic formal request, used once.

In Latin America (and the Canary Islands and part of Andalusia) ustedes is the only plural, for friends and strangers alike, so formality comes from greetings, vocabulary and polite tenses. In most of Spain vosotros is the informal plural and ustedes the formal one, so an email to another institution uses ustedes.
Every form is third person, consistent with usted.
Le + lo becomes se lo; te would break the usted.

As you saw in lesson 176, a gerund should not report an event that happens later than the main verb. The Academy grammar is more tolerant when the second event follows immediately as a consequence, but in a formal text “y” + finite verb is always safe.
Con base en is the recommended form here.
Presentar una queja is the exact collocation.
Consistent institutional we and no “later event” gerund.
Grammatical but overloaded with softeners; one formula is clearer and just as polite.
Felipe, the minutes are almost ready, but here you wrote “people talked about the money thing”. In official minutes that says nothing.
So what do I write? That’s what happened: we talked about money.
Write exactly what was done: the budget was reviewed and a ten per cent increase was approved.
OK. And I made a real effort with the conclusions: “It is recommended that the contract be subjected to review.”
It’s correct, but heavy: proceder adds nothing. Better to say the management should review the contract before Friday. That way it’s clear who and when.
Good morning. Is that the minutes? Add the capacity problem: it is worth noting that over three hundred people came last year and the hall has two hundred seats.
I put it further down: “Capacity-wise, the hall falls short.”
There’s no “level” there, Felipe. Write that the hall’s capacity is insufficient. And if the sports hall doesn’t confirm by Friday, the proper step is to look for another venue.
Speaking of the sports hall: Felipe had written to the manager “Hi Liliana, I’m writing about the sports hall thing.”
Too familiar for a first contact. Start formally, and to make the request, use “we would be grateful if you could confirm the booking”.
And at the end, do I write “I think the date suits everyone”?
You’re writing on behalf of the association, so use “we consider”. And no “en base a”: on the basis of her reply, we’ll draw up the contract and send it to her.
Why does Natalia correct that sentence?
What does Natalia’s version gain?
