Why “consideramos” rather than “creo”?
A specific subject after the verb needs que + subjunctive.
No procede + infinitive: “it is not in order to”.
An evaluative expression with que takes the subjunctive.
Recalling a fact: indicative.
Hacer is the catch-all here; impartir is the exact verb for workshops.
Name the actual problem instead of “the chairs thing”.
Presentar una queja is the precise collocation.
Drop the filler and make the volunteers the subject.
It should be noted that the deadline is Friday: a fact, so the indicative.
We would be grateful if you could send us the signed contract.
We consider it advisable for the fair to be held in November: institutional we plus subjunctive.
What is the main purpose of the message?
Why is the venue changing?
What are exhibitors asked to do before the 5th?
What time should exhibitors arrive?
What should volunteers who cannot come do?
The director mixes impersonal resources with an institutional “we” and a warm closing. Formal style is not cold; it is precise and respectful.
Recommending or evaluating takes the subjunctive (or an infinitive for anyone); stating or highlighting a fact takes the indicative.
Keep one person throughout, speak as “we” for an institution, and use one well-placed polite formula rather than a pile of softeners.
Replace catch-all words with the exact verb or noun, so the reader knows exactly what happened or what is being asked.
Formal does not mean padded: drop empty verbs, “a nivel de” without real levels, “en base a” and gerunds for later events.

Three questions before sending: am I evaluating or stating (subjunctive or indicative)? Who is speaking to whom (institutional we, consistent usted, one polite formula)? Does every word say something concrete (no catch-all words, empty verbs or discouraged phrases)?
“It would be advisable for the report to be handed in before the 15th.”
“I would be grateful if you could send me the invoice.”
“The visitors were surveyed.”
“The programme was designed on the basis of residents’ proposals.”
“The library closed in January for works and reopened in June.”

Seville, Spain. A university department secretary checks three sentences an intern wants to send to heads of other departments he doesn’t know. In Spain, the formal plural for strangers is ustedes, not vosotros.

Minutes and administrative emails have fixed formulas: se acuerda + infinitive for decisions, se procede a la votación as an established formula, se levanta la sesión to close. Adjunto is an adjective and agrees with what is attached; se ruega + infinitive is always singular.
Adjunto agrees with the noun: adjuntas las facturas.
Se acuerda + infinitive records a decision.
With an infinitive, se ruega stays singular.

Today you wrote with maximum distance: impersonal, polite and precise. The natural next step is the opposite end: how colloquial conversation intensifies, leaves sentences hanging and tells stories with feeling. Knowing both ends lets you move freely between them.

The writers’ room of a comedy web series set in a Madrid apartment building. Gabriel’s first scene is grammatically flawless but sounds like a police report. Today you learn the grammar of spontaneous conversation: how people tell stories vividly, how they leave sentences hanging for the listener to finish, and, just as important, where none of this belongs.
Correct, but it reads like a report: aunque, además and en resumen are the connectors of careful written prose.
The degree becomes a surprise, the action sounds sudden and outrageous, one sentence is left hanging for the listener, and total, que wraps the story up.
Va y + verb does not mean anyone went anywhere: it frames the action as sudden or outrageous.
A suspended phrase: the intonation asks the listener to imagine just how bad it was.

In pseudo-coordination, ir y + verb (va y se pone, fue y se puso) does not describe any movement: it presents the second action as sudden, unexpected or outrageous. Both verbs share tense and person. Encima adds one more grievance (“on top of that”), y eso que + indicative adds an afterthought that makes the fact more surprising (“even though”), and total, que wraps the story up and jumps to the result. All of them are colloquial and very frequent in spoken narrative.
We told him to turn it down and he went and turned it up: both verbs in the past.
The narrative present makes the story vivid; ir stays in the present too.
Encima adds insult to injury; y eso que adds an ironic fact (“and he’s the one who…”).
Total, que skips the details and lands on the outcome.
In a past-tense story, ir also goes in the preterite: fue y se echó a llorar.
Y eso que introduces a fact, so the verb is indicative: she has three cats herself.

Con lo + adjective or adverb + que + indicative takes the degree you saw in class 192 (lo tarde que era) and turns it into a reason (“seeing how tired I am…”) or a contrast (“late as it was, he still…”); context decides which. The adjective agrees with its noun. Con lo que + verb and con la de + noun + que work the same way with actions and quantities. De + adjective + que (de despistado que es) gives a cause: he is so absent-minded that…; it is mainly for recognition at this level.
Concessive: shy as she is, she gave the residents’ president a piece of her mind (cantar las cuarenta = to tell someone off).
Causal: seeing how nice it is at home, why go out? With an adverb nothing agrees.
Con lo que + verb: given how much we pay in building fees…
De + agreeing adjective + que: she was so tired that she fell asleep. A variant is de lo cansada que estaba.
Expensive as the flat is, it leaks: the second part goes against what the degree leads you to expect.
Seeing how expensive the flat is, I may not be able to stay: the degree is the reason.
The adjective agrees with Merche, even though lo is neuter.
Punctual as he is, Paco was late: the fact goes against expectations, so it is concessive.

Spoken Spanish often leaves a sentence unfinished on purpose. The listener completes it from context and intonation: an excuse (Es que mañana madrugo… = so I can’t), a story too big to tell (¡Si yo te contara…!), a warning (Como no te des prisa… = or else), an intensity beyond words (Tiene un genio…), or a reproach (Con lo que yo he hecho por ti…). Es que on its own is the standard way to justify or excuse yourself without saying no directly.
An excuse: the no is never said, but it is understood.
How did the residents’ meeting go? If only you knew! There is a lot, and none of it good.
Como no + present subjunctive = if you don’t; the threat can be said or left in the air.
He has such a temper (you can imagine). / After everything I’ve done for you… (and this is how you repay me).
Es que gives the reason and leaves the refusal unsaid.
Como no + present subjunctive means “if you don’t”; the consequence is left unsaid.

O sea (que) rephrases or draws a conclusion (“so what you’re saying is…”). Pues nada closes a topic or accepts something with resignation (“oh well”). Es más raises the stakes with a stronger point (“in fact”). A sentence starting with que repeats an order (¡Que te calles! = I said be quiet), relays or repeats a question (Que si vienes mañana = she’s asking whether…), or echoes something with surprise (¿Que no lo sabías?). Repetition insists (Que sí, que sí). A diminutive often softens a request or a criticism rather than meaning “small”.
So the lift is still broken. Oh well, we’ll take the stairs.
Es más adds a stronger point; it also works in careful speech and writing.
I said be quiet! / She’s asking if you’re coming for lunch on Sunday. / They’ve put your rent up? (surprise)
The diminutives soften the request; in fact the table is heavy.

In Spain, ¡Anda que + verb! ironically reproaches what someone failed to do (“thanks for telling me!”), while ¡Anda que no…! is an emphatic yes. Outside Spain it is much less common and usage varies, so recognise it rather than use it as a general formula. Diminutive suffixes also vary by region.
An ironic complaint: you never call me.
Que si… relays or repeats a yes-no question.
Indicative after con lo… que, and both verbs of the ir y pattern in the same tense.
A formal email to a company needs neutral, complete sentences.
Morning, Encarna. Did you sleep well?
Sleep? If only you knew! Didn’t you hear anything last night?
Nothing, I sleep with earplugs. What happened?
The new guy in 4B. At one in the morning, late as it was, he goes and starts ringing every doorbell.
Every one? How come?
Well, he’d left his keys inside. And on top of that he was singing, with a voice like… you can imagine.
Come on, that could happen to anyone.
Not to anyone. He’s so absent-minded he even rang his own doorbell. In fact, he kept at it for quite a while.
So there was nobody to let him in.
Nobody. Paco from the first floor let him sleep on his sofa, even though he doesn’t know him from Adam. Anyway, at three I was still awake.
Right, well, I’m off, I’m running late.
And you’re leaving me here with the bags? Thanks for offering! Go on, carry this one up for me, it’s a little heavy.
Why did the new neighbour ring all the doorbells?
Where did he end up sleeping?
What does Encarna complain about at the end?
In a past-tense story, both verbs go in the preterite.
Calm as Merche is, I didn’t expect her to shout like that.
I failed my driving test, even though I practised all month.
If you don’t turn it down… (or else).
A formal email to the property manager needs a neutral connector.
Es que introduces the excuse for saying no.
Late as it was, he goes and starts singing.
He failed the exam, even though he studied really hard.
Long story short, we were without a lift all weekend.
Why does Lucía send Gabriel this message?
Why did Merche ring Lucía?
What did the downstairs neighbour threaten to do?
How did the night end?
What is implied by this unfinished sentence?
Ir y + verb makes an action sound sudden; both verbs share tense and person. Encima adds a grievance, y eso que an ironic fact, and total, que jumps to the outcome.
Con lo… que turns a degree into a contrast (despite) or a reason (because); de + adjective + que presents it as the cause.
Unfinished sentences let the listener fill in an intrigue, a warning, an intensity or a reproach; diminutives soften requests.
Es que justifies, o sea concludes, pues nada closes, es más raises the stakes, and an initial que repeats or relays; ¡anda que…! is typical of Spain.

Ask yourself two things: am I talking to someone close, and is this pattern general or regional? Colloquial Spanish is not incorrect Spanish; it has its own grammar. But it has no place in a formal email, a report or a complaint.
I told him not to touch anything and he went and unplugged the fridge.
Seeing how wet the streets are, we’d better stay in.
An excuse that avoids saying no.
If only I could tell you what the landlord said!
A formal email needs a formal connector.
Valparaíso, Chile. Javiera is recording a voice message for her sister about her day at the office. She drafted it like a report; help her say it the way people actually talk.

Each colloquial device has a formal counterpart; va y has none, so a formal text simply narrates the action. Two patterns to recognise: de + adjective + que (“she was so fed up that…”) and con la de + noun + que (“after all the times we’ve said it…”), very common in Spain.
Moreover, the lift has been out of order for a month.
In short, no solution has been offered to us to date.
We called three times, despite having been told it was not necessary.
She was so fed up with the leaks that she moved out.

Today you narrated past events with va y se pone, a present tense about yesterday. The natural next step is seeing why tenses do not always mean their time: the historical present, the polite imperfect (“I was coming to ask you…”) and the future of conjecture. It is the other half of the living grammar of conversation.

An amateur theatre group rehearses at a neighbourhood cultural centre. The director needs more rehearsal time, a spotlight and an actress. In this group people ask favours, play, give orders and tell stories, and the verb is rarely in the tense you would expect. That is today’s topic: a tense can step out of its own time to express an attitude.
Literal use: a wish she had back then.
Polite imperfect: the request is happening now; the past form just adds distance, like “I was wondering if…”.
Imperfect of make-believe: it sets up the fiction of a game or an improvisation, “let’s say I’m the queen…”.
“I came to ask you a favour.” When is the favour being asked?
“The premiere was going to be on Friday, but we’ve moved it to Saturday.” When is it now?

Two present-time uses of the imperfect. Polite: with verbs of wishing, needing, coming or calling (querer, desear, necesitar, venir a, llamar para), the imperfect softens a request made now, like English “I wanted to ask…”, “I was calling to…”. Quoting: “¿Cómo te llamabas?” means “remind me of your name”: you were told before and you are recovering it. The preterite never has these uses.
I came to ask whether you could help me with the set (a request now; «si podrías»: “whether”, so the conditional is fine).
Ramiro, I’m calling to confirm the rehearsal time.
Sorry, what was your name again? You told me yesterday. · Aren’t you from Cali? (I think you said so)
“Good afternoon, I came to ask about the theatre workshop.”
Sorry, what was your name again?

The imperfect can describe a world that is not real: the make-believe of children’s games and of improvisation (“Yo era el médico y tú venías con fiebre”), and the events of a dream. It can also point to the future from a past viewpoint: “Mañana me iba de viaje” presents a plan as it stood, and usually announces that something got in the way.
Let’s improvise: I’m the doctor and you come in with a fever.
Last night I dreamt the theatre flooded and the audience just stayed in their seats, perfectly calm.
I was supposed to leave tomorrow, but the flight was cancelled. · Weren’t you leaving for Lima today?
“I was going to the beach with my family on Saturday…” What does Olga understand?
“You’re a lost tourist and I sell you a fake map.” What is the imperfect doing?

The present can bring a past event closer, as if it were happening before our eyes (in history writing and in lively anecdotes: “So yesterday I’m at the door and the caretaker comes up and says…”). With a time expression it presents a future event as decided (“Mañana te llamo”). And in the second person it can give an order, neutral in directions and instructions but very firm between people (“Tú te callas y escuchas”).
Yesterday I’m at the door of the centre, the caretaker comes over and tells me they close in August.
I’ll call you tomorrow and we’ll talk it over. · On Saturday we rehearse from ten to two (it is settled).
Today you sit down and watch (firm). · You go up to the second floor and ask there (neutral directions).
“I’ll get the corrected script to you tomorrow.” What does the present express?
“Ramiro, you are not touching the lights tonight.” What tone does it have?

The future can command with authority: the old commandments (“No matarás”), rules and regulations (“Los participantes entregarán…”) and a parent or boss who will not be argued with (“Harás lo que te digo”). In exclamations it shows surprise or indignation (“¡Será posible!”: “I can’t believe it!”). You already know the concessive future (“Será caro, pero…”). The conditional softens requests (“¿Podrías…?”) and opinions (“Yo diría que…”). In the press it can mark unconfirmed news, which class 208 studies in depth.
Thou shalt not kill. · Tomorrow you will be here at nine, understood? (an order, not a prediction)
I can’t believe it! The spotlight has blown again. · It may be expensive, I’m not saying it isn’t, but we need it.
Could you bring the printed script? · I’d say the second scene is too long (a softened opinion).
“I can’t believe it!” What does «será» express here?
“I’d say the ending is too sad.” What does the conditional do?
Which sentence asks a favour politely?
If you could come earlier, I’d be grateful.
Good afternoon. I came to ask about the theatre workshop. Is it here?
Yes, come in. Sorry, what was your name again? You told me on the phone yesterday and it’s gone.
Nerea Lozano. I wanted to know whether there’s still room in the group.
Of course. We’re improvising right now. Simón, explain the game to her.
Easy: I’m a lost taxi driver and you get into the taxi in a huge hurry.
I can’t believe it! The big spotlight has blown again, and the premiere is in two weeks.
Ramiro, today you sit down and watch the scene. The lights can wait.
Look, I was going to the beach with my family on Saturday, so someone will have to buy that spotlight. It may be urgent, I’m not saying it isn’t, but it costs a fortune.
I’ll talk to Mrs Valverde tomorrow. I’d say two new spotlights will do.
By the way, yesterday I’m at the door of the centre, the caretaker comes over and tells me they close in August.
Sorry, Olga, could you tell me what time rehearsals are?
Mondays and Wednesdays at seven. And there’s only one rule here: nobody will be late.
Why does Olga ask “what was your name”?
What happens to Ramiro’s Saturday plan?
What kind of statement is the punctuality rule?
“Hi Ramiro, I’m calling to ask if you can take me to rehearsal tomorrow.”
“Hey, aren’t you from Barranquilla?” (I think you told me)
“I was supposed to leave early for Medellín tomorrow, but they’ve moved my flight to the evening.”
“You are staying here until the scene works.” What does the present express?
“How inconsiderate can you be! You’ve eaten my lunch.” What does the future express?
I came to ask whether you could help me with the set.
I was supposed to go on a trip tomorrow, but the flight was cancelled.
I’m the director and you come to ask me for a part (a game).
She reports on the meeting, announces changes and hands out jobs.
What did Olga get?
When is the premiere now?
What does Simón have to do?
What does Olga think about the new spotlight?
politeness, recalling what was said, make-believe and dreams, a plan seen as it stood
brings things closer: vivid past, settled future, firm order
commands from authority, reacts with indignation, or concedes
softens requests and opinions; in the press, unconfirmed news (class 208)

First ask when the event really happens. If it doesn’t match the tense, look for the intention: distance, recall, make-believe, vividness, authority or reaction. Politeness belongs to the imperfect (never the preterite) and the conditional; the commanding future belongs to whoever is in charge.
“Good morning, how can I help you?” (what would you like)
“In 1810 the city rises against the governor.” When does it happen?
“Tomorrow at eight you will be here, no excuses.”
“What time was tomorrow’s meeting again?” Why the imperfect?
“You’re the wolf and I hide in the house.” What does the imperfect describe?
A patient phones her health centre to change an appointment. Rewrite her sentences so they sound more polite or clearer.

For strong students or spare time. Headlines use the present for past events; reports use the “narrative imperfect” for a single, completed event shown as a scene (“Minutes later, the train set off again”); and the conditional of rumour presents unconfirmed information (“The director has reportedly resigned”), which class 208 covers in depth.
Headline: “Neighbourhood theatre reopens after two years of building work.” When did it happen?
“At a quarter past ten, the referee blew the final whistle.” What kind of event is this?
“According to local radio, the cultural centre is set to close in August.” How sure is the journalist?

You now know that a tense can step out of its time to ask, imagine, narrate or command, and you read the context to find its real value. Class 201 keeps you reading tenses closely, now in literature: the past anterior (“apenas hubo terminado, se fue”), a form that lives almost only in writing and is worth recognising.

On Thursday the school sent a circular whose commas turned a note about twelve students into a statement about all 120. In this class you work on the C1 side of relative clauses: punctuation as meaning, the relative a careful text requires, and register.
Restrictive: only the students who passed went out. The clause picks out a subset, so removing it changes the claim.
Non-restrictive: all the students passed and all went out. The clause is an aside about the whole group.
With commas, the clause applies to the whole group, so families read it as “nobody has handed it in”.
No commas: the clause selects the twelve. A single comma is never right here.
In speech, the non-restrictive clause is set off by pauses and a lower pitch.
Which ones? The clause narrows down what the noun refers to; without it, you would be talking about a different (larger) set.
Only the teachers supervising the exam arrive at eight; the others don’t.
We need a room that holds thirty people (any room, not a known one: subjunctive).
The teacher I’m covering for comes back in May. «Quien» is fine here because of the preposition.
What else can I tell you about it? The noun is already identified; the clause adds a comment, like a parenthesis.
Elisa Navarro, who has run the school since 2019, will sign the letter. The name already identifies her.
The library, which was refurbished in the summer, now opens in the afternoons. «La cual» marks a formal written register.
My sister, who lives in Lima, will come to the graduation: I have only one sister, or I’m not contrasting her with others.
Without commas, the clause implies a contrast with other sisters.
Restrictive, no preposition: only «que» works.

If the verb inside the relative clause takes a preposition, it moves to the front of the relative, usually with an article. Dropping it is common in casual speech but reads as an error in careful writing.
It’s the company Iván’s mother works for (trabajar para → para la que).
This is the topic I told you about yesterday (hablar de → del que).
It was support without which the project would not have got off the ground: a long preposition, so «el cual».
“Which” referring to the whole previous clause; also works with no antecedent (“whatever you can”).
Same meaning, more formal; it always needs an antecedent, so it cannot replace «lo que» in “haz lo que puedas”.
It’s the foundation Rubén works for in the summer.
The power went off in the hall, which is why the rehearsal was cancelled.
I remember perfectly the day you started here.
Whose. It agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed (the noun after it), never with the owner. It belongs to writing and formal speech.
She’s the student whose parents organised the fair: cuyos agrees with padres.
We congratulate the department whose proposal won the competition: cuya agrees with propuesta.
She is an author about whose work very little has been written: preposition + cuya.
It’s the best project we have received: stated as a fact about a known set.
Same meaning, with emphasis on the judgement; very common and natural, especially with “ever” (nunca, jamás).

After a superlative and after “the only one / the first / the last who”, both moods are correct and common; the subjunctive adds emphasis. These clauses are always restrictive, so no commas. With “la primera vez que” the indicative is the norm.
It’s the cheapest study trip we have (ever) organised.
He is a teacher whose daughters study here.
He is a colleague I can always count on.
Lima, which is the capital of Peru, has almost ten million inhabitants.
Rubén, I’ve got forty messages from families. Apparently yesterday’s circular says no student in cuarto has handed in the project.
Let’s see… “The cuarto students, who haven’t handed in the project, must come in on Monday.” There it is: it’s the commas.
But there are only twelve! What I meant was “the students who still haven’t handed it in”, without commas.
Exactly. With commas you’re talking about the whole year; without them, only those twelve. Let’s send a correction and review the annual report now, which saves us another meeting.
OK. Look at this paragraph: “We thank the Ribera Foundation for its support, without which the trip to Lima would not have been possible.”
Perfect. But two lines further down it says “the company that Iván’s father works”. The preposition is missing: it’s “the company he works for”.
True. And here? “The teacher who coordinated the trip…”. Something sounds off.
With no commas and no preposition, only «que». But if you write “Carmen Ibáñez, who coordinated the trip, …”, between commas, it’s perfect.
I like it. Add a line about Nuria Campos too, whose project has won the regional prize.
Of course! Her tutor says it’s the best piece of work he has ever read in twenty years of teaching.
Then put it exactly like that. And from today, we both read every circular before it goes out.
Why did so many families write in?
What is wrong with “la empresa que trabaja el padre de Iván”?
Why does Rubén accept “Carmen Ibáñez, quien coordinó el viaje”?
Rubén has removed every comma from the draft to check them one by one. Read the context in brackets and decide whether each clause restricts (no commas) or adds information (commas).
Without commas, the clause restricts the group.
With commas, the clause describes the whole group.
A unique antecedent takes a non-restrictive clause, with both commas.
Choosing one cousin among three: restrictive.
Restrictive with subjunctive; never a comma between subject and verb.
It’s the company Iván works for.
The head, who signed the circular, apologised.
Two flights were cancelled, as a result of which we changed the plan.
She clears up the misunderstanding, gives practical details and shares good news.
How many students must come on Monday?
Who will email the families concerned?
Why will the session be in the library?
What does Nuria’s tutor say about her project?
restricts the set; no commas; may take the subjunctive
adds a comment about the whole set; a comma on each side
keep the verb’s preposition; lo cual for a whole clause; cuyo agrees with the thing owned
both moods are correct; the subjunctive adds emphasis

Before you add a comma, ask yourself: all of them or only some? Restrictive clauses take no commas; non-restrictive ones take two. Then choose the relative: in a restrictive clause without a preposition, only «que». And never drop the verb’s preposition.
The lift, which broke down yesterday, is working again.
It’s the supplier we depend on for materials.
Two speakers didn’t turn up, because of which the conference finished early.
The author, whose novels are read in many schools, will visit the city.
The person who called this morning was the inspector.
The public library is preparing its monthly newsletter. Join the sentences in a formal register and decide each time whether the clause restricts or adds information.
Between commas, «la que» works as an identifying apposition: “my sister, the one who lives in Lima”.
It introduces the consequence of the whole previous clause, like “so” or “which is why”.
The rule was approved, under which families will be able to appeal grades.
Both are correct in a formal non-restrictive clause.

You can now punctuate relative clauses by meaning and choose the relative a careful text needs. In class 204 you move from the paragraph to the whole text: you revise an argumentative piece for coherence, cohesion and nuance. It is the natural next step: «lo cual» and «a raíz de lo cual» are already cohesion devices, and a well-placed comma is part of nuance.

Raúl, head of people at a furniture cooperative, is writing an op-ed for the regional paper in favour of trying a four-day week. Beatriz, a copy editor, tells him: “You’re right, but your text doesn’t prove it yet.” No new structures today: you revise a whole argumentative text with the C1 tools you already have.
It claims more than it can prove, repeats the same phrase, piles up connectors and slips into casual speech.
It sizes the claim to the evidence, refers back with a summarising noun and grants the objection before holding its ground.
Why is the revision more persuasive? Precision, not vocabulary.
The speaker grants the point but says it isn’t enough to change their conclusion.

Coherence is about the plan. The thesis comes early, in one clear sentence. Each paragraph develops one main idea, announced in its first sentence. Arguments follow an order the reader can see. The strongest objection is acknowledged and answered. The conclusion restates the thesis in new words and opens a way forward; it doesn’t copy the introduction.
A thesis: one sentence, one clear position; the conditional makes it a proposal, not an order.
A topic sentence: the reader knows what this paragraph is about before reading it.
A conclusion that restates the thesis in new words instead of copying it.
Which works best as the thesis of an op-ed? A thesis takes a position that can be argued.
What should the conclusion do? Restate and propose, not copy or open new arguments.

An encapsulator is a general noun with a demonstrative (esta medida, este problema) that sums up everything said before, a sentence or a whole paragraph, and makes it the topic of the next sentence. The noun you pick also interprets: “this measure”, “this risk” and “this opportunity” are not neutral. Dicho / dicha without an article is formal and written. Ello is formal and refers to a whole idea, never to a person.
“This problem” sums up the whole previous sentence and labels it as a problem.
“Dicha” is formal written Spanish and takes no article.
“Ello” picks up the whole idea, not a single noun: formal register.
Ellipsis: the verb and object are understood, so they are not repeated.
The cooperative cut working hours in 2025. This decision improved the atmosphere at work.
The shifts can’t be changed without an agreement. For that reason, the proposal includes a negotiation.

A connector names the relationship between two ideas. Pick one that doesn’t fit (por tanto where nothing follows) and the reader loses the thread; repeat the same one (además… además…) and every argument seems to weigh the same. Use few, varied and exact connectors: sometimes paragraph order and a good encapsulator already do the job. Aun así and con todo don’t contrast two facts: they grant what was said and keep your conclusion.
I grant that point; even so, I stand by the proposal.
Formal contrast: the second fact limits the weight of the first.
Reformulation: the same idea, made concrete.
A consequence presented as explained by the previous fact: subjunctive after de ahí que.
The plant is a difficult case. Even so, two local cooperatives have already solved it with shifts.
Which version is correctly punctuated?

A C1 text persuades because it sizes its claims. A proven fact goes in the indicative, without detours; what is likely or debatable is hedged or attributed to its source; what you deny or question takes the subjunctive. Hedging everything is as bad as hedging nothing. And keep one register: an op-ed has no room for o sea, un montón or generic “you” (si trabajas cuatro días…); use quien trabaja…, se, or la plantilla.
A measured claim: strong, but limited to what the evidence covers.
Questioning a claim: the subjunctive marks that you don’t assert it.
Attribution: the figure belongs to the source, not to you.
Generic subject in formal register, instead of the casual “si trabajas…”.
Which sentence is pitched right for an op-ed?
It isn’t clear that the measure works equally well in every job.
Revise from big to small: plan first, punctuation last.
I like the idea, but I don’t know what you’re arguing until the third paragraph. Why not start there?
I wanted a bit of suspense, to be honest. OK, I’ll open with the thesis. Like that?
Exactly. Also, you write “the four-day week” eleven times. Once you’ve introduced it, you can call it “this measure”, “that model” or just “the proposal”.
Yes, but I was afraid it wouldn’t be clear. What if I use “la misma”?
Better not: it sounds like an official report. Use a possessive, a pronoun or, for a whole idea, something like “This requires reorganising the shifts”.
Got it. And the production paragraph? People at the plant say it’s impossible to stop for a whole day.
That could be your best paragraph. Don’t hide the objection: acknowledge it and answer it.
So agreeing with the other side doesn’t weaken me.
Quite the opposite: it makes you credible. What does undermine you is this. All of them? Proven by whom?
By the Labour Observatory report… which, well, looked at forty companies.
Then say exactly that. It’s less spectacular, but nobody can argue with it.
You’ve convinced me. And I’ll cut the four “además” in a row in the second paragraph. In short: fewer frills, more arguments.
What is the first problem Beatriz points out?
Why does Beatriz want to keep the production paragraph?
What changes in the productivity sentence?
Paragraph 1 is all background: there is no position.
Paragraph 2 repeats the same phrase and stacks “además”.
Paragraph 3 dismisses the objection and attacks the people who raise it.
Paragraph 4 over-claims and slips into casual register.
The measure is not meant to cut production, but wear and tear.
Everything suggests the trial has worked, at least in offices.
She praises the improvement and suggests three specific changes before he sends it.
What problem remains in the conclusion?
What does she suggest instead of “la implantación de la misma”?
Why does she like the plant paragraph?
What does she ask him to do with the “nobody in their right mind” sentence?
What must Raúl add to the 20% figure?
the reader knows your position after two sentences and can follow the plan
refer back with summarising nouns, pronouns or nothing at all, never with “el mismo” as a pronoun
each connector names one exact relationship; grant and hold with aun así or con todo
size every claim to the evidence, attribute what isn’t yours, and keep one register

Revising isn’t hunting for typos: it’s rereading with one question at a time, from big to small. A C1 text doesn’t persuade through difficult words, but because it never says more, or less, than it can back up.
The council closed the centre to traffic in May. This measure has cut noise by 30%.
I admit the cycle lane takes away parking spaces. Even so, I think it’s worth it.
Which sentence fits a formal argumentative text?
It hasn’t been shown that the measure harms shops in the centre.
Lucía, secretary of a residents’ association, is writing to the council about the new cycle lane. Her draft repeats itself, over-claims and concedes nothing. Revise three sentences.

For strong students or spare time. In academic or very formal texts, si bien + indicative concedes, no es menos cierto que (“it is no less true that”) adds a counterweight, and cabe objetar que (“one might object that”) anticipates an objection impersonally. Summarising nouns can also judge: “this measure” is neutral, but “this absurdity” takes sides. Fine in an op-ed that justifies it; not in a neutral report.
What does “si bien” do here?
What does the second half add?
A neutral technical report: which summarising noun fits?

You have finished the C1 argumentation block: you can revise a whole text and decide what to say, how to refer back to it and how strongly to claim it. The next step opens C2 with the other side of precision: reading old or legal formal texts. In class 205 you learn to recognise the future perfect subjunctive, a form you won’t write but will come across.

A small publisher is preparing an anthology of historical texts from an imaginary town: bylaws, an old chronicle, a 19th-century novel and recent press reviews, each printed with a version in present-day Spanish for readers in Spain and Latin America. You already know the pretérito anterior and the two subjunctive futures; today you combine them with other historical forms and learn to rephrase them without changing the meaning. The goal is reading and rewording, never using these forms yourself.
Which excerpt could appear in this week’s newspaper?
What does the modern version do with “El que hiciere fuego”?

The -re future subjunctive does not have a single modern equivalent: the replacement depends on what introduces it. After a relative or cuando it becomes the present subjunctive (el que haga, cuando llegue). After conditional si, Spanish never uses the present subjunctive, so it becomes the present indicative (si reincide). The compound form follows the same split: haya + participle after quien or cuando, ha + participle after si.
Whoever causes damage to the bridge will pay for it: any person, if it happens.
After si, the modern form is the present indicative, never “si no pague”.
Once the constable has drawn up the report: the action must be completed first.
If he has not appeared within eight days: si + present perfect indicative.
If any resident fails to attend the council meeting, he will pay a fine.
Anyone who has lost the receipt will not be able to make a claim.

The pretérito anterior marks an action completed immediately before another past action. It is confined to literary and very formal prose. Today the same immediacy is expressed with the simple past and a connector (apenas, en cuanto, tan pronto como) or with después de + infinitive. Llegado que hubo is an even more archaic variant with the same meaning.
As soon as she read the letter, she burst into tears.
As soon as the viceroy arrived, he ordered the port closed.

In written Spanish, especially literary and journalistic prose, the -ra form sometimes keeps its original indicative value: pluperfect (que había publicado) or, in the press, a plain past (que publicó). It nearly always appears in relative clauses. It is a legitimate usage, since it is the historical meaning of the form, but several newspaper style guides advise against it, especially when it simply replaces the preterite.
The bridge, designed by a French engineer, turns a hundred: a fact, not a hypothesis.
It reports a fact: you can replace it with an indicative past without changing the meaning.
Here the subjunctive is required by “quería que”: no indicative can replace it.
As soon as she closed the shop, it started to rain.
The singer, who was a hit in the eighties, performs in Valdeloma today.

In older texts and in literary prose up to the early 20th century, the pronoun was often attached to the end of a conjugated verb. Today, with indicative forms, it goes before the verb as a separate word. Attached pronouns remain normal with infinitives, gerunds, imperatives and subjunctives used as commands (véase, siéntese). A few old formulas survive: érase una vez, ¡habrase visto!
A great silence fell over the square.
She sat down by the window. Older editions spell it “sentóse”; current spelling rules drop the accent.
They gave him the keys to the archive.
Edition for Spain only: which modern version fits?
Whatever the case, the town did not surrender. What does the adapter do with the formula?
Which of these is normal in a present-day text? (See chapter three.)

If the tenant has not paid by the end of the month…
I’ll start with the 1868 bylaw. You’ve put the present subjunctive there. That works for me.
It’s any person at all, a possible case. But the next sentence can’t be handled the same way: “should he reoffend…”.
Of course: after “si” the present subjunctive isn’t possible. And the bit about the constable?
“When the constable shall have drawn up the report” becomes “once he has drawn it up”: first the report, then the appeal.
Perfect. On to the chronicle: “No sooner had the governor arrived than he summoned the townspeople and told them the port was closing.”
I went with the simple past and “en cuanto”, and moved the pronoun in front. The sense of immediacy is still there.
The novel is trickier: a reader today might think “enviudara” is a subjunctive.
That’s why I changed it to the pluperfect. It’s the same usage you still see in the papers.
I read it almost every day and it always grates a little. Now for the hard one: the proclamation.

Hugo addresses his listeners as “ustedes”, as everywhere in Latin America. Notice how he reads the old forms naturally and always follows them straight away with the modern version: that is the clearest way to present a historical text to a general audience.
After a relative or cuando, use the present (or perfect) subjunctive; after si, the present (or perfect) indicative
The pretérito anterior becomes a simple past with a connector of immediacy; an -ra form that reports a fact becomes an indicative past
Move pronouns before conjugated indicative verbs and choose vosotros or ustedes according to the readers
Fixed formulas are kept as they are, and explained if necessary

Before modernising, ask three questions: is it a living formula (then keep it)? What comes before the form (si takes the indicative; quien, el que and cuando take the subjunctive)? Does it report a fact or raise a possibility (an -ra form reporting a fact is an indicative past)? Then adjust pronouns and forms of address to your readers.
If the buyer does not collect the goods within three days, he will lose the deposit.
As soon as she had closed the door, she lit the oil lamp.
The actress, who made her debut at this theatre in 1975, returns tonight.
Anyone who has lost their card must apply for a new one.
Night fell and the travellers looked for an inn.

Irene finds two letters from her great-great-grandfather, who emigrated to Mexico in 1862: one written before he sailed, one on arrival. She wants to copy them out in present-day Spanish for the family album; the family lives in Spain. Reword three sentences.

For strong students or spare time. 1. The -ra form can also stand for a conditional, especially with querer, deber, poder and valer: “quisiera” is the normal polite form today, “debiera” and “pudiera ser” sound formal, and “más te valiera” is literary. 2. In old texts, “vos” was a respectful form for one person, with plural verb forms. Today you would use “usted”. Present-day American voseo comes historically from it, but it is now an informal form with its own verb endings.
What does “Más te valiera callar” mean? (You’d do better to keep quiet.)
How many people is the writer addressing?
Is “Quisiera hablar con la directora” archaic?
It might be that the manuscript is a forgery: which version is more neutral?

You can now read historical forms and decide from the context whether their modern equivalent takes the indicative or the subjunctive. Class 207 takes the opposite step: in present-day texts, you choose the mood yourself according to the speaker’s perspective, where both moods are correct but say different things.

At Estudio Contraluz in Bogotá, the team subtitles a British documentary series into Spanish. Margaret runs a fish restaurant in Cornwall and her son Owen wants to sell it. English does not mark mood, but Spanish has to choose. You already know the aunque contrast. At C2 you work on cases where both moods are grammatical and the mood reveals perspective: what you assert as new information, and what you leave as background, evaluation, hypothesis or request.
Indicative: Margaret takes note of a fact (“I gather you’re tired”) and acts on it.
Subjunctive: the tiredness is already known; she is not reporting it but saying it is understandable.

When both moods are possible, don’t ask which word comes before. Ask whether you are asserting the content as new information. If so, indicative; if you take it for granted, evaluate it, imagine it or request it, subjunctive.
What does Margaret express?
What does the speaker do with “tiene razón”?

A “que” clause placed first as the subject, or introduced by “el hecho de que”, usually presents its content as the topic, something already on the table that you now comment on. That is why the subjunctive is normal here even with facts everyone knows. With “el hecho de que” the indicative is also possible, above all when the clause comes after the verb and adds new information (“se debe al hecho de que…”).
Owen coming back to the village doesn’t mean he wants to stay. (His return is a fact, but it is the topic, not the news.)
The fact that the restaurant has debts doesn’t make it unsellable.
The closure is due to the fact that tourists no longer come in winter. (New, explanatory information: indicative is natural.)
Margaret not answering the bank’s calls worries the whole family.
Where is the indicative most natural?
What is Ruth doing?
What does “comprendió” mean here?

“No digo que sea…” means you are not asserting the content. “No digo que es…, digo que…” corrects how your words were reported: the focus is the formulation, so the indicative appears. “No es que + subjunctive” corrects an interpretation. “No creo que + indicative” does occur in speech, but it is rare and marked; in careful usage, use the subjunctive.
I’m not saying the subtitle is wrong; I’m saying it loses the irony.
It’s not that Owen doesn’t love his mother; he just can’t take any more.
I don’t think Margaret will change her mind.
What is the speaker doing?
Maybe Margaret will accept the buyer’s offer.
Indicative: a specific, known wish or manner. Clause-initial “como” with the indicative gives a cause (“since you didn’t come…”).
Subjunctive: whatever or however, not identified. “Como” with the subjunctive is a condition, often a warning (“if you’re not here by ten…”).
What does “como” express?
What does it express now?
Ruth has written asking us to shorten the subtitle at minute 40: she thinks it’s too long.
I don’t think the dubbed version is better than the subtitled one.
Darío, minute 12. Margaret says “I understand you’re tired” and you put the indicative. Are you sure?
Yes. Owen has just told her he hasn’t slept for weeks; she’s simply registering the fact.
I don’t see it that way. She puts her hand on his shoulder and lowers her voice. To me it’s empathy, so subjunctive.
English doesn’t choose; we do. And here the image decides: the fact that she touches his shoulder says it all.
Fine, I’ll change it. But I won’t budge on minute 15: “I’m not saying you’re wrong” stays with the subjunctive.
Agreed. And “Mum said to wait”? Here it says “Mum said she was waiting”.
Oops! That reports that she was waiting. Owen means she asked them to be patient: “Mum told us to wait”.
And watch out for minute 20: “Maybe she knew”. Indicative or subjunctive?
It depends on how much Owen believes it. The letters don’t turn up until episode four, so he still has doubts: subjunctive.
And at the end Margaret snaps “Do what you want with the restaurant”. I went for the subjunctive.
Good: it’s a hurt “I don’t care”. If she knew what he wanted and approved, it would be the indicative. One more thing: if we don’t deliver on Friday, we miss the premiere.
We’ll probably finish on Thursday. There don’t seem to be any doubts left.
Why does Darío change the subtitle at minute 12?
What was wrong with “Mamá dijo que esperaba”?
Why do they choose “quizá lo supiera”?
Which subtitle reflects Owen’s certainty?
Let me remind you that the channel wants the files in SRT format, not any other.
A subtitle being faithful isn’t enough: it has to be readable in two seconds.
Which version says Owen is asking for something?
Maybe Ruth will send us the final version today; she said it was almost ready.
Owen having doubts doesn’t mean anything.
It’s not that he doesn’t want to; he can’t.
If we don’t deliver today, we miss the deadline.
What is the main idea?
When, according to Irene, is the indicative used?
What is the difference between the two?
What does she ask the translators to do?
What should they do if the client wants a literal version?
a known fact you comment on takes the subjunctive; new explanatory content can take the indicative
noting or reporting (indicative) versus evaluating, regretting or requesting (subjunctive)
mood grades how much you assert; a lo mejor and igual only take the indicative
something specific and real, or open and possible

When both moods are correct, mood does not correct anything: it decides the perspective. Indicative: you assert it as information. Subjunctive: you take it as known and comment on it, evaluate it, imagine it or request it. Before choosing, look at the context: the gesture, what has already been said, what happens next.
The flight leaving late doesn’t justify nobody informing us.
My doctor told me to drink less coffee; she says that’s why I sleep badly.
The sun might come out tomorrow; the forecast has changed.
What does it mean?
If you don’t give the book back before Friday, I’ll charge you for it.
Your building’s residents’ association is debating whether to install solar panels on the roof. Rewrite each sentence with the perspective given.

For strong students or spare time. Two register cases: when a “que” clause is moved to the front and picked up again by a pronoun before a verb like saber or negar, the indicative is possible, because the speaker does assert the content. And in legal texts and contracts, “se entiende que” + indicative means “it is understood / deemed that”.
Translation contract: if the client doesn’t respond within ten days, they are deemed to accept the version.
Why is the subjunctive more natural here?

You can now choose mood to decide what you assert and what you don’t. In class 208 you go further in controlling commitment: the “rumour” conditional lets you pass on information without taking responsibility for it (“according to sources, the series would have a second season”). It is the natural next step: another tool for grading what you assert.

A public radio station. The listeners’ ombudswoman reads a complaint: the Friday headline said the public works secretary “had reportedly hidden” a report on cost overruns, and the listener only kept “hidden”. You already know the conditional of rumour; today you look at what it does in discourse, what it leaves unsaid, and what the alternatives are.
The conditional signals second-hand, unconfirmed information, roughly “reportedly”, without naming the source.
The claim is in the indicative, but it clearly belongs to the named source, not to the station.
The station has seen the document and vouches for the fact itself.
The conditional of rumour reports someone else’s unconfirmed claim; it is neither the station’s own guess nor a hypothesis.
Only explicit attribution tells the audience who is making the claim.

The simple conditional reports an unconfirmed present state or a planned future event (sería, estaría negociando, viajaría mañana). The compound conditional reports an unconfirmed past event (habría rechazado) and covers what the indicative splits into rechazó, ha rechazado and había rechazado. The source may be named (según…) or left implicit: the conditional alone already tells you the information is second-hand.
The minister reportedly turned the proposal down at Thursday’s meeting.
According to police sources, the detainee is the construction firm’s manager (not yet confirmed).
The city government is said to be negotiating a new contract with another company.
The secretary is expected to appear before the committee on Tuesday, according to his team: a plan, not a fact.
A past event, unconfirmed: which form?
A present attitude, reported by his lawyer: which form?
Someone else’s claim: “reportedly left before dawn”.
The speaker’s own estimate: “it must have been about ten”.
Softens a request or an opinion: “Could you…? I’d say…”.
An unreal situation: “would not have gone unnoticed”.

Same form, two values: with “cuando llegaron, ya habría salido” the speaker is inferring; with “según los vecinos, habría salido” the speaker is relaying an unconfirmed report. The source of the information decides.
She is estimating the witness’s age herself.
A politeness conditional in a request.

Be precise here. The academic grammar describes it as a frequent journalistic use that presents information as second-hand and unconfirmed. Several style guides, such as El País’s, and the Fundéu advise against it as a calque of French that blurs who answers for the claim. It is nonetheless very common in the press of Spain and Latin America. It is not a grammatical error, nor a neutral choice: it is a stylistic decision with consequences.
Which statement matches what the sources actually say?
Only the investigation itself is verified.

Under the presumption of innocence, nobody is guilty until a final judgment. “Presunto” (alleged) goes before the noun and protects a person who has not been convicted; it can also qualify the offence when it is not established that a crime took place. “Presuntamente” is the adverb. The conditional of rumour is no legal shield: an unconfirmed accusation is still an accusation, and many journalism handbooks warn against using it to insinuate.
The alleged forger of the invoices has been arrested.
The company allegedly charged twice for the same work.
Once there is a final conviction, “presunto” no longer applies.
He has been arrested but not tried.
He has a final conviction: is “presunto” still appropriate?
The station has the minutes in hand.
Thanks for coming. It’s about Friday’s headline: “Public works secretary reportedly hid a report on cost overruns.”
I guessed as much. But the conditional was there precisely so as not to assert it: it’s what our sources say, not our accusation.
That’s exactly her point. Nobody hears the nuance of the conditional; what sticks is “hidden”. And the headline never said according to whom.
The source was in the body of the story: “investigation sources consulted by this station”. You can’t fit everything into an eight-second headline.
It fits if you want it to: “Investigation sources claim Public Works hid a report.” Almost as short, and it makes clear who answers for it.
Sure, but with “hid” in the indicative it sounds more categorical, as if we were confirming it.
No, because “claim” is their verb. The conditional only says that somebody says it, not who. Attribution does.
I’ll grant you that. And the businessman? We said he was reportedly the construction firm’s manager.
That’s less serious: identifying someone isn’t accusing them. The delicate part was calling him “the forger”. With no ruling, at the very least “alleged”.
You’re right. In the rush before the deadline, it must have been half past nine when we recorded it, and nobody checked it.
I understand. Could you send me today’s script before it airs? I’ll answer Mercedes myself in my Friday slot.
What is the listener’s complaint?
Why doesn’t the indicative commit the station here?
What does Rodrigo’s “serían” express?
A past event reported by judicial sources.
An unconfirmed future event.
Which headline handles an unverified accusation most responsibly?
He was acquitted yesterday.
The audit report is published and the source is named.
According to judicial sources, the businessman reportedly destroyed several documents.
Prosecutors are investigating whether the secretary hid the report.
City hall sources say the contract has been cancelled.
He keeps confirmed facts apart from sourced claims and corrects other outlets.
What is Medina’s answer?
Which fact is confirmed?
What has the station checked about the alleged escape?
What does “podría” express here?
Why does he mention the presumption of innocence?
It marks information as second-hand and unconfirmed, but it does not name the source.
The option style guides prefer: the claim has an owner, and the indicative does not commit the outlet.
A safeguard for people not yet convicted, not a sign of the journalist’s doubt; drop it after a final conviction.
Same form, other jobs: the source of the information tells you which value it has.

Ask “according to whom?” of every conditional. If the answer is “my own estimate”, it is probability; if it is “someone I don’t name”, it is rumour, and it is worth asking whether you could name them. If the story accuses someone without a ruling, use “presunto”.
The candidate reportedly submitted her resignation last night.
Your own estimate of the time.
Which headline respects the presumption of innocence?
The court has ruled.
What does “estaría” express?

For strong students or spare time. After a past reporting verb, “habría + participle” can be ambiguous: a transposed conjecture (“habrá llegado tarde”, it probably arrived late) or a relayed rumour. Interrogative headlines assert nothing yet plant suspicion. Quotation headlines attribute word for word, but once the attribution is lost, only the quoted words remain.
In reported speech, a conjecture with “habrá” becomes “habría”.
What does an interrogative headline do?
What is the risk of a quotation headline on air?

Today you saw how one conditional changes value depending on the discourse level: the source’s claim, the speaker’s estimate, reported speech. Class 209 works on that temporal architecture in complex sentences: sequences such as “Quería que lo hubieran revisado antes de que llegase” and shifts between time planes within a text.
